    X = torch.randn(shape)
    out = torch.einsum("...i,ji->...j", X, W)         # one string for all ranks
    print(f"input {str(shape):10s} -> output {str(tuple(out.shape)):10s} same as X @ W.T: {torch.allclose(out, X @ W.T, atol=1e-6)}")

Mb = torch.randn(2, 6, 3, 4); Nb = torch.randn(2, 6, 4, 5)       # two batch axes in front
print("...ij,...jk->...ik :", tuple(torch.einsum("...ij,...jk->...ik", Mb, Nb).shape),
      " same as @:", torch.allclose(torch.einsum("...ij,...jk->...ik", Mb, Nb), Mb @ Nb, atol=1e-6))
Sq = torch.randn(2, 6, 3, 3)
print("...ii->...         :", tuple(torch.einsum("...ii->...", Sq).shape),
      " same as traces:", torch.allclose(torch.einsum("...ii->...", Sq), Sq.diagonal(dim1=-2, dim2=-1).sum(-1)))


input (4,)       -> output (3,)       same as X @ W.T: True
input (5, 4)     -> output (5, 3)     same as X @ W.T: True
input (2, 5, 4)  -> output (2, 5, 3)  same as X @ W.T: True
...ij,...jk->...ik : (2, 6, 3, 5)  same as @: True
...ii->...         : (2, 6)  same as traces: True


2. Building the string in code. Sometimes the axis that takes part in the contraction is only known when the program runs, e.g. “apply the matrix \(M\) to axis \(k\) of a tensor \(T\) with \(N\) axes”, where \(N\) and \(k\) are variables. The string is then assembled from letters: one letter per axis of \(T\), the letter of axis \(k\) is shared with \(M\), and in the output it is replaced by a new letter: \[T'_{a_1 \dots a_{k-1}\, b\, a_{k+1} \dots a_N} = \sum_{a_k} M_{b\, a_k}\, T_{a_1 \dots a_k \dots a_N}.\] This operation appears, for example, when an operator acts on one index of a many-index object (in quantum mechanics: a one-qubit gate acting on the state of \(N\) qubits, stored as a tensor with \(N\) axes of length 2).
Python details of the cell: the module string provides string.ascii_lowercase, the string 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz'; a string is sliced like a list (letters[:4] is 'abcd'); f"..." inserts the values of the expressions in braces; and a function can return several values separated by commas, which the caller unpacks into several variables (out, spec = ...).


Code
import string

def apply_along_axis(M, T, k):
    """Contract the matrix M (shape (n_out, n_k)) with axis k of the tensor T; the new axis stays at position k."""
    letters = string.ascii_lowercase                 # 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz'
    t_idx = letters[:T.ndim]                         # one letter per axis of T, e.g. 'abcd'
    new = letters[T.ndim]                            # an unused letter for the output axis
    out_idx = t_idx[:k] + new + t_idx[k + 1:]        # axis k replaced by the new letter
    spec = f"{new}{t_idx[k]},{t_idx}->{out_idx}"     # e.g. 'ec,abcd->abed' for k = 2
    return torch.einsum(spec, M, T), spec

torch.manual_seed(7)
T = torch.randn(2, 3, 4, 5)                          # N = 4 axes
M = torch.randn(6, 4)                                # acts on an axis of length 4
out, spec = apply_along_axis(M, T, k=2)
# check: move axis k to the end, multiply with M^T, move the new axis back to position k
reference = (T.movedim(2, -1) @ M.T).movedim(-1, 2)
print("generated string:", spec)
print("result shape    :", tuple(out.shape), "  same as movedim + @:", torch.allclose(out, reference, atol=1e-6))


generated string: ec,abcd->abed
result shape    : (2, 3, 6, 5)   same as movedim + @: True


movedim(source, destination) moves one axis to another position (a permute that changes only one axis). The same contraction can also be done with torch.tensordot(M, T, dims=([1], [k])), which contracts axis 1 of M with axis k of T and puts the remaining axes of M first; einsum has the advantage that the order of the output axes is written explicitly.
Summary of the rules. One letter per axis; equal letters are the same index; letters missing after -> are summed; letters kept after -> are not summed (if they appear in several inputs they act as batch indices); the order of the letters after -> is the order of the output axes. ... stands for any number of further axes, so that one string works for tensors of different rank; strings can also be assembled in code. When an operation has a standard function (@, .T, sum), that function is usually at least as fast; einsum is most useful when several axes are contracted at once or when the index notation makes the code easier to compare with a formula.

title: Lab 003: PyTorch tensors, devices and layers
text:
6. Layers: nn.Linear and activation functions
nn.Linear(n_in, n_out) is the dense (fully connected) layer \(\mathbf z \mapsto \mathbf W\mathbf z + \mathbf b\). It creates and randomly initialises its own parameters weight (shape (n_out, n_in)) and bias (shape (n_out,)): by default all of them are drawn uniformly from \([-1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}},\, 1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}]\). The factor \(1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}\) keeps the outputs of the layer of order one, independently of the number of inputs (the reason is given in Section 7). Input: a batch of shape (B, n_in); output: (B, n_out).
In the printout, .data gives the bare numbers of a parameter without its gradient bookkeeping; it is used here only for a shorter printout. In computations .data should be avoided, because changes made through it are invisible to autograd; the safe alternatives are .detach() and torch.no_grad().


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
layer = nn.Linear(in_features=3, out_features=2)
print(layer)
print("weight:", layer.weight.shape, "\n", layer.weight.data)
print("weight.requires_grad:", layer.weight.requires_grad)
print("bias  :", layer.bias.shape, layer.bias.data)

Z = torch.randn(5, 3)            # batch of 5 inputs with 3 features each
out = layer(Z)                   # calling the layer = forward pass
print("output shape:", out.shape)

# check: it is really Z @ W^T + b
print("same as manual:", torch.allclose(out, Z @ layer.weight.T + layer.bias))


Linear(in_features=3, out_features=2, bias=True)
weight: torch.Size([2, 3]) 
 tensor([[-0.0043,  0.3097, -0.4752],
        [-0.4249, -0.2224,  0.1548]])
weight.requires_grad: True
bias  : torch.Size([2]) tensor([-0.0114,  0.4578])
output shape: torch.Size([5, 2])
same as manual: True


layer.weight.requires_grad is True: these are trainable parameters, and PyTorch will compute gradients with respect to them.
Activation functions exist both as layers (nn.Tanh(), nn.ReLU(), …) and as functions (torch.tanh, torch.relu, …). The six plotted below are (in the plots, \(\sigma\) denotes a generic activation function)







name
formula




Sigmoid
\(1/(1 + e^{-z})\)


Tanh
\(\tanh z\)


ReLU
\(\max(0, z)\)


LeakyReLU(\(\alpha\))
\(z\) for \(z \ge 0\), \(\alpha z\) for \(z < 0\); the slope \(\alpha\) is a free choice (0.01 is PyTorch’s default, 0.1 is used here to make it visible)


GELU
\(z\,\Phi(z)\), with \(\Phi\) the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution


Softplus
\(\ln(1 + e^{z})\), a smooth version of ReLU



In the code, acts is a dictionary (name \(\to\) layer); acts.items() yields the pairs (name, layer). axes.flatten() turns the \(2\times3\) array of subplots into a list of 6, and zip walks through the two sequences in parallel. The range \([-4, 4]\) covers the region where the functions bend; 300 points are only needed for smooth curves.


Code
z = torch.linspace(-4, 4, 300)
acts = {"Sigmoid": nn.Sigmoid(), "Tanh": nn.Tanh(), "ReLU": nn.ReLU(),
        "LeakyReLU(0.1)": nn.LeakyReLU(0.1), "GELU": nn.GELU(), "Softplus": nn.Softplus()}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(12, 6), sharex=True)
for ax, (name, act) in zip(axes.flatten(), acts.items()):
    ax.plot(z, act(z), lw=2)
    ax.axhline(0, color="gray", lw=0.5); ax.axvline(0, color="gray", lw=0.5)
    ax.set_title(name); ax.set_xlabel("$z$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\sigma(z)$")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()






nn.Sequential: stacking layers
The single-hidden-layer network \(f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} W^{(2)}_i\,\sigma(W^{(1)}_i x + b_i) + b^{(2)}\), with \(\sigma = \tanh\), is Linear(1, N) → Tanh → Linear(N, 1). By the Universal Approximation Theorem (see the lecture), such a network can approximate any continuous function on an interval when \(N\) is large enough. The width \(N = 16\) is arbitrary.
The parameter count is \(3N + 1\): the first layer has \(N\) weights and \(N\) biases, the second \(N\) weights and 1 bias. In the code, model.parameters() yields the trainable tensors of the model one after another, named_parameters() yields them together with their names, and p.numel() is the number of elements of a tensor. sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) adds up p.numel() for every parameter tensor without first building a list.


Code
torch.manual_seed(1)
N = 16
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(1, N),     # W^(1), b      : x -> N hidden pre-activations
    nn.Tanh(),           # sigma, element-wise
    nn.Linear(N, 1),     # W^(2), b^(2)  : N hidden activations -> 1 output
)
print(model)

n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print("number of trainable parameters:", n_params, "= 3N + 1 =", 3 * N + 1)
for name, p in model.named_parameters():
    print(f"  {name:10s} {tuple(p.shape)}")


Sequential(
  (0): Linear(in_features=1, out_features=16, bias=True)
  (1): Tanh()
  (2): Linear(in_features=16, out_features=1, bias=True)
)
number of trainable parameters: 49 = 3N + 1 = 49
  0.weight   (16, 1)
  0.bias     (16,)
  2.weight   (1, 16)
  2.bias     (1,)


The untrained network evaluated on a grid of 400 inputs (a batch of shape (400, 1); range and number of points are arbitrary choices for the plot).
A with block switches a setting on for the indented lines only and restores it afterwards. Inside with torch.no_grad(): PyTorch does not record the operations needed to compute gradients, which saves memory and time when a network is only evaluated.


Code
x = torch.linspace(-3, 3, 400)[:, None]       # shape (400, 1): batch of 1D inputs
with torch.no_grad():                         # we only evaluate; no gradients needed
    y = model(x)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.plot(x.squeeze(), y.squeeze())
ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$f_\theta(x)$"); ax.set_title("an untrained network")
plt.show()





The curve is smooth, but its shape and its small values (here between about \(-0.14\) and \(0.01\)) are determined only by the random initial values of the 49 parameters; another seed gives another curve. .squeeze() turns the shapes (400, 1) into (400,) for plotting. Fitting such a network to a given function means changing its parameters until the curve follows the target: this is training.

title: Lab 003: PyTorch tensors, devices and layers
text:
7. A model class: subclassing nn.Module
For anything non-trivial we write a class. Two methods are required: - __init__: create the layers / parameters (always call super().__init__() first); - forward(x): describe the computation. The model is then called as model(x), not model.forward(x).
Parameters wrapped in nn.Parameter (and all parameters of sub-layers) are registered automatically. The reasons for the two rules: super().__init__() runs the __init__ of nn.Module, which creates the internal lists in which parameters and sub-layers are registered; assigning an nn.Parameter before this call fails with AttributeError: cannot assign parameters before Module.__init__() call. Calling model(x) runs forward together with additional bookkeeping of PyTorch (so-called hooks), which a direct call of forward would skip.
Below, the UAT ansatz written explicitly — exactly the formula from the lecture. In def __init__(self, N, activation=torch.tanh) the argument activation has a default value: it is used when the caller does not give this argument. A function such as torch.tanh can be passed and stored like any other object.
Initial values: W1 and b are drawn from the standard normal distribution. Neuron \(i\) switches (its \(\tanh\) changes sign) at \(x = -b_i/W^{(1)}_i\); with W1 and b of order one, most of these points (about 80 %) lie in \([-3, 3]\), the range of inputs used below, so most neurons are not saturated there. The output bias c (\(b^{(2)}\) above) only shifts \(f\) up or down; there is no reason to start with a shift, so it starts at 0.


Code
class UATNet(nn.Module):
    """f(x) = sum_i W2_i * sigma(W1_i * x + b_i) + c   (single hidden layer, N neurons)."""

    def __init__(self, N, activation=torch.tanh):
        super().__init__()
        self.W1 = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N))        # input weights
        self.b = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N))         # biases
        self.W2 = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N) / N**0.5)  # output weights, scaled by 1/sqrt(N) (explained below)
        self.c = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1))         # output bias
        self.activation = activation

    def forward(self, x):                             # x: shape (B,) -> output (B,)
        hidden = self.activation(self.W1 * x[:, None] + self.b)   # (B, N) by broadcasting
        return hidden @ self.W2 + self.c

torch.manual_seed(0)
net = UATNet(N=8)
print(net)            # prints only sub-modules (layers); our parameters are listed separately:
print("parameters:", [(n, tuple(p.shape)) for n, p in net.named_parameters()])
x = torch.linspace(-3, 3, 200)    # shape (200,): this class takes a 1D tensor, nn.Sequential above needed shape (200, 1)
print("output shape:", net(x).shape)


UATNet()
parameters: [('W1', (8,)), ('b', (8,)), ('W2', (8,)), ('c', (1,))]
output shape: torch.Size([200])


Output weights divided by \(\sqrt N\). The output is a sum of \(N\) terms, \(f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} W^{(2)}_i h_i(x) + c\) with \(h_i = \tanh(\dots)\in[-1,1]\). If the \(W^{(2)}_i\) are independent random numbers with mean 0 and variance \(\sigma_W^2\), the terms are uncorrelated with mean zero and their variances add: \[\mathrm{Var}\, f(x) = N\,\sigma_W^2\,\overline{h^2}, \qquad \text{standard deviation of } f \;\propto\; \sqrt{N}\,\sigma_W ,\] where \(\overline{h^2} = \frac1N\sum_i h_i(x)^2 \le 1\) is the mean squared hidden activation (the variance is taken over random \(W^{(2)}\) at fixed \(x\), with \(c = 0\)). With \(\sigma_W = 1\) an untrained network with many neurons would produce outputs that grow like \(\sqrt N\), far from the order-one values of typical targets. With \(\sigma_W = 1/\sqrt N\) the variance of the output is of order one for every \(N\). The same rule, weights scaled by \(1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}\) with \(n_{\rm in}\) the number of inputs of the layer, is the basis of the standard initialisations (LeCun, Xavier/Glorot), and nn.Linear uses it by default. For the first layer \(n_{\rm in} = 1\), so W1 is not scaled. The cell below measures the standard deviation of \(f\) over the inputs and 50 random initialisations, with and without the factor: the 50 outputs of shape (200,) are joined by torch.cat into one vector of \(50\times200 = 10\,000\) values, of which std() computes the sample standard deviation (normalised by the number of values minus one, which makes no difference for 10 000 values).


Code
x_test = torch.linspace(-3, 3, 200)[:, None]                   # shape (200, 1)
print("   N   std of f, W2 ~ N(0, 1)   std of f, W2 ~ N(0, 1/N)")
for n_hidden in [1, 10, 100, 1000]:
    stds = {}
    for scaled in [False, True]:
        outputs = []
        for seed in range(50):                                 # 50 random networks
            torch.manual_seed(seed)
            W1, b1 = torch.randn(n_hidden), torch.randn(n_hidden)
            W2 = torch.randn(n_hidden) / (n_hidden**0.5 if scaled else 1.0)
            outputs.append(torch.tanh(x_test * W1 + b1) @ W2)  # (200,) for this network
        stds[scaled] = torch.cat(outputs).std().item()
    print(f"{n_hidden:5d}   {stds[False]:20.2f}   {stds[True]:22.2f}")


   N   std of f, W2 ~ N(0, 1)   std of f, W2 ~ N(0, 1/N)
    1                   0.67                     0.67
   10                   2.77                     0.87


  100                   7.52                     0.75
 1000                  21.90                     0.69


Without the factor the standard deviation grows by roughly a factor of 3 for every tenfold increase of \(N\) (expected: \(\sqrt{10}\approx3.2\); with 50 random networks the estimate fluctuates); with the factor it stays of order one, independent of \(N\).
A model can be moved to the GPU with model.to(device), and switched to double precision with model.double().

title: Lab 003: PyTorch tensors, devices and layers
text:
8. Summary

Tensors ≈ NumPy arrays (+ GPU + autograd). Default dtype float32; use float64 for precise physics.
torch.from_numpy shares memory, torch.tensor copies; .numpy(), .item(), .cpu() to go back.
Shapes: reshape/view change the shape (row-by-row order), transpose/permute reorder axes (non-contiguous views), unsqueeze/squeeze add/remove axes of length 1, cat joins along an existing axis, stack along a new one; batched products with @ or einsum.
device = "cuda" if available else "cpu"; everything in one operation on the same device.
nn.Linear(n_in, n_out) = \(\mathbf W\mathbf z+\mathbf b\) on batches (B, n_in); nn.Sequential stacks layers; own models subclass nn.Module with __init__ and forward.
with torch.no_grad(): when only evaluating.

9. Exercises


Exercise 1 — Ising chain energy in PyTorch
Implement the vectorised energy of a periodic Ising chain, \(E = -\sum_{i=1}^{L} s_i s_{i+1}\) with \(s_{L+1} = s_1\), in PyTorch (torch.roll, torch.sum(..., dim=1)). Generate the random spins with torch.randint(0, 2, (M, L)) * 2 - 1. Run it on 100 000 configurations with \(L = 64\) and check the mean and standard deviation of the energy (\(\approx 0\) and \(\approx\sqrt{L}\)).

Solution


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
M, L, J = 100_000, 64, 1.0

# torch.randint(0, 2, ...) gives 0 or 1; *2 - 1 maps them to -1 or +1.
# .float() converts integers to floats so that sums and std() work as expected.
spins = (torch.randint(0, 2, (M, L)) * 2 - 1).float()

# np.roll -> torch.roll, axis -> dims/dim (for readers who know NumPy)
E = -J * torch.sum(spins * torch.roll(spins, shifts=-1, dims=1), dim=1)

# .item() converts a one-element tensor to a Python number for printing
print(f"mean = {E.mean().item():.3f},  std = {E.std().item():.3f},  sqrt(L) = {L**0.5:.3f}")
# Why sqrt(L): with periodic boundaries the L products s_i s_{i+1} of independent random spins are pairwise independent
# (uncorrelated) numbers +-1 with mean 0 and variance 1, so their variances add: the sum has mean 0 and variance L,
# hence standard deviation sqrt(L).


mean = 0.050,  std = 7.986,  sqrt(L) = 8.000





Exercise 2 — Tensor shapes in a multilayer network
Build model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10)) — the classic network for MNIST (a data set of 70 000 grey-scale images of handwritten digits 0–9, each of \(28\times28\) pixels) from the next lecture. 1. Feed a random batch of 32 “images” of shape (32, 28, 28). It fails; read the error message and fix the problem with reshape. 2. Print the shape of the output. What do the 10 numbers per image represent? 3. Count the parameters (by hand from the formula \(\sum_l n_l(n_{l-1}+1)\) for layer sizes \(n_0, n_1, \dots\), and with sum(p.numel() ...)). 4. The softmax \(p_k = e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}\) turns the 10 outputs \(z_k\) into probabilities. Apply torch.softmax(out, dim=1) and check that each row sums to 1.

Solution


Code
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10))
images = torch.rand(32, 28, 28)               # 32 random 28x28 "images", values uniform in [0, 1) like pixel intensities

# 1) The first layer expects input of shape (batch, 784). A (32, 28, 28) tensor is interpreted as
#    32*28 = 896 rows of length 28, which does not match 784 -> error.
try:
    model(images)
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("Error:", e)

# Fix: flatten every image into a vector of 28*28 = 784 numbers; with -1, PyTorch computes that size.
flat = images.reshape(32, -1)
print("flattened shape:", flat.shape)
out = model(flat)

# 2) One row per image, 10 numbers per row: one score (logit) per digit class 0..9
print("output shape:", out.shape)

# 3) Parameters: layer n_in -> n_out has n_out * n_in weights and n_out biases
by_hand = 128 * (784 + 1) + 64 * (128 + 1) + 10 * (64 + 1)
print("parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()), " by hand:", by_hand)

# 4) Softmax over the class dimension (dim=1) turns the scores into probabilities: p_k = exp(z_k) / sum_j exp(z_j)
#    is positive and the p_k sum to 1. The unnormalised scores z_k that enter the softmax are called logits.
with torch.no_grad():                   # no gradient tracking needed here (otherwise the output shows grad_fn)
    probs = torch.softmax(out, dim=1)
print("row sums:", probs.sum(dim=1)[:5])


Error: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (896x28 and 784x128)
flattened shape: torch.Size([32, 784])
output shape: torch.Size([32, 10])
parameters: 109386  by hand: 109386
row sums: tensor([1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000])





Exercise 3 — Random networks of different depth
Using nn.Sequential, build networks \(1\to W\to\cdots\to W\to 1\) with \(\tanh\) activations, width \(W=64\) and depth (number of hidden layers) \(1, 3, 10\). For each depth draw 5 random initialisations and plot \(f(x)\) on \(x\in[-5,5]\). Do this twice: (a) with PyTorch’s default initialisation, (b) with all weights redrawn from \(\mathcal N(0, (3/\sqrt{n_\text{in}})^2)\), where \(n_\text{in}\) is the number of inputs of the layer. How does the shape of a random function change with depth in the two cases? (The factor 3 is one choice among many; for \(\tanh\) networks the boundary between the two kinds of behaviour shown by (a) and (b) lies at a factor of about 1, and any factor well above 1 shows the effect of (b).) Hint: build the list of layers in a loop and pass it as nn.Sequential(*layers); torch.nn.init.normal_(layer.weight, std=...) redraws the weights of a layer.

Solution


Code
def make_mlp(depth, width=64, activation=nn.Tanh, weight_std_factor=None):
    """1 -> width -> ... -> width -> 1 network with `depth` hidden layers.
    weight_std_factor=None: PyTorch default initialisation; otherwise weights ~ N(0, (factor/sqrt(n_in))^2)."""
    layers = [nn.Linear(1, width), activation()]                  # activation is a class (nn.Tanh); activation() creates a layer object
    for _ in range(depth - 1):                                    # remaining hidden layers
        layers += [nn.Linear(width, width), activation()]
    layers.append(nn.Linear(width, 1))                            # linear output layer
    if weight_std_factor is not None:
        for layer in layers:
            if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear):                      # True if layer is an nn.Linear object; only these have weights
                n_in = layer.weight.shape[1]
                # the trailing underscore of normal_ marks an in-place operation: the existing weight tensor is overwritten
                nn.init.normal_(layer.weight, mean=0.0, std=weight_std_factor / n_in**0.5)
    return nn.Sequential(*layers)                                 # *layers passes the list elements as separate arguments

x = torch.linspace(-5, 5, 500)[:, None]                           # shape (500, 1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(15, 7))
for row, (factor, row_name, plain_name) in enumerate([(None, "default init", "default init"),
                                                     (3.0, r"std $3/\sqrt{n_{in}}$", "std 3/sqrt(n_in)")]):
    for ax, depth in zip(axes[row], [1, 3, 10]):
        ranges = []
        for seed in range(5):
            torch.manual_seed(seed)                               # a different random network for each seed
            with torch.no_grad():                                 # evaluation only, no gradients
                y = make_mlp(depth, weight_std_factor=factor)(x).squeeze()
            ax.plot(x.squeeze(), y)
            ranges.append((y.max() - y.min()).item())
        ax.set_title(f"{row_name}, depth = {depth}")
        ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$f(x)$")
        print(f"{plain_name:17s} depth {depth:2d}: range of f over [-5, 5] for the 5 networks:", np.round(ranges, 4))

#     10-layer networks vary by less than 1e-2 over the whole interval, i.e. they are almost constant.
# (b) With larger weights each layer stretches the signal and folds it through tanh; deep random networks
#     then become rapidly oscillating functions; the larger the factor, the more local maxima and minima
#     the deep networks have on [-5, 5].
# Depth can produce complicated functions, but only if the weights have a suitable scale; this is one

Exercise 4 (advanced) — A custom layer
Write an nn.Module called GaussianRBF implementing \(f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} a_i\, \exp\!\big(-(x-\mu_i)^2 / (2 s_i^2)\big)\) with trainable \(a_i, \mu_i, s_i\) (nn.Parameter). Initialise \(\mu_i\) on a uniform grid on \([-3,3]\), \(s_i = 0.5\), \(a_i \sim \mathcal N(0,1)\). Plot the output and the individual Gaussians for \(N=6\). (Radial-basis-function networks are also universal approximators.)

Solution


Code
class GaussianRBF(nn.Module):
    """f(x) = sum_i a_i exp(-(x - mu_i)^2 / (2 s_i^2)) with trainable a, mu, s."""

    def __init__(self, N):
        super().__init__()
        # nn.Parameter registers the tensor as a trainable parameter of the module
        self.a = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N))                 # amplitudes
        self.mu = nn.Parameter(torch.linspace(-3, 3, N))      # centres on a uniform grid
        self.s = nn.Parameter(0.5 * torch.ones(N))            # widths; for N = 6 the centres are 1.2 apart, so neighbouring
                                                              # Gaussians of width 0.5 overlap and their sum is a smooth curve

    def basis(self, x):
        """The N Gaussians evaluated at all points: shape (B, N)."""
        return torch.exp(-(x[:, None] - self.mu)**2 / (2 * self.s**2))

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.basis(x) @ self.a                         # weighted sum -> shape (B,)

torch.manual_seed(0)
rbf = GaussianRBF(6)
print("parameters:", [(name, tuple(p.shape)) for name, p in rbf.named_parameters()])

x = torch.linspace(-4, 4, 400)
with torch.no_grad():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
    ax.plot(x, rbf.basis(x) * rbf.a, lw=1, alpha=0.7)        # (400, 6): ax.plot draws one curve per column = one weighted Gaussian
    ax.plot(x, rbf(x), "k", lw=2.5, label="sum $f(x)$")
    ax.legend(); ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$f(x)$ and its Gaussian terms"); plt.show()

Exercise 7 — A batch of rotations

For \(B = 6\) angles \(\varphi_b = b\pi/6\) build a tensor R of shape (B, 2, 2) of rotation matrices \(\begin{pmatrix}\cos\varphi & -\sin\varphi\\ \sin\varphi & \cos\varphi\end{pmatrix}\) using torch.stack (no loop).

Solution

n_rot = 6
phi = torch.arange(n_rot) * torch.pi / 6                  # shape (n_rot,)

# 1) stack the four entries: first the two rows (each of shape (B, 2)), then the rows into matrices
row1 = torch.stack([c, -s], dim=1)                        # (n_rot, 2)
row2 = torch.stack([s, c], dim=1)                         # (n_rot, 2)
R = torch.stack([row1, row2], dim=1)                      # (n_rot, 2, 2): R[b] = [[c, -s], [s, c]]

rot2 = torch.einsum("bij,bj->bi", R, e_x)
rot3 = torch.bmm(R, e_x.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2)
print("all three agree:", torch.allclose(rot1, rot2) and torch.allclose(rot1, rot3))

Exercise 8 — Applying a layer to every time step
A batch of \(B = 8\) time series, each with \(T = 50\) time steps and \(F = 3\) measured quantities per step, is stored as a tensor of shape (B, T, F). 1. Apply nn.Linear(3, 5) to every time step by reshaping to (B*T, F), applying the layer, and reshaping back to (B, T, 5). 2. Apply the layer directly to the (B, T, F) tensor and compare: nn.Linear acts on the last axis and treats all other axes as batch axes. 3. What goes wrong if the tensor is stored as (B, F, T) instead? Fix it with transpose.

Solution

n_series, T, F = 8, 50, 3
torch.manual_seed(0)
series = torch.randn(n_series, T, F)
lin = nn.Linear(F, 5)

# 1) merge batch and time axes, apply the layer, split them again

# 2) directly: Linear acts on the last axis

    lin(series_ft)

    # (the stored weight has shape (5, 3)): the inner dimensions 50 and 3 do not match
out3 = lin(series_ft.transpose(1, 2))                     # back to (B, T, F) before the layer
print("after transposing back:", tuple(out3.shape), "  agrees:", torch.allclose(out3, out1))

title: Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
text:
1. Three ways to compute derivatives

1.1 Finite differences
From the definition of the derivative, for small \(h\): \[\text{forward: } \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} \approx \frac{f(\vec x + h\vec e_i) - f(\vec x)}{h} \quad (\text{error } \mathcal O(h)), \qquad
\text{central: } \frac{f(\vec x + h\vec e_i) - f(\vec x - h\vec e_i)}{2h} \quad (\text{error } \mathcal O(h^2)).\] Here \(\vec e_i\) is the unit vector along axis \(i\) (only \(x_i\) is changed), and “error \(\mathcal O(h)\)” means that the error is proportional to \(h\) for small \(h\). Two problems: 1. cost — a gradient in \(m\) dimensions needs \(\mathcal O(m)\) evaluations of \(f\) (impossible for \(m=10^9\)); 2. accuracy — the computer stores \(f(x+h)\) and \(f(x)\) with a relative rounding error of about the machine epsilon \(\epsilon_\text{machine}\). For small \(h\) the two values are nearly equal; their difference keeps an absolute error of about \(\epsilon_\text{machine}|f|\), and dividing by \(h\) enlarges it. This round-off error therefore grows as \(\epsilon_\text{machine}/h\). There is an optimal \(h\), and it is not known in advance.
The second problem for \(f(x) = \sin x\) at \(x=1\) (exact derivative \(\cos 1\)) is shown below. We evaluate both formulas for 100 values of \(h\) between \(10^{-16}\) and \(1\), spaced evenly on a logarithmic scale (np.logspace), and plot the absolute error on log–log axes, where power laws such as \(h\) or \(1/h\) appear as straight lines. The two dotted and dashed reference lines show only the slopes: the round-off line \(10^{-16}/h\) uses a constant of the order of the machine precision \(\epsilon \approx 2.2\times10^{-16}\), and the truncation line \(0.5\,h\) uses a constant close to \(|f''(1)|/2 = \sin(1)/2 \approx 0.42\), the prefactor of the forward-difference error.


Code
f, df_exact, x0 = np.sin, np.cos(1.0), 1.0
hs = np.logspace(-16, 0, 100)
err_fwd = np.abs((f(x0 + hs) - f(x0)) / hs - df_exact)
err_cen = np.abs((f(x0 + hs) - f(x0 - hs)) / (2 * hs) - df_exact)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.loglog(hs, err_fwd, label="forward difference")
ax.loglog(hs, err_cen, label="central difference")
ax.loglog(hs, 1e-16 / hs, "k:", lw=1, label=r"round-off $\sim\epsilon/h$")
ax.loglog(hs, 0.5 * hs, "k--", lw=1, label=r"truncation $\sim h$")
ax.set_xlabel("step $h$"); ax.set_ylabel("absolute error of $f'(1)$")
ax.set_ylim(1e-13, 1); ax.legend()
plt.show()





The plot is read from the right. For large \(h\) the error decreases along the truncation line (as \(h\) for the forward and as \(h^2\) for the central difference). Below the optimum it grows again along the round-off line, and the curves become jagged because rounding errors behave like random numbers. The best achievable accuracy is about \(10^{-9}\) (forward, at \(h\approx10^{-8}\)) or \(10^{-11}\)–\(10^{-12}\) (central, at \(h\approx10^{-6}\)–\(10^{-5}\)), far from machine precision \(\sim10^{-16}\). The position of the optimum follows from adding the two errors. The Taylor expansion \(f(x+h) = f + hf' + \tfrac12h^2f'' + \tfrac16h^3f''' + \dots\) gives the truncation error \(\tfrac12 h f''\) of the forward formula; in the central formula the \(f''\) terms of \(f(x+h)\) and \(f(x-h)\) cancel, and the first remaining term is \(\tfrac16 h^2 f'''\). For the forward difference the total error is about \(\epsilon/h + |f''|\,h/2\), smallest at \(h\sim\sqrt{\epsilon}\approx10^{-8}\). For the central difference it is about \(\epsilon/h + |f'''|\,h^2/6\), smallest at \(h\sim\epsilon^{1/3}\approx10^{-5}\). Both estimates agree with the positions of the minima in the plot to within an order of magnitude.


1.2 Symbolic differentiation
Computer algebra (Mathematica, sympy) applies the rules of calculus to expressions. The result is exact and interpretable, but expressions can grow enormously (“expression swell”) and the approach does not work for functions defined by programs (loops, if statements, matrix diagonalisation…).


Code
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols("x")
expr = x
for _ in range(4):                     # a 'deep network' of 4 nested layers sin(x*sin(...))
    expr = sp.sin(x * expr)
d = sp.diff(expr, x)                   # symbolic derivative
print("function  :", expr)
# sp.count_ops counts the elementary operations (+, *, sin, cos, ...) in an expression
print("derivative has", sp.count_ops(d), "operations (function has", sp.count_ops(expr), ")")
print("first part of derivative:", str(d)[:200], "...")


function  : sin(x*sin(x*sin(x*sin(x**2))))
derivative has 43 operations (function has 8 )
first part of derivative: (x*(x*(2*x**2*cos(x**2) + sin(x**2))*cos(x*sin(x**2)) + sin(x*sin(x**2)))*cos(x*sin(x*sin(x**2))) + sin(x*sin(x*sin(x**2))))*cos(x*sin(x*sin(x*sin(x**2)))) ...


The function with 4 nested layers has 8 operations, its derivative 43. With 6 layers the numbers are 12 and 89: the derivative grows much faster than the function. This growth is the expression swell.


1.3 Automatic differentiation
AD sits in between: every program — however complicated — is a composition of elementary operations (\(+,\times,\sin,\exp,\log,\dots\)) whose derivatives are known. AD records these operations and combines their local derivatives with the chain rule, giving derivatives that are exact to machine precision at a cost of a small multiple of evaluating \(f\) itself.

title: Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
text:
2. The computational graph
Consider the following function (adapted from the example in Baydin et al., Automatic differentiation in machine learning: a survey, JMLR 2018): \[y = f(x_1, x_2) = \ln x_1 + \cos x_2 - x_1 x_2 .\] A computational graph is a diagram of a calculation: each node is one intermediate value, and an arrow from \(v_a\) to \(v_b\) means that \(v_a\) is used to compute \(v_b\). We break the function into elementary steps. Following Baydin et al., the inputs get the indices \(-1\) and \(0\), \(v_{-1}=x_1\), \(v_0 = x_2\), so that the intermediate variables are numbered \(v_1,\dots,v_5\):



computational-graph.png


Forward evaluation at \((x_1,x_2) = (2, 1)\) — read the graph from left to right:



step
value




\(v_{-1} = x_1\)
\(2\)


\(v_0 = x_2\)
\(1\)


\(v_1 = \ln v_{-1}\)
\(\ln 2 = 0.693\)


\(v_2 = v_{-1} \times v_0\)
\(2\)


\(v_3 = \cos v_0\)
\(\cos 1 = 0.540\)


\(v_4 = v_1 - v_2\)
\(-1.307\)


\(v_5 = v_3 + v_4\)
\(-0.767\)


\(y = v_5\)
\(-0.767\)



Analytically: \(\partial f/\partial x_1 = 1/x_1 - x_2 = -0.5\) and \(\partial f/\partial x_2 = -\sin x_2 - x_1 = -2.841\). Below we obtain these numbers automatically.

title: Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
text:
3. Forward-mode AD and dual numbers
Idea: carry along with every intermediate value \(v_i\) its derivative with respect to one chosen input, \(\dot v_i = \partial v_i/\partial x_1\). Each elementary step updates both by the chain rule. In the table, the primal is the ordinary value and the tangent is the derivative carried along with it (“w.r.t.” = with respect to). The seed is the derivative we give to the inputs at the start: \(\partial x_1/\partial x_1 = 1\) for the input we differentiate with respect to, and \(\partial x_2/\partial x_1 = 0\) for the other one.








primal (value)
tangent (derivative w.r.t. \(x_1\))
at \((2,1)\)




\(v_{-1} = x_1 = 2\)
\(\dot v_{-1} = 1\) (seed)
\(1\)


\(v_0 = x_2 = 1\)
\(\dot v_0 = 0\)
\(0\)


\(v_1 = \ln v_{-1}\)
\(\dot v_1 = \dot v_{-1}/v_{-1}\)
\(0.5\)


\(v_2 = v_{-1}v_0\)
\(\dot v_2 = \dot v_{-1}v_0 + v_{-1}\dot v_0\)
\(1\)


\(v_3 = \cos v_0\)
\(\dot v_3 = -\dot v_0\sin v_0\)
\(0\)


\(v_4 = v_1 - v_2\)
\(\dot v_4 = \dot v_1 - \dot v_2\)
\(-0.5\)


\(v_5 = v_3 + v_4\)
\(\dot v_5 = \dot v_3 + \dot v_4\)
\(\mathbf{-0.5}\) (check)



Dual numbers make this automatic. Extend real numbers by an element \(\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon^2=0\) (like the imaginary unit, but nilpotent): \(z = a + b\,\varepsilon\). Then \[(a_1 + b_1\varepsilon) + (a_2 + b_2\varepsilon) = (a_1+a_2) + (b_1+b_2)\varepsilon,\qquad (a_1 + b_1\varepsilon)(a_2 + b_2\varepsilon) = a_1a_2 + (a_1b_2 + b_1a_2)\varepsilon,\] and from the Taylor series \(g(a + b\varepsilon) = g(a) + g'(a)\,b\varepsilon + \tfrac12 g''(a)\,b^2\varepsilon^2 + \dots\), in which every term containing \(\varepsilon^2\) vanishes: \[g(a + b\varepsilon) = g(a) + g'(a)\,b\,\varepsilon .\] So evaluating \(f\) on \(x_1 + 1\cdot\varepsilon\) returns \(f(x) + \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}\varepsilon\): the coefficient of \(\varepsilon\) in the result is the derivative. In code: a small class with operator overloading: defining __add__ and __mul__ makes + and * work on Dual objects. Three Python details appear in the class for the first time: - isinstance(z, Dual) checks whether z is already a dual number. If it is a plain number such as 3, the method lift turns it into Dual(3, 0) (a constant has derivative zero), so that expressions like x1 * 3 work. - @staticmethod marks a function that belongs to the class but does not receive self; it is called as Dual.lift(z). - __radd__ and __rmul__ are used by Python when the plain number stands on the left, as in 3 + Dual(...).


Code
class Dual:
    """Dual number a + b*eps with eps^2 = 0.  'a' = value, 'b' = derivative."""

    def __init__(self, a, b=0.0):
        self.a, self.b = a, b

    @staticmethod
    def lift(z):                      # turn plain numbers into duals with zero derivative
        return z if isinstance(z, Dual) else Dual(z, 0.0)

    def __add__(self, other):
        other = Dual.lift(other)
        return Dual(self.a + other.a, self.b + other.b)

    def __sub__(self, other):
        other = Dual.lift(other)
        return Dual(self.a - other.a, self.b - other.b)

    def __mul__(self, other):         # product rule
        other = Dual.lift(other)
        return Dual(self.a * other.a, self.a * other.b + self.b * other.a)

    __radd__ = __add__                # so that 3 + Dual(...) also works
    __rmul__ = __mul__

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Dual(value={self.a:.6f}, derivative={self.b:.6f})"

# elementary functions: g(a + b eps) = g(a) + g'(a) b eps
def d_log(z): return Dual(math.log(z.a), z.b / z.a)
def d_cos(z): return Dual(math.cos(z.a), -math.sin(z.a) * z.b)
def d_sin(z): return Dual(math.sin(z.a), math.cos(z.a) * z.b)


The function of Section 2 written with dual-number operations. The derivative with respect to \(x_1\) is obtained by giving \(x_1\) the derivative part 1 and \(x_2\) the derivative part 0:


Code
def f_dual(x1, x2):
    return d_log(x1) + d_cos(x2) - x1 * x2

# derivative w.r.t. x1: seed x1 with derivative 1, x2 with 0
print("d/dx1:", f_dual(Dual(2.0, 1.0), Dual(1.0, 0.0)))
# derivative w.r.t. x2: a SECOND forward pass with a different seed
print("d/dx2:", f_dual(Dual(2.0, 0.0), Dual(1.0, 1.0)))
print("exact:", 1/2 - 1, -math.sin(1) - 2)


d/dx1: Dual(value=-0.766551, derivative=-0.500000)
d/dx2: Dual(value=-0.766551, derivative=-2.841471)
exact: -0.5 -2.8414709848078967


Both passes return the value \(-0.7666\) of the table in Section 2 together with one derivative each, and both derivatives equal the exact results.
Cost of forward mode: one pass per input variable. Efficient for \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^m\) (few inputs, many outputs), inefficient for a loss \(\mathcal L:\mathbb R^{10^9}\to\mathbb R\), which would need \(10^9\) passes.

title: Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
text:
4. Reverse-mode AD = backpropagation
Idea: first run the program forward and record the graph. Then go backwards from the output, computing the adjoints \[\bar v_i = \frac{\partial y}{\partial v_i}.\] Start with \(\bar v_5 = \partial y/\partial y = 1\). The chain rule says: the adjoint of a node is the sum, over all nodes \(v_j\) that use it, of \(\bar v_j\,\partial v_j/\partial v_i\).







backward step
at \((2,1)\)




\(\bar v_5 = 1\)
\(1\)


\(\bar v_4 = \bar v_5\,\partial v_5/\partial v_4 = \bar v_5\)
\(1\)


\(\bar v_3 = \bar v_5\,\partial v_5/\partial v_3 = \bar v_5\)
\(1\)


\(\bar v_2 = \bar v_4\,\partial v_4/\partial v_2 = -\bar v_4\)
\(-1\)


\(\bar v_1 = \bar v_4\,\partial v_4/\partial v_1 = \bar v_4\)
\(1\)


\(\bar v_0 = \bar v_3\,(-\sin v_0) + \bar v_2\, v_{-1}\)
\(-0.841 - 2 = \mathbf{-2.841}\) (check)


\(\bar v_{-1} = \bar v_1 / v_{-1} + \bar v_2\, v_0\)
\(0.5 - 1 = \mathbf{-0.5}\) (check)



One backward pass gives the derivatives with respect to all inputs. Cost: a small constant times one evaluation of \(f\), independent of the number of parameters. This is why reverse mode (= backpropagation in the neural-network language) is the method used to train neural networks.
Below is a minimal implementation of what PyTorch does internally (in the spirit of A. Karpathy’s micrograd). Each Var stores its value, the Vars it was computed from (parents) and the local derivatives with respect to them. The method backward must visit the nodes in an order in which every node comes after all nodes it depends on (a topological order). The inner function build produces it: it first calls itself on all parents and only then appends the node (a depth-first traversal). id(v) is a number that identifies the Python object v; the set visited records the nodes already placed, so that a node used twice, such as \(x_1\), appears in the list only once. Going through this list in reverse order then visits the output first and the inputs last.


Code
class Var:
    """A scalar that remembers how it was computed, so that gradients can flow back."""

    def __init__(self, value, parents=(), local_grads=(), name=""):
        self.value = value
        self.grad = 0.0                  # will hold dy/d(this) after backward()
        self.parents = parents           # the Vars this one was computed from
        self.local_grads = local_grads   # d(this)/d(parent) for each parent
        self.name = name

    def __add__(self, other): return Var(self.value + other.value, (self, other), (1.0, 1.0))
    def __sub__(self, other): return Var(self.value - other.value, (self, other), (1.0, -1.0))
    def __mul__(self, other): return Var(self.value * other.value, (self, other), (other.value, self.value))

    def backward(self):
        # 1) order the graph so that every node comes after all nodes it depends on (topological sort)
        order, visited = [], set()
        def build(v):
            if id(v) not in visited:
                visited.add(id(v))
                for p in v.parents:
                    build(p)
                order.append(v)
        build(self)
        # 2) seed and propagate adjoints from the output back to the inputs
        self.grad = 1.0
        for v in reversed(order):
            for parent, local in zip(v.parents, v.local_grads):
                parent.grad += v.grad * local     # chain rule; '+=' sums over all paths

def v_log(v): return Var(math.log(v.value), (v,), (1.0 / v.value,))
def v_cos(v): return Var(math.cos(v.value), (v,), (-math.sin(v.value),))


The same function with Var objects: the forward pass builds the graph, and one backward pass gives both derivatives:


Code
x1, x2 = Var(2.0, name="x1"), Var(1.0, name="x2")
y = v_log(x1) + v_cos(x2) - x1 * x2       # forward pass builds the graph
y.backward()                              # ONE backward pass
print(f"y = {y.value:.4f}")
print(f"dy/dx1 = {x1.grad:.4f},  dy/dx2 = {x2.grad:.4f}")


y = -0.7666
dy/dx1 = -0.5000,  dy/dx2 = -2.8415

title: Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
text:
5. torch.autograd
PyTorch implements exactly this reverse-mode machinery for tensors and hundreds of operations (including matmul, eigh, fft, …). - requires_grad=True marks a tensor as a variable we want derivatives with respect to; - every operation on it records a node of the graph (grad_fn); - y.backward() runs the backward pass; the gradients land in .grad of the leaf tensors. A leaf is a tensor created directly by us (below: x1 and x2), not as the result of an operation; the leaves are the inputs of the graph.


Code
x1 = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True)
x2 = torch.tensor(1.0, requires_grad=True)

y = torch.log(x1) + torch.cos(x2) - x1 * x2
print("y       :", y)                     # grad_fn=<SubBackward0>: the last operation recorded in the graph
y.backward()
print("dy/dx1  :", x1.grad.item())      # .item() converts a one-element tensor to a Python number
print("dy/dx2  :", x2.grad.item())


y       : tensor(-0.7666, grad_fn=<SubBackward0>)
dy/dx1  : -0.5
dy/dx2  : -2.8414709848078967


The recorded graph can be traversed backwards from y.grad_fn. It contains the same elementary operations as the graph in Section 2; the grouping differs because Python evaluates log(x1) + cos(x2) first and subtracts x1*x2 last.


Code
def show_graph(fn, depth=0):
    # Print the name of each graph node, indented by its distance from the output.
    # fn.next_functions lists the nodes that fn received its inputs from (pairs (node, index));
    # type(fn).__name__ is the class name of the node, e.g. 'MulBackward0' for a multiplication.
    if fn is None:                                   # inputs that need no gradient appear as None
        return
    print("  " * depth + type(fn).__name__)
    for parent, _ in fn.next_functions:
        show_graph(parent, depth + 1)

y = torch.log(x1) + torch.cos(x2) - x1 * x2
show_graph(y.grad_fn)     # 'AccumulateGrad' = a leaf: the place where .grad is stored


SubBackward0
  AddBackward0
    LogBackward0
      AccumulateGrad
    CosBackward0
      AccumulateGrad
  MulBackward0
    AccumulateGrad
    AccumulateGrad



5.1 Derivatives of a whole curve at once
backward() starts from a single number (a scalar), so for a tensor \(x\) of many points we sum the outputs first. Since each term of the sum depends only on its own point, \(\partial\big(\sum_j f(x_j)\big)/\partial x_i = f'(x_i)\): the gradient is the derivative at every point. Here: \(\frac{d}{dx}\big[e^{-x^2/2}\sin 3x\big]\), compared with the analytic result.


Code
x = torch.linspace(-4, 4, 400, requires_grad=True)
y = torch.exp(-x**2 / 2) * torch.sin(3 * x)
y.sum().backward()

xd = x.detach()                                   # detach: a plain tensor without graph, for plotting
analytic = torch.exp(-xd**2 / 2) * (3 * torch.cos(3 * xd) - xd * torch.sin(3 * xd))
print("max |autograd - analytic| =", (x.grad - analytic).abs().max().item())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.plot(xd, y.detach(), label="$f(x)$")
ax.plot(xd, x.grad, label="$f'(x)$  (autograd)")
ax.plot(xd[::15], analytic[::15], "k.", label="$f'(x)$  (analytic)")
ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.legend(); plt.show()


max |autograd - analytic| = 4.440892098500626e-16





The largest difference, about \(4\times10^{-16}\), is at the level of float64 rounding: the autograd derivative is exact up to machine precision.


5.2 Higher derivatives: torch.autograd.grad with create_graph=True
torch.autograd.grad(y, x) returns the gradient instead of storing it in .grad. With create_graph=True the gradient computation itself is recorded, so it can be differentiated again. Physics example: a potential \(V(x)\) → force \(F = -V'(x)\) and curvature \(V''(x)\); the curvature at the minimum gives the vibration frequency \(\omega = \sqrt{V''(r_0)/\mu}\) (\(\mu\) = reduced mass). Take the Morse potential \(V(r) = D\,(1 - e^{-a(r - r_0)})^2\), a model of the bond between two atoms (\(D\) is the depth of the well, \(r_0\) the bond length, \(a\) sets the width), for which \(V''(r_0) = 2Da^2\) (the values of \(D\), \(a\), \(r_0\) below are arbitrary).
torch.autograd.grad returns a tuple with one gradient per input tensor, even when there is only one input. The notation (dV,) = ... unpacks this one-element tuple; it is equivalent to dV = torch.autograd.grad(...)[0].


Code
D, a, r0 = 4.0, 1.5, 1.0
r = torch.tensor(r0, requires_grad=True)
V = D * (1 - torch.exp(-a * (r - r0)))**2

(dV,) = torch.autograd.grad(V, r, create_graph=True)   # first derivative, still differentiable
(d2V,) = torch.autograd.grad(dV, r)                    # second derivative
print(f"V'(r0)  = {dV.item():.3e}   (equilibrium -> 0)")
print(f"V''(r0) = {d2V.item():.6f}   exact 2 D a^2 = {2*D*a**2}")


V'(r0)  = 0.000e+00   (equilibrium -> 0)
V''(r0) = 18.000000   exact 2 D a^2 = 18.0




5.3 Four common pitfalls


Code
# Pitfall 1: gradients ACCUMULATE. Calling backward twice adds up the gradients.
w = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
for i in range(3):
    loss = w**2
    loss.backward()
    print(f"iteration {i}: w.grad = {w.grad.item()}   (true gradient: 6)")
# -> every training loop must reset them: w.grad = None  or  optimizer.zero_grad()  (Section 7)


iteration 0: w.grad = 6.0   (true gradient: 6)
iteration 1: w.grad = 12.0   (true gradient: 6)
iteration 2: w.grad = 18.0   (true gradient: 6)


Pitfall 2: the graph is freed after backward() to save memory. A second gradient needs a new forward pass, which every training step makes anyway:


Code
# Pitfall 2: the graph is freed after backward(); calling backward on it again raises an error
w = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
loss = w**2
loss.backward()
try:
    loss.backward()
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("RuntimeError:", str(e)[:90], "...")


RuntimeError: Trying to backward through the graph a second time (or directly access saved tensors after ...


Pitfall 3: converting a tensor that requires gradients to NumPy:


Code
# Pitfall 3: .numpy() cannot be called on a tensor that requires grad -> use .detach() first
w = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0], requires_grad=True)
try:
    (w**2).numpy()
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("RuntimeError:", str(e)[:80], "...")
print("fixed:", (w**2).detach().numpy())


RuntimeError: Can't call numpy() on Tensor that requires grad. Use tensor.detach().numpy() ins ...
fixed: [1. 4.]


Pitfall 4: updating parameters by hand. The update itself is an operation on w; if it were recorded, the graph would keep growing from one step to the next. Inside with torch.no_grad(): nothing is recorded. The update must also be in place (w -= ...): it changes the numbers stored in the existing tensor w, which stays the same leaf tensor with requires_grad=True. Writing w = w - 0.1 * w.grad would instead create a new tensor and bind the name w to it. Inside no_grad the new tensor does not require gradients at all; outside no_grad it is not a leaf and its .grad stays None after the next backward pass. In both cases the training stops working.


Code
# Pitfall 4: parameter updates must NOT be recorded in the graph -> wrap them in torch.no_grad()
w = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
loss = w**2
loss.backward()
with torch.no_grad():
    w -= 0.1 * w.grad          # an in-place update of a leaf, outside the graph
w.grad = None                  # reset for the next step (pitfall 1)
print("updated w:", w)


updated w: tensor(2.4000, requires_grad=True)

title: Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
text:
6. Physics: differentiating through a diagonalisation
Consider the double-well potential (harmonic trap + Gaussian barrier of height \(\kappa\)): \[\hat H(\kappa) = -\frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \kappa\, e^{-x^2/2}.\] Question: how do the energies \(E_n(\kappa)\) respond to changes of the barrier, \(dE_n/d\kappa\)?
The program is: build the matrix \(\bar H(\kappa)\) (the bar denotes the matrix of \(\hat H\) on the grid) → diagonalise → pick eigenvalue \(n\). There is no closed formula, but every step (including torch.linalg.eigh) is differentiable, so autograd gives \(dE_n/d\kappa\) exactly (up to the grid discretisation).
Why two wells appear: \(V'(x) = x\,(1 - \kappa e^{-x^2/2})\) and \(V''(0) = 1-\kappa\). For \(\kappa > 1\) the point \(x = 0\) becomes a maximum, and two minima appear at \(x = \pm\sqrt{2\ln\kappa}\) (for example \(\pm1.67\) at \(\kappa = 4\)).
The box \([-6, 6]\) is much wider than the low-lying states. With \(N_x = 300\) points the spacing is \(\Delta x \approx 0.04\), small compared with the scale (of order 1) on which these states vary. The lowest four energies at \(\kappa = 4\) change by less than \(10^{-3}\) (relative change below \(2\cdot10^{-4}\)) when \(N_x\) is increased from 300 to 1000, so any \(N_x\) of a few hundred gives the same picture; larger \(N_x\) only makes the diagonalisation slower.
Functions used for the first time: - torch.diag(v, k) applied to a vector v builds a matrix with v on the \(k\)-th diagonal (\(k = 1\): the diagonal above the main one, \(k = -1\): the diagonal below it, \(k = 0\) or omitted: the main diagonal). - torch.linalg.eigvalsh(H) returns only the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix; torch.linalg.eigh(H) returns the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors. Both return the eigenvalues in ascending order, so [:n_levels] selects the lowest levels. We use eigvalsh whenever the eigenvectors are not needed: it does less work.


Code
# Grid: psi''(x_i) ~ (psi_{i+1} - 2 psi_i + psi_{i-1}) / dx^2, and psi = 0 beyond the ends of the grid
# (hard walls at x = -6 and x = 6, far from where the wavefunctions live).
L_box, Nx = 12.0, 300
x = torch.linspace(-L_box / 2, L_box / 2, Nx)
dx = x[1] - x[0]

# kinetic part (does not depend on kappa): built once
ones = torch.ones(Nx - 1)
H_kin = -0.5 / dx**2 * (torch.diag(ones, 1) - 2 * torch.eye(Nx) + torch.diag(ones, -1))

def potential(x, kappa):
    return 0.5 * x**2 + kappa * torch.exp(-x**2 / 2)

def hamiltonian(kappa):
    """Matrix of H(kappa) on the grid; differentiable w.r.t. kappa."""
    return H_kin + torch.diag(potential(x, kappa))

def energies(kappa, n_levels=4):
    return torch.linalg.eigvalsh(hamiltonian(kappa))[:n_levels]


The potential and the densities of the four lowest states (shifted by their energies) for four barrier heights. eigh returns the eigenvectors as the columns of the matrix psi: psi[:, n] (all rows, column \(n\)) is the \(n\)-th eigenstate, belonging to E[n]. Taking a row, psi[n], would be a mistake. The eigenvectors are normalised as vectors, \(\sum_i|\psi_n(x_i)|^2 = 1\); dividing by \(\Delta x\) turns this into a probability density with \(\sum_i |\psi_n(x_i)|^2/\Delta x\cdot\Delta x = 1\), the discrete form of \(\int|\psi|^2dx = 1\). The extra factor 1.5 only enlarges the curves for visibility.


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(15, 3.5), sharey=True)
for ax, kappa in zip(axes, [0.0, 2.0, 4.0, 10.0]):
    E, psi = torch.linalg.eigh(hamiltonian(torch.tensor(kappa)))
    ax.plot(x, potential(x, torch.tensor(kappa)), "k", lw=2)
    for n in range(4):
        ax.plot(x, E[n] + 1.5 * psi[:, n]**2 / dx, lw=1.5)       # |psi_n|^2 (scaled by 1.5) shifted by E_n
        ax.axhline(E[n], color="gray", lw=0.4)
    ax.set_title(rf"$\kappa = {kappa}$"); ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_xlim(-5, 5); ax.set_ylim(0, 9)
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$V(x)$, $\;E_n + |\psi_n(x)|^2$")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





In the figure, for \(\kappa = 0\) the levels are those of the harmonic oscillator, \(E_n = n + \tfrac12\). As \(\kappa\) grows, the barrier pushes the states out of the centre and the levels move up. At \(\kappa = 10\) they form pairs of almost equal energy, \(E_1 - E_0 \approx 5\times10^{-4}\) and \(E_3 - E_2 \approx 9\times10^{-3}\), and the two curves of each pair lie on top of each other.
One derivative with autograd. The value \(\kappa = 4\) is an arbitrary choice in the double-well regime \(\kappa > 1\); the checks below agree equally well for other values.


Code
kappa = torch.tensor(4.0, requires_grad=True)
E0 = energies(kappa)[0]
E0.backward()
print(f"E_0(kappa=4) = {E0.item():.6f},   dE_0/dkappa = {kappa.grad.item():.6f}")


E_0(kappa=4) = 3.089526,   dE_0/dkappa = 0.388432


Check 1 — Hellmann–Feynman theorem. For a normalised eigenstate, \(\dfrac{dE_n}{d\kappa} = \Big\langle\psi_n\Big|\dfrac{\partial\hat H}{\partial\kappa}\Big|\psi_n\Big\rangle = \langle\psi_n|\,e^{-x^2/2}\,|\psi_n\rangle\). Here \(\langle\psi_n|\hat A|\psi_n\rangle\) is the expectation value of \(\hat A\) in the state \(\psi_n\). On the grid (eigenvectors from eigh are normalised as vectors) it is \(\sum_i |\psi_n(x_i)|^2 e^{-x_i^2/2}\), because \(d\bar H/d\kappa = \mathrm{diag}(e^{-x_i^2/2})\). On the grid the theorem follows in one line. With \(E_n = \vec\psi_n^T\bar H\vec\psi_n\) and \(\vec\psi_n^T\vec\psi_n = 1\), the product rule gives \(dE_n/d\kappa = \vec\psi_n^T(d\bar H/d\kappa)\vec\psi_n + 2\,\vec\psi_n^T\bar H\,(d\vec\psi_n/d\kappa)\). Since \(\bar H\) is symmetric, \(\vec\psi_n^T\bar H = E_n\vec\psi_n^T\), and the last term is \(2E_n\vec\psi_n^T d\vec\psi_n/d\kappa = E_n\,d(\vec\psi_n^T\vec\psi_n)/d\kappa = 0\). The change of the eigenvector does not contribute.
Check 2 — central finite differences. Section 1 found the optimal step near \(10^{-6}\)–\(10^{-5}\) for \(\sin x\). Here any \(h\) between about \(10^{-3}\) and \(10^{-5}\) gives agreement with autograd to better than \(10^{-8}\); we take the middle value \(h = 10^{-4}\).


Code
k0 = 4.0
_, psi = torch.linalg.eigh(hamiltonian(torch.tensor(k0)))
hf = torch.sum(psi[:, 0]**2 * torch.exp(-x**2 / 2)).item()
h = 1e-4
fd = ((energies(torch.tensor(k0 + h))[0] - energies(torch.tensor(k0 - h))[0]) / (2 * h)).item()
print(f"autograd          : {kappa.grad.item():.10f}")
print(f"Hellmann-Feynman  : {hf:.10f}")
print(f"finite difference : {fd:.10f}")


autograd          : 0.3884316631
Hellmann-Feynman  : 0.3884316631
finite difference : 0.3884316634


The full picture: \(E_n(\kappa)\) and \(dE_n/d\kappa\) for the four lowest levels, \(\kappa\in[0,12]\). For each of 121 values of \(\kappa\) (step 0.1) we compute all four derivatives with torch.autograd.functional.jacobian. For a function \(\vec f\) of \(\vec x\), jacobian(f, x) evaluates \(\vec f\) at x and returns the matrix of derivatives \(\partial f_i/\partial x_j\) (one backward pass per output \(f_i\)). Here \(f\) maps one number \(\kappa\) to four energies, so the result is a vector of four derivatives. jacobian switches on gradient tracking for its input argument itself, so k needs no requires_grad=True. The energies themselves are stored with .detach(), which keeps only the numbers and not the computational graph (otherwise 121 graphs would be kept in memory). At the end, torch.stack turns the list of 121 tensors of shape (4,) into one tensor of shape (121, 4).


Code
kappas = torch.linspace(0, 12, 121)
E_all, dE_all = [], []
for k in kappas:
    E_all.append(energies(k).detach())
    dE_all.append(torch.autograd.functional.jacobian(energies, k))   # shape (4,): dE_n/dkappa
E_all, dE_all = torch.stack(E_all), torch.stack(dE_all)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.5))
for n in range(4):
    axes[0].plot(kappas, E_all[:, n], label=f"$n={n}$")
    axes[1].plot(kappas, dE_all[:, n], label=f"$n={n}$")
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$E_n(\kappa)$"); axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$dE_n/d\kappa$  (autograd)")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel(r"barrier height $\kappa$"); ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





Interpretation. \(dE_n/d\kappa = \langle e^{-x^2/2}\rangle_n\) is the probability-weighted overlap of the state with the barrier. For large \(\kappa\) all four states are pushed out of the centre and \(dE_n/d\kappa\) decreases (for \(n=2\) only above \(\kappa\approx4\); below that it first increases); pairs of levels \((0,1)\), \((2,3)\) merge into quasi-degenerate tunnelling doublets (pairs of nearly equal energy; the two states of a pair are spread symmetrically and antisymmetrically over the two wells, and their small splitting is caused by tunnelling through the barrier) — and their derivatives become equal, because both states of a doublet see the barrier the same way.

A subtle point. Derivatives of eigenvalues are well defined. Derivatives of eigenvectors contain factors \(1/(E_n - E_m)\) and blow up at (near-)degeneracies. PyTorch’s backward formula for eigh builds the full matrix of factors \(1/(E_j - E_i)\), so exact degeneracies anywhere in the spectrum give inf, and inf multiplied by zero gives nan, even for pairs that do not contribute mathematically. The PyTorch documentation of eigh warns about this.

To summarise this section: any computation built from differentiable operations can be differentiated. The same mechanism that trains neural networks is used to optimise Hamiltonians, quantum circuits (the variational quantum eigensolver VQE and the quantum approximate optimisation algorithm QAOA, later in the course) and control pulses.

title: Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
text:
7. From gradients to optimisation

7.1 Gradient descent written by hand
Minimise the Rosenbrock function \(f(x, y) = (1-x)^2 + 100\,(y - x^2)^2\) (minimum at \((1,1)\) at the bottom of a long, curved, flat valley — a simple model of a hard loss landscape).
The starting point \((-1.5, 2)\) lies on the far side of the curved valley, so the path has to follow its whole length; other starts at a distance of order 1–3 from \((1,1)\) show the same behaviour. The 3000 steps are chosen to show the slow motion along the valley, not to reach convergence. The positions are stored with p.detach().clone(): detach() alone would return a tensor that shares memory with p, and since p is changed in place in every step, all stored entries would change with it and end up equal to the final position. clone() makes an independent copy.


Code
def rosenbrock(p):
    return (1 - p[0])**2 + 100 * (p[1] - p[0]**2)**2

def gradient_descent(lr, n_steps=3000, start=(-1.5, 2.0)):
    p = torch.tensor(start, requires_grad=True)
    path = [p.detach().clone()]
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        loss = rosenbrock(p)
        loss.backward()                  # 1) gradient by autograd
        with torch.no_grad():
            p -= lr * p.grad             # 2) step downhill
        p.grad = None                    # 3) reset accumulated gradient
        path.append(p.detach().clone())
    return torch.stack(path)

path = gradient_descent(lr=1e-3)
print("final point:", path[-1], " f =", rosenbrock(path[-1]).item())


final point: tensor([0.7796, 0.6068])  f = 0.048669156394873424


The path of gradient descent drawn on the Rosenbrock landscape (the red star is the minimum). torch.meshgrid(xg, yg, indexing="xy") builds two 2D arrays XG, YG holding the \(x\) and \(y\) coordinates of every point of the plotting grid, in the layout of shape (len(yg), len(xg)) that contourf expects. The values of \(f\) on the plot range from 0 to about \(2.5\times10^3\), so the colour scale shows \(\log_{10}(f + 10^{-3})\); the small constant avoids \(\log 0\) at the minimum, and any value well below the plotted levels of \(f\) works.


Code
xg, yg = torch.linspace(-2, 2, 300), torch.linspace(-1, 3, 300)
XG, YG = torch.meshgrid(xg, yg, indexing="xy")
FG = rosenbrock(torch.stack([XG, YG]))

def landscape(ax):
    ax.contourf(XG, YG, torch.log10(FG + 1e-3), levels=40, cmap="Greys_r", alpha=0.8)
    ax.plot(1, 1, "r*", ms=15)
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
landscape(ax)
ax.plot(path[:, 0], path[:, 1], ".-", color="C0", ms=2, lw=1, label="gradient descent, $\\eta=10^{-3}$")
ax.legend(loc="lower right"); plt.show()





Gradient descent (GD) quickly falls into the valley, then crawls slowly along it. A larger learning rate helps along the valley — but makes the steps across the steep walls unstable. The limit can be computed. Near a minimum, \(f\) is approximately quadratic with the Hessian matrix \(\partial^2 f/\partial x_i\partial x_j\) as curvature. There the gradient is approximately \(\nabla f \approx \nabla^2 f\,(\vec x - \vec x^\ast)\), where \(\nabla^2 f\) is the Hessian and \(\vec x^\ast\) the minimum, so one GD step maps \(\vec x - \vec x^\ast \to (\mathbf 1 - \eta\,\nabla^2 f)(\vec x - \vec x^\ast)\). Along an eigenvector of the Hessian with eigenvalue \(\lambda\), one step therefore multiplies the distance from the minimum by \((1 - \eta\lambda)\). The iteration converges only if \(|1-\eta\lambda| < 1\) for all eigenvalues, i.e. \(\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}\). At the Rosenbrock minimum the eigenvalues are \(0.40\) and \(1001.6\), so \(\eta\) must stay below \(2/1001.6 \approx 2.0\times10^{-3}\). The flat direction (\(\lambda = 0.4\)) then shrinks by only a factor \(1 - 0.4\,\eta \approx 0.9992\) per step, which is why GD is slow.
The cell below compares \(\eta = 10^{-3}\), \(\eta = 1.9\times10^{-3}\) (slightly below the limit, much closer to the minimum after 3000 steps) and \(\eta = 2.5\times10^{-3}\) (above the limit: the iteration diverges, and the result is nan, “not a number”). The range of usable learning rates is narrow. Better optimisers address the mismatch between flat and steep directions.


Code
for lr in [1e-3, 1.9e-3, 2.5e-3]:
    final = gradient_descent(lr=lr)[-1]
    print(f"eta = {lr:.1e}:  final point = {final.numpy().round(4)},  f = {rosenbrock(final).item():.2e}")


eta = 1.0e-03:  final point = [0.7796 0.6068],  f = 4.87e-02


eta = 1.9e-03:  final point = [0.9756 0.9517],  f = 5.97e-04


eta = 2.5e-03:  final point = [nan nan],  f = nan




7.2 torch.optim: the optimiser zoo
PyTorch’s optimisers implement the update rule. For most optimisers the training loop has the same 4 lines (L-BFGS, used in Section 8, is an exception):
optimizer.zero_grad()   # reset gradients
loss = f(params)        # forward pass
loss.backward()         # backward pass
optimizer.step()        # update parameters
We compare (see Lecture Notes, The Zoo of Optimization Algorithms): - SGD: \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta g\), with \(g\) the gradient. The name stochastic gradient descent refers to estimating \(g\) from a random part of the training data. Here there are no data, \(g\) is exact, and SGD is plain gradient descent. - SGD + momentum: \(v \leftarrow \gamma v - \eta g\), \(\theta\leftarrow\theta + v\) — a “heavy ball” that builds up speed along the valley. \(\gamma = 0.9\) is the conventional value: the velocity is then an average over roughly the last \(1/(1-\gamma) = 10\) gradients. - RMSprop: per-parameter step \(\eta\,g/\sqrt{E[g^2]}\) — rescales steep and flat directions. Here \(E[g^2]\) is a running average of the squared gradient, updated in every step as \(E \leftarrow \rho E + (1-\rho)\,g^2\) (PyTorch default \(\rho = 0.99\)), separately for each parameter. - Adam: momentum + RMSprop. Both running averages start at zero, which makes them too small in the first steps; the bias correction divides them by \(1-\beta^t\) to compensate (\(t\) = step number; \(\beta\) = the decay factor of the average, by default \(0.9\) for the gradient and \(0.999\) for its square). Adam is the default choice in deep learning.
The learning rates differ between the optimisers because \(\eta\) means different things. With momentum \(\gamma = 0.9\), on a steady slope the steps add up to \(\eta/(1-\gamma) = 10\,\eta\), so \(\eta\) is reduced. RMSprop and Adam divide the gradient by its typical size, so their \(\eta\) is roughly the step length in parameter space and can be much larger. Each value was set by hand to give a stable run; the comparison shows typical behaviour, not the best possible setting of each method.
Python details in the code: a class such as torch.optim.Adam can be passed to a function like any other object. In the definition def run(opt_class, ..., **opt_kwargs), **opt_kwargs collects all remaining keyword arguments into a dictionary, and in the call opt_class([p], **opt_kwargs) the ** unpacks the dictionary back into keyword arguments. The line results = {...} is a dictionary comprehension: it runs every set-up and stores the result under its name.


Code
def run(opt_class, n_steps=3000, start=(-1.5, 2.0), **opt_kwargs):
    p = torch.tensor(start, requires_grad=True)
    opt = opt_class([p], **opt_kwargs)
    path, losses = [p.detach().clone()], []
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = rosenbrock(p)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
        path.append(p.detach().clone()); losses.append(loss.item())
    return torch.stack(path), losses

setups = {
    "SGD (lr=1e-3)":               (torch.optim.SGD, dict(lr=1e-3)),
    "SGD + momentum (lr=3e-4, 0.9)": (torch.optim.SGD, dict(lr=3e-4, momentum=0.9)),
    "RMSprop (lr=1e-2)":           (torch.optim.RMSprop, dict(lr=1e-2)),
    "Adam (lr=5e-2)":              (torch.optim.Adam, dict(lr=5e-2)),
}
results = {name: run(cls, **kw) for name, (cls, kw) in setups.items()}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))
landscape(axes[0])
for i, (name, (path, losses)) in enumerate(results.items()):
    axes[0].plot(path[:, 0], path[:, 1], "-", color=f"C{i}", lw=1.5, label=name)
    axes[1].semilogy(losses, color=f"C{i}", label=name)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right"); axes[0].set_xlim(-2, 2); axes[0].set_ylim(-1, 3)
axes[1].set_xlabel("iteration"); axes[1].set_ylabel("$f$"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
for name, (path, losses) in results.items():
    print(f"{name:32s} final f = {losses[-1]:.2e}   final point = {path[-1].numpy().round(4)}")





SGD (lr=1e-3)                    final f = 4.87e-02   final point = [0.7796 0.6068]
SGD + momentum (lr=3e-4, 0.9)    final f = 1.95e-04   final point = [0.9861 0.9723]
RMSprop (lr=1e-2)                final f = 2.24e-02   final point = [0.9678 0.9514]
Adam (lr=5e-2)                   final f = 5.82e-29   final point = [1. 1.]


Reading the result: Adam reaches the minimum \((1, 1)\) to machine precision within 3000 steps, momentum comes close (\(f \approx 2\times10^{-4}\)), and plain SGD is still moving slowly along the valley. RMSprop gets stuck at \(f\approx2\times10^{-2}\), about 0.06 from the minimum. Since it divides the gradient by its own typical size, its steps stay about as long as \(\eta\) even near the minimum (0.014 on average over the last 500 steps), so it keeps jumping across the narrow valley (the spikes in its loss curve). A smaller \(\eta\) lowers this final error (\(f\approx3\times10^{-3}\) with \(\eta = 3\times10^{-3}\)), but makes the start slower (\(f\approx0.2\) after 3000 steps with \(\eta = 10^{-3}\)).
No optimiser is universally best, and each has hyperparameters (here: the learning rate) that strongly affect the result. The same tools are used to fit neural networks, where the loss landscape has millions or more dimensions instead of two.

title: Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
text:
8. The inverse Schrödinger problem

8.1 Motivation
The usual (direct) problem of quantum mechanics is: given a potential \(V(x)\), find the eigenstates and energies. Many questions in physics are inverse: which potential produces a prescribed state? - In experiments with ultracold atoms, the trapping potential is shaped with laser beams; one wants the potential that gives a desired density profile of the atomic cloud. - In semiconductor quantum dots, gate voltages define the confining potential; one wants electrons localised in a prescribed way. - In density-functional theory, the Kohn–Sham inversion problem asks for the potential whose ground-state density equals a given density.
Here we solve the simplest version: for one particle in 1D, find \(V(x)\) such that the ground-state probability density \(|\psi_0(x)|^2\) is as close as possible to a target density \(\rho_\ast(x)\).


8.2 Formulation as an optimisation problem
On the grid of Section 6 the potential is a vector of \(N_x\) numbers \(V_i = V(x_i)\); these are our trainable parameters (here \(N_x = 300\)). For given \(V\) we build \(\bar H = \bar H_{\rm kin} + \mathrm{diag}(V)\), diagonalise it and take the ground state \(\psi_0\). The loss compares amplitudes: \[\mathcal L(V) = \sum_i \Big(|\psi_0(x_i)| - \sqrt{\rho_\ast(x_i)}\Big)^2\,\Delta x .\] The factor \(\Delta x\) makes the sum an approximation of the integral \(\int\big(|\psi_0| - \sqrt{\rho_\ast}\big)^2dx\), so its value does not depend on the number of grid points. We compare \(|\psi_0|\) with \(\sqrt{\rho_\ast}\) rather than \(|\psi_0|^2\) with \(\rho_\ast\): the square root gives more weight to regions where the density is small, which otherwise hardly influence the loss. The gradient \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial V_i\) for all 300 components comes from one backward pass through eigh. We minimise with L-BFGS, a quasi-Newton method. Newton’s method jumps to the minimum of the local quadratic approximation of the loss, \(\Delta\vec V = -(\nabla^2\mathcal L)^{-1}\nabla\mathcal L\), with the Hessian \(\nabla^2\mathcal L\) (Section 7). Computing and inverting the \(300\times300\) Hessian at every step is expensive; a quasi-Newton method instead builds an approximation of \((\nabla^2\mathcal L)^{-1}\) from the gradients of previous steps. This makes it fast for smooth problems with exact (non-stochastic) gradients. Within one step it evaluates the loss several times (a line search: several step lengths are tried along the chosen direction), so opt.step receives a function, called closure, that recomputes the loss and its gradient. (In Python, a function defined inside another function that uses that function’s variables, here opt, V and amp_target, is called a closure.) One L-BFGS step contains up to max_iter such iterations (a setting explained in 8.3).
Starting point. We start from \(V = 0\), not from a harmonic potential. The backward pass of eigh contains factors \(1/(E_i - E_j)\) for all pairs of eigenvalues, also those of highly excited states that do not enter the loss. In a symmetric potential with high walls at the edges of the grid, such as \(x^2/2\) on \([-6, 6]\), the highest states come in pairs localised at the left and right edge with numerically equal energies; the factor \(1/0\) then turns the gradient into nan (this is the warning of Section 6 in practice). The spectrum of the flat potential has no such degeneracies.
Two properties of the problem are worth knowing in advance: - \(V\) is determined only up to a constant: \(V \to V + c\) shifts all energies by \(c\) and leaves the states unchanged. We fix it by a shift: in 8.3 the potential is matched to the exact one in the high-density region, in 8.4 its minimum in that region is set to zero. - Where the target density is practically zero, the potential has almost no influence on the loss, so it is not determined there.


8.3 A test with a known answer
For a node-less ground state the Schrödinger equation can be inverted exactly. Dividing \(-\frac12\psi_0'' + V\psi_0 = E_0\psi_0\) by \(\psi_0\), which is allowed because \(\psi_0 \neq 0\) everywhere (no nodes), gives \(V(x) = E_0 + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\psi_0''(x)}{\psi_0(x)}\). For the Gaussian \(\psi_\ast(x)\propto e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}\) we have \(\psi_\ast''/\psi_\ast = x^2/\sigma^4 - 1/\sigma^2\), so \(V(x) = \frac{x^2}{2\sigma^4} + \text{const}\), a harmonic potential. We use this case to test the method. The target density is \(\rho_\ast = |\psi_\ast|^2 \propto e^{-x^2/\sigma^2}\).
Details of the code: - torch.zeros_like(x) creates a tensor of zeros with the shape and type of x. The trailing underscore in requires_grad_(True) marks a PyTorch method that modifies the tensor in place, here switching on gradient tracking. - An eigensolver may return \(\psi\) or \(-\psi\) (both are eigenvectors), and the sign can change from one iteration to the next. The ground state has no nodes, so torch.abs(psi[:, 0]) removes this ambiguity. Dividing by \(\sqrt{\Delta x}\) converts the vector normalisation \(\sum_i|\psi_i|^2 = 1\) of eigh into \(\sum_i|\psi_i|^2\Delta x = 1\), as in Section 6. - \(\sigma = 0.7\) is arbitrary. Any width works that is much larger than \(\Delta x \approx 0.04\) (so that the grid resolves the density) and much smaller than the half-width 6 of the box (so that the density vanishes at the walls). - Settings of torch.optim.LBFGS: - lr=1 means a full quasi-Newton step; the line_search_fn="strong_wolfe" then shortens or lengthens each step so that the loss really decreases by a sufficient amount. Without the line search a fixed step is taken; without it the run still converged, but to a noticeably larger loss. - history_size=50 is the number of past gradients used to estimate the curvature; values from 10 to 100 give a final loss of the same order. - tolerance_grad and tolerance_change are the thresholds below which L-BFGS stops. The defaults (\(10^{-7}\) and \(10^{-9}\)) are of the size of the loss reached here, and with them the optimisation stops early (after roughly 150–200 evaluations) at a loss a few times larger. We set them so small that they never stop the run. - Each call opt.step(closure) makes up to max_iter=50 iterations, and the line search adds further loss evaluations: the default n_steps=5 outer steps make about 270 evaluations of the loss, each with one diagonalisation and one backward pass. n_steps is kept small so that the notebook runs quickly. For the Gaussian target this costs little accuracy: with n_steps=20 (about 1200 evaluations, four times longer) the final loss decreased in our tests by less than a factor of two and the plots looked the same. Harder targets profit more from extra steps (Section 8.4). - opt.step(closure) returns the loss at the beginning of the step. To record the loss after the last step, closure() is called once more at the end.


Code
def ground_state_amplitude(V):
    # |psi_0| on the grid, normalised so that sum |psi_0|^2 dx = 1
    E, psi = torch.linalg.eigh(H_kin + torch.diag(V))
    return torch.abs(psi[:, 0]) / torch.sqrt(dx)

def invert(rho_target, n_steps=5):
    # Find V on the grid whose ground-state density is closest to rho_target (a tensor on the grid x)
    rho_target = rho_target / (rho_target.sum() * dx)            # normalise the target
    amp_target = torch.sqrt(rho_target)
    V = torch.zeros_like(x).requires_grad_(True)                 # start from a flat potential (see 'Starting point' in 8.2)
    opt = torch.optim.LBFGS([V], lr=1, max_iter=50, history_size=50, line_search_fn="strong_wolfe",
                            tolerance_grad=1e-12, tolerance_change=1e-16)
    history = []

    def closure():
        opt.zero_grad()
        amp = ground_state_amplitude(V)
        loss = torch.sum((amp - amp_target)**2) * dx
        loss.backward()                                          # gradient w.r.t. all components of V
        return loss

    for _ in range(n_steps):
        history.append(opt.step(closure).item())                 # step() returns the loss at the START of the step
    history.append(closure().item())                             # loss after the last step
    amp = ground_state_amplitude(V.detach())
    return V.detach(), amp**2, rho_target, history

sigma = 0.7
t0 = time.perf_counter()
V_opt, rho_opt, rho_star, hist = invert(torch.exp(-x**2 / sigma**2))
print(f"optimisation took {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s, final loss {hist[-1]:.2e}")
print(f"max |rho_0 - rho_target| = {torch.max(torch.abs(rho_opt - rho_star)).item():.1e}")


optimisation took 1.8 s, final loss 1.26e-07
max |rho_0 - rho_target| = 1.9e-04


Loss history, target and achieved densities, and the optimised potential compared with the exact harmonic potential (shifted by a constant). To fix the constant, we take the region where the target density exceeds \(10^{-3}\) of its maximum, where the loss carries information about \(V\), and shift \(V\) so that its mean difference from the exact potential in that region is zero. The threshold is arbitrary: with \(10^{-2}\) or \(10^{-4}\) the shift changes by about 0.02 and the picture is the same. Matching the potentials at \(x = 0\) would be an equally valid choice.


Code
