V_exact = x**2 / (2 * sigma**4)
inside = rho_star > 1e-3 * rho_star.max()                    # region where the density is not negligible
shift = torch.mean((V_opt - V_exact)[inside])                # remove the arbitrary constant

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4))
axes[0].semilogy(hist); axes[0].set_xlabel("L-BFGS step"); axes[0].set_ylabel("loss")
axes[1].plot(x, rho_star, "k", lw=3, alpha=0.4, label=r"target $\rho_\ast$")
axes[1].plot(x, rho_opt, "--", label=r"$|\psi_0|^2$ of the optimised $V$")
axes[1].set_xlim(-4, 4); axes[1].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[2].plot(x, V_exact, "k", lw=3, alpha=0.4, label=r"exact: $x^2/(2\sigma^4)$")
axes[2].plot(x, V_opt - shift, "--", label="optimised $V$ (shifted)")
axes[2].fill_between(x, -2, 30, where=~inside, color="gray", alpha=0.15, label=r"$\rho_\ast < 10^{-3}\max\rho_\ast$")
axes[2].set_xlim(-4, 4); axes[2].set_ylim(-1, 25); axes[2].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[2].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
for R in [1.0, 1.5, 2.0]:
    m = x.abs() < R
    print(f"max |V_opt - V_exact| for |x| < {R}: {torch.max(torch.abs(V_opt - shift - V_exact)[m]).item():.3f}"
          f"   (V_exact reaches {V_exact[m].max().item():.1f} there)")





max |V_opt - V_exact| for |x| < 1.0: 0.120   (V_exact reaches 2.0 there)
max |V_opt - V_exact| for |x| < 1.5: 0.251   (V_exact reaches 4.5 there)
max |V_opt - V_exact| for |x| < 2.0: 0.878   (V_exact reaches 8.2 there)


The density is reproduced closely, and in the central region the optimised potential agrees with the exact harmonic one. The deviation grows towards the edges, where the density is small and the loss is almost insensitive to \(V\); in the grey region the potential is not determined at all. This is a general feature of inverse problems: the data constrain the answer only partly, and the result is meaningful only where the data carry information.


8.4 Non-trivial target densities
On the grid, a strictly positive density is the ground state of some potential, \(V_i = E - (\bar H_{\rm kin}\psi)_i/\psi_i\) (row \(i\) of the eigenvalue equation \((\bar H_{\rm kin}\vec\psi)_i + V_i\psi_i = E\psi_i\) solved for \(V_i\)), but this potential can be very large and irregular. A density with exact zeros, such as the triangle below, cannot be reached at all. In both cases the minimisation returns the potential whose ground-state density is closest to the target in the sense of the loss. Three examples: - a triangular density, \(\rho_\ast \propto \max(0, 1 - |x|/1.5)\), with kinks and exact zeros; - a flat-top density, nearly constant on \([-1.5, 1.5]\) and falling off steeply; - an asymmetric density with three peaks of heights 1, 0.6 and 0.4 (before normalisation).
The widths, positions and heights in these formulas are arbitrary choices that give three distinct shapes. torch.clamp(t, min=0.0) replaces all negative entries of t by 0. The flat top \(1/\big(1 + e^{(|x| - 1.5)/0.1}\big)\) is a smoothed step (the Fermi function): close to 1 for \(|x| < 1.5\) and close to 0 outside, with edges of width about 0.1. In the loop, for col, (name, target) in enumerate(targets.items()) unpacks in one line the column number and the (name, density) pair.
All three use the default n_steps=5 (about 280 loss evaluations each); the cell prints its own run time. The value is kept small so that the cell runs in a few seconds. With n_steps=20 the densities improve somewhat further (for the triangle the largest density error drops from about \(8\times10^{-3}\) to \(5\times10^{-3}\)), at about four times the run time. The three peaks are deliberately not too narrow: with narrower, more separated peaks the low density between them requires very high barriers, and the optimisation needs many more steps.


Code
targets = {
    "triangle":    torch.clamp(1 - x.abs() / 1.5, min=0.0),
    "flat top":    1 / (1 + torch.exp((x.abs() - 1.5) / 0.1)),
    "three peaks": torch.exp(-(x + 1.5)**2 / 0.4**2) + 0.6 * torch.exp(-x**2 / 0.4**2)
                   + 0.4 * torch.exp(-(x - 1.5)**2 / 0.4**2),
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(16, 7))
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for col, (name, target) in enumerate(targets.items()):
    V_opt, rho_opt, rho_star, hist = invert(target)
    inside = rho_star > 1e-3 * rho_star.max()
    V_plot = V_opt - V_opt[inside].min()                       # fix the constant: minimum of V in the relevant region = 0
    axes[0, col].plot(x, rho_star, "k", lw=3, alpha=0.4, label=r"target $\rho_\ast$")
    axes[0, col].plot(x, rho_opt, "--", label=r"$|\psi_0|^2$ achieved")
    axes[0, col].set_title(f"{name}:  max |difference| = {torch.max(torch.abs(rho_opt - rho_star)).item():.1e}", fontsize=10)
    axes[1, col].plot(x[inside], V_plot[inside], color="C1")
    axes[1, col].set_ylabel("optimised $V(x)$")
    for ax in axes[:, col]:
        ax.set_xlim(-4, 4); ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
    axes[0, col].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"three inversions took {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")





three inversions took 6 s


The potentials are shown only where the target density is non-negligible. The three-peak density requires three wells separated by barriers; the relative heights of the peaks are set by the depths and the widths of the wells together, so the deepest well need not be under the highest peak (check this in your own run). The flat-top density requires a potential that is flat in the middle, has narrow dips immediately inside the edges of the plateau (they make the density rise steeply there), and rises steeply outside. The triangular density is reproduced to the accuracy printed in the panel title, although it has exact zeros: the potential outside \(|x| = 1.5\) is much higher than inside (not shown; on average about three times the value inside in our run), which pushes the density there almost (but on the grid never exactly) to zero. Inside, the optimised potential oscillates from one grid point to the next. Such grid-scale structure is a sign that the target cannot be produced by any smooth potential: the optimisation uses every degree of freedom of \(V\) on the grid to approach it. Details of such optimised potentials, especially in regions of small density, can differ between computers (different linear-algebra libraries); the densities they produce do not.
This is the same scheme as training a neural network: a parametrised model (here: \(V \mapsto \psi_0\) through the Schrödinger equation), a loss comparing the output with a target, and gradients by automatic differentiation. Only the “model” is a physics computation instead of a network.

title: Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
text:
9. Summary

Finite differences: \(\mathcal O(m)\) cost, limited accuracy. Symbolic: exact but expression swell, no programs.
AD: exact derivatives of programs via the chain rule on the computational graph.

forward mode (dual numbers): cost ∝ number of inputs;
reverse mode (backpropagation): cost ∝ number of outputs → ideal for a scalar loss of many parameters.

PyTorch: requires_grad=True, loss.backward(), .grad; torch.autograd.grad(..., create_graph=True) for higher derivatives.
Pitfalls: gradients accumulate → zero_grad(); the graph is freed after backward(); updates inside torch.no_grad(); .detach() before .numpy().
AD through eigh gives \(dE_n/d\kappa\); agrees with Hellmann–Feynman.
Training loop: zero_grad → loss → backward → step.
Inverse Schrödinger problem: 300 grid values of \(V\) optimised through eigh so that \(|\psi_0|^2\) matches a target density.

10. Exercises


Exercise 1 — By hand, then by machine
For \(f(x_1, x_2) = x_1 x_2 + \sin x_1\) at \((x_1,x_2) = (\pi/2, 3)\): 1. Draw the computational graph and fill the forward (primal) table. 2. Compute \(\partial f/\partial x_1\) and \(\partial f/\partial x_2\) with the reverse-mode adjoint table (on paper). 3. Check with (a) the Dual class (two passes), (b) the Var class (add the missing v_sin), (c) torch.autograd.

Solution


Code
# On paper, at (x1, x2) = (pi/2, 3):
#   forward:  v_-1 = x1 = pi/2,  v_0 = x2 = 3,  v_1 = v_-1 * v_0 = 3pi/2,  v_2 = sin(v_-1) = 1,  v_3 = v_1 + v_2 = y
#   backward: vbar_3 = 1,  vbar_1 = vbar_3 = 1,  vbar_2 = vbar_3 = 1,
#             vbar_0  = vbar_1 * v_-1                       = pi/2
#             vbar_-1 = vbar_1 * v_0 + vbar_2 * cos(v_-1)   = 3 + 0 = 3

# (a) forward mode with dual numbers: one pass per input, the seed (derivative part = 1) selects the input
a, b = math.pi / 2, 3.0
dy_dx1 = (Dual(a, 1) * Dual(b, 0) + d_sin(Dual(a, 1))).b     # seed x1
dy_dx2 = (Dual(a, 0) * Dual(b, 1) + d_sin(Dual(a, 0))).b     # seed x2
print("Dual :", dy_dx1, dy_dx2)

# (b) reverse mode with our Var class: we need the missing sin node.
#     Its local derivative d sin(v)/dv = cos(v) is stored for the backward pass.
def v_sin(v):
    return Var(math.sin(v.value), (v,), (math.cos(v.value),))

x1, x2 = Var(a), Var(b)
y = x1 * x2 + v_sin(x1)
y.backward()                      # one backward pass gives both derivatives
print("Var  :", x1.grad, x2.grad)

# (c) PyTorch
t1 = torch.tensor(a, requires_grad=True)
t2 = torch.tensor(b, requires_grad=True)
(t1 * t2 + torch.sin(t1)).backward()
print("torch:", t1.grad.item(), t2.grad.item())
print("exact: dy/dx1 = x2 + cos(x1) = 3,  dy/dx2 = x1 = pi/2 =", math.pi / 2)


Dual : 3.0 1.5707963267948966
Var  : 3.0 1.5707963267948966
torch: 3.0 1.5707963267948966
exact: dy/dx1 = x2 + cos(x1) = 3,  dy/dx2 = x1 = pi/2 = 1.5707963267948966





Exercise 2 — Dual numbers for a neuron

Add __truediv__ (quotient rule) and functions d_exp, d_tanh to the dual-number toolbox.
Using duals, compute the derivative of a single neuron’s output \(y = w_2\tanh(w_1 x + b)\) with respect to \(w_1\) at \(x=0.5\), \(w_1=2\), \(b=-1\), \(w_2=1.5\).
Compare with torch.autograd and with the analytic result \(w_2\,x\,(1-\tanh^2(w_1x+b))\).


Solution


Code
# 1) Quotient rule for dual numbers: (a1 + b1 eps) / (a2 + b2 eps) = a1/a2 + (b1 a2 - a1 b2)/a2^2 eps
def _truediv(self, other):
    other = Dual.lift(other)
    return Dual(self.a / other.a, (self.b * other.a - self.a * other.b) / other.a**2)
Dual.__truediv__ = _truediv          # attach the method to the existing class

#    Elementary functions: g(a + b eps) = g(a) + g'(a) b eps
def d_exp(z):
    return Dual(math.exp(z.a), math.exp(z.a) * z.b)

def d_tanh(z):
    return Dual(math.tanh(z.a), (1 - math.tanh(z.a)**2) * z.b)     # tanh' = 1 - tanh^2

print("check exp: d/dz e^z at z=1 :", d_exp(Dual(1.0, 1.0)).b, "=", math.e)
print("check div: d/dz 1/z at z=2 :", (Dual(1.0) / Dual(2.0, 1.0)).b, "= -1/4")

# 2) Derivative of y = w2 tanh(w1 x + b) with respect to w1.
#    We want d/dw1, so w1 is the dual number with derivative part 1; x, b, w2 are plain constants.
x_in, w1, b, w2 = 0.5, 2.0, -1.0, 1.5
y = w2 * d_tanh(Dual(w1, 1.0) * x_in + b)
print("dual    :", y.b)

# 3) Comparison
tw1 = torch.tensor(w1, requires_grad=True)
(w2 * torch.tanh(tw1 * x_in + b)).backward()
print("torch   :", tw1.grad.item())
print("analytic:", w2 * x_in * (1 - math.tanh(w1 * x_in + b)**2))


check exp: d/dz e^z at z=1 : 2.718281828459045 = 2.718281828459045
check div: d/dz 1/z at z=2 : -0.25 = -1/4
dual    : 0.75
torch   : 0.75
analytic: 0.75





Exercise 3 — Autodiff meets perturbation theory
Consider the anharmonic oscillator \(\hat H(\lambda) = -\tfrac12\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + \tfrac12x^2 + \lambda x^4\). First-order perturbation theory gives \(E_n(\lambda) \approx (n+\tfrac12) + \lambda\,\langle n|x^4|n\rangle\) with \(\langle n|x^4|n\rangle = \tfrac34\,(2n^2 + 2n + 1)\) for the harmonic-oscillator eigenstates \(|n\rangle\). 1. Using the grid Hamiltonian of Section 6 (H_kin and the grid x), compute \(dE_n/d\lambda\) at \(\lambda = 0\) for \(n = 0,\dots,3\) with autograd (torch.autograd.functional.jacobian on a function returning the four lowest eigenvalues). 2. Compare with \(\tfrac34(2n^2+2n+1)\). By the Hellmann–Feynman theorem the two must agree; what limits the agreement here? 3. Plot \(E_n(\lambda)\) for \(\lambda\in[0, 0.2]\) together with the first-order lines \((n+\tfrac12) + \lambda\,\tfrac34(2n^2+2n+1)\). For which \(n\) does first-order perturbation theory fail first? Give the reason.

Solution


Code
def levels(lam, n_levels=4):
    # Four lowest eigenvalues of H(lambda) = H_kin + x^2/2 + lambda x^4 on the grid
    return torch.linalg.eigvalsh(H_kin + torch.diag(0.5 * x**2 + lam * x**4))[:n_levels]

# 1) derivatives at lambda = 0: the jacobian of a function R -> R^4 is a vector of 4 numbers
dE = torch.autograd.functional.jacobian(levels, torch.tensor(0.0))

# 2) comparison with first-order perturbation theory
for n in range(4):
    pt = 0.75 * (2 * n**2 + 2 * n + 1)
    print(f"n = {n}:  autograd dE/dlambda = {dE[n].item():8.4f}   <n|x^4|n> = {pt:6.3f}")
# By Hellmann-Feynman, dE_n/dlambda at lambda = 0 equals <n|x^4|n> exactly. The small difference
# (about 0.1 % for n = 3) is the error of the finite-difference grid (dx = 0.04): the grid
# eigenstates are not exactly the harmonic-oscillator states. A finer grid reduces it.

# 3) E_n(lambda) vs the first-order approximation
lams = torch.linspace(0, 0.2, 41)
E_grid = torch.stack([levels(l) for l in lams])           # shape (41, 4)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
for n in range(4):
    ax.plot(lams, E_grid[:, n], color=f"C{n}", label=f"$n={n}$ exact (grid)")
    ax.plot(lams, (n + 0.5) + lams * 0.75 * (2 * n**2 + 2 * n + 1), "--", color=f"C{n}")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\lambda$"); ax.set_ylabel("$E_n$"); ax.set_title("solid: exact, dashed: first order")
ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show()
# The first-order correction grows like n^2, while the level spacing is 1. Perturbation theory is
# reliable only while lambda <n|x^4|n> << 1, so it fails first for the highest level shown (n = 3).


n = 0:  autograd dE/dlambda =   0.7497   <n|x^4|n> =  0.750
n = 1:  autograd dE/dlambda =   3.7477   <n|x^4|n> =  3.750
n = 2:  autograd dE/dlambda =   9.7412   <n|x^4|n> =  9.750
n = 3:  autograd dE/dlambda =  18.7271   <n|x^4|n> = 18.750








Exercise 4 — Inverse problem: design the barrier
We want a double well whose tunnelling gap is exactly \(\Delta E^{\ast} = E_1 - E_0 = 0.05\). Find \(\kappa\) by gradient-based optimisation: minimise \(\mathcal L(\kappa) = \big(\log\Delta E(\kappa) - \log\Delta E^{\ast}\big)^2\) with torch.optim.Adam (start at \(\kappa=1\), lr=0.1, 300 steps). With Adam the parameter changes by at most about lr per step, so going from \(\kappa = 1\) to a value near 5 takes at least about 40 steps; the 300 steps leave room for the final convergence. Plot \(\mathcal L\) and \(\kappa\) versus iteration and check the result on the \(E_n(\kappa)\) plot of Section 6. Why is it a good idea to compare logarithms?

Solution


Code
target_gap = 0.05
kappa = torch.tensor(1.0, requires_grad=True)       # starting value of the parameter we optimise
opt = torch.optim.Adam([kappa], lr=0.1)

hist_loss, hist_kappa = [], []
for step in range(300):
    opt.zero_grad()                                  # reset the gradient from the previous step
    E = energies(kappa, 2)                           # the two lowest levels (diagonalisation inside)
    gap = E[1] - E[0]
    # torch.log on gap, because the gradient must flow through it; the target is a fixed number, so math.log suffices
    loss = (torch.log(gap) - math.log(target_gap))**2
    loss.backward()                                  # d loss / d kappa, through eigvalsh
    opt.step()                                       # update kappa
    hist_loss.append(loss.item())
    hist_kappa.append(kappa.item())

E = energies(kappa.detach(), 2)
print(f"kappa* = {kappa.item():.4f},  gap = {(E[1] - E[0]).item():.5f}  (target {target_gap})")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 3.5))
axes[0].semilogy(hist_loss); axes[0].set_ylabel("loss")
axes[1].plot(hist_kappa); axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$\kappa$")
# check with the data of Section 6: the gap E_1 - E_0 as a function of kappa, and the optimised kappa*
axes[2].semilogy(kappas, E_all[:, 1] - E_all[:, 0], label="$E_1 - E_0$ (Section 6)")
axes[2].axhline(target_gap, color="gray", ls=":", label="target gap")
axes[2].axvline(kappa.item(), color="C3", ls="--", label=r"optimised $\kappa^*$")
axes[2].set_xlabel(r"$\kappa$"); axes[2].legend(fontsize=8)
for ax in axes[:2]: ax.set_xlabel("iteration")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
# The gap decreases roughly exponentially with kappa. In log(gap) the dependence is almost linear,
# so the loss is a simple parabola in kappa. With (gap - target)^2 the loss and its gradient would be
# extremely small for large kappa, and the optimiser would hardly move.


kappa* = 4.7285,  gap = 0.05000  (target 0.05)








Exercise 5 (advanced) — The variational principle with autograd
For the anharmonic oscillator \(V(x) = \tfrac12 x^2 + \lambda x^4\) with \(\lambda = 0.5\), take the trial wavefunction \(\psi_{\alpha,\beta}(x) \propto \exp(-\alpha x^2 - \beta x^4)\) on the grid of Section 6 (with \(\alpha, \beta>0\); parametrise them as exp of trainable numbers to keep them positive). The Rayleigh quotient \(E = \vec\psi^{T}\bar H\vec\psi/\vec\psi^{T}\vec\psi\) is, by the variational principle, never below the lowest eigenvalue of \(\bar H\), whatever \(\vec\psi\) is. Minimising it over \(\alpha, \beta\) therefore gives the best upper bound on the ground-state energy within this family of wavefunctions. 1. Write \(E(\alpha,\beta) = \dfrac{\vec\psi^{T}\bar H\vec\psi}{\vec\psi^{T}\vec\psi}\) using the grid Hamiltonian. 2. Minimise it with Adam (for example lr=0.03, 1500 steps, starting from \(\alpha = 1\), \(\beta = e^{-3}\approx0.05\)). Compare with the exact ground-state energy from eigvalsh, and with the best pure Gaussian (\(\beta = 0\)). 3. Plot the exact ground state and both variational wavefunctions.

Solution


Code
lam = 0.5
H_anh = H_kin + torch.diag(0.5 * x**2 + lam * x**4)     # grid Hamiltonian of the anharmonic oscillator
evals, evecs = torch.linalg.eigh(H_anh)                 # reference: exact diagonalisation

def variational(use_beta, steps=1500):
    """Minimise E(alpha, beta) = <psi|H|psi>/<psi|psi> for psi = exp(-alpha x^2 - beta x^4)."""
    # alpha = exp(log_a) and beta = exp(log_b) are always positive, whatever value log_a, log_b take.
    # Start: alpha = 1 (the harmonic value is 1/2) and a small quartic correction beta = e^-3 ~ 0.05. Other starts of this
    # order give the same result. With lr = 0.03 the energy stops changing after about 500 steps; 1500 steps is a safe margin.
    log_a = torch.tensor(0.0, requires_grad=True)
    log_b = torch.tensor(-3.0, requires_grad=use_beta)
    params = [log_a] + ([log_b] if use_beta else [])
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(params, lr=0.03)
    for _ in range(steps):
        opt.zero_grad()
        beta = torch.exp(log_b) if use_beta else 0.0
        psi = torch.exp(-torch.exp(log_a) * x**2 - beta * x**4)    # trial wavefunction on the grid
        # @ is matrix multiplication; for a vector psi and a matrix H, psi @ H @ psi is the number psi^T H psi.
        # The quotient (Rayleigh quotient) is never below the lowest eigenvalue: the variational principle.
        E = psi @ H_anh @ psi / (psi @ psi)
        E.backward()
        opt.step()
    return E.item(), (psi / psi.norm()).detach()

E_g, psi_g = variational(use_beta=False)        # pure Gaussian
E_gb, psi_gb = variational(use_beta=True)       # Gaussian times exp(-beta x^4)
print(f"exact      E0 = {evals[0].item():.6f}")
print(f"Gaussian   E  = {E_g:.6f}")
print(f"Gauss+x^4  E  = {E_gb:.6f}")
# Variational principle: both values lie above the exact E0; the richer ansatz is closer.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.plot(x, evecs[:, 0].abs(), "k", lw=3, label="exact")   # abs(): eigh may return -psi
ax.plot(x, psi_g, "--", label="Gaussian")
ax.plot(x, psi_gb, ":", lw=2, label="Gaussian + quartic")
ax.set_xlim(-3, 3); ax.legend(); ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); plt.show()


exact      E0 = 0.696046
Gaussian   E  = 0.701521
Gauss+x^4  E  = 0.696061








Exercise 6 (advanced, optional) — Quantum phase transition in the transverse-field Ising chain
This exercise uses a many-body quantum system, which we will study properly later in the course. For \(L\) spins-1/2 with periodic boundaries, \[\hat H(h) = -\sum_{i=1}^{L}\hat\sigma^z_i\hat\sigma^z_{i+1} - h\sum_{i=1}^{L}\hat\sigma^x_i .\] In the thermodynamic limit there is a quantum phase transition at \(h_c=1\) (ferromagnet \(\to\) paramagnet). 1. Build \(\hat H(h)\) as a \(2^L\times2^L\) matrix for \(L=6\) using torch.kron: write a helper site_op(op, i, L) that returns the operator op acting on site i of an L-site chain (identity elsewhere). torch.kron(A, B) is the Kronecker product \(A\otimes B\), the block matrix whose block \((i, j)\) is \(A_{ij}B\). An operator acting on site \(i\) of the chain is \(\mathbb 1\otimes\dots\otimes\hat\sigma\otimes\dots\otimes\mathbb 1\), with \(\hat\sigma\) at position \(i\). 2. With autograd compute \(e_0'(h) = \frac{d}{dh}\frac{E_0}{L}\) for \(h\in[0.2, 2]\). Verify it against Hellmann–Feynman: \(e_0'(h) = -\frac{1}{L}\langle\psi_0|\sum_i\hat\sigma^x_i|\psi_0\rangle\) (minus the transverse magnetisation per site, \(-m_x\)). 3. Compute \(e_0''(h)\) by central finite differences of the autograd derivative and plot it. Where is its extremum? Repeat for \(L=8\). What happens as \(L\) grows? (\(L = 10\) also works but is much slower: the matrix is \(1024\times1024\) and one diagonalisation takes about 30 times longer than for \(L = 8\).) 4. Try computing \(e_0''(h)\) by differentiating twice with autograd (create_graph=True). The result is nan; explain the reason using the remark about degeneracies in Section 6.

Solution


Code
# Pauli matrices and the 2x2 identity
sx = torch.tensor([[0., 1.], [1., 0.]])
sz = torch.tensor([[1., 0.], [0., -1.]])
id2 = torch.eye(2)

def site_op(op, i, L):
    """op acting on site i of an L-site chain: id x ... x op x ... x id (Kronecker products)."""
    out = torch.ones(1, 1)
    for j in range(L):
        out = torch.kron(out, op if j == i else id2)
    return out

hs = torch.linspace(0.2, 2.0, 61)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4))
for L in [6, 8]:                                     # L = 10 works too, but takes about 10 s
    # 1) Hamiltonian pieces. (i + 1) % L connects the last site to the first (periodic boundaries).
    ZZ = sum(site_op(sz, i, L) @ site_op(sz, (i + 1) % L, L) for i in range(L))
    X = sum(site_op(sx, i, L) for i in range(L))

    # 2) e0'(h) by autograd, and the Hellmann-Feynman value for comparison
    d1, hf = [], []
    for hv in hs:
        h = hv.clone().requires_grad_(True)          # a fresh leaf tensor for each h
        E, V = torch.linalg.eigh(-ZZ - h * X)
        (E[0] / L).backward()                        # d(E0/L)/dh  ->  h.grad
        d1.append(h.grad.item())
        psi0 = V[:, 0].detach()                      # ground state (detached: no gradient needed here)
        hf.append(-(psi0 @ X @ psi0).item() / L)     # <psi0| dH/dh |psi0> / L  with dH/dh = -X
    d1, hf = np.array(d1), np.array(hf)
    print(f"L={L}: max |autograd - Hellmann-Feynman| = {np.abs(d1 - hf).max():.2e}")

    # 3) second derivative by central finite differences of the autograd first derivative
    d2 = np.gradient(d1, hs.numpy())
    print(f"       minimum of e0''(h) at h = {hs[np.argmin(d2)].item():.3f}")
    axes[0].plot(hs, d1, label=f"L={L}")
    axes[1].plot(hs, d2, label=f"L={L}")

axes[0].set_ylabel("$de_0/dh$"); axes[1].set_ylabel("$d^2e_0/dh^2$")
for ax in axes:
    ax.axvline(1, color="gray", ls=":")             # h_c = 1 of the infinite chain
    ax.set_xlabel("$h$"); ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
# The extremum of e0'' moves towards h_c = 1 as L grows: a finite-size precursor of the
# quantum phase transition (in the infinite chain e0'' diverges logarithmically at h_c).

# 4) Second derivative by applying autograd twice
h = torch.tensor(1.0, requires_grad=True)
e0 = torch.linalg.eigvalsh(-ZZ - h * X)[0] / L
(g1,) = torch.autograd.grad(e0, h, create_graph=True)   # keep the graph of the first derivative
(g2,) = torch.autograd.grad(g1, h)
print("second derivative with autograd twice:", g2.item())
# Mathematically e0'' is finite: by second-order perturbation theory it involves only the gaps E_m - E_0 to the
# non-degenerate ground state. The nan is an artefact of the implementation: PyTorch's backward formula for eigh builds
# the full matrix of factors 1/(E_j - E_i) for ALL pairs of levels. The TFIM spectrum has exactly degenerate excited
# levels (momenta +k and -k), so this matrix contains inf, and inf * 0 = nan. The finite-difference route above avoids this.


L=6: max |autograd - Hellmann-Feynman| = 3.33e-16
       minimum of e0''(h) at h = 0.830


L=8: max |autograd - Hellmann-Feynman| = 1.11e-16
       minimum of e0''(h) at h = 0.890





second derivative with autograd twice: nan

title: Lab 005: The N-link pendulum with SymPy and automatic differentiation
text:
1. SymPy: a short tutorial
SymPy is a Python library for symbolic mathematics (a computer algebra system, like Mathematica or Maple). Variables are symbols, not numbers, and results are exact formulas.

1.1 Symbols and expressions
sp.symbols creates symbols. Assumptions such as positive=True help SymPy simplify (e.g. \(\sqrt{x^2} = x\) for \(x>0\)).


Code
x, y = sp.symbols("x y")                     # two real-or-complex symbols
a, b = sp.symbols("a b", positive=True)      # symbols known to be positive

expr = (x + y)**2 - x * y
print(expr)                                  # plain text
show(r"\text{expr} = ", expr)                # rendered as a formula


-x*y + (x + y)**2


\(\displaystyle \text{expr} = - x y + \left(x + y\right)^{2}\)


Substituting numbers and evaluating numerically; the last line shows how the assumption positive=True changes the simplification of \(\sqrt{a^2}\):


Code
# substitution and numerical evaluation
print(expr.subs({x: 1, y: 2}))               # exact result (an integer here)
print(sp.sqrt(2) * sp.pi)                    # exact: stays symbolic
print(sp.N(sp.sqrt(2) * sp.pi, 30))          # numerical value with 30 digits
print(sp.sqrt(a**2), "   vs   ", sp.sqrt(x**2))   # the assumption a > 0 matters


7
sqrt(2)*pi
4.44288293815836624701588099006
a    vs    sqrt(x**2)




1.2 Simplification
SymPy does not simplify automatically; simplification has to be requested. expand, factor, trigsimp and simplify are the most useful.


Code
show(r"\text{expand}: ", sp.expand((x + y)**3))
show(r"\text{factor}: ", sp.factor(x**2 - y**2))
show(r"\text{trigsimp}: ", sp.trigsimp(sp.sin(x)**2 + sp.cos(x)**2))
show(r"\text{simplify}: ", sp.simplify(sp.sin(x) * sp.cos(y) - sp.cos(x) * sp.sin(y)))


\(\displaystyle \text{expand}: x^{3} + 3 x^{2} y + 3 x y^{2} + y^{3}\)


\(\displaystyle \text{factor}: \left(x - y\right) \left(x + y\right)\)


\(\displaystyle \text{trigsimp}: 1\)


\(\displaystyle \text{simplify}: \sin{\left(x - y \right)}\)




1.3 Derivatives, integrals, series
sp.diff(f, x, a) differentiates first with respect to \(x\), then with respect to \(a\). sp.integrate(f, (x, lower, upper)) computes a definite integral; sp.oo (two letters o) is SymPy’s symbol for \(\infty\). sp.series(f, x, x0, n) expands \(f\) around \(x_0\) and keeps the powers up to \(x^{n-1}\); the remainder is written as \(O(x^n)\). With \(n = 8\) the expansion of \(\cos x\) below stops at \(x^6\) (the \(x^7\) term of \(\cos\) vanishes).


Code
f = sp.exp(-a * x**2) * sp.sin(x)
show(r"\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = ", sp.diff(f, x))
show(r"\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial a} = ", sp.diff(f, x, a))
show(r"\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-a x^2}\,dx = ", sp.integrate(sp.exp(-a * x**2), (x, -sp.oo, sp.oo)))
show(r"\cos x = ", sp.series(sp.cos(x), x, 0, 8))


\(\displaystyle \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = - 2 a x e^{- a x^{2}} \sin{\left(x \right)} + e^{- a x^{2}} \cos{\left(x \right)}\)


\(\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial a} = x \left(2 a x^{2} \sin{\left(x \right)} - x \cos{\left(x \right)} - 2 \sin{\left(x \right)}\right) e^{- a x^{2}}\)


\(\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-a x^2}\,dx = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{\sqrt{a}}\)


\(\displaystyle \cos x = 1 - \frac{x^{2}}{2} + \frac{x^{4}}{24} - \frac{x^{6}}{720} + O\left(x^{8}\right)\)




1.4 Solving equations
sp.solve(equation, unknown); an expression without = is understood as “expression \(= 0\)”. sp.Eq(lhs, rhs) writes an equation explicitly (the Python symbol = is reserved for assignment, and == compares two objects, so neither can be used to write an equation). sp.solve returns a list of solutions for one unknown and, for a linear system with a unique solution, a dictionary {unknown: value} (other cases return a list; dict=True always gives a list of dictionaries).


Code
print(sp.solve(x**2 - 3 * x + 2, x))                         # roots of a quadratic
sol = sp.solve([sp.Eq(2 * x + y, 5), sp.Eq(x - y, 1)], [x, y])  # a linear system
print(sol)


[1, 2]
{x: 2, y: 1}




1.5 Matrices


Code
A = sp.Matrix([[a, 1], [1, a]])
show(r"A = ", A, r",\quad \det A = ", A.det(), r",\quad A^{-1} = ", sp.simplify(A.inv()))
print("eigenvalues:", A.eigenvals())                         # {eigenvalue: multiplicity}


\(\displaystyle A = \left[\begin{matrix}a & 1\\1 & a\end{matrix}\right] ,\quad \det A = a^{2} - 1 ,\quad A^{-1} = \left[\begin{matrix}\frac{a}{a^{2} - 1} & - \frac{1}{a^{2} - 1}\\- \frac{1}{a^{2} - 1} & \frac{a}{a^{2} - 1}\end{matrix}\right]\)


eigenvalues: {a - 1: 1, a + 1: 1}




1.6 Functions of time and differential equations
For mechanics we need unknown functions of time, e.g. \(\theta(t)\). sp.Function("theta")(t) creates one; sp.diff differentiates it. sp.dsolve solves (simple) ordinary differential equations exactly.


Code
t = sp.symbols("t", real=True)
omega = sp.symbols("omega", positive=True)
theta = sp.Function("theta")(t)

ode = sp.Eq(sp.diff(theta, t, 2), -omega**2 * theta)         # harmonic oscillator
show(r"\text{ODE: } ", ode)
show(r"\text{solution: } ", sp.dsolve(ode))


\(\displaystyle \text{ODE: } \frac{d^{2}}{d t^{2}} \theta{\left(t \right)} = - \omega^{2} \theta{\left(t \right)}\)


\(\displaystyle \text{solution: } \theta{\left(t \right)} = C_{1} \sin{\left(\omega t \right)} + C_{2} \cos{\left(\omega t \right)}\)




1.7 From formulas to fast numerical functions: lambdify
To compute numbers with a SymPy formula (many times, on arrays), convert it into a NumPy function with sp.lambdify(arguments, expression, "numpy"). This is the bridge between symbolic derivation and numerical simulation.


Code
dfdx = sp.diff(f, x)                                 # symbolic derivative from 1.3
dfdx_num = sp.lambdify((x, a), dfdx, "numpy")        # a Python function of (x, a) using NumPy

xs = np.linspace(-4, 4, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
ax.plot(xs, sp.lambdify((x, a), f, "numpy")(xs, 0.3), label="$f(x)$")
ax.plot(xs, dfdx_num(xs, 0.3), label=r"$\partial f/\partial x$ (from SymPy)")
ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.legend(); plt.show()

title: Lab 005: The N-link pendulum with SymPy and automatic differentiation
text:
2. Lagrangian mechanics in one paragraph
Describe the system with generalised coordinates \(q_1,\dots,q_N\) that automatically respect the constraints (for a pendulum: angles, not Cartesian positions, so the rod length is fixed by construction). Write the kinetic energy \(T(q,\dot q)\) and the potential energy \(V(q)\), and form the Lagrangian \[L(q,\dot q) = T(q,\dot q) - V(q).\] The motion satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equations, one per coordinate: \[\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q_i} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i} = 0,\qquad i = 1,\dots,N.\] For a time-independent \(L\) whose kinetic energy is a homogeneous quadratic function of the velocities \(\dot q\) (no linear terms) (true for all systems in this notebook), the energy \(E = T + V\) is conserved. We use this as a check of every simulation.
Reading the partial derivatives. In \(\partial L/\partial q_i\) and \(\partial L/\partial\dot q_i\) the coordinates and the velocities are treated as independent variables: \(L\) is an ordinary function of \(2N\) numbers, and each derivative is taken with the other \(2N-1\) held fixed. Only afterwards, in \(\frac{d}{dt}\), are \(q(t)\) and \(\dot q(t)\) the functions of time along the motion. A check with one particle on a line, \(L = \tfrac12 m\dot x^2 - V(x)\): \(\partial L/\partial\dot x = m\dot x\) (the momentum), \(\frac{d}{dt}(m\dot x) = m\ddot x\), and \(\partial L/\partial x = -V'(x)\), so the Euler–Lagrange equation is \(m\ddot x = -V'(x)\), Newton’s second law. The advantage of the Lagrangian form appears with constraints: in angle coordinates the forces of the rods never have to be computed.

title: Lab 005: The N-link pendulum with SymPy and automatic differentiation
text:
3. The single pendulum
A mass \(m\) on a massless rod of length \(l\); the angle \(\theta\) is measured from the downward vertical. The position of the mass is \(x = l\sin\theta\), \(y = -l\cos\theta\). We let SymPy do every step.


Code
t = sp.symbols("t", real=True)
m, l, g = sp.symbols("m l g", positive=True)
theta = sp.Function("theta")(t)

# Cartesian position of the mass, expressed through the generalised coordinate theta(t)
x_pos = l * sp.sin(theta)
y_pos = -l * sp.cos(theta)

# Kinetic and potential energy. sp.Rational(1, 2) is the exact fraction 1/2; writing 0.5 would put a
# floating-point number into the formula, and SymPy would then print and simplify it with decimals.
T = sp.Rational(1, 2) * m * (sp.diff(x_pos, t)**2 + sp.diff(y_pos, t)**2)
V = m * g * y_pos
L = sp.simplify(T - V)
show(r"T = ", sp.simplify(T), r",\qquad V = ", V)
show(r"L = ", L)


\(\displaystyle T = \frac{l^{2} m \left(\frac{d}{d t} \theta{\left(t \right)}\right)^{2}}{2} ,\qquad V = - g l m \cos{\left(\theta{\left(t \right)} \right)}\)


\(\displaystyle L = \frac{l m \left(2 g \cos{\left(\theta{\left(t \right)} \right)} + l \left(\frac{d}{d t} \theta{\left(t \right)}\right)^{2}\right)}{2}\)


The Euler–Lagrange equation for \(\theta\), and its solution for \(\ddot\theta\):


Code
theta_dot = sp.diff(theta, t)

# Euler-Lagrange equation:  d/dt (dL/d theta_dot) - dL/d theta = 0
EL = sp.diff(sp.diff(L, theta_dot), t) - sp.diff(L, theta)
show(r"\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot\theta} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta} = ", sp.simplify(EL), " = 0")

# Solve for the angular acceleration. sp.solve returns a list of solutions; the equation is linear in
# theta'' and has exactly one, which [0] takes out of the list.
theta_ddot = sp.solve(EL, sp.diff(theta, t, 2))[0]
show(r"\ddot\theta = ", theta_ddot)


\(\displaystyle \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot\theta} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta} = l m \left(g \sin{\left(\theta{\left(t \right)} \right)} + l \frac{d^{2}}{d t^{2}} \theta{\left(t \right)}\right) = 0\)


\(\displaystyle \ddot\theta = - \frac{g \sin{\left(\theta{\left(t \right)} \right)}}{l}\)


For small angles \(\sin\theta\approx\theta\) and the equation becomes the harmonic oscillator with \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{g/l}\). SymPy can check this and solve it. sp.series expands in a symbol, not in a function such as \(\theta(t)\), so \(\theta(t)\) is first replaced by a plain symbol \(\vartheta\), expanded to first order, and substituted back; .removeO() deletes the remainder term \(O(\vartheta^2)\), leaving an ordinary expression. sp.dsolve returns an equation \(\theta(t) = \dots\); .rhs (right-hand side) takes the expression after the equals sign. \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) in the result are the two integration constants of a second-order equation, fixed by the initial angle and angular velocity.


Code
small = sp.series(theta_ddot.subs(theta, sp.Symbol("vartheta")), sp.Symbol("vartheta"), 0, 2).removeO()
show(r"\ddot\theta \approx ", small.subs(sp.Symbol("vartheta"), theta))
show(r"\theta(t) = ", sp.dsolve(sp.Eq(sp.diff(theta, t, 2), small.subs(sp.Symbol("vartheta"), theta))).rhs)


\(\displaystyle \ddot\theta \approx - \frac{g \theta{\left(t \right)}}{l}\)


\(\displaystyle \theta(t) = C_{1} \sin{\left(\frac{\sqrt{g} t}{\sqrt{l}} \right)} + C_{2} \cos{\left(\frac{\sqrt{g} t}{\sqrt{l}} \right)}\)



3.1 Phase portrait
The state of the pendulum is the point \((\theta, \dot\theta)\) in phase space. Since the energy \(E(\theta,\dot\theta) = \tfrac12 m l^2\dot\theta^2 - m g l\cos\theta\) is conserved, every trajectory lies on a contour line of \(E\). We plot these contours with the energy from SymPy (lambdify), with \(m = l = 1\), \(g = 9.81\).
Two technical steps in the code: for clarity we first replace \(\dot\theta(t)\) by a plain symbol (its LaTeX name only changes how it is printed) and \(\theta(t)\) by the symbol q (lambdify could also take \(\theta(t)\) and \(\dot\theta(t)\) directly as arguments). np.meshgrid turns two 1D grids into two 2D arrays holding the \(\theta\) and \(\dot\theta\) coordinates of every point of the plane; contour needs the function values on such a grid.

\(E < mgl\): closed curves around \((0,0)\) — oscillations;
\(E > mgl\): open curves — rotations (the pendulum goes over the top);
\(E = mgl\): the separatrix, which ends at the unstable equilibrium \(\theta = \pm\pi\) (pendulum pointing up).

The picture repeats every \(2\pi\) along the \(\theta\) axis because \(\theta\) and \(\theta + 2\pi\) are the same position of the pendulum; the plotted range \([-2\pi, 2\pi]\) shows two copies so that the rotations, which run from one copy into the next, are visible.


Code
w = sp.symbols(r"\dot\theta")                                # a plain symbol standing for the angular velocity
E_expr = (T + V).subs(sp.diff(theta, t), w).subs(theta, sp.Symbol("q"))
E_num = sp.lambdify((sp.Symbol("q"), w, m, l, g), E_expr, "numpy")
show(r"E = ", sp.simplify(E_expr))

qq, ww = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-2 * np.pi, 2 * np.pi, 500), np.linspace(-10, 10, 400))
EE = E_num(qq, ww, 1.0, 1.0, 9.81)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
# the lowest energy is -m g l = -9.81 (at rest at the bottom); the 25 levels from -9 to 40 are a display choice
ax.contour(qq, ww, EE, levels=np.linspace(-9, 40, 25), cmap="viridis", linewidths=1)
ax.contour(qq, ww, EE, levels=[9.81], colors="red", linewidths=2)        # separatrix E = m g l
ax.plot([-np.pi, np.pi], [0, 0], "rx", ms=10, mew=2, label="unstable equilibria")
ax.plot([-2 * np.pi, 0, 2 * np.pi], [0, 0, 0], "ko", ms=6, label="stable equilibria")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta$ [rad]"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\dot\theta$ [rad/s]")
ax.set_title("single pendulum: contours of $E(\\theta,\\dot\\theta)$; red = separatrix")
ax.legend(loc="upper right"); plt.show()


\(\displaystyle E = \frac{l m \left(\dot\theta^{2} l - 2 g \cos{\left(q \right)}\right)}{2}\)

title: Lab 005: The N-link pendulum with SymPy and automatic differentiation
text:
4. The N-link pendulum with SymPy

4.1 Geometry
Masses \(m_1,\dots,m_N\) sit at the ends of massless rods of lengths \(l_1,\dots,l_N\); rod 1 hangs from the fixed pivot at the origin. Each angle \(\theta_i\) is measured from the downward vertical. The position of mass \(k\) is the sum of the rod vectors up to \(k\): \[x_k = \sum_{j=1}^{k} l_j\sin\theta_j,\qquad y_k = -\sum_{j=1}^{k} l_j\cos\theta_j .\] Then \[T = \frac12\sum_{k=1}^{N} m_k\big(\dot x_k^2 + \dot y_k^2\big),\qquad V = g\sum_{k=1}^{N} m_k\,y_k,\qquad L = T - V .\]
The next cell only draws the sketch below. draw_chain uses only basic Matplotlib plotting commands and does not need to be studied in detail; the part that matters is the first two lines of the function, which are the formulas for \(x_k\), \(y_k\) above (np.cumsum gives the running sums).


Code
from matplotlib.patches import Arc

def draw_chain(ax, theta, lengths, masses=None, labels=True):
    # Draw an N-link pendulum with angles theta (from the downward vertical) and rod lengths.
    N = len(theta)
    xs = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(lengths * np.sin(theta))])     # pivot + N masses
    ys = np.concatenate([[0.0], -np.cumsum(lengths * np.cos(theta))])
    ax.plot([-0.4, 0.4], [0, 0], color="k", lw=3)                           # ceiling
    ax.plot(xs, ys, "-", color="0.35", lw=2.5, zorder=1)                    # rods
    sizes = 120 * (np.ones(N) if masses is None else np.asarray(masses) / np.max(masses))
    ax.scatter(xs[1:], ys[1:], s=sizes * 2, color="C0", zorder=3, edgecolor="k")
    ax.plot(0, 0, "o", color="k", ms=6, zorder=4)                           # pivot
    if labels:
        for k in range(N):
            ax.plot([xs[k], xs[k]], [ys[k], ys[k] - 0.55 * lengths[k]], "k:", lw=1)       # vertical reference
            start, end = (-90, -90 + np.rad2deg(theta[k])) if theta[k] > 0 else (-90 + np.rad2deg(theta[k]), -90)
            ax.add_patch(Arc((xs[k], ys[k]), 0.6 * lengths[k], 0.6 * lengths[k], theta1=start, theta2=end, color="C3", lw=1.5))
            mid = np.deg2rad(-90) + theta[k] / 2
            ax.text(xs[k] + 0.42 * lengths[k] * np.cos(mid), ys[k] + 0.42 * lengths[k] * np.sin(mid),
                    rf"$\theta_{k+1}$", color="C3", fontsize=13, ha="center", va="center")
            # rod label: 60 % along the rod, shifted perpendicular to it, away from the angle arc
            normal = np.array([np.cos(theta[k]), np.sin(theta[k])])
            pos = np.array([xs[k], ys[k]]) + 0.6 * np.array([xs[k + 1] - xs[k], ys[k + 1] - ys[k]]) + 0.13 * normal
            ax.text(pos[0], pos[1], rf"$l_{k+1}$", fontsize=12, ha="center", va="center")
            # mass label: lower left of the mass (free of rods, arcs and the vertical reference line)
            ax.text(xs[k + 1] - 0.1, ys[k + 1] - 0.1, rf"$m_{k+1}$", fontsize=12, color="C0", ha="right", va="top")
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))
draw_chain(ax, theta=np.array([0.45, 1.0, 0.25, 1.3]), lengths=np.array([1.0, 0.8, 0.9, 0.7]), masses=[1.0, 0.8, 1.2, 0.6])
ax.text(-0.42, 0.06, "pivot", fontsize=11, ha="right")
ax.set_title("N-link pendulum, N = 4\n(angles from the downward vertical)", fontsize=11)
plt.show()







4.2 Deriving the equations for any N
The function below follows the recipe of Section 3 for arbitrary \(N\). After forming the Euler–Lagrange expressions we replace \(\theta_i(t), \dot\theta_i, \ddot\theta_i\) by plain symbols \(q_i, w_i, a_i\) (easier to handle). Each Euler–Lagrange equation is linear in the accelerations \(a_i = \ddot\theta_i\), so the system can be written as \[M(q)\,\ddot q = F(q,\dot q),\] with the mass matrix \(M\) and a right-hand side \(F\) (gravity and centrifugal terms). sp.linear_eq_to_matrix extracts \(M\) and \(F\). \(M\) is the matrix of second derivatives of \(T\) with respect to the velocities, \(M_{ij} = \partial^2 T/\partial\dot q_i\,\partial\dot q_j\), because \(T\) is quadratic in \(\dot q\). It is therefore symmetric, and positive definite, since \(T = \tfrac12\dot q^{\top} M\dot q > 0\) for every non-zero velocity. Hence \(M\) is invertible, and the equations can always be solved for the accelerations.
Two SymPy details used below. sp.symbols("m1:4") creates the numbered symbols m1, m2, m3; as in Python’s range, the upper end is excluded, hence f"m1:{N + 1}" for \(N\) symbols. The substitutions must start with the highest derivative: \(\ddot\theta_i\) is the derivative of \(\dot\theta_i\), so if \(\dot\theta_i\) were replaced by the symbol \(w_i\) first, \(\ddot\theta_i\) would turn into the time derivative of a constant symbol, i.e. \(0\), and the accelerations would disappear from the equations.


Code
def derive_n_pendulum(N):
    """Symbolic equations of motion M(q) a = F(q, w) of the N-link pendulum, and its energy."""
    t = sp.symbols("t", real=True)
    g = sp.symbols("g", positive=True)
    m = sp.symbols(f"m1:{N + 1}", positive=True)          # (m1, ..., mN)
    l = sp.symbols(f"l1:{N + 1}", positive=True)          # (l1, ..., lN)
    th = [sp.Function(f"theta{i + 1}")(t) for i in range(N)]

    # positions as running sums, kinetic and potential energy
    x_k, y_k, T, V = 0, 0, 0, 0
    for k in range(N):
        x_k += l[k] * sp.sin(th[k])
        y_k += -l[k] * sp.cos(th[k])
        T += sp.Rational(1, 2) * m[k] * (sp.diff(x_k, t)**2 + sp.diff(y_k, t)**2)
        V += m[k] * g * y_k
    L = T - V

    # Euler-Lagrange expressions  d/dt dL/d(theta_dot) - dL/d(theta),  one per coordinate
    EL = [sp.diff(sp.diff(L, sp.diff(th_i, t)), t) - sp.diff(L, th_i) for th_i in th]

    # replace theta_i'' -> a_i, theta_i' -> w_i, theta_i -> q_i  (order matters: highest derivative first, see above)
    q = sp.symbols(f"q1:{N + 1}"); w = sp.symbols(f"w1:{N + 1}"); a = sp.symbols(f"a1:{N + 1}")
    replace = {}
    for i in range(N):
        replace[sp.diff(th[i], t, 2)] = a[i]
    for i in range(N):
        replace[sp.diff(th[i], t)] = w[i]
    EL = [e.subs(replace).subs(dict(zip(th, q))) for e in EL]
    energy = (T + V).subs(replace).subs(dict(zip(th, q)))

    # EL_i = sum_j M_ij a_j - F_i = 0   ->   M a = F
    M, F = sp.linear_eq_to_matrix(EL, a)
    # M and F are simplified; L and the energy are returned unsimplified, because simplifying them is the
    # slowest step and the numerical functions built from them do not need it
    return dict(M=sp.simplify(M), F=sp.simplify(F), L=L.subs(replace).subs(dict(zip(th, q))),
                E=energy, q=q, w=w, m=m, l=l, g=g)

t_derive = {}                                         # derivation times, used again in the cost table below
t0 = time.perf_counter()
dp = derive_n_pendulum(2)
t_derive[2] = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"N = 2 derived in {t_derive[2]:.1f} s")
show(r"L = ", sp.simplify(dp["L"]))
show(r"M(q) = ", dp["M"])
show(r"F(q, w) = ", dp["F"])


N = 2 derived in 0.7 s


\(\displaystyle L = g l_{1} m_{1} \cos{\left(q_{1} \right)} + g m_{2} \left(l_{1} \cos{\left(q_{1} \right)} + l_{2} \cos{\left(q_{2} \right)}\right) + \frac{l_{1}^{2} m_{1} w_{1}^{2}}{2} + \frac{m_{2} \left(l_{1}^{2} w_{1}^{2} + 2 l_{1} l_{2} w_{1} w_{2} \cos{\left(q_{1} - q_{2} \right)} + l_{2}^{2} w_{2}^{2}\right)}{2}\)


\(\displaystyle M(q) = \left[\begin{matrix}l_{1}^{2} \left(m_{1} + m_{2}\right) & l_{1} l_{2} m_{2} \cos{\left(q_{1} - q_{2} \right)}\\l_{1} l_{2} m_{2} \cos{\left(q_{1} - q_{2} \right)} & l_{2}^{2} m_{2}\end{matrix}\right]\)


\(\displaystyle F(q, w) = \left[\begin{matrix}- l_{1} \left(g m_{1} \sin{\left(q_{1} \right)} + g m_{2} \sin{\left(q_{1} \right)} + l_{2} m_{2} w_{2}^{2} \sin{\left(q_{1} - q_{2} \right)}\right)\\l_{2} m_{2} \left(- g \sin{\left(q_{2} \right)} + l_{1} w_{1}^{2} \sin{\left(q_{1} - q_{2} \right)}\right)\end{matrix}\right]\)


Compare with the textbook double pendulum. Dividing the first row by \(l_1\) and the second by \(m_2 l_2\): \[(m_1+m_2)\,l_1\ddot\theta_1 + m_2 l_2\cos(\theta_1-\theta_2)\,\ddot\theta_2 = -m_2 l_2\dot\theta_2^2\sin(\theta_1-\theta_2) - (m_1+m_2)\,g\sin\theta_1,\] \[l_1\cos(\theta_1-\theta_2)\,\ddot\theta_1 + l_2\ddot\theta_2 = l_1\dot\theta_1^2\sin(\theta_1-\theta_2) - g\sin\theta_2 .\] SymPy checks the agreement. In SymPy, == compares the form of two expressions, not their mathematical value: sp.sin(x)**2 + sp.cos(x)**2 == 1 is False. Two formulas are therefore compared by simplifying their difference and testing whether the result is the zero matrix.


Code
q1, q2 = dp["q"]; w1, w2 = dp["w"]; m1, m2 = dp["m"]; l1, l2 = dp["l"]; g_ = dp["g"]
d = q1 - q2
M_book = sp.Matrix([[(m1 + m2) * l1, m2 * l2 * sp.cos(d)], [l1 * sp.cos(d), l2]])
F_book = sp.Matrix([-m2 * l2 * w2**2 * sp.sin(d) - (m1 + m2) * g_ * sp.sin(q1), l1 * w1**2 * sp.sin(d) - g_ * sp.sin(q2)])
scale = sp.diag(1 / l1, 1 / (m2 * l2))                       # row scaling described above
print("M agrees:", sp.simplify(scale * dp["M"] - M_book) == sp.zeros(2, 2))
print("F agrees:", sp.simplify(scale * dp["F"] - F_book) == sp.zeros(2, 1))


M agrees: True
F agrees: True




4.3 Structure of the mass matrix
For \(N = 3\) the matrix shows a pattern: \[M_{ij} = l_i\,l_j\cos(\theta_i - \theta_j)\sum_{k\ge\max(i,j)} m_k .\] (Rod \(i\) “carries” all masses below it.) We verify the formula for \(N=3\) symbolically.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()
tp = derive_n_pendulum(3)
t_derive[3] = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"N = 3 derived in {t_derive[3]:.1f} s")
show(r"M = ", tp["M"])

q, m_, l_ = tp["q"], tp["m"], tp["l"]
M_formula = sp.Matrix(3, 3, lambda i, j: l_[i] * l_[j] * sp.cos(q[i] - q[j]) * sum(m_[max(i, j):]))
print("formula agrees:", sp.simplify(tp["M"] - M_formula) == sp.zeros(3, 3))


N = 3 derived in 2.0 s

4.4 From SymPy to a numerical acceleration function
We turn \(M\) and \(F\) into NumPy functions with lambdify and solve \(M\ddot q = F\) numerically. The function accepts either one state (arrays of shape (N,)) or a batch of states (shape (N, B)) — we will need batches for the Poincaré sections.
How the matrix is assembled and solved: - Iterating over a SymPy matrix gives its entries row by row (\(M_{11}, M_{12}, \dots, M_{1N}, M_{21}, \dots\)), so the flat list of evaluated entries is reshaped to (N, N, *shape); *shape appends the batch shape, which is empty for a single state. - np.linalg.solve(M, F) solves the linear system \(M a = F\). It is cheaper and more accurate than computing the inverse \(M^{-1}\) and multiplying, and \(M\) (a mass matrix, positive definite) always has a unique solution. For a stack of systems, solve requires the matrix indices to be the last two axes, shape (B, N, N), and the right-hand side to have shape (B, N, 1). np.moveaxis moves the batch axis to the front, [..., None] appends an axis of length 1, and [..., 0] removes it again from the result.


Code
def make_sympy_accel(res, m_vals, l_vals, g_val):
    """Return accel(q, w) = M(q)^{-1} F(q, w) for given numerical masses, lengths and g."""
    N = len(res["q"])
    # one dictionary {symbol: number}: ** unpacks the two dictionaries into the new one, and g is added as a third entry
    params = {**dict(zip(res["m"], m_vals)), **dict(zip(res["l"], l_vals)), res["g"]: g_val}
    # one NumPy function per matrix entry (entries that are constants, e.g. l1**2 (m1 + m2), return a plain number)
    M_funs = [sp.lambdify(res["q"], e, "numpy") for e in res["M"].subs(params)]
    F_funs = [sp.lambdify(res["q"] + res["w"], e, "numpy") for e in res["F"].subs(params)]
    E_fun = sp.lambdify(res["q"] + res["w"], res["E"].subs(params), "numpy")

    def evaluate(funs, args, shape):
        # evaluate all entries and broadcast constant entries to the batch shape
        return np.array([np.broadcast_to(np.asarray(f(*args), dtype=float), shape) for f in funs])

    def accel(q, w):
        shape = np.shape(q[0])                                   # () for one state, (B,) for a batch
        M = evaluate(M_funs, q, shape).reshape(N, N, *shape)
        F = evaluate(F_funs, list(q) + list(w), shape).reshape(N, *shape)
        # move the batch axis to the front for np.linalg.solve, then back
        M = np.moveaxis(M, (0, 1), (-2, -1)); F = np.moveaxis(F, 0, -1)[..., None]
        return np.moveaxis(np.linalg.solve(M, F)[..., 0], -1, 0)

    def energy(q, w):
        return E_fun(*q, *w)
    return accel, energy

# double pendulum with m = l = 1, g = 9.81
accel_dp, energy_dp = make_sympy_accel(dp, [1.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0], 9.81)
print("one state :", accel_dp(np.array([0.3, -0.2]), np.array([0.1, 0.5])))
print("batch of 3:", accel_dp(np.array([[0.3, 1.0, 2.0], [-0.2, 0.0, 0.5]]), np.zeros((2, 3))).shape)

title: Lab 005: The N-link pendulum with SymPy and automatic differentiation
section: 5. The N-link pendulum with automatic differentiation
text:
5. The N-link pendulum with automatic differentiation
In this approach no equations of motion are derived. We only need \(L(q,\dot q)\) as a function that computes a number. Expanding the time derivative in the Euler–Lagrange equation with the chain rule, \[\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i} = \sum_j \frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial\dot q_i\,\partial\dot q_j}\,\ddot q_j + \sum_j\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial\dot q_i\,\partial q_j}\,\dot q_j ,\] so the Euler–Lagrange equations become \[\underbrace{\Big[\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial\dot q\,\partial\dot q}\Big]}_{M}\ddot q = \frac{\partial L}{\partial q} - \Big[\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial\dot q\,\partial q}\Big]\dot q
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\ddot q = M^{-1}\Big(\nabla_q L - \big(\nabla_q\nabla_{\dot q}L\big)\,\dot q\Big).\] Here \(\big(\nabla_q\nabla_{\dot q}L\big)\) is the matrix with elements \(C_{ij} = \partial^2 L/\partial\dot q_i\,\partial q_j\), so that \((C\dot q)_i = \sum_j C_{ij}\dot q_j\). Everything on the right is a derivative of the scalar function \(L\), which autodiff computes exactly up to rounding errors: - grad(L, argnums=0) — the gradient \(\nabla_q L\). grad does not return a number: it returns a new Python function which, called with (q, qd), returns \(\partial L/\partial q\). argnums selects the argument with respect to which the derivative is taken (0 = q, 1 = qd); - hessian(L, argnums=1) — the matrix \(M = \partial^2 L/\partial\dot q\,\partial\dot q\), again as a function of (q, qd); - the product \(\big(\nabla_q\nabla_{\dot q}L\big)\dot q\) is a Jacobian-vector product of the function \(q\mapsto\nabla_{\dot q}L(q,\dot q)\) with the vector \(\dot q\): jvp computes it without building the full matrix. jvp(f, (x,), (v,)) returns two results, \(f(x)\) and the directional derivative \(J_f(x)\,v\); only the second is needed, so the first is assigned to _ (a name conventionally used for a discarded value). The lambda fixes qd, so that the function given to jvp depends on q only; - torch.linalg.solve(M, b) solves \(M\ddot q = b\) without forming \(M^{-1}\), as np.linalg.solve in Section 4.4.
torch.func provides these operations as functions that transform functions (like in the mathematical notation).
The Lagrangian of the chain, written with cumsum (the velocities follow from differentiating the running sums of Section 4.1): \[\dot x_k = \sum_{j\le k} l_j\cos\theta_j\,\dot\theta_j,\qquad \dot y_k = \sum_{j\le k} l_j\sin\theta_j\,\dot\theta_j .\]


Code
def lagrangian_chain(q, qd, m, l, g):
    """L = T - V of the N-link pendulum; m, l have length N; q, qd have shape (N,), or (B, N) for B chains."""
    vx = torch.cumsum(l * torch.cos(q) * qd, dim=-1)        # dim=-1: sums run over the last axis (the links)
    vy = torch.cumsum(l * torch.sin(q) * qd, dim=-1)
    T = 0.5 * torch.sum(m * (vx**2 + vy**2), dim=-1)
    y = -torch.cumsum(l * torch.cos(q), dim=-1)
    V = g * torch.sum(m * y, dim=-1)
    return T - V

def energy_chain(q, qd, m, l, g):
    vx = torch.cumsum(l * torch.cos(q) * qd, dim=-1)
    vy = torch.cumsum(l * torch.sin(q) * qd, dim=-1)
    y = -torch.cumsum(l * torch.cos(q), dim=-1)
    return 0.5 * torch.sum(m * (vx**2 + vy**2), dim=-1) + g * torch.sum(m * y, dim=-1)

def accel_from_lagrangian(L, q, qd):
    """Accelerations q_ddot from the Euler-Lagrange equations of ANY Lagrangian L(q, qd), by autodiff."""
    dL_dq = grad(L, argnums=0)(q, qd)                       # nabla_q L
    M = hessian(L, argnums=1)(q, qd)                        # d^2 L / d qd d qd
    dL_dqd = lambda qq: grad(L, argnums=1)(qq, qd)          # q -> nabla_qd L(q, qd)
    _, C_qd = jvp(dL_dqd, (q,), (qd,))                      # (d^2 L / d qd d q) @ qd
    return torch.linalg.solve(M, dL_dq - C_qd)


Check against SymPy. We draw random states (angles and angular velocities) and deliberately unequal masses and lengths, so that an error cannot cancel by symmetry, and compare the accelerations from both routes for \(N = 2\) and \(N = 3\).


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for res, N in [(dp, 2), (tp, 3)]:
    m_vals, l_vals = np.array([1.7, 0.9, 1.3])[:N], np.array([1.3, 0.6, 0.8])[:N]
    accel_sym, _ = make_sympy_accel(res, m_vals, l_vals, 9.81)
    m_t, l_t = torch.tensor(m_vals), torch.tensor(l_vals)
    L = lambda q, qd: lagrangian_chain(q, qd, m_t, l_t, 9.81)

    max_diff = 0.0
    for _ in range(100):
        q = rng.uniform(-np.pi, np.pi, N); w = rng.uniform(-8, 8, N)
        a_sym = accel_sym(q, w)
        a_ad = accel_from_lagrangian(L, torch.tensor(q), torch.tensor(w)).numpy()
        max_diff = max(max_diff, np.max(np.abs(a_sym - a_ad)))
    print(f"N = {N}: max |a_SymPy - a_autodiff| over 100 random states = {max_diff:.1e}")


N = 2: max |a_SymPy - a_autodiff| over 100 random states = 9.9e-14


N = 3: max |a_SymPy - a_autodiff| over 100 random states = 1.1e-13


The angles cover a full period and the velocities \(\pm 8\) rad/s, a range typical of the motions simulated later; 100 states are more than enough to expose an error in a formula (500 states, tried when preparing the notebook, also agree to about \(10^{-13}\) but take five times longer), and the exact numbers are arbitrary. The two routes agree to about \(10^{-13}\), i.e. to rounding error: the accelerations at these states reach up to about 170 rad/s\(^2\), and float64 resolves relative differences of about \(10^{-16}\), so \(10^{-13}\) is a relative difference of order \(10^{-15}\), a few rounding steps. The autodiff route needed only the few lines of lagrangian_chain, works for any \(N\) without new derivations, and for any other Lagrangian (Exercise 4).
The price: every call performs several automatic-differentiation passes, so it is slower than evaluating the formulas from lambdify (measured below). The first call of a function includes one-time set-up work and is slower than the following ones, so every time is an average over repeated calls after one warm-up call; the numbers of repetitions are arbitrary. As a rule, the symbolic route is preferable when the formulas are manageable and speed matters, autodiff when the model is large, changes often, or when \(L\) is itself learned (Lagrangian neural networks).

L10 = lambda q, qd: lagrangian_chain(q, qd, m_t, l_t, 9.81)
q, qd = torch.rand(10), torch.rand(10)

# (the SymPy derivation time in Section 4.3 grows by a factor of about 3 per additional link from N = 2 on; N = 10 is not attempted)

# cost of one acceleration evaluation for N = 2: lambdify formulas vs autodiff
q2, w2 = np.array([0.3, -0.2]), np.array([0.1, 0.5])
L2_chain = lambda q, qd: lagrangian_chain(q, qd, torch.ones(2), torch.ones(2), 9.81)
accel_dp(q2, w2); accel_from_lagrangian(L2_chain, torch.tensor(q2), torch.tensor(w2))     # warm-up calls
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(200):
    accel_dp(q2, w2)
t_sym = (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 200
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(50):
    accel_from_lagrangian(L2_chain, torch.tensor(q2), torch.tensor(w2))
t_ad = (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 50
print(f"one acceleration, N = 2:  lambdify {1e6 * t_sym:.0f} microseconds,  autodiff {1e6 * t_ad:.0f} microseconds")

one acceleration, N = 2:  lambdify 57 microseconds,  autodiff 7926 microseconds


Reading the printed times (they depend on the computer): for \(N = 2\) the autodiff acceleration is about two orders of magnitude slower than the lambdify formulas. The autodiff time for \(N = 10\) is about the same as for \(N = 2\): at these sizes the cost is dominated by the fixed overhead of the torch.func calls, not by the arithmetic (in our tests the time per call stayed of order 10 ms, about 8 ms in the run above, from \(N = 2\) to \(N = 20\)). Section 9 shows how this overhead is reduced for long simulations.

title: Lab 005: The N-link pendulum with SymPy and automatic differentiation
text:
6. Integrating the equations of motion
Integration methods are formulated for first-order equations \(\dot s = f(s)\). A second-order equation is brought into this form by treating the velocity \(w = \dot q\) as an additional unknown; the equations of motion then form a first-order system for the state \(s = (q, \dot q)\): \[\frac{d}{dt}\begin{pmatrix} q\\ \dot q\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\dot q \\ \ddot q(q,\dot q)\end{pmatrix}.\] We integrate it with the classical 4th-order Runge–Kutta method (RK4): with time step \(\Delta t\), \[k_1 = f(s),\; k_2 = f(s + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}k_1),\; k_3 = f(s + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}k_2),\; k_4 = f(s + \Delta t\,k_3),\qquad
s \leftarrow s + \tfrac{\Delta t}{6}(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4).\] The error after a fixed time is proportional to \(\Delta t^4\). The four \(k\)’s are estimates of the slope \(ds/dt\): at the start of the step (\(k_1\)), twice at the midpoint (\(k_2\), \(k_3\), each using the previous estimate to get there) and at the end (\(k_4\)). The step uses their weighted average, like Simpson’s rule for an integral.
Why RK4: it is the standard general-purpose method for such systems. Each step needs four evaluations of the acceleration, and halving \(\Delta t\) reduces the error 16 times, whereas for the simplest (Euler) method, \(s \leftarrow s + \Delta t\, f(s)\), the error is proportional to \(\Delta t\) and halving the step only halves it. RK4 does not conserve energy exactly; the energy slowly drifts, and Section 6.2 uses this drift to measure the accuracy. A derivation of the formulas is found in numerical-analysis textbooks, e.g. W. H. Press et al., Numerical Recipes (3rd ed.), Ch. 17.
In simulate, the number of steps is int(round(T / dt)). In floating-point arithmetic a quotient can come out slightly too small, e.g. 0.3 / 0.1 gives 2.9999999999999996, and int cuts off the fractional part (giving 2); rounding first gives the intended number.
Both functions also work for a batch: with q and w of shape (N, B), the B columns are independent pendulums that are advanced together. Most of the time of one step is fixed overhead (Python calls, building small arrays), so a batch of several trajectories costs little more than a single one. The notebook uses this throughout to stay fast enough for the free Colab CPU.
simulate stores the state after every step in a list and converts the list with np.array at the end; time is the first axis, so Q has shape (n_steps + 1, N) for one pendulum and (n_steps + 1, N, B) for a batch.


Code
def rk4_step(accel, q, w, dt):
    """One RK4 step for q'' = accel(q, q'). Works for single states and batches."""
    k1q, k1w = w, accel(q, w)
    k2q, k2w = w + 0.5 * dt * k1w, accel(q + 0.5 * dt * k1q, w + 0.5 * dt * k1w)
    k3q, k3w = w + 0.5 * dt * k2w, accel(q + 0.5 * dt * k2q, w + 0.5 * dt * k2w)
    k4q, k4w = w + dt * k3w, accel(q + dt * k3q, w + dt * k3w)
    q_new = q + dt / 6 * (k1q + 2 * k2q + 2 * k3q + k4q)
    w_new = w + dt / 6 * (k1w + 2 * k2w + 2 * k3w + k4w)
    return q_new, w_new

def simulate(accel, q0, w0, T, dt):
    """Integrate from (q0, w0) up to time T; return times and arrays of q and w (time along axis 0)."""
    n_steps = int(round(T / dt))
    q, w = np.array(q0, float), np.array(w0, float)
    Q, W = [q], [w]
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        q, w = rk4_step(accel, q, w, dt)
        Q.append(q); W.append(w)
    return np.arange(n_steps + 1) * dt, np.array(Q), np.array(W)



6.1 A double-pendulum trajectory
Released from rest at \(\theta_1 = 120^\circ\), \(\theta_2 = -10^\circ\) (\(m = l = 1\), \(g = 9.81\)).
Choice of \(\Delta t\) and \(T\). The natural time scale of a pendulum is \(\sqrt{l/g} \approx 0.32\) s; the two small-oscillation periods of the double pendulum are \(2.6\) s and \(1.1\) s (Exercise 2). A step \(\Delta t = 2\cdot10^{-3}\) s resolves these scales with hundreds of steps. Measured for this trajectory over 10 s, the largest relative energy error is \(1.4\cdot10^{-7}\) for \(\Delta t = 10^{-3}\) s, \(2\cdot10^{-6}\) for \(2\cdot10^{-3}\) s and \(3\cdot10^{-5}\) for \(4\cdot10^{-3}\) s, so any of these steps gives the same plots. \(T = 10\) s covers about four periods of the slower oscillation; it is kept short for speed, and \(T = 30\) s shows more of the irregular motion. (The energy at the start is \(E(0) \approx 0.15\) J, i.e. \(\approx 0.015\,mgl\), just above the energy \(E = 0\) of both rods horizontal.)
Left: both angles as functions of time. Right: the paths of the two masses in the plane; mass 1 always stays on the circle of radius \(l_1 = 1\) around the pivot (the rod is rigid), while mass 2 can reach any point within distance \(l_1 + l_2 = 2\).


Code
t_arr, Q, W = simulate(accel_dp, [np.deg2rad(120), np.deg2rad(-10)], [0.0, 0.0], T=10.0, dt=2e-3)
E = energy_dp(Q.T, W.T)
print(f"relative energy drift over 10 s: {np.max(np.abs(E - E[0])) / abs(E[0]):.1e}")

# Cartesian positions of both masses for the trajectory plot
x1, y1 = np.sin(Q[:, 0]), -np.cos(Q[:, 0])
x2, y2 = x1 + np.sin(Q[:, 1]), y1 - np.cos(Q[:, 1])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.5), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.6, 1]})
axes[0].plot(t_arr, Q[:, 0], label=r"$\theta_1$"); axes[0].plot(t_arr, Q[:, 1], label=r"$\theta_2$")
axes[0].set_xlabel("$t$ [s]"); axes[0].set_ylabel("angle [rad]"); axes[0].legend()
axes[1].plot(x2, y2, lw=0.5, color="C1", label="mass 2")
axes[1].plot(x1, y1, lw=0.8, color="C0", label="mass 1")
axes[1].plot(0, 0, "ks"); axes[1].set_aspect("equal"); axes[1].legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_title("paths in the $(x, y)$ plane"); axes[1].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[1].set_ylabel("$y$")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


relative energy drift over 10 s: 2.1e-06







6.2 Energy conservation as a test of the integrator
The exact motion conserves \(E\); the numerical one does not, and the drift tells us how accurate the integration is. For RK4 the error should scale as \(\Delta t^4\) — a slope of 4 on a log-log plot.
The step is halved from \(0.04\) s to \(0.0025\) s, which gives equally spaced points on the logarithmic axis; \(T = 3\) s keeps the cell fast. The dashed line only shows the slope 4; it is drawn through the last point, and its vertical position has no other meaning. The asymptotic law \(\propto\Delta t^4\) holds only when \(\Delta t\) is small enough: between the two largest steps the error falls about 28 times (slope \(\approx 4.8\); at \(\Delta t = 0.04\) s the energy error is \(0.14\), not small), between the two smallest about 15 times (slope \(\approx 3.9\)).


Code
dts = [0.04, 0.02, 0.01, 0.005, 0.0025]
drifts = []
for dt in dts:
    _, Qd_, Wd_ = simulate(accel_dp, [np.deg2rad(120), np.deg2rad(-10)], [0.0, 0.0], T=3.0, dt=dt)
    Ed = energy_dp(Qd_.T, Wd_.T)
    drifts.append(np.max(np.abs(Ed - Ed[0])))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.loglog(dts, drifts, "o-", label="max $|E(t) - E(0)|$ over 3 s")
ax.loglog(dts, drifts[-1] * (np.array(dts) / dts[-1])**4, "k--", label=r"$\propto \Delta t^4$")
ax.set_xlabel(r"time step $\Delta t$"); ax.set_ylabel("energy error"); ax.legend()
plt.show()







6.3 Animation: small, large and very large amplitudes
Equal masses and lengths (\(m_1 = m_2 = 1\), \(l_1 = l_2 = 1\)), released from rest with \(\theta_1 = \theta_2 = \alpha\) for \(\alpha = 10^\circ\), \(90^\circ\) and \(170^\circ\). In every panel a second pendulum (drawn in a paler colour) starts with \(\theta_1\) larger by \(10^{-3}\) rad; the line behind the lower mass shows its recent path.
matplotlib.animation.FuncAnimation calls a function update(frame) for every frame, and to_jshtml() turns the result into an interactive player (play, pause, step) that works in Colab and Jupyter. The time needed is printed below the player.
Choices in the code, all of them for display only: - all six pendulums are integrated as one batch, with \(\Delta t = 4\cdot10^{-3}\) s (energy error \(3\cdot10^{-5}\), Section 6.1); only every 30th state is drawn: one frame every \(0.12\) s, about 8 frames per second. The frame rate and the resolution (dpi=50) are kept low so that the notebook file stays small; frame_dt = 0.04 (a multiple of the integration step) and dpi=100 give a smoother, sharper animation at several times the file size; - the shift of \(10^{-3}\) rad of the twin is chosen so that the separation becomes visible within the simulated 12 s; the trail shows the last 17 frames (about 2 s at frame_dt = 0.12; the number of frames is fixed, so a smaller frame_dt shortens the trail); “separated” means that the lower masses are more than \(0.1\,l\) apart; all these values are arbitrary; - animation.embed_limit raises matplotlib’s default limit (20 MB) on the size of an animation stored inside the notebook; - blit=True makes matplotlib redraw only the objects returned by update in each frame (faster), which is why update returns them; default_mode="once" makes the player stop at the end instead of looping.

q0[0, 1::2] += 1e-3                                  # columns 1, 3, 5 are the twins
_, Qa, _ = simulate(accel_dp, q0, np.zeros_like(q0), T=T_anim, dt=dt_sim)        # Qa: (steps, 2, 6)
Qa = Qa[::every]                                     # angles at the frame times
runs = []
for j in range(6):
    x1, y1 = np.sin(Qa[:, 0, j]), -np.cos(Qa[:, 0, j])                 # l1 = l2 = 1

n_frames = len(runs[0][0])

# when do the lower masses of reference and twin first differ by more than 0.1 (in units of l)?
for k, a in enumerate(amplitudes):

for k, ax in enumerate(axes):

    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
