title: Lab 005: The N-link pendulum with SymPy and automatic differentiation
text:
7. Chaos: sensitivity to initial conditions
Two double pendulums released from angles differing by \(10^{-9}\) rad. We follow the distance between them in phase space, \(d(t) = \|s_A(t) - s_B(t)\|\). In a chaotic system it grows on average exponentially, \(d(t)\sim d(0)\,e^{\lambda t}\), until it reaches the size of the accessible phase space. \(\lambda\) is the (largest) Lyapunov exponent. On a logarithmic vertical axis, as in the right panel below, exponential growth appears as a straight line: \(\ln d(t) = \ln d(0) + \lambda t\), with slope \(\lambda\).
Choices in the code: - The perturbation \(10^{-9}\) rad is very small, so that the exponential phase lasts long before the distance saturates; any value well above the rounding level \(10^{-16}\) would do. (The shifts of \(10^{-3}\) rad in Section 6.3 and \(10^{-4}\) rad in Section 9 were instead chosen so that the separation becomes visible within the simulated time.) - The distance \(d\) adds angles (rad) and angular velocities (rad/s), quantities with different units. This is acceptable: changing the weights of the coordinates in the distance changes only the prefactor of \(d(t)\), not its exponential growth rate \(\lambda\). - \(\lambda\) is the slope of \(\ln d(t)\) versus \(t\), obtained with np.polyfit(t, ln d, 1), a least-squares fit of a straight line (polynomial of degree 1) that returns the slope and the intercept. The fit uses \(1\,\mathrm{s} < t < 8\,\mathrm{s}\): at the start \(d\) does not yet grow steadily (the perturbation first has to turn into the most unstable direction; here \(d\) rises and falls again, staying of order \(10^{-8}\), up to \(t \approx 2\) s). The first second is left out; the remaining dip before \(t = 2\) s barely affects the slope of a fit over seven seconds (starting the window at 2 s instead of 1 s changes \(\lambda\) by about 2 %). The upper limit keeps the fit far from saturation, which sets in after about 20 s. - Both pendulums are integrated as one batch (two columns) with \(\Delta t = 5\cdot10^{-3}\) s for 25 s. With \(\Delta t = 10^{-3}\) s the separation time and \(\lambda\) change by less than 1 %.


Code
q0 = np.deg2rad([120.0, -10.0])
q_AB = np.column_stack([q0, q0 + np.array([1e-9, 0])])          # shape (2, 2): column 0 = A, column 1 = B
t_arr, Q, W = simulate(accel_dp, q_AB, np.zeros((2, 2)), T=25.0, dt=5e-3)
QA, QB, WA, WB = Q[:, :, 0], Q[:, :, 1], W[:, :, 0], W[:, :, 1]
dist = np.sqrt(np.sum((QA - QB)**2 + (WA - WB)**2, axis=1))
t_sep = t_arr[np.argmax(np.abs(QA[:, 1] - QB[:, 1]) > 0.1)]       # first time theta2 differs by more than 0.1 rad
print(f"theta2 of A and B first differ by more than 0.1 rad at t = {t_sep:.1f} s")

# slope of log(d) in the growth phase: a straight-line fit for 1 s < t < 8 s
sel = (t_arr > 1) & (t_arr < 8)
lam, c = np.polyfit(t_arr[sel], np.log(dist[sel]), 1)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4))
axes[0].plot(t_arr, QA[:, 1], label="pendulum A"); axes[0].plot(t_arr, QB[:, 1], "--", label="pendulum B")
axes[0].set_xlabel("$t$ [s]"); axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$\theta_2$ [rad]"); axes[0].legend()
axes[1].semilogy(t_arr, dist, label="$d(t)$")
axes[1].semilogy(t_arr[sel], np.exp(c + lam * t_arr[sel]), "k--", label=rf"fit $\propto e^{{\lambda t}}$, $\lambda \approx {lam:.2f}$ s$^{{-1}}$")
axes[1].set_xlabel("$t$ [s]"); axes[1].set_ylabel("phase-space distance"); axes[1].legend()
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


theta2 of A and B first differ by more than 0.1 rad at t = 19.2 s





After an initial transient (in the first one to two seconds \(d\) fluctuates without growing) the distance grows exponentially on average, but it becomes visible in the angles only when it reaches order \(10^{-1}\) (time printed above); after that the two pendulums, which started \(10^{-9}\) rad apart, move completely differently. The estimate of \(\lambda\) from a single pair of trajectories is rough: it depends on the fitting window (windows between 1 s and 15 s give \(0.9\)–\(1.1\) s\(^{-1}\), the window 0–3 s gives \(0.7\) s\(^{-1}\)); a reliable method is the subject of Exercise 3. A practical consequence: no numerical method can follow an individual chaotic trajectory for long times — rounding errors of \(10^{-16}\) are amplified in the same way. Statistical properties (such as the Poincaré sections below) are nevertheless reproducible.

title: Lab 005: The N-link pendulum with SymPy and automatic differentiation
text:
8. Phase space and Poincaré sections
The double pendulum has a 4-dimensional phase space \((\theta_1, \theta_2, \dot\theta_1, \dot\theta_2)\), and energy conservation restricts each trajectory to a 3-dimensional surface \(E = \text{const}\). That is still hard to draw. Projections onto two coordinates are a first look. We show two trajectories, released from rest at \(\theta_1=\theta_2=10^\circ\) (small angles) and at \(\theta_1=120^\circ,\theta_2=-10^\circ\) (large angles); both are integrated as one batch with \(\Delta t = 5\cdot10^{-3}\) s for 30 s, to save time; for a picture of this kind the accuracy is more than sufficient (for the trajectory of Section 6.1 this step gives a relative energy error of \(8\cdot10^{-5}\) over 10 s). With \(T = 100\) s the filling of the plane is easier to see.


Code
q0_pair = np.deg2rad([[10.0, 120.0], [10.0, -10.0]])        # columns: (10, 10) deg and (120, -10) deg
_, Qp, Wp = simulate(accel_dp, q0_pair, np.zeros((2, 2)), T=30.0, dt=5e-3)
titles = [r"small angles: $\theta_1=\theta_2=10^\circ$", r"large angles: $\theta_1=120^\circ, \theta_2=-10^\circ$"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))
for j, (ax, title) in enumerate(zip(axes, titles)):
    ax.plot(Qp[:, 0, j], Wp[:, 0, j], lw=0.3)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta_1$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\dot\theta_1$"); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





Left (small angles): the curve stays inside a band and is woven in a regular pattern; two oscillations with different frequencies are superposed, and the trajectory never exactly repeats. Right (large angles): the curve wanders irregularly over a larger region. In both cases the lines cross each other, because the plot shows only two of the four coordinates. A projection of a chaotic trajectory fills an area and hides the structure. The tool for looking inside is the Poincaré section. It is introduced here step by step.
1. Phase space and flow. The state of the double pendulum is the point \(z = (\theta_1, \theta_2, \dot\theta_1, \dot\theta_2) \in \mathbb R^4\). The equations of motion \(\dot z = F(z)\) determine, for every initial state \(z_0\), a unique trajectory \(z(t) = \varphi_t(z_0)\); the map \(\varphi_t\) is called the flow. Trajectories of an autonomous system (one whose equations do not contain the time explicitly, \(\dot z = F(z)\) and not \(F(z, t)\)) never cross each other in phase space: through every point passes exactly one trajectory.
2. The energy surface. The energy \(E(z) = T + V\) is conserved, so a trajectory never leaves the 3-dimensional surface \(\{z : E(z) = E\}\). Each trajectory is a curve on this 3D surface, which still cannot be drawn on paper. A projection onto two coordinates, as in the figure above, squashes the curve and makes it cross itself everywhere.
3. The surface of section. Choose a surface that trajectories keep passing through, here \[\Sigma = \{\, z :\ \theta_1 = 0,\ \ \dot\theta_1 > 0,\ \ E(z) = E \,\}.\] In words: the first rod passes through the vertical, moving to the right. The condition \(\dot\theta_1 > 0\) is needed because during one swing the rod passes the vertical twice, once in each direction; counting only one direction makes every recorded point correspond to “the same phase” of the motion, and it guarantees that the trajectory really crosses \(\Sigma\) instead of touching it. \(\Sigma\) is 2-dimensional: \(\theta_1 = 0\) removes one coordinate, and on this set the energy equation, quadratic in \(\dot\theta_1\), fixes \(\dot\theta_1 > 0\) once \(\theta_2\) and \(\dot\theta_2\) are given (the formula is derived below). The pair \((\theta_2, \dot\theta_2)\) is therefore a complete set of coordinates on \(\Sigma\) (up to a two-fold ambiguity where both roots of the quadratic are positive; we then take the larger one, see below).
4. The Poincaré map. Start at a point \(z \in \Sigma\), follow the flow, and stop when the trajectory comes back to \(\Sigma\) for the first time; call this time \(\tau(z)\), the return time. The point of return defines the Poincaré map \[P : \Sigma \to \Sigma, \qquad P(z) = \varphi_{\tau(z)}(z).\] A trajectory is thus turned into a sequence of points \(z_1,\ z_2 = P(z_1),\ z_3 = P(z_2), \dots\) in a plane: a continuous flow in 4 dimensions is replaced by a discrete map in 2 dimensions, without losing information, because every \(z_n\) determines the whole trajectory through it.
5. What the patterns mean. - A periodic orbit that crosses \(\Sigma\) \(k\) times per period returns to the same \(k\) points: a fixed point of \(P^k\) (the map applied \(k\) times). - Quasi-periodic motion combines two frequencies whose ratio is irrational; the trajectory then winds forever around a 2-dimensional torus in phase space without closing. (Each of the two oscillations is described by a phase angle that runs around a circle; the pair of angles lives on the surface of a doughnut, the torus.) The torus intersects \(\Sigma\) in a closed curve, and the points \(z_n\) fill this invariant curve densely. - Chaotic motion lies on no torus; its points \(z_n\) scatter over a 2-dimensional region of \(\Sigma\).
For small oscillations the double pendulum is close to two coupled harmonic oscillators (Exercise 2), and all motion is quasi-periodic. With growing energy the nonlinearity grows; the Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser (KAM) theorem states that most tori survive a weak perturbation but are progressively destroyed as it becomes stronger, leaving chains of islands (remnants of resonant tori) embedded in a chaotic sea. The four panels below show this sequence.
6. A remark on coordinates. For Hamiltonian systems (conservative systems without friction, such as all systems described by a Lagrangian \(L = T - V\)) the Poincaré map preserves area, but in the canonical coordinates \((\theta_2, p_2)\) with the canonical momentum \(p_2 = \partial L / \partial\dot\theta_2\) (for a single particle \(\partial L/\partial\dot x = m\dot x\), the ordinary momentum, Section 2), which on \(\Sigma\) (with \(m = l = 1\)) equals \(\dot\theta_2 + \dot\theta_1\cos\theta_2\). We plot \((\theta_2, \dot\theta_2)\), which is more intuitive; it shows the same curves, islands and chaotic regions, but areas are slightly distorted.
7. How the crossings are found numerically. The integrator produces states \(z_n\) at times \(t_n = n\,\Delta t\). A crossing of \(\Sigma\) between steps \(n\) and \(n+1\) is detected by a sign change of \(s = \sin\theta_1\) from \(s_n < 0\) to \(s_{n+1} \ge 0\) (the rod moves to the right) together with \(\cos\theta_1 > 0\) (the rod points down; this excludes the passage through the upright position \(\theta_1 = \pi\), where \(\sin\theta_1\) also changes sign). The sine is tested instead of \(\theta_1\) itself because the integrator does not reduce the angle to one period: after the first rod has gone over the top, \(\theta_1\) continues to \(2\pi, 4\pi, \dots\), and \(\sin\theta_1\) detects every passage through the downward vertical, modulo \(2\pi\). Within the step the motion is approximated by a straight line: the crossing happens at the fraction \[\beta = \frac{s_n}{s_n - s_{n+1}} \in (0, 1]\] of the step, and the state on \(\Sigma\) is estimated as \(z^\ast \approx z_n + \beta\,(z_{n+1} - z_n)\). The error of this linear interpolation is of order \(\Delta t^2\) (here \(\Delta t = 10^{-2}\) s). We measured it by locating the crossings exactly (by repeating the last step with an adjusted step size until \(\sin\theta_1 = 0\)): the typical error in \(\dot\theta_2\) is below \(10^{-3}\) rad/s and the largest about \(2\cdot10^{-2}\) rad/s, invisible on axes that span \(\pm 10\) rad/s. The angle \(\theta_2\) is also brought back to one period with np.arctan2(np.sin(th2), np.cos(th2)): arctan2 returns the angle in \((-\pi, \pi]\) with the given sine and cosine, i.e. \(\theta_2\) shifted by a multiple of \(2\pi\).
Initial conditions at fixed energy. We start every trajectory on the section: choose \(\theta_1 = 0\), a random \(\theta_2\) and \(\dot\theta_2\), and compute \(\dot\theta_1>0\) from \(E\). With \(m = l = 1\), the energy at \(\theta_1 = 0\) is \[E = \dot\theta_1^2 + \dot\theta_1\dot\theta_2\cos\theta_2 + \tfrac12\dot\theta_2^2 - 2g - g\cos\theta_2 ,\] a quadratic equation for \(\dot\theta_1\). We let SymPy confirm the formula and solve it.
\(\theta_2\) and \(\dot\theta_2\) are drawn at random, and a draw is rejected when no real \(\dot\theta_1 > 0\) gives the required energy (the energy is too low for these values); this is called rejection sampling. Minimising the kinetic part of the formula over \(\dot\theta_1\) (the minimum is at \(\dot\theta_1 = -\tfrac12\dot\theta_2\cos\theta_2\)) gives \(E \ge \tfrac14\dot\theta_2^2(2 - \cos^2\theta_2) - 2g - g\cos\theta_2 \ge \tfrac14\dot\theta_2^2 - 3g\), so on the section \(|\dot\theta_2| \le 2\sqrt{E + 3g}\): \(4.2\) rad/s at \(E = -25\) and \(10.8\) rad/s at \(E = 0\). The sampling range \(\pm 10\) rad/s therefore covers almost the whole allowed region (at \(E = 0\) the narrow strips \(10 < |\dot\theta_2| < 10.8\) are not sampled), and at low energy most draws are rejected (about 91 % at \(E = -25\)), which costs only a little time. When both roots are positive, both give valid states with the same energy; taking the larger one is an arbitrary convention.


Code
q1s, q2s = dp["q"]; w1s, w2s = dp["w"]
E_sec = dp["E"].subs({**dict(zip(dp["m"], [1, 1])), **dict(zip(dp["l"], [1, 1]))}).subs(q1s, 0)
show(r"E\big|_{\theta_1 = 0} = ", sp.expand(sp.simplify(E_sec)))

E_sym = sp.symbols("E")
roots = sp.solve(sp.Eq(E_sec, E_sym), w1s)
show(r"\dot\theta_1 = ", roots[0], r"\quad\text{or}\quad", roots[1])
w1_of = sp.lambdify((q2s, w2s, E_sym, dp["g"]), roots, "numpy")     # both roots as NumPy functions


\(\displaystyle E\big|_{\theta_1 = 0} = - g \cos{\left(q_{2} \right)} - 2 g + w_{1}^{2} + w_{1} w_{2} \cos{\left(q_{2} \right)} + \frac{w_{2}^{2}}{2}\)


\(\displaystyle \dot\theta_1 = - \frac{w_{2} \cos{\left(q_{2} \right)}}{2} - \frac{\sqrt{4 E + 4 g \cos{\left(q_{2} \right)} + 8 g - w_{2}^{2} \sin^{2}{\left(q_{2} \right)} - w_{2}^{2}}}{2} \quad\text{or}\quad - \frac{w_{2} \cos{\left(q_{2} \right)}}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{4 E + 4 g \cos{\left(q_{2} \right)} + 8 g - w_{2}^{2} \sin^{2}{\left(q_{2} \right)} - w_{2}^{2}}}{2}\)


Two functions: the first creates initial states on the section with a given energy, the second integrates a batch of trajectories and records where they cross the section. poincare_sections integrates the trajectories of all requested energies as one batch (4 energies \(\times\) 30 trajectories = 120 columns), which costs little more than a single trajectory. For speed the step is \(\Delta t = 10^{-2}\) s and \(T = 100\) s (10 000 steps, a few seconds); each trajectory then crosses the section about 50 times. The accuracy is monitored by the largest energy error at the end, printed in each panel title. These values are kept small for the free Colab CPU; T=300.0, dt=5e-3 (about a minute) gives denser and sharper pictures.
New NumPy functions in the code: np.isfinite is True for ordinary numbers and False for nan (the square root of a negative number) and infinity; np.repeat(energies, n_traj) repeats every energy n_traj times, giving the energy of each column; np.nonzero(crossed)[0] gives the column indices where crossed is True, so that every section point is stored together with the number of its trajectory.


Code
def initial_conditions_on_section(E, n, rng, g=9.81):
    """n states with theta1 = 0, theta1_dot > 0 and energy E (m = l = 1)."""
    states = []
    while len(states) < n:
        th2, w2 = rng.uniform(-np.pi, np.pi), rng.uniform(-10, 10)
        with np.errstate(invalid="ignore"):                 # sqrt of a negative number -> nan (energy not reachable)
            w1_candidates = np.array(w1_of(th2, w2, E, g), dtype=float)
        w1_ok = w1_candidates[np.isfinite(w1_candidates) & (w1_candidates > 0)]
        if w1_ok.size > 0:
            states.append([0.0, th2, w1_ok.max(), w2])       # if both roots are positive, take the larger one
    return np.array(states).T                               # shape (4, n): rows q1, q2, w1, w2

def poincare_sections(energies, n_traj=30, T=100.0, dt=1e-2, seed=0):
    """n_traj trajectories for each energy, all integrated as one batch; collect crossings of theta1 = 0 with theta1_dot > 0.
    Returns the points (column index, theta2, theta2_dot) and the largest energy error for each energy."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    s = np.hstack([initial_conditions_on_section(E, n_traj, rng) for E in energies])   # shape (4, n_energies * n_traj)
    E_target = np.repeat(energies, n_traj)                  # energy of every column
    q, w = s[:2], s[2:]
    points = []
    for _ in range(int(round(T / dt))):
        q_new, w_new = rk4_step(accel_dp, q, w, dt)
        # crossing: sin(theta1) changes sign from - to + while the rod points down (cos theta1 > 0)
        before, after = np.sin(q[0]), np.sin(q_new[0])
        crossed = (before < 0) & (after >= 0) & (np.cos(q_new[0]) > 0)
        if crossed.any():
            frac = before[crossed] / (before[crossed] - after[crossed])        # linear interpolation in time
            th2 = q[1, crossed] + frac * (q_new[1, crossed] - q[1, crossed])
            w2 = w[1, crossed] + frac * (w_new[1, crossed] - w[1, crossed])
            th2 = np.arctan2(np.sin(th2), np.cos(th2))                       # wrap the angle to (-pi, pi]
            points += list(zip(np.nonzero(crossed)[0], th2, w2))
        q, w = q_new, w_new
    dE = np.abs(energy_dp(q, w) - E_target).reshape(len(energies), n_traj).max(axis=1)
    return np.array(points), dE

print("minimum energy (both rods hanging down):", -3 * 9.81)


minimum energy (both rods hanging down): -29.43


Section versus projection, for a single trajectory. Before computing many trajectories, the difference between a projection and a section is shown for one regular trajectory (\(E = -25\)) and one chaotic trajectory (\(E = 0\)), integrated together as a batch of two for 80 s with \(\Delta t = 10^{-2}\) s. Left: the whole trajectory projected onto the plane \((\theta_2, \dot\theta_2)\) (thin line), with the crossings of the section \(\theta_1 = 0\), \(\dot\theta_1 > 0\) marked as dots. Right: the crossings alone, which is the Poincaré section of this trajectory. seed=1 only selects which random initial condition is shown.


Code
def single_trajectories_and_crossings(energies, T=80.0, dt=1e-2, seed=1):
    # one trajectory per energy, started on the section; returns the full paths and the section points of each
    s0 = np.hstack([initial_conditions_on_section(E, 1, np.random.default_rng(seed)) for E in energies])
    q, w = s0[:2].copy(), s0[2:].copy()                         # shapes (2, number of energies)
    path, crossings = [np.vstack([q, w])], [[] for _ in energies]
    for _ in range(int(round(T / dt))):
        q_new, w_new = rk4_step(accel_dp, q, w, dt)
        before, after = np.sin(q[0]), np.sin(q_new[0])
        for j in np.nonzero((before < 0) & (after >= 0) & (np.cos(q_new[0]) > 0))[0]:   # same condition as above
            frac = before[j] / (before[j] - after[j])
            crossings[j].append([q[1, j] + frac * (q_new[1, j] - q[1, j]), w[1, j] + frac * (w_new[1, j] - w[1, j])])
        q, w = q_new, w_new
        path.append(np.vstack([q, w]))
    return np.array(path), [np.array(c) for c in crossings]         # path: (steps, 4, number of energies)

paths, crossings = single_trajectories_and_crossings([-25.0, 0.0])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 9))
for row, E in enumerate([-25.0, 0.0]):
    path, cross = paths[:, :, row], crossings[row]
    th2 = np.arctan2(np.sin(path[:, 1]), np.cos(path[:, 1]))        # theta2 wrapped to (-pi, pi]
    th2[1:][np.abs(np.diff(th2)) > np.pi] = np.nan                   # break the line where the angle jumps by 2 pi
    axes[row, 0].plot(th2, path[:, 3], color="0.75", lw=0.4)
    axes[row, 0].plot(np.arctan2(np.sin(cross[:, 0]), np.cos(cross[:, 0])), cross[:, 1], "o", color="C3", ms=3)
    axes[row, 0].set_title(f"E = {E:g}: projection of the whole trajectory (grey) and section points (red)", fontsize=9)
    axes[row, 1].plot(np.arctan2(np.sin(cross[:, 0]), np.cos(cross[:, 0])), cross[:, 1], "o", color="C3", ms=3)
    axes[row, 1].set_title(f"E = {E:g}: Poincaré section only ({len(cross)} points)", fontsize=9)
    for ax in axes[row]:
        ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta_2$ [rad]"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\dot\theta_2$ [rad/s]")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





In the projection (left) the trajectory crosses itself everywhere, although in the 4D phase space it never does: the projection discards two coordinates. The section (right) keeps only the moments at which the state passes through the same surface, and there the structure is clear: for the regular trajectory the points line up on a closed curve (the cut through the torus on which the motion takes place), for the chaotic trajectory they scatter over an area. Each point of the section determines the next one (the Poincaré map), so the section is a 2D picture of the dynamics, not of a single moment.
Four energies, from slightly above the minimum \(E_{\min} = -3g \approx -29.4\) to \(E = 0\). For orientation: released from rest with \(\theta_1 = \theta_2 = \alpha\), the pendulum has \(E = -3g\cos\alpha\), so \(E = -25, -15, -10, 0\) correspond to \(\alpha \approx 32^\circ, 59^\circ, 70^\circ, 90^\circ\) (both rods horizontal at \(E = 0\)). The values were picked to show the regular, mixed and chaotic regimes; nearby values show the same picture. Each panel: 30 trajectories, 100 s each, one colour per trajectory (colours repeat after 20).


Code
energies = [-25.0, -15.0, -10.0, 0.0]
n_traj = 30
t0 = time.perf_counter()
pts, dE = poincare_sections(energies, n_traj=n_traj)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(20, 5))
for k, (ax, E) in enumerate(zip(axes, energies)):
    mine = (pts[:, 0] >= k * n_traj) & (pts[:, 0] < (k + 1) * n_traj)        # columns that belong to energy k
    ax.scatter(pts[mine, 1], pts[mine, 2], c=pts[mine, 0] % 20, cmap="tab20", vmin=0, vmax=19, s=1.0)
    ax.set_title(f"E = {E:g}   (energy error {dE[k]:.0e})", fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta_2$ [rad]"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\dot\theta_2$ [rad/s]")
fig.suptitle(r"Poincaré sections of the double pendulum: $\theta_1 = 0$, $\dot\theta_1 > 0$", y=1.02)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"computed in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")





computed in 5 s


Interpretation. - \(E = -25\) (small oscillations): every trajectory draws a closed curve or a chain of small islands — the motion is regular. Near the minimum the double pendulum is close to two coupled harmonic oscillators (Exercise 2). - \(E = -15\): closed curves and chains of small islands coexist with regions of scattered points — mixed phase space. - \(E = -10\): most of the section is a chaotic sea; a few islands of regular motion survive. - \(E = 0\): almost all initial conditions are chaotic.
How to read the panels: points of one colour belong to one trajectory (with 30 trajectories and 20 colours, two trajectories share a colour). A regular trajectory puts all its points on one curve, a chaotic one scatters them. The points fill a region whose outer edge is the edge of the energetically allowed part of \(\Sigma\). It is not symmetric under \(\dot\theta_2 \to -\dot\theta_2\) because of the condition \(\dot\theta_1 > 0\): from the quadratic equation above, at \(\theta_2 = 0\) and \(E = -25\) the allowed range is \(-4.2 < \dot\theta_2 < 3.0\) rad/s, in agreement with the vertical extent of the points in the first panel.
The gradual break-up of the invariant curves with growing perturbation is described by the Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser (KAM) theorem.

title: Lab 005: The N-link pendulum with SymPy and automatic differentiation
text:
9. A 5-link chain with autodiff only
For \(N = 5\) we skip SymPy: the accelerations come from the Lagrangian alone, by autodiff. We integrate 20 chains at once: all released horizontally (\(\theta_i = 90^\circ\)), with the first angle shifted by \(k\cdot 10^{-4}\) rad, \(k=0,\dots,19\).
accel_from_lagrangian of Section 5 is written for one state: one Hessian and one linear solve. vmap turns it into a function that processes a whole batch along the first axis, without rewriting it. This is exact but slow: every call of the torch.func transformations carries a fixed overhead of of order 10 ms (about 8 ms in the run of Section 5), and RK4 needs four calls per step, i.e. thousands of calls for one simulation. For long simulations we therefore write a second, batched version, accel_batch, with torch.autograd.grad, which computes the same quantities with fewer and cheaper passes: - The chains are independent, so the gradient of the sum of their Lagrangians with respect to q (shape (B, N)) contains \(\partial L_b/\partial q\) for every chain \(b\) at once; the same holds for qd. lagrangian_chain sums over the last axis, so it already returns the \(B\) Lagrangians of a batch. - create_graph=True keeps the computational graph of these first derivatives, so that they can be differentiated once more. - Differentiating \(\sum_b \partial L_b/\partial\dot q_{b,i}\) with respect to qd and q gives row \(i\) of \(M\) and row \(i\) of \(C\) for all chains; \(N\) such passes give the whole matrices. retain_graph=True keeps the graph alive between the passes. - .detach() returns the result without the graph, as plain numbers.
The first cell checks that both versions agree and compares their cost.


Code
N_chain, n_copies = 5, 20
m_c, l_c, g_c = torch.ones(N_chain), torch.full((N_chain,), 0.4), 9.81
L_chain = lambda q, qd: lagrangian_chain(q, qd, m_c, l_c, g_c)

def accel_batch(L, q, qd):
    """Accelerations of B independent systems; q and qd have shape (B, N), L(q, qd) returns the B Lagrangians."""
    q = q.detach().requires_grad_(True)
    qd = qd.detach().requires_grad_(True)
    dL_dq, dL_dqd = torch.autograd.grad(L(q, qd).sum(), (q, qd), create_graph=True)
    M_rows, C_qd = [], []
    for i in range(q.shape[1]):
        # row i of M and of C, for all chains at once: derivatives of dL/dqd_i with respect to qd and q
        d_q, d_qd = torch.autograd.grad(dL_dqd[:, i].sum(), (q, qd), retain_graph=True)
        M_rows.append(d_qd)
        C_qd.append((d_q * qd).sum(dim=1))                  # (C qd)_i for every chain
    M, C_qd = torch.stack(M_rows, dim=1), torch.stack(C_qd, dim=1)       # shapes (B, N, N) and (B, N)
    return torch.linalg.solve(M, dL_dq - C_qd).detach()

# the torch.func version of Section 5, applied to a batch with vmap
accel_vmap = vmap(lambda q, qd: accel_from_lagrangian(L_chain, q, qd))

torch.manual_seed(0)
q_test, qd_test = 3 * torch.rand(n_copies, N_chain), torch.randn(n_copies, N_chain)     # random test states
print(f"max |accel_vmap - accel_batch| = {(accel_vmap(q_test, qd_test) - accel_batch(L_chain, q_test, qd_test)).abs().max():.1e}")
for name, f in [("vmap(accel_from_lagrangian)", lambda: accel_vmap(q_test, qd_test)),
                ("accel_batch", lambda: accel_batch(L_chain, q_test, qd_test))]:
    f()                                                     # warm-up call
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(10):
        f()
    print(f"{name:28s}: {1e3 * (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 10:.1f} ms per call for {n_copies} chains")


max |accel_vmap - accel_batch| = 3.6e-14
vmap(accel_from_lagrangian) : 9.7 ms per call for 20 chains
accel_batch                 : 1.4 ms per call for 20 chains


The simulation uses accel_batch. Choices: with \(l_i = 0.4\) the chain has total length 2, the same as the double pendulum with \(l = 1\), so the pictures have the same scale. The step \(\Delta t = 8\cdot10^{-3}\) s resolves the time scale \(\sqrt{l/g} \approx 0.2\) s with 25 steps and keeps the cell at a few seconds. The energy error at the end is printed; the chains start horizontally, where \(E = 0\), so it is an absolute error, to be compared with the potential energy, which changes by up to about 60 during the motion. Halving the step reduces the error about 20 times (with twice the run time). \(T = 6\) s is long enough for the chains to separate. energy_chain also sums over the last axis, so it accepts the whole batch.


Code
def accel_chain(q, w):
    """NumPy wrapper with the (N, B) layout used by rk4_step (accel_batch uses (B, N), hence the transposes .T)."""
    return accel_batch(L_chain, torch.tensor(q.T), torch.tensor(w.T)).numpy().T

q = np.full((N_chain, n_copies), np.pi / 2)
q[0] += 1e-4 * np.arange(n_copies)                       # small differences in the first angle
w = np.zeros((N_chain, n_copies))
E_start = energy_chain(torch.tensor(q.T), torch.tensor(w.T), m_c, l_c, g_c).numpy()

dt, T_end = 8e-3, 6.0
n_steps = int(round(T_end / dt))
snapshot_steps = [int(round(t / dt)) for t in (0, 2, 4, 6)]     # store the configuration at t = 0, 2, 4, 6 s
snapshots, frames_chain0 = {}, []
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for step in range(n_steps + 1):
    if step in snapshot_steps:
        snapshots[step * dt] = q.copy()
    if step % 10 == 0:                                       # every 0.08 s: angles of chain 0, for the animation
        frames_chain0.append(q[:, 0].copy())
    if step < n_steps:
        q, w = rk4_step(accel_chain, q, w, dt)
E_end = energy_chain(torch.tensor(q.T), torch.tensor(w.T), m_c, l_c, g_c).numpy()
print(f"integration took {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s;  max energy error: {np.max(np.abs(E_end - E_start)):.1e}")


integration took 5 s;  max energy error: 2.8e-02

title: Lab 005: The N-link pendulum with SymPy and automatic differentiation
text:
10. Summary

SymPy: symbols, simplify, diff, solve, Matrix, dsolve, lambdify. Exact formulas, but expressions and derivation time grow quickly with system size.
Lagrangian mechanics: \(L = T - V\) in generalised coordinates, Euler–Lagrange equations; for the \(N\)-link pendulum they take the form \(M(q)\ddot q = F(q,\dot q)\).
Autodiff: \(\ddot q = M^{-1}\big(\nabla_q L - (\nabla_q\nabla_{\dot q}L)\dot q\big)\) with \(M = \nabla_{\dot q}\nabla_{\dot q} L\) — only \(L\) has to be written. Agreement with SymPy to \(10^{-13}\).
Numerics: RK4 with error \(\propto\Delta t^4\); energy conservation as a test.
Dynamics: exponential separation of nearby trajectories (Lyapunov exponent); Poincaré sections show the transition from regular to chaotic motion with growing energy.

title: Lab 005: The N-link pendulum with SymPy and automatic differentiation
text:
11. Exercises (with solutions)

Exercise 1 — The elastic pendulum
Replace the rigid rod of the single pendulum by a spring of stiffness \(k\) and rest length \(l_0\). The generalised coordinates are the length \(r\) and the angle \(\varphi\): \[L = \tfrac12 m\big(\dot r^2 + r^2\dot\varphi^2\big) + m g\, r\cos\varphi - \tfrac12 k\,(r - l_0)^2 .\] 1. Derive the two Euler–Lagrange equations with SymPy and solve them for \(\ddot r\) and \(\ddot\varphi\). 2. Write the same Lagrangian as a PyTorch function of q = (r, phi), qd = (r_dot, phi_dot) and check that accel_from_lagrangian gives the same accelerations at a few random states. 3. Simulate \(m=1\), \(k=40\), \(l_0=1\), \(g=9.81\) from \(r = 1.2\), \(\varphi = 0.6\), at rest, for 20 s (\(\Delta t = 2\cdot10^{-3}\) s) with the SymPy accelerations. Plot the path of the mass in the \((x, y)\) plane and check energy conservation.
The parameters are arbitrary. With \(k = 40\) the spring oscillates with \(\sqrt{k/m} \approx 6.3\) rad/s, and the pendulum, whose length at equilibrium is \(l_0 + mg/k \approx 1.25\), with \(\sqrt{g/1.25} \approx 2.8\) rad/s; the two motions have comparable frequencies and are coupled, so the mass does not move on a simple arc but traces loops.
In the solution, sp.solve(equations, unknowns, dict=True) returns a list of dictionaries {unknown: value}, one per solution; [0] takes the only one.

Solution


Code
# 1) SymPy derivation
t = sp.symbols("t", real=True)
m, g, k, l0 = sp.symbols("m g k l_0", positive=True)
r = sp.Function("r")(t); phi = sp.Function("varphi")(t)
L_el = (sp.Rational(1, 2) * m * (sp.diff(r, t)**2 + r**2 * sp.diff(phi, t)**2)
        + m * g * r * sp.cos(phi) - sp.Rational(1, 2) * k * (r - l0)**2)
EL = [sp.diff(sp.diff(L_el, sp.diff(c, t)), t) - sp.diff(L_el, c) for c in (r, phi)]
sol = sp.solve(EL, [sp.diff(r, t, 2), sp.diff(phi, t, 2)], dict=True)[0]
r_dd, phi_dd = sp.simplify(sol[sp.diff(r, t, 2)]), sp.simplify(sol[sp.diff(phi, t, 2)])
show(r"\ddot r = ", r_dd)
show(r"\ddot\varphi = ", phi_dd)

# replace functions by plain symbols, then lambdify with the parameters fixed
R, P, Rd, Pd = sp.symbols("R P R_d P_d")
to_plain = lambda e: e.subs({sp.diff(r, t): Rd, sp.diff(phi, t): Pd}).subs({r: R, phi: P})
par = {m: 1.0, g: 9.81, k: 40.0, l0: 1.0}
acc_r = sp.lambdify((R, P, Rd, Pd), to_plain(r_dd).subs(par), "numpy")
acc_p = sp.lambdify((R, P, Rd, Pd), to_plain(phi_dd).subs(par), "numpy")
def accel_elastic(q, w):
    return np.array([acc_r(q[0], q[1], w[0], w[1]), acc_p(q[0], q[1], w[0], w[1])])

# 2) the same Lagrangian for autodiff (r = q[0], phi = q[1])
def L_elastic_torch(q, qd, m=1.0, g=9.81, k=40.0, l0=1.0):
    return 0.5 * m * (qd[0]**2 + q[0]**2 * qd[1]**2) + m * g * q[0] * torch.cos(q[1]) - 0.5 * k * (q[0] - l0)**2

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
for _ in range(3):
    q = np.array([rng.uniform(0.5, 1.5), rng.uniform(-1, 1)]); w = rng.uniform(-2, 2, 2)
    a_ad = accel_from_lagrangian(L_elastic_torch, torch.tensor(q), torch.tensor(w)).numpy()
    print("SymPy:", accel_elastic(q, w), "  autodiff:", a_ad)

# 3) simulation and energy check
t_arr, Q, W = simulate(accel_elastic, [1.2, 0.6], [0.0, 0.0], T=20.0, dt=2e-3)
E = 0.5 * (W[:, 0]**2 + Q[:, 0]**2 * W[:, 1]**2) - 9.81 * Q[:, 0] * np.cos(Q[:, 1]) + 0.5 * 40 * (Q[:, 0] - 1)**2
print(f"relative energy drift: {np.max(np.abs(E - E[0])) / abs(E[0]):.1e}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))
ax.plot(Q[:, 0] * np.sin(Q[:, 1]), -Q[:, 0] * np.cos(Q[:, 1]), lw=0.6)
ax.plot(0, 0, "ks"); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$")
ax.set_title("elastic pendulum: path of the mass"); plt.show()


\(\displaystyle \ddot r = \frac{k l_{0} - k r{\left(t \right)} + m \left(g \cos{\left(\varphi{\left(t \right)} \right)} + r{\left(t \right)} \left(\frac{d}{d t} \varphi{\left(t \right)}\right)^{2}\right)}{m}\)


\(\displaystyle \ddot\varphi = - \frac{g \sin{\left(\varphi{\left(t \right)} \right)} + 2 \frac{d}{d t} r{\left(t \right)} \frac{d}{d t} \varphi{\left(t \right)}}{r{\left(t \right)}}\)


SymPy: [ 8.87665341 -2.55120653]   autodiff: [ 8.87665341 -2.55120653]
SymPy: [17.32871922  3.01864123]   autodiff: [17.32871922  3.01864123]
SymPy: [3.78776318 7.27982747]   autodiff: [3.78776318 7.27982747]


relative energy drift: 2.2e-11








Exercise 2 — Normal modes of the N-link pendulum
For small oscillations around \(q = 0\) the Lagrangian is quadratic, \(L \approx \tfrac12\dot q^{\top} M_0\,\dot q - \tfrac12 q^{\top} K q\) with \(M_0 = \partial^2 L/\partial\dot q\,\partial\dot q\,\big|_{0}\) and \(K = -\partial^2 L/\partial q\,\partial q\,\big|_{0}\). The Euler–Lagrange equations of this quadratic Lagrangian are linear, \(M_0\ddot q = -K q\). Inserting the ansatz \(q(t) = v\cos\omega t\) (all angles oscillate with one frequency and fixed amplitude ratios \(v\)) gives \(-\omega^2 M_0 v\cos\omega t = -K v\cos\omega t\), so the normal modes solve the generalised eigenvalue problem \(K v = \omega^2 M_0 v\). 1. For \(N=2\), \(m_1=m_2=m\), \(l_1=l_2=l\): compute \(M_0\) and \(K\) with SymPy (from dp["M"] and the energy) and show that \(\omega^2 = \frac{g}{l}(2\mp\sqrt2)\). 2. Compute \(M_0\) and \(K\) by autodiff (hessian of lagrangian_chain) for \(N = 2\) and check the numbers; then for \(N = 5\) (\(m_i = 1\), \(l_i = 0.4\)) compute all frequencies with scipy.linalg.eigh(K, M0) and draw the five mode shapes. scipy.linalg.eigh(K, M0) solves the generalised eigenvalue problem \(K v = \omega^2 M_0 v\) for a symmetric \(K\) and a positive-definite \(M_0\); it returns the values \(\omega^2\) in increasing order and the vectors \(v\) as the columns of a matrix. In SymPy, sp.hessian(V, q) builds the matrix of second derivatives \(\partial^2 V/\partial q_i\,\partial q_j\). 3. Start the double pendulum (\(m=l=1\)) at rest in the slow mode with amplitude \(0.01\) rad. Check by simulation that the ratio \(\theta_2/\theta_1\) stays constant and that the period is \(2\pi/\omega_1\).

Solution


Code
import scipy.linalg

# 1) SymPy, N = 2 with equal masses and lengths
msym, lsym = sp.symbols("m l", positive=True)
eq_par = {dp["m"][0]: msym, dp["m"][1]: msym, dp["l"][0]: lsym, dp["l"][1]: lsym}
zero = {qq: 0 for qq in dp["q"]}
M0_sym = dp["M"].subs(eq_par).subs(zero)
V_sym = dp["E"].subs({ww: 0 for ww in dp["w"]}).subs(eq_par)            # energy at rest = potential energy
K_sym = sp.hessian(V_sym, dp["q"]).subs(zero)                           # K = d^2 V / dq dq at q = 0
show(r"M_0 = ", M0_sym, r",\quad K = ", K_sym)
omega2 = sp.Symbol("omega^2")
roots = sp.solve(sp.det(K_sym - omega2 * M0_sym), omega2)              # det(K - w^2 M0) = 0
show(r"\omega^2 = ", [sp.simplify(rt) for rt in roots])

# 2) autodiff: M0 = d^2L/dqd dqd, K = -d^2L/dq dq, both at q = qd = 0
def M0_K(N, m_vals, l_vals, g=9.81):
    L = lambda q, qd: lagrangian_chain(q, qd, torch.tensor(m_vals), torch.tensor(l_vals), g)
    z = torch.zeros(N)
    return hessian(L, argnums=1)(z, z).numpy(), -hessian(L, argnums=0)(z, z).numpy()

M0, K = M0_K(2, [1.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0])
omega_sq2, modes2 = scipy.linalg.eigh(K, M0)                              # generalised eigenproblem: omega^2 and modes
print("autodiff N=2: omega^2 =", omega_sq2, "  exact:", 9.81 * (2 - np.sqrt(2)), 9.81 * (2 + np.sqrt(2)))

M0, K = M0_K(5, [1.0] * 5, [0.4] * 5)
omega_sq5, modes5 = scipy.linalg.eigh(K, M0)
print("N=5 frequencies omega [rad/s]:", np.sqrt(omega_sq5).round(3))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(16, 4), sharey=True)
for j, ax in enumerate(axes):
    v = modes5[:, j] / np.max(np.abs(modes5[:, j])) * 0.3                # small angles, scaled for display
    X = np.r_[0, np.cumsum(0.4 * np.sin(v))]; Y = np.r_[0, -np.cumsum(0.4 * np.cos(v))]
    ax.plot(X, Y, "-o"); ax.plot(0, 0, "ks"); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 0.6)
    ax.set_title(rf"mode {j+1}, $\omega$ = {np.sqrt(omega_sq5[j]):.2f} rad/s")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Exercise 3 — The largest Lyapunov exponent
The fit in Section 7 is rough. A standard method (Benettin et al., 1980): follow a reference trajectory \(A\) and a neighbour \(B\) at distance \(d_0 = 10^{-8}\); after every interval \(\tau\) measure their distance \(d\), add \(\ln(d/d_0)\) to a running sum, and move \(B\) back to distance \(d_0\) along the line joining it with \(A\). Then \(\lambda \approx \frac{1}{T}\sum \ln(d/d_0)\) for total time \(T\). The resetting keeps the separation small, so that it always grows at the exponential rate and never saturates. \(d_0\) must be small enough that the separation stays in this linear regime during one interval, yet far above the rounding level \(10^{-16}\); \(\tau\) must be short enough that \(d\) grows only by a modest factor within it (\(e^{\lambda\tau} \approx 1.1\) for \(\lambda \approx 1\) s\(^{-1}\) and \(\tau = 0.1\) s). For this system, \(d_0\) between \(10^{-9}\) and \(10^{-7}\) and \(\tau\) between \(0.05\) and \(1\) s give the same \(\lambda\) to three digits (checked for release from rest at \(\theta_1=\theta_2=\alpha\) with \(\alpha = 90^\circ\) and \(130^\circ\)). 1. Implement the method for the double pendulum (\(m = l = 1\)) with \(\tau = 0.1\) s, \(T = 50\) s, \(\Delta t = 10^{-2}\) s. (These values keep the run at a few seconds; \(T = 200\) s and \(\Delta t = 5\cdot10^{-3}\) s give better converged estimates.) 2. Start from rest with \(\theta_1 = \theta_2 = \alpha\) for \(\alpha = 10^\circ, 30^\circ, \dots, 150^\circ\) and plot \(\lambda(\alpha)\). Integrate all angles as one batch. 3. Where does chaos set in? Compare with the Poincaré sections (compute the energy for each \(\alpha\)).

Solution


Code
alphas = np.deg2rad(np.arange(10, 151, 20))
n = alphas.size
d0, tau, T_total, dt = 1e-8, 0.1, 50.0, 1e-2
steps_per_tau = int(round(tau / dt))

# reference trajectories A and perturbed trajectories B, all in one batch of 2n states
qA = np.vstack([alphas, alphas]); wA = np.zeros((2, n))
qB = qA + np.array([[d0], [0.0]]);  wB = wA.copy()
q = np.hstack([qA, qB]); w = np.hstack([wA, wB])          # shape (2, 2n): columns 0..n-1 = A, n..2n-1 = B

log_sum = np.zeros(n)
for _ in range(int(T_total / tau)):
    for _ in range(steps_per_tau):
        q, w = rk4_step(accel_dp, q, w, dt)
    # distance between A and B in the 4D phase space
    dq, dw = q[:, n:] - q[:, :n], w[:, n:] - w[:, :n]
    d = np.sqrt(np.sum(dq**2 + dw**2, axis=0))
    log_sum += np.log(d / d0)
    # renormalise: put B back at distance d0 from A, in the same direction
    q[:, n:] = q[:, :n] + dq * d0 / d
    w[:, n:] = w[:, :n] + dw * d0 / d
lyap = log_sum / T_total

E_alpha = energy_dp(np.vstack([alphas, alphas]), np.zeros((2, n)))
for a, E, lam in zip(np.rad2deg(alphas), E_alpha, lyap):
    print(f"alpha = {a:5.0f} deg   E = {E:7.2f}   lambda = {lam:.3f} 1/s")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.plot(np.rad2deg(alphas), lyap, "o-")
ax.set_xlabel(r"initial angle $\alpha$ [deg]"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\lambda$ [1/s]")
plt.show()

# between 70 and 90 deg. Small non-zero values do not prove chaos: for regular motion the finite-time estimate

# depends on the initial condition, not only on the energy.

Exercise 4 (advanced) — A pendulum made of rigid rods
Replace the point masses by uniform rigid rods of mass \(m_k\) and length \(l_k\) (no point masses). The kinetic energy of rod \(k\) is the energy of its centre of mass plus the rotational energy about it: \[T_k = \tfrac12 m_k |\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm},k}|^2 + \tfrac12\,\frac{m_k l_k^2}{12}\,\dot\theta_k^2,\qquad
\mathbf r_{\mathrm{cm},k} = \mathbf r_{\mathrm{joint},k-1} + \tfrac12 l_k(\sin\theta_k, -\cos\theta_k),\] and \(V = g\sum_k m_k y_{\mathrm{cm},k}\). 1. Write lagrangian_rods(q, qd, m, l, g) in PyTorch (hint: the velocity of joint \(k-1\) is the cumulative sum up to \(k\) minus the term of rod \(k\)). 2. For one rod the exact equation is \(\ddot\theta = -\frac{3g}{2l}\sin\theta\). Check accel_from_lagrangian against it at random states. (Derivation: \(m l^2/12\) is the moment of inertia of a uniform rod about its centre; about the pivot it is \(m l^2/12 + m (l/2)^2 = m l^2/3\) by the parallel-axis theorem. The gravitational torque is \(-m g\,(l/2)\sin\theta\), and \(\tfrac{m l^2}{3}\ddot\theta = -\tfrac{m g l}{2}\sin\theta\).) 3. Simulate a double rod pendulum (\(m_k = 1\), \(l_k = 1\)) from \(\theta_1 = \theta_2 = 90^\circ\) at rest for 3 s (\(\Delta t = 10^{-2}\) s) with autodiff accelerations (accel_batch of Section 9, with a batch of one), and check energy conservation. Nothing except the Lagrangian has to be changed. Writing all sums over the last axis (dim=-1) makes the functions work for single states and for batches.

Solution


Code
def rod_kinematics(q, qd, l):
    """Centre-of-mass positions and velocities of a chain of uniform rods."""
    # joint velocities: cumulative sums over the last axis, as for the point-mass chain
    jvx = torch.cumsum(l * torch.cos(q) * qd, dim=-1)
    jvy = torch.cumsum(l * torch.sin(q) * qd, dim=-1)
    jy = -torch.cumsum(l * torch.cos(q), dim=-1)
    # velocity/position of the joint ABOVE rod k = cumulative sum minus the term of rod k itself
    prev_vx = jvx - l * torch.cos(q) * qd
    prev_vy = jvy - l * torch.sin(q) * qd
    prev_y = jy + l * torch.cos(q)
    # centre of mass: half-way along rod k
    vcx = prev_vx + 0.5 * l * torch.cos(q) * qd
    vcy = prev_vy + 0.5 * l * torch.sin(q) * qd
    ycm = prev_y - 0.5 * l * torch.cos(q)
    return vcx, vcy, ycm

def lagrangian_rods(q, qd, m, l, g):
    vcx, vcy, ycm = rod_kinematics(q, qd, l)
    T = 0.5 * torch.sum(m * (vcx**2 + vcy**2), dim=-1) + 0.5 * torch.sum(m * l**2 / 12 * qd**2, dim=-1)
    V = g * torch.sum(m * ycm, dim=-1)
    return T - V

def energy_rods(q, qd, m, l, g):
    vcx, vcy, ycm = rod_kinematics(q, qd, l)
    return (0.5 * torch.sum(m * (vcx**2 + vcy**2), dim=-1) + 0.5 * torch.sum(m * l**2 / 12 * qd**2, dim=-1)
            + g * torch.sum(m * ycm, dim=-1))

# 2) single rod: compare with the exact theta'' = -(3g/2l) sin(theta)
m1t, l1t = torch.tensor([1.0]), torch.tensor([0.7])
L1 = lambda q, qd: lagrangian_rods(q, qd, m1t, l1t, 9.81)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
err = 0.0
for _ in range(20):
    th, om = rng.uniform(-np.pi, np.pi), rng.uniform(-5, 5)
    a = accel_from_lagrangian(L1, torch.tensor([th]), torch.tensor([om])).item()
    err = max(err, abs(a - (-1.5 * 9.81 / 0.7 * np.sin(th))))
print(f"single rod: max |autodiff - exact| = {err:.1e}")

# 3) double rod pendulum with autodiff accelerations only
m2t, l2t = torch.ones(2), torch.ones(2)
L2 = lambda q, qd: lagrangian_rods(q, qd, m2t, l2t, 9.81)
def accel_rods(q, w):
    # one state of shape (N,) -> a batch of one, shape (1, N), for accel_batch, and back
    return accel_batch(L2, torch.tensor(q)[None], torch.tensor(w)[None])[0].numpy()

t0 = time.perf_counter()
t_arr, Q, W = simulate(accel_rods, [np.pi / 2, np.pi / 2], [0.0, 0.0], T=3.0, dt=1e-2)
E = energy_rods(torch.tensor(Q), torch.tensor(W), m2t, l2t, 9.81).numpy()       # all time steps at once (batch)
print(f"simulated in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s;  max |E(t) - E(0)| = {np.max(np.abs(E - E[0])):.1e}  (E(0) = {E[0]:.3f})")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.5))
ax.plot(t_arr, Q[:, 0], label=r"$\theta_1$"); ax.plot(t_arr, Q[:, 1], label=r"$\theta_2$")

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
1. Target function and dataset
We use the example from the Lecture Notes, \[g(x) = x^2\sin(\pi x) - \frac{1}{2+\cos x}, \qquad x\in[-2, 2],\] and a training set \(\mathcal D = \{(x_k, g(x_k))\}_{k=1}^{K}\) of \(K=100\) points \(x_k\) drawn at random (uniformly) from the interval. We deliberately do not use an equally spaced grid: in real experiments and simulations the sampling points are rarely regular, and a fit should be judged on how well it reproduces \(g\) between the sampling points. Therefore all fits are plotted on a separate dense grid x_plot.
Why \(K = 100\): the networks below have a few tens of parameters (30 for \(N = 10\)), and the number of data points should be several times larger than the number of parameters, otherwise the data do not determine the fit. Any \(K\) of order 100 serves the purpose. The seed 2026 of the random generator fixes the points, so that every run of the notebook gives the same numbers; its value is arbitrary (the same holds for all other seeds in this notebook).


Code
def g(x):
    """Target function from the Lecture Notes (Chapter 2)."""
    return x**2 * np.sin(np.pi * x) - 1.0 / (2.0 + np.cos(x))

K = 100
rng_data = np.random.default_rng(2026)
x_train = np.sort(rng_data.uniform(-2, 2, K))     # random, non-equidistant sampling points (sorted for convenience)
y_train = g(x_train)
x_plot = np.linspace(-2, 2, 1000)                 # dense grid, used only for plotting and for judging fits

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.plot(x_plot, g(x_plot), "k", lw=2, label="$g(x)$")
ax.plot(x_train, y_train, "o", color="C3", ms=4, label=f"{K} random sampling points")
ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$"); ax.legend()
plt.show()

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
2. Building blocks

2.1 One neuron
A single hidden neuron contributes \(W^{(2)}\tanh(W^{(1)}x + b)\). The weight \(W^{(1)}\) sets the steepness, the ratio \(-b/W^{(1)}\) sets the position of the step, and \(W^{(2)}\) sets its height.
In the plotting code the labels are f-strings that contain LaTeX. Inside an f-string single braces {w} insert the value of a variable, so a literal brace, needed for the LaTeX superscript W^{(1)}, is written twice: f"$W^{{(1)}} = {w}$" produces the text $W^{(1)} = 0.5$.


Code
x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 400)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8))
for w in [0.5, 1, 3, 10]:
    axes[0].plot(x, np.tanh(w * x), label=f"$W^{{(1)}} = {w}$")
for b in [-2, 0, 2]:
    axes[1].plot(x, np.tanh(3 * x + b), label=f"$b = {b}$  (step at $x = {-b/3:.2f}$)")
axes[0].set_title(r"$\tanh(W^{(1)} x)$: steepness"); axes[1].set_title(r"$\tanh(3x + b)$: position")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()







2.2 Two neurons make a bump
The difference of two shifted steps is a localised bump: \(\tfrac12\big[\tanh(s(x - a)) - \tanh(s(x - c))\big] \approx 1\) for \(a < x < c\) and \(\approx 0\) elsewhere. A sum of such bumps with suitable heights can follow any continuous curve — this is the intuition behind the UAT. Each \(\tanh\) goes from \(-1\) to \(+1\), i.e. changes by 2 across its step; the difference of two steps therefore has height 2, and the factor \(\tfrac12\) normalises the bump to height 1. The values \(s = 8\), \(a = -0.5\), \(c = 1\) below are arbitrary illustration values.


Code
s, a, c = 8.0, -0.5, 1.0
step1, step2 = np.tanh(s * (x - a)), np.tanh(s * (x - c))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
ax.plot(x, step1, "--", label=r"$\tanh(s(x-a))$")
ax.plot(x, -step2, "--", label=r"$-\tanh(s(x-c))$")
ax.plot(x, 0.5 * (step1 - step2), "k", lw=2.5, label="half of the sum: a bump on $[a, c]$")
ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.show()

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
3. A constructive approximation (no optimisation)
Divide \([-2,2]\) into \(N\) intervals with nodes \(x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_N\). A staircase that jumps by \(g(x_j) - g(x_{j-1})\) at the midpoint \(m_j\) of each interval is \[f_N(x) = g(x_0) + \sum_{j=1}^{N}\big[g(x_j) - g(x_{j-1})\big]\;\frac{1 + \tanh\big(s\,(x - m_j)\big)}{2}.\] The function \(\tfrac12\big(1+\tanh(s(x-m_j))\big)\) is a smooth step that goes from 0 (for \(x \ll m_j\)) to 1 (for \(x \gg m_j\)), so each term adds the jump \(g(x_j)-g(x_{j-1})\) once \(x\) has passed \(m_j\). This is a one-hidden-layer network with \(N\) neurons (plus a constant). We chose all parameters by hand: \(W^{(1)}_j = s\), \(b_j = -s m_j\), \(W^{(2)}_j = [g(x_j)-g(x_{j-1})]/2\). The factor \(\tfrac12\) in \(W^{(2)}_j\) comes from \(\tfrac12(1+\tanh z) = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12\tanh z\): each term is half a jump times \(\tanh\), plus half a jump as a constant. All these constants add up to the constant of the network, \(g(x_0) + \tfrac12\sum_j[g(x_j)-g(x_{j-1})] = \tfrac12[g(x_0)+g(x_N)]\). As \(N\to\infty\) (with \(s\) growing so that steps stay sharp) the error goes to zero — a constructive version of the theorem.
Two details of the code: - Steepness. The intervals have width \(h = 4/N\), and we take \(s = 4N\), so \(s\,h = 16\): each step rises from 0 to 1 within a small fraction of its interval, and the network is a genuine staircase. The factor 4 is arbitrary. Smaller factors make neighbouring steps overlap; the sum then becomes a smoother interpolation and is in fact somewhat more accurate (with factor 1 the error for \(N \ge 64\) is about 2.5 times smaller), but the sharp version shows the construction better. - Broadcasting. Indexing with None adds an axis of length 1: x[:, None] is a column of shape \((K, 1)\) and mids[None, :] a row of shape \((1, N)\). Their difference is broadcast to a \((K, N)\) table whose entry \((k, j)\) is \(x_k - m_j\), i.e. neuron \(j\) evaluated at point \(k\). The product hidden @ jumps then sums over the neurons.


Code
def staircase(x, N, steepness_factor=4.0):
    """Hand-built one-hidden-layer tanh network approximating g with N neurons."""
    nodes = np.linspace(-2, 2, N + 1)
    mids = 0.5 * (nodes[1:] + nodes[:-1])
    jumps = g(nodes[1:]) - g(nodes[:-1])
    s = steepness_factor * N                       # steps get sharper as intervals shrink
    hidden = 0.5 * (1 + np.tanh(s * (x[:, None] - mids[None, :])))   # shape (len(x), N)
    return g(nodes[0]) + hidden @ jumps

x_fine = np.linspace(-2, 2, 2000)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4))
axes[0].plot(x_fine, g(x_fine), "k", lw=2, label="$g(x)$")
for N in [5, 10, 40]:
    axes[0].plot(x_fine, staircase(x_fine, N), label=f"$N = {N}$")
axes[0].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[0].legend()

Ns = np.array([4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512])
sup_err = [np.max(np.abs(staircase(x_fine, N) - g(x_fine))) for N in Ns]
axes[1].loglog(Ns, sup_err, "o-", label=r"$\max_x |f_N(x) - g(x)|$")
axes[1].loglog(Ns, 20 / Ns, "k--", label=r"$\propto 1/N$")   # guide line; the prefactor 20 only places it near the points
axes[1].set_xlabel("number of neurons $N$"); axes[1].set_ylabel("sup error"); axes[1].legend()
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The construction works but is inefficient: the error decreases only like \(1/N\), and it needs \(g\) at equally spaced nodes of our choice. The \(1/N\) law follows from the shape of a staircase: within one interval it is (nearly) constant, while \(g\) changes by up to \(|g'|_{\max}\,h\) with \(h = 4/N\). The error is therefore at most about half of such a change, \(\tfrac12|g'|_{\max}\cdot 4/N \approx 26/N\) for \(|g'|_{\max}\approx 12.9\) on \([-2,2]\); the measured error is about \(18/N\) for large \(N\). In practice the sampling points are given, and a minimiser has to choose all \(3N\) parameters, including the positions of the steps. Section 7 shows that an optimised network with \(N \approx 8\) neurons is more accurate than the staircase with \(N = 512\).

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
section: 4. The loss function as a function of a parameter vector
text:
4. The loss function as a function of a parameter vector
Most minimisers (in particular scipy.optimize.minimize) work with a flat vector of parameters \(\vec\theta\in\mathbb R^{3N}\). We store \(\vec\theta = (W^{(1)}_1,\dots,W^{(1)}_N,\; b_1,\dots,b_N,\; W^{(2)}_1,\dots,W^{(2)}_N)\) and unpack it inside the model.
The model. np.outer(x, W1) is the \(K\times N\) matrix with entries \(x_k W^{(1)}_i\). Adding the length-\(N\) vector b adds \(b_i\) to every entry of column \(i\) (broadcasting), so entry \((k, i)\) of the table is the argument of neuron \(i\) at point \(k\). Multiplying by W2 with @ sums the neurons with their output weights.
The random initial parameters are not arbitrary in their order of magnitude: - \(W^{(1)}_i, b_i \sim \mathcal N(0, 2^2)\). With \(x\in[-2,2]\) a neuron \(\tanh(W^{(1)}x+b)\) is a step at \(x = -b/W^{(1)}\) of width about \(1/|W^{(1)}|\). Values of order 2 give steps that are narrower than the interval and positions \(-b/W^{(1)}\) that are of order 1, i.e. mostly inside the interval. Much smaller values give nearly linear neurons, much larger values give very sharp steps with vanishing slope almost everywhere. - \(W^{(2)}_i \sim \mathcal N(0, 1/N)\). The output is a sum of \(N\) terms of random sign, so its variance is \(N\cdot\mathrm{Var}(W^{(2)})\) times a number of order 1. With \(\mathrm{Var}(W^{(2)}) = 1/N\) the initial \(f(x)\) is of order 1, comparable to \(g\), for every \(N\) (the standard deviation of \(W^{(2)}\) scales as \(1/\sqrt N\)).
\(N = 10\) (30 parameters) is small enough for the gradient-free methods and the finite-difference gradients below to finish in seconds, and large enough for a good fit.


Code
def unpack(theta):
    """Split the flat parameter vector into (W1, b, W2), each of length N."""
    N = theta.size // 3                         # // is integer division: 30 // 3 = 10 (an integer, usable as an index)
    return theta[:N], theta[N:2 * N], theta[2 * N:]

def model(theta, x):
    """f(x; theta) = sum_i W2_i tanh(W1_i x + b_i), evaluated for all x at once."""
    W1, b, W2 = unpack(theta)
    hidden = np.tanh(np.outer(x, W1) + b)       # shape (K, N): neuron i evaluated at point k
    return hidden @ W2                          # shape (K,)

def loss(theta, x=x_train, y=y_train):
    """Mean squared error on the training set."""
    return np.mean((model(theta, x) - y)**2)

def init_theta(N, seed):
    """Random initial parameters: input weights and biases ~ N(0, 2^2), output weights ~ N(0, 1/N)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    # np.concatenate joins the three length-N arrays into one flat vector of length 3N
    return np.concatenate([rng.normal(0, 2, N), rng.normal(0, 2, N), rng.normal(0, 1, N) / np.sqrt(N)])

N = 10
theta0 = init_theta(N, seed=0)        # ONE common starting point for all minimisers below
print("number of parameters:", theta0.size, "  initial loss:", loss(theta0))


number of parameters: 30   initial loss: 1.0398383815103345



4.1 The gradient, derived by hand (backpropagation for one hidden layer)
With \(a_{ki} = W^{(1)}_i x_k + b_i\), \(h_{ki} = \tanh a_{ki}\), \(f_k = \sum_i W^{(2)}_i h_{ki}\) and residuals \(r_k = f_k - y_k\): \[\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial W^{(2)}_i} = \frac{2}{K}\sum_k r_k\,h_{ki},\qquad
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial b_i} = \frac{2}{K}\sum_k r_k\,W^{(2)}_i\,(1 - h_{ki}^2),\qquad
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial W^{(1)}_i} = \frac{2}{K}\sum_k r_k\,W^{(2)}_i\,(1 - h_{ki}^2)\,x_k .\] The factors come from the chain rule: \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial f_k = 2r_k/K\); then \(\partial f_k/\partial W^{(2)}_i = h_{ki}\), \(\partial f_k/\partial h_{ki} = W^{(2)}_i\), \(\partial h_{ki}/\partial a_{ki} = 1-h_{ki}^2\), and \(\partial a_{ki}/\partial b_i = 1\), \(\partial a_{ki}/\partial W^{(1)}_i = x_k\). Each parameter affects \(\mathcal L\) through all \(K\) points, hence the sums over \(k\). (We used \(\tanh' = 1 - \tanh^2\).) This is the chain rule applied backwards through the network; autograd performs the same computation automatically.
A hand-derived gradient is easy to get wrong, so we compare it with the central difference \([\mathcal L(\vec\theta+\delta\vec e) - \mathcal L(\vec\theta-\delta\vec e)]/(2\delta)\) for every unit vector \(\vec e\), with step \(\delta\) (eps in the code). Its truncation error is of order \(\delta^2\) and its round-off error of order \(10^{-16}/\delta\), so \(\delta\) between about \(10^{-4}\) and \(10^{-7}\) gives differences of \(10^{-9}\) or smaller; we take \(\delta = 10^{-6}\). The gradient components here are of order 1, so a mistake in one of the formulas would show up as a difference of order 1, not \(10^{-10}\).


Code
def grad(theta, x=x_train, y=y_train):
    """Analytic gradient of the MSE loss with respect to theta = (W1, b, W2)."""
    W1, b, W2 = unpack(theta)
    K = x.size
    h = np.tanh(np.outer(x, W1) + b)            # (K, N) hidden activations
    r = h @ W2 - y                              # (K,)   residuals
    dW2 = 2 / K * h.T @ r                       # (N,)   (2/K) sum_k r_k h_ki
    delta = 2 / K * r[:, None] * W2[None, :] * (1 - h**2)   # (K, N) dL/da_ki
    db = delta.sum(axis=0)                      # (N,)   sum over the points k
    dW1 = delta.T @ x                           # (N,)   sum_k delta_ki x_k
    return np.concatenate([dW1, db, dW2])

# Always check a hand-written gradient against finite differences before using it.
# The rows of np.eye(n) are the unit vectors e; each one perturbs a single parameter.
eps = 1e-6
fd = np.array([(loss(theta0 + eps * e) - loss(theta0 - eps * e)) / (2 * eps) for e in np.eye(theta0.size)])
print("max |analytic - finite difference| =", np.max(np.abs(grad(theta0) - fd)))


max |analytic - finite difference| = 2.181130831502287e-10

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
5. Minimisers in SciPy
scipy.optimize.minimize(fun, x0, method=..., jac=...) gives access to many classical algorithms. We compare two families:








method
uses
idea




Nelder–Mead
only \(\mathcal L\)
moves a simplex of \(3N+1\) points by reflections/contractions


Powell
only \(\mathcal L\)
successive 1D line minimisations along a set of directions


CG
\(\mathcal L\), \(\nabla\mathcal L\)
line searches along conjugate-gradient directions: each new direction is the gradient corrected so that it does not undo the progress along the previous directions


BFGS
\(\mathcal L\), \(\nabla\mathcal L\)
quasi-Newton: builds an approximation of the inverse Hessian from gradient history


L-BFGS-B
\(\mathcal L\), \(\nabla\mathcal L\)
BFGS with limited memory (stores the last few differences of parameters and gradients) — usable for many parameters; “-B”: optional bounds on the parameters, not used here



Two terms used in the table: a simplex in \(n\) dimensions is a set of \(n+1\) points (a triangle for \(n = 2\), a tetrahedron for \(n = 3\)); Nelder–Mead compares \(\mathcal L\) at its corners and moves the worst corner. A line search (line minimisation) is a one-dimensional minimisation of \(\mathcal L(\vec\theta + \alpha\vec d)\) over the step length \(\alpha\) along a chosen direction \(\vec d\).
To follow the progress we pass a callback, which SciPy calls after every iteration with the current \(\vec\theta\). We also count how many times \(\mathcal L\) was evaluated (nfev) and, for the methods that use it, how many times the gradient was evaluated (njev); with the analytic gradient one gradient costs about as much as a few evaluations of \(\mathcal L\). message reports why the minimiser stopped.
Details of the code below: - minimize returns an OptimizeResult object: res.x is the parameter vector at the end of the run, res.fun the loss there, res.nfev/res.njev the numbers of loss and gradient evaluations. - Results of the gradient-free methods have no attribute njev. getattr(obj, "name", default) returns the attribute if it exists and default otherwise, so the code works for all methods. - maxiter = 5000: the default limits differ between methods; with a common limit every method can stop on its own convergence criterion, except Nelder–Mead, which reaches the limit (with 20000 iterations it gets to \(5\cdot10^{-2}\), still far from the other methods, at four times the cost). Each method has its own default stopping tolerance, so the final losses are not compared at equal accuracy; they show what each method delivers with its standard settings.


Code
def run_scipy(method, use_grad, theta_start=theta0, maxiter=5000):
    """Minimise the loss with scipy; return a dict with the history and statistics."""
    history = [loss(theta_start)]
    callback = lambda th: history.append(loss(th))       # record loss after each iteration
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    res = minimize(loss, theta_start, method=method,
                   jac=grad if use_grad else None,       # None -> scipy uses finite differences (if it needs a gradient)
                   callback=callback,
                   options={"maxiter": maxiter})
    return dict(theta=res.x, history=history, final_loss=res.fun, nfev=res.nfev,
                njev=getattr(res, "njev", 0), message=res.message, time=time.perf_counter() - t0)

scipy_runs = {
    "Nelder-Mead":           run_scipy("Nelder-Mead", use_grad=False),
    "Powell":                run_scipy("Powell", use_grad=False),
    "CG":                    run_scipy("CG", use_grad=True),
    "BFGS":                  run_scipy("BFGS", use_grad=True),
    "BFGS (finite-diff grad)": run_scipy("BFGS", use_grad=False),
    "L-BFGS-B":              run_scipy("L-BFGS-B", use_grad=True),
}
for name, r in scipy_runs.items():
    print(f"{name:25s} loss = {r['final_loss']:.2e}   nfev = {r['nfev']:6d}   njev = {r['njev']:5d}   time = {r['time']:.2f} s   ({r['message']})")


Nelder-Mead               loss = 8.06e-02   nfev =   5986   njev =     0   time = 0.32 s   (Maximum number of iterations has been exceeded.)
Powell                    loss = 4.95e-03   nfev =  28849   njev =     0   time = 0.80 s   (Optimization terminated successfully.)
CG                        loss = 2.69e-06   nfev =   3107   njev =  3107   time = 0.35 s   (Optimization terminated successfully.)
BFGS                      loss = 1.11e-06   nfev =    592   njev =   592   time = 0.09 s   (Optimization terminated successfully.)
BFGS (finite-diff grad)   loss = 2.19e-06   nfev =  16089   njev =   519   time = 0.48 s   (Optimization terminated successfully.)
L-BFGS-B                  loss = 1.34e-05   nfev =    703   njev =   703   time = 0.06 s   (CONVERGENCE: RELATIVE REDUCTION OF F <= FACTR*EPSMCH)


Reading the table: BFGS reaches a loss of about \(10^{-6}\) with about 600 evaluations, while Powell needs almost \(3\cdot10^4\) evaluations and stops at a loss several thousand times larger, and Nelder–Mead stops at the iteration limit with a loss of about 0.08. The line BFGS (finite-diff grad) reaches a similar loss, but needs many more function evaluations, because every gradient costs \(3N+1\) evaluations of \(\mathcal L\). With \(10^6\) parameters this is not feasible; deep learning therefore relies on backpropagation.

5.1 Plain gradient descent with the hand-written gradient
\(\vec\theta_{t+1} = \vec\theta_t - \eta\,\nabla\mathcal L(\vec\theta_t)\) with fixed learning rate \(\eta\).
How large may \(\eta\) be? Near a minimum \(\mathcal L\) is approximately quadratic, and along the eigenvector of the Hessian with the largest eigenvalue \(\lambda_{\max}\) one step multiplies the distance to the minimum by \((1-\eta\lambda_{\max})\). The iteration is stable only if \(|1-\eta\lambda_{\max}|<1\), i.e. \(\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}\); otherwise the parameters oscillate with growing amplitude. For our start \(\lambda_{\max}\approx 9\), so the limit is \(\eta\approx 0.2\). We measured: \(\eta = 0.5\) diverges within 10 steps, while \(\eta\) up to \(0.3\) does not diverge in 20000 steps: the parameters drift into a region where the landscape is flatter (at the end of the run with \(\eta = 0.3\), \(\lambda_{\max}\approx 6.7 \approx 2/0.3\)), so the estimate from the starting point is only a rough guide. The value \(\eta = 0.05\) is a safe choice well below the limit, not an optimal one (\(\eta = 0.1\) reaches a loss about 3 times lower here); Exercise 3 scans \(\eta\) systematically. Because each step is small, the loss decreases slowly along the flat directions of the landscape, hence the large number of steps.


Code
eta, n_steps = 0.05, 20000
theta = theta0.copy()
gd_history = [loss(theta)]
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for t in range(n_steps):
    theta = theta - eta * grad(theta)
    gd_history.append(loss(theta))
gd_run = dict(theta=theta, history=gd_history, final_loss=gd_history[-1], nfev=n_steps, time=time.perf_counter() - t0)
print(f"gradient descent: loss = {gd_run['final_loss']:.2e} after {n_steps} steps")


gradient descent: loss = 3.70e-03 after 20000 steps




5.2 Comparison
Loss vs. iteration (left) and the resulting fits (right). An “iteration” means different things for different methods (one simplex move, one line search, one gradient step), so the table of function and gradient evaluations above is also relevant. What to look at: on the left, Powell decreases fastest during the first iterations (but each of its iterations costs many evaluations of \(\mathcal L\)); BFGS (with analytic or finite-difference gradient) and CG reach the lowest losses (about \(10^{-6}\)), while L-BFGS-B stops about ten times higher with its default tolerance; gradient descent decreases slowly over \(2\cdot10^4\) steps, and Nelder–Mead hardly moves during the first few hundred iterations. On the right, most fits lie on top of \(g\); the Nelder–Mead fit is visibly wrong near the ends of the interval and around \(x = 0\).


Code
all_np = {**scipy_runs, "gradient descent": gd_run}     # new dict: all entries of scipy_runs plus one more
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.8))
for i, (name, r) in enumerate(all_np.items()):
    axes[0].loglog(np.arange(1, len(r["history"]) + 1), r["history"], color=f"C{i}", label=name)
    axes[1].plot(x_plot, model(r["theta"], x_plot), color=f"C{i}", lw=1.2)
axes[1].plot(x_plot, g(x_plot), "k", lw=3, alpha=0.4, label="$g(x)$")
axes[1].plot(x_train, y_train, "k.", ms=4, label="sampling points")
axes[0].set_xlabel("iteration"); axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$\mathcal{L}$"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[1].legend()
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
section: 6. The same problem in PyTorch: autograd + torch.optim
text:
6. The same problem in PyTorch: autograd + torch.optim
Here autograd computes the gradient, and we compare the optimisers used in deep learning (see The Zoo of Optimization Algorithms in the Lecture Notes). We start from the same \(\vec\theta_0\). L-BFGS in PyTorch needs a closure — a function that recomputes the loss and gradient, because it evaluates them several times per step (line search).
Details of the code below: - getattr(torch.optim, "Adam") is the same object as torch.optim.Adam: the optimiser class is selected from its name given as a string, so one function run_torch serves all optimisers. - **opt_kwargs in the definition of a function collects all extra keyword arguments into a dictionary; **kw in a call unpacks a dictionary into keyword arguments, so run_torch("SGD", 2000, **dict(lr=0.05)) is the same as run_torch("SGD", 2000, lr=0.05). - opt.step(closure) returns the loss computed by the (first) call of the closure, i.e. the loss before the update of this step. .item() turns the one-element tensor into a Python number, so the list history does not keep the computational graph in memory.
Different learning rates. With momentum \(\beta = 0.9\) the steps accumulate along a steady slope to about \(\mathrm{lr}/(1-\beta) = 10\,\mathrm{lr}\), so momentum needs a smaller lr than plain SGD. RMSprop and Adam divide the gradient by a running average of its size, so for them lr is roughly the step length in parameter units, independent of the size of the gradient. All these values were tuned by hand to give stable runs; they are typical, not optimal (Exercise 3 scans the learning rate).
L-BFGS settings. max_iter = 20 is the number of inner quasi-Newton iterations per call of step, so 50 outer steps allow up to 1000 iterations (each with several evaluations of the loss in the line search), comparable in cost to the 2000 steps of the first-order methods. The numbers of steps are kept small so that the cell runs in a few seconds; with 5000 steps the first-order methods reach lower losses (we measured Adam \(9\cdot10^{-5}\), momentum \(4\cdot10^{-3}\), RMSprop \(10^{-2}\), SGD \(6\cdot10^{-2}\)). lr = 1 is the natural step length, because a quasi-Newton direction already has the scale of a Newton step. Without a line search PyTorch takes this fixed step, which can increase the loss; with line_search_fn="strong_wolfe" the step length is adjusted at every iteration so that the loss decreases sufficiently (the Wolfe conditions).


Code
xt, yt = torch.tensor(x_train), torch.tensor(y_train)

def model_torch(theta, x):
    """Same network as `model`, written with torch operations."""
    N = theta.numel() // 3
    W1, b, W2 = theta[:N], theta[N:2 * N], theta[2 * N:]
    return torch.tanh(x[:, None] * W1 + b) @ W2

def run_torch(opt_name, n_steps, **opt_kwargs):
    theta = torch.tensor(theta0, requires_grad=True)          # fresh copy of the common start
    opt = getattr(torch.optim, opt_name)([theta], **opt_kwargs)
    history = []

    def closure():                                            # forward + backward; used by every optimiser
        opt.zero_grad()
        L = torch.mean((model_torch(theta, xt) - yt)**2)
        L.backward()
        return L

    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        L = opt.step(closure)                                 # SGD/Adam call closure once, LBFGS several times
        history.append(L.item())
    return dict(theta=theta.detach().numpy(), history=history, final_loss=history[-1],
                time=time.perf_counter() - t0)

torch_setups = {
    "SGD":             ("SGD",     2000, dict(lr=0.05)),
    "SGD + momentum":  ("SGD",     2000, dict(lr=0.02, momentum=0.9)),
    "RMSprop":         ("RMSprop", 2000, dict(lr=3e-3)),
    "Adam":            ("Adam",    2000, dict(lr=1e-2)),
    "L-BFGS (torch)":  ("LBFGS",     50, dict(lr=1, max_iter=20, line_search_fn="strong_wolfe")),
}
torch_runs = {name: run_torch(opt, n, **kw) for name, (opt, n, kw) in torch_setups.items()}
for name, r in torch_runs.items():
    print(f"{name:16s} loss = {r['final_loss']:.2e}   time = {r['time']:.2f} s")


SGD              loss = 1.12e-01   time = 0.53 s
SGD + momentum   loss = 2.43e-02   time = 0.51 s
RMSprop          loss = 3.54e-02   time = 0.54 s
Adam             loss = 4.29e-03   time = 0.58 s
L-BFGS (torch)   loss = 6.82e-06   time = 1.09 s


Loss versus optimiser step (left) and the error of the final fits on the dense grid (right). A perfect fit would give the horizontal line at zero in the right panel. L-BFGS is close to this line everywhere. After 2000 steps Adam has errors of a few tenths, SGD, momentum and RMSprop of order 1 even inside the interval, and the largest errors (up to almost 2 for SGD) are at the ends \(x = \pm 2\), where the data constrain the fit only from one side.

for i, (name, r) in enumerate(torch_runs.items()):

    axes[1].plot(x_plot, model(r["theta"], x_plot) - g(x_plot), color=f"C{i}", lw=1.2, label=name)

axes[1].axhline(0, color="gray", lw=0.5)

Observations (the exact numbers depend on the random start and on the hyperparameters): - Gradient-free methods (Nelder–Mead, Powell) need many function evaluations already for 30 parameters; Nelder–Mead stopped at the iteration limit without converging (see its message above). - Methods that use curvature information (BFGS, L-BFGS), which build an approximation of the curvature (the Hessian) from the history of gradients, or conjugate directions (CG) are the most accurate for this small, smooth, full-batch problem. - First-order methods (SGD, momentum, RMSprop, Adam) are slower to converge here, but they are the only ones that remain practical for millions of parameters and mini-batches of data (at every step the gradient is computed from a random subset of the data, which makes it noisy), which is the situation in deep learning. - Every method has hyperparameters (learning rate, momentum, number of steps); with other values the ranking can change (Exercise 3).

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
section: 7. The UAT numerically: loss vs. number of neurons
text:
7. The UAT numerically: loss vs. number of neurons
For each \(N\) we run BFGS from a few random starting points and keep the best result.

Restarts. The landscape is non-convex (Section 9), so a single run can end in a poor minimum. Three starts per \(N\) (seeds 0, 1, 2) are a compromise between cost and the chance of missing a good minimum; any small number (3–10) is reasonable.
gtol. BFGS stops when the largest component of the gradient falls below gtol (default \(10^{-5}\)), or after maxiter iterations. With the default, the run for \(N = 8\) stops at a loss of about \(10^{-6}\), although much lower losses exist: near such a small minimum the gradient is already tiny. We therefore set gtol = 1e-8.
maxiter. To keep the cell fast we allow at most 1000 iterations, and for \(N \ge 6\) the runs stop at this limit. The losses for \(N \ge 6\) (of order \(10^{-7}\)) are therefore set by the iteration budget, not by \(N\). With max_iter = 5000 (about four times longer) we measured \(1.6\cdot10^{-9}\) for \(N = 8\) and \(10^{-10}\) for \(N = 12\).



Code
Ns = [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12]
max_iter = 1000          # kept small so that the cell runs in a few seconds; 5000 gives lower losses for N >= 6
best_loss, best_theta = {}, {}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for N in Ns:
    results = [minimize(loss, init_theta(N, seed), jac=grad, method="BFGS",
                        options={"maxiter": max_iter, "gtol": 1e-8}) for seed in range(3)]
    best = min(results, key=lambda r: r.fun)      # the result with the smallest r.fun (final loss)
    best_loss[N], best_theta[N] = best.fun, best.x
    print(f"N = {N:2d}   ({3*N:2d} parameters)   best loss = {best.fun:.2e}")
print(f"total time {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")

axes[0].semilogy(Ns, [best_loss[N] for N in Ns], "o-")
