title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
8. Building approximators for other functions
We now collect everything into one tool that builds the approximator \[f(x;\vec W^{(1)},\vec b,\vec W^{(2)}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} W^{(2)}_i\,\sigma\big(W^{(1)}_i x + b_i\big) + c\] for any target \(g(x)\) on an interval \([x_\min, x_\max]\), with a chosen number of hidden nodes \(N\) (we use ‘node’ and ‘neuron’ interchangeably), activation \(\sigma\), number of sampling points \(K\) and minimiser. We add an output bias \(c\): for activations that are not odd, i.e. do not satisfy \(\sigma(-z) = -\sigma(z)\) (sigmoid, ReLU, …), it is needed to shift the output; for \(\tanh\) it changes little.
The steps inside fit_uat are exactly the ones from the lecture: 1. data — sample \(K\) points \(x_k\) in the interval and compute \(y_k = g(x_k)\); 2. model — parameters \(\vec\theta = (\vec W^{(1)}, \vec b, \vec W^{(2)}, c)\), initialised randomly; 3. loss — \(\mathcal L(\vec\theta) = \frac1K\sum_k \big(y_k - f(x_k;\vec\theta)\big)^2\); 4. minimisation — repeat: compute \(\mathcal L\), compute \(\nabla_{\vec\theta}\mathcal L\) by autograd, update \(\vec\theta\); 5. since the landscape is non-convex, optionally repeat from a few random starts (n_restarts) and keep the best result.
Choices made inside fit_uat, and why: - Rescaling of the input. \(x\) is mapped linearly to \([-1, 1]\) before entering the network. The random initial steps have positions \(-b_i/W^{(1)}_i\) of order 1 and widths \(1/|W^{(1)}_i|\) of order \(1/3\), so they cover \([-1,1]\) well. On an interval far from this scale the same initialisation fails: for \(g\) shifted to \([100, 104]\) (8 nodes) the loss stays at 1.4, which is the variance of the data (no fit at all, every \(\tanh\) is saturated), while with rescaling it reaches \(3\cdot10^{-6}\); on \([-0.02, 0.02]\) the numbers are 0.13 and \(2\cdot10^{-5}\). For the intervals used below, all of width 2–6 around 0, rescaling makes little difference, but it costs nothing. The output \(y\) is not rescaled; the targets below are of order 1. - Initial weights. \(W^{(1)}_i, b_i \sim \mathcal N(0, 3^2)\) and \(W^{(2)}_i\sim\mathcal N(0, 1/N)\) (Section 4). The value 3 is arbitrary. We tested standard deviations 1, 3, 5 and 10 with 8 nodes: for the smooth targets all of them give small final losses, with no systematic trend; for the sawtooth the final loss ranges from \(10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-1}\) and depends mainly on which minimum the run happens to reach (Section 9), not on this value. - Output bias \(c\) starts at the mean of the data, so the nodes only have to represent the deviations from the mean. Starting from \(c = 0\) also works. - Default steps and learning rates follow Section 6: L-BFGS needs some tens of outer steps with lr \(= 1\), first-order methods need thousands of steps with a small lr. The defaults (30 L-BFGS steps of up to 20 inner iterations each, 2000 Adam/SGD steps, a single start) are kept small so that every figure below takes only a few seconds; larger values (e.g. n_steps=100, n_restarts=5) give lower losses for the larger \(N\), at a correspondingly higher cost.


Code
import torch.nn.functional as F    # PyTorch module with activation functions written as plain functions, e.g. F.elu(z)

# Activation functions from the lecture slide
ACTIVATIONS = {
    "sigmoid":   torch.sigmoid,
    "tanh":      torch.tanh,
    "ReLU":      torch.relu,
    "LeakyReLU": lambda z: F.leaky_relu(z, negative_slope=0.1),
    "ELU":       F.elu,
}

def fit_uat(g, x_range, N, K=30, activation="tanh", optimizer="LBFGS",
            n_steps=None, lr=None, n_restarts=1, sampling="random", seed=0):
    """
    Fit f(x) = sum_i W2_i * sigma(W1_i * x + b_i) + c  to the function g on the interval x_range.

    g          : function of a NumPy array (the target)
    x_range    : (x_min, x_max)
    N          : number of nodes in the single hidden layer
    K          : number of sampling (training) points
    activation : key of ACTIVATIONS
    optimizer  : "LBFGS", "Adam" or "SGD"
    n_restarts : number of random initialisations; the best one is returned
    sampling   : "random" (uniformly random points) or "grid" (equally spaced points)
    Returns a dict with the fitted predictor, the data, the final loss and the loss history.
    """
    sigma = ACTIVATIONS[activation]
    x_min, x_max = x_range
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)

    # ---- 1. data -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    if sampling == "random":
        x_data = np.sort(rng.uniform(x_min, x_max, K))
    else:
        x_data = np.linspace(x_min, x_max, K)
    y_data = g(x_data)
    to_unit = lambda x: 2 * (x - x_min) / (x_max - x_min) - 1      # rescale input to [-1, 1]
    xt, yt = torch.tensor(to_unit(x_data)), torch.tensor(y_data)

    # default number of steps and learning rate for each optimiser
    defaults = {"LBFGS": (30, 1.0), "Adam": (2000, 1e-2), "SGD": (2000, 1e-2)}
    # `a or b` gives b when a is None (or 0): the default is used only when no value was passed
    n_steps = n_steps or defaults[optimizer][0]
    lr = lr or defaults[optimizer][1]

    best = None
    for restart in range(n_restarts):
        torch.manual_seed(seed + restart)
        # ---- 2. model parameters (random initialisation) -----------------------------
        W1 = (3 * torch.randn(N)).requires_grad_()               # steepness of each node
        b = (3 * torch.randn(N)).requires_grad_()                # position of each node
        W2 = (torch.randn(N) / np.sqrt(N)).requires_grad_()      # height of each node
        c = torch.tensor([float(y_data.mean())], requires_grad=True)  # output bias
        params = [W1, b, W2, c]

        def f(x):                                                # the approximator f(x; theta)
            return sigma(x[:, None] * W1 + b) @ W2 + c

        # ---- 3. loss -----------------------------------------------------------------
        # closure uses opt, which is created only further down: Python looks up the name opt when closure is CALLED
        # (inside opt.step), not when it is defined, and by then opt exists.
        def closure():
            opt.zero_grad()
            L = torch.mean((yt - f(xt))**2)
            L.backward()                                         # gradient by autograd
            return L

        # ---- 4. minimisation ---------------------------------------------------------
        if optimizer == "LBFGS":
            opt = torch.optim.LBFGS(params, lr=lr, max_iter=20, line_search_fn="strong_wolfe")
        else:
            opt = getattr(torch.optim, optimizer)(params, lr=lr)
        history = []
        for step in range(n_steps):
            L = opt.step(closure)
            history.append(L.item())
            if not np.isfinite(history[-1]):                     # stop a diverging run
                break

        # ---- 5. keep the best restart ------------------------------------------------
        # keep this restart if it is the first one, if the best so far diverged (nan), or if it is better
        if best is None or not np.isfinite(best["loss"]) or history[-1] < best["loss"]:
            # detach().clone(): an independent copy outside the autograd graph, not changed by later restarts.
            # The default argument frozen=frozen is evaluated when predict is defined, so predict keeps the
            # parameters of THIS restart (a direct reference to W1, b, ... would see the names of the last restart).
            frozen = [p.detach().clone() for p in params]
            def predict(x, frozen=frozen):
                W1_, b_, W2_, c_ = frozen
                return (sigma(torch.tensor(to_unit(np.asarray(x)))[:, None] * W1_ + b_) @ W2_ + c_).numpy()
            best = dict(predict=predict, loss=history[-1], history=history,
                        x_data=x_data, y_data=y_data, N=N, activation=activation)
    return best


And a plotting function that reproduces the figure from the lecture slide: the target \(g(x)\), the sampling points, and the approximations for several \(N\); on the right, the loss during minimisation.


Code
def plot_approximations(g, x_range, N_list, title="", **fit_kwargs):
    """Fit and plot f(x) for every N in N_list (as on the lecture slide), plus the loss curves."""
    x_plot = np.linspace(*x_range, 600)          # *x_range unpacks the pair: same as np.linspace(x_range[0], x_range[1], 600)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.5), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.6, 1]})   # left panel 1.6 times wider
    axes[0].plot(x_plot, g(x_plot), "k", lw=2, label="$g(x)$")
    for i, N in enumerate(N_list):
        res = fit_uat(g, x_range, N, **fit_kwargs)
        axes[0].plot(x_plot, res["predict"](x_plot), "--", lw=2, color=f"C{i}",
                     label=f"$f(x)$, $N = {N}$")
        axes[1].semilogy(res["history"], color=f"C{i}", label=f"$N = {N}$: final $\\mathcal{{L}}$ = {res['loss']:.1e}")
    axes[0].plot(res["x_data"], res["y_data"], "o", color="k", ms=6, label="sampling points of $g(x)$")
    # limit the vertical range: between sampling points a fit can make very large excursions, which would hide everything else
    g_min, g_max = g(x_plot).min(), g(x_plot).max()
    span = g_max - g_min
    axes[0].set_ylim(g_min - 0.5 * span, g_max + 0.5 * span)
    axes[0].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[0].set_ylabel("$g(x)$"); axes[0].set_title(title)
    axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
    axes[1].set_xlabel("optimiser step"); axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$\mathcal{L}$"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
    fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# The example from the slide: g(x) on [-2, 2], K = 30 random sampling points, N = 2, 3, 4
plot_approximations(g, (-2, 2), N_list=[2, 3, 4], K=30, title="lecture example")





This is the situation of the lecture slide. With \(N = 2\) and \(N = 3\) the fits are made of a few steep steps, and their loss curves become flat after a few steps: the minimiser has stopped in a minimum and more steps do not help (with n_steps=100 the final losses for this seed are unchanged). The result depends on the starting point: for \(N = 3\) the seeds 0–5 give final losses between \(9\cdot10^{-3}\) and \(5\cdot10^{-1}\). With \(N = 4\) the fit follows \(g\) closely.

8.1 A gallery of harder targets
Some functions are harder than others. The number of nodes needed depends on how many “features” (bumps, kinks, steps) the function has on the interval, and how sharp they are. Examples: - a Gaussian wave packet \(e^{-x^2}\cos(8x)\): many oscillations; - \(|x|\): a kink (not differentiable at 0); - a smoothed step \(\tanh(30x)\): very steep; - a sawtooth: several jumps; - the Lennard-Jones potential \(4(r^{-12} - r^{-6})\): steep wall plus shallow minimum (in its panel the horizontal axis is the distance \(r\)); - the ground state of the double well \(V = \tfrac12x^2 + \kappa e^{-x^2/2}\) (\(\kappa = 6\), units \(\hbar = m = 1\)). It is computed by discretising \(H = -\tfrac12\, d^2/dx^2 + V\) with the three-point stencil on 400 equally spaced points in \([-6, 6]\) and diagonalising the resulting matrix.


Code
def double_well_ground_state(x, kappa=6.0):
    """Ground-state wavefunction of V = x^2/2 + kappa exp(-x^2/2), interpolated onto x."""
    grid = np.linspace(-6, 6, 400); dx = grid[1] - grid[0]
    H = (-0.5 / dx**2 * (np.diag(np.ones(399), 1) - 2 * np.eye(400) + np.diag(np.ones(399), -1))
         + np.diag(0.5 * grid**2 + kappa * np.exp(-grid**2 / 2)))
    psi0 = np.linalg.eigh(H)[1][:, 0]
    # eigh normalises sum(psi0**2) = 1; dividing by sqrt(dx) gives sum(psi0**2) * dx = 1, the discrete form of
    # the integral normalisation. abs() removes the arbitrary overall sign (the ground state has no nodes).
    psi0 = np.abs(psi0) / np.sqrt(dx)
    return np.interp(x, grid, psi0)          # linear interpolation of the grid values psi0 at the points x

TARGETS = {
    # name: (function, interval)
    "lecture g(x)":            (g, (-2, 2)),
    "wave packet":             (lambda x: np.exp(-x**2) * np.cos(8 * x), (-3, 3)),
    "|x|":                     (np.abs, (-1, 1)),
    "steep step tanh(30x)":    (lambda x: np.tanh(30 * x), (-1, 1)),
    "sawtooth":                (lambda x: 2 * (x - np.floor(x + 0.5)), (-2, 2)),   # x - floor(x + 1/2): signed distance to the nearest integer, in [-1/2, 1/2)
    "Lennard-Jones":           (lambda r: 4 * (r**-12 - r**-6), (0.95, 3.0)),
    "double-well ground state": (double_well_ground_state, (-4, 4)),
}

# K = 60 sampling points (instead of 30): the harder targets need more points to resolve their oscillations and jumps.
# For N = 16 the network has 49 parameters (3N + 1 with the output bias c), comparable to K; experiment 3 of Section 8.2
# shows what happens when K is smaller than the number of parameters.
# The intervals contain the region where each function has its features; their exact limits are arbitrary.
for name in ["wave packet", "|x|"]:
    func, interval = TARGETS[name]
    plot_approximations(func, interval, N_list=[2, 4, 8, 16], K=60, title=name)








The sawtooth and the Lennard-Jones potential, with the same settings:


Code
for name in ["sawtooth", "Lennard-Jones"]:
    func, interval = TARGETS[name]
    plot_approximations(func, interval, N_list=[2, 4, 8, 16], K=60, title=name)








Observations: - the wave packet has 9 maxima and minima of visible size; \(N = 8\) still misses several of them, while \(N = 16\) (about two nodes per extremum) follows all of them; - for \(|x|\) a ReLU network would need only two nodes (\(|x| = \mathrm{ReLU}(x) + \mathrm{ReLU}(-x)\)), while \(\tanh\) needs several — the choice of \(\sigma\) matters; - jumps (sawtooth) are approximated by very steep \(\tanh\) nodes; between sampling points the fit can do anything. For \(N = 16\) the loss is still decreasing after the 30 default L-BFGS steps; n_steps=100 gives a much better fit; - on \([0.95, 3]\) the Lennard-Jones potential varies only between \(-1\) and \(2\) and is fitted well already with a few nodes; closer to \(r = 0.9\) the wall would grow much faster and the fit would become harder.

section: 9. A non-convex landscape: different starts, different minima
text:
9. A non-convex landscape: different starts, different minima
\(\mathcal L(\vec\theta)\) is not convex. Running the same minimiser (BFGS) from 10 random starting points gives a whole distribution of final losses. We use \(N = 6\): small enough for 10 BFGS runs (at most 1000 iterations each) to take only seconds, and large enough for the final losses to spread over several orders of magnitude (from about \(10^{-6}\) to \(3\cdot10^{-3}\) here).


Code
N = 6
finals, thetas = [], []
for seed in range(10):       # 10 starts keep the cell fast; 30 or more give a smoother histogram
    # seeds 100..109: starting points different from those of Section 7 (the value 100 is arbitrary)
    r = minimize(loss, init_theta(N, seed=100 + seed), jac=grad, method="BFGS", options={"maxiter": 1000, "gtol": 1e-8})
    finals.append(r.fun); thetas.append(r.x)
finals = np.array(finals)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.hist(np.log10(finals), bins=10)
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\log_{10}$ of final loss"); ax.set_ylabel("number of runs")
ax.set_title(f"BFGS from {len(finals)} random starts, N = {N}")
plt.show()





Take the best solution \(\vec\theta_A\) and a worse one \(\vec\theta_B\), and evaluate the loss along the straight line between them, \(\mathcal L\big((1-t)\vec\theta_A + t\vec\theta_B\big)\). If the landscape were convex, this curve could not have a maximum between the two minima.


Code
order = np.argsort(finals)
theta_A, theta_B = thetas[order[0]], thetas[order[len(order) // 2]]   # best and median run
ts = np.linspace(-0.2, 1.2, 281)          # step 0.005: the grid contains t = 0 and t = 1 exactly
# t < 0 and t > 1 are included to show that the loss also rises on the outer side of each minimum
path_loss = [loss((1 - t) * theta_A + t * theta_B) for t in ts]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.semilogy(ts, path_loss)
ax.axvline(0, color="C2", ls=":", label=r"$\theta_A$ (best)")
ax.axvline(1, color="C3", ls=":", label=r"$\theta_B$ (median)")
ax.set_xlabel("$t$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\mathcal{L}((1-t)\theta_A + t\theta_B)$"); ax.legend()
plt.show()





There is a barrier between the two minima. The valleys around the minima are very narrow (the parameters have large values, so a small relative change of \(\vec\theta\) changes \(f\) strongly); this is why the curve must be evaluated exactly at \(t=0\) and \(t=1\) to show the minimal losses. Part of the multiplicity is trivial: permuting the \(N\) neurons, or flipping the signs \((W^{(1)}_i, b_i, W^{(2)}_i)\to(-W^{(1)}_i, -b_i, -W^{(2)}_i)\) (since \(\tanh\) is odd), does not change \(f\). So a generic minimum has \(N!\,2^N\) equivalent copies (\(N!\) orderings of the neurons times two signs for each of them) (fewer if some neurons are identical).

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
10. Interpolation is not extrapolation
The network was fitted on \([-2, 2]\). Its predictions outside this interval:


Code
x_wide = np.linspace(-4, 4, 800)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.plot(x_wide, g(x_wide), "k", lw=2, label="$g(x)$")
for N in [4, 8, 12]:
    ax.plot(x_wide, model(best_theta[N], x_wide), label=f"network, $N = {N}$")
ax.axvspan(-2, 2, color="gray", alpha=0.15, label="training interval")
ax.set_ylim(-20, 20); ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$g(x)$, $f(x)$"); ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.show()





Outside the training interval the network continues the trend of its outermost neurons and, far away, tends to a constant once all \(\tanh\) saturate; it has no information about the oscillations of \(g\). The UAT is a statement about a compact set; the network has learned the data, not the formula for \(g(x)\). The same limitation applies whenever a network is applied to physical parameters outside its training range.

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
11. Summary

One hidden layer = a weighted sum of shifted, stretched \(\tanh\) steps; pairs of steps make bumps, sums of bumps approximate any continuous function.
The UAT guarantees existence of good parameters; finding them is a non-convex minimisation of \(\mathcal L(\vec\theta)\).
Gradient-free methods need no derivatives but scale badly; finite-difference gradients cost \(\mathcal O(\dim\vec\theta)\) evaluations (a number proportional to the number of parameters); backpropagation/autograd gives the exact gradient at the cost of a few evaluations of \(\mathcal L\), independently of \(\dim\vec\theta\).
For small smooth problems quasi-Newton methods (BFGS, L-BFGS) are very effective; for large networks and mini-batches, first-order methods (SGD, Adam) are used.
Different initialisations lead to different minima.
A fitted network interpolates; it does not extrapolate.

12. Exercises


Exercise 1 — Activation functions
Repeat the experiment of Section 7, with an additional output bias \(c\), for three activations: \(\tanh\), the sigmoid \(1/(1+e^{-z})\) and ReLU \(\max(0,z)\). Use PyTorch with Adam (lr=1e-2, 1000 steps; more steps give lower losses but take longer), \(N\in\{4, 8, 16\}\), and plot the final loss vs. \(N\) for each activation. Plot the ReLU fit for \(N = 8\): what kind of function is it?

Solution


Code
activations = {name: ACTIVATIONS[name] for name in ["tanh", "sigmoid", "ReLU"]}   # from Section 8

def fit_adam(N, act, n_steps=1000, lr=1e-2, seed=0):
    """Fit f(x) = sum_i W2_i act(W1_i x + b_i) + c with Adam; return the final loss and the parameters."""
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    # the initialisation of Section 4 (input x in [-2, 2], not rescaled as in fit_uat)
    W1 = (2 * torch.randn(N)).requires_grad_()
    b = (2 * torch.randn(N)).requires_grad_()
    W2 = (torch.randn(N) / N**0.5).requires_grad_()
    c = torch.zeros(1, requires_grad=True)          # output bias: sigmoid and ReLU are not odd, a shift helps
    opt = torch.optim.Adam([W1, b, W2, c], lr=lr)
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        opt.zero_grad()
        pred = act(xt[:, None] * W1 + b) @ W2 + c
        L = torch.mean((pred - yt)**2)
        L.backward()
        opt.step()
    return L.item(), (W1, b, W2, c)

Ns_act = [4, 8, 16]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4))
for name, act in activations.items():
    losses = [fit_adam(N, act)[0] for N in Ns_act]
    print(f"{name:8s} final losses for N = {Ns_act}: " + ", ".join(f"{L:.1e}" for L in losses))
    axes[0].semilogy(Ns_act, losses, "o-", label=name)
axes[0].set_xlabel("$N$"); axes[0].set_ylabel("final loss"); axes[0].legend()

# the ReLU network is piecewise linear: N kinks at x = -b_i / W1_i
_, (W1, b, W2, c) = fit_adam(8, torch.relu)
with torch.no_grad():
    xp = torch.tensor(x_plot)
    f_relu = (torch.relu(xp[:, None] * W1 + b) @ W2 + c).numpy()      # ReLU network on the dense grid
    axes[1].plot(x_plot, g(x_plot), "k", lw=3, alpha=0.4, label="$g(x)$")
    axes[1].plot(x_plot, f_relu, label="ReLU network, N = 8")
    kinks = (-b / W1).numpy()
    kinks = kinks[(kinks > -2) & (kinks < 2)]
    axes[1].plot(kinks, np.interp(kinks, x_plot, f_relu),
                 "rx", ms=10, label="kinks $x = -b_i/W^{(1)}_i$")
axes[1].legend(); axes[1].set_xlabel("$x$")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
# tanh gives the lowest loss for every N. All losses (printed above) are of order 1e-2 to 1e-1, far above the BFGS
# results of Section 7: 1000 Adam steps are not enough to converge, which is also why the loss does not always
# decrease with N (tanh, N = 8 vs N = 4). The ReLU fit is piecewise linear: straight segments joined at the kinks.


tanh     final losses for N = [4, 8, 16]: 6.5e-02, 7.2e-02, 3.1e-02


sigmoid  final losses for N = [4, 8, 16]: 1.2e-01, 1.1e-01, 4.6e-02


ReLU     final losses for N = [4, 8, 16]: 2.2e-01, 1.0e-01, 5.4e-02








Exercise 2 — Noisy data and overfitting
Real data are noisy and scarce. Generate \(K=20\) training points \(y_k = g(x_k) + \xi_k\), \(\xi_k\sim\mathcal N(0, \sigma_\xi^2)\) with noise standard deviation \(\sigma_\xi = 0.3\), with \(x_k\) uniformly random in \([-2,2]\), and a separate validation set of 200 noisy points. 1. Fit networks with \(N \in\{2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64\}\) using BFGS (with the functions loss and grad, passing the data through args=). minimize calls loss(theta, *args) and grad(theta, *args); so far args was not given and the default arguments x=x_train, y=y_train were used. 2. Plot the training and the validation loss vs. \(N\). 3. Plot the fits for a small and for the largest \(N\) and explain the result. (This is the starting point of the next lecture: regularisation.)

Solution


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
noise = 0.3
x_tr = np.sort(rng.uniform(-2, 2, 20)); y_tr = g(x_tr) + noise * rng.normal(size=20)
x_val = rng.uniform(-2, 2, 200);        y_val = g(x_val) + noise * rng.normal(size=200)

Ns_of = [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64]
train_loss, val_loss, fits = [], [], {}
for N in Ns_of:
    # best of 3 starts, judged on the TRAINING loss (the validation set must not be used for fitting).
    # At most 2000 iterations per run (for speed). The networks with N >= 16 nevertheless pass through
    # all 20 points: their training losses are of order 1e-12 or smaller.
    runs = [minimize(loss, init_theta(N, s), args=(x_tr, y_tr), jac=grad, method="BFGS",
                     options={"maxiter": 2000}) for s in range(3)]
    best = min(runs, key=lambda r: r.fun)
    fits[N] = best.x
    train_loss.append(best.fun)
    val_loss.append(loss(best.x, x_val, y_val))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.2))
axes[0].loglog(Ns_of, train_loss, "o-", label="training loss")
axes[0].loglog(Ns_of, val_loss, "s-", label="validation loss")
axes[0].axhline(noise**2, color="gray", ls=":", label=r"noise variance $0.3^2$")
axes[0].set_xlabel("$N$"); axes[0].legend()

axes[1].plot(x_plot, g(x_plot), "k", lw=2, alpha=0.4, label="$g(x)$ (unknown in practice)")
axes[1].plot(x_tr, y_tr, "o", color="k", label="training data")
for N in [4, 64]:
    axes[1].plot(x_plot, model(fits[N], x_plot), label=f"N = {N}")
axes[1].set_ylim(-6, 6); axes[1].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
for N, tr, va in zip(Ns_of, train_loss, val_loss):
    print(f"N = {N:3d}:  training loss = {tr:.1e},  validation loss = {va:.1e}")
print("smallest validation loss at N =", Ns_of[int(np.argmin(val_loss))])
# The training loss decreases with N and drops far below the noise variance 0.3^2 = 0.09: a large network
# passes through the 20 noisy points and oscillates strongly between them. The validation loss is smallest for a
# small network (printed above) and becomes orders of magnitude larger for large N: overfitting.
# The validation loss is not monotonic in N: it peaks at N = 8 (5.4e+03) and is lower again for N = 16, 32 (about 2e+02).
# Even its smallest value (0.8 at N = 2) is well above the noise variance 0.09, so none of these fits reproduces g closely.





N =   2:  training loss = 5.8e-02,  validation loss = 8.0e-01
N =   4:  training loss = 4.4e-02,  validation loss = 8.3e-01
N =   8:  training loss = 8.1e-03,  validation loss = 5.4e+03
N =  16:  training loss = 5.6e-13,  validation loss = 2.3e+02
N =  32:  training loss = 3.4e-12,  validation loss = 2.1e+02
N =  64:  training loss = 1.1e-14,  validation loss = 8.6e+02
smallest validation loss at N = 2





Exercise 3 — Learning-rate scan
For \(N=10\) and the common start \(\vec\theta_0\), run SGD and Adam for 1000 steps with learning rates \(\eta\in\{10^{-4}, 10^{-3}, \dots, 1\}\) (use np.logspace(-4, 0, 5); a finer scan with np.logspace(-4, 0, 9) and 2000 steps takes about 3.5 times longer) and plot the final loss vs. \(\eta\) (log-log). Mark runs that diverged (nan or inf). Which optimiser is less sensitive to the choice of \(\eta\)?

Solution


Code
lrs = np.logspace(-4, 0, 5)          # 5 values and 1000 steps keep the cell fast; 9 values and 2000 steps give a finer picture
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
for i, opt_name in enumerate(["SGD", "Adam"]):
    finals = np.array([run_torch(opt_name, 1000, lr=lr)["final_loss"] for lr in lrs])
    ok = np.isfinite(finals) & (finals < 1e3)           # diverged: nan/inf, or far above the initial loss of about 1
    # ~ok is the element-wise NOT of the boolean array: True for the diverged runs; np.full(n, 1e1) is an array of n values 10
    ax.loglog(lrs[ok], finals[ok], "o-", color=f"C{i}", label=opt_name)
    ax.loglog(lrs[~ok], np.full((~ok).sum(), 1e1), "x", color=f"C{i}", ms=12)   # crosses at an arbitrary height 10
ax.set_xlabel(r"learning rate $\eta$"); ax.set_ylabel("final loss (x = diverged)")
ax.legend(); plt.show()
# SGD converges slowly for small eta and diverges once eta exceeds a threshold (the crosses).
# Adam divides each step by the square root of a running average of the squared gradient, so its step length is
# about eta independently of the size of the gradient; it does not diverge in the scanned range and reaches much
# lower losses, with an optimum at an intermediate eta.








Exercise 4 — A network as a surrogate for a quantum calculation
The ground-state energy \(E_0(\kappa)\) of the double well \(V = \tfrac12x^2 + \kappa e^{-x^2/2}\) can be computed by exact diagonalisation of the finite-difference Hamiltonian. Suppose each diagonalisation were expensive and we could afford only 12 of them. 1. Compute \(E_0(\kappa_j)\) for 12 randomly chosen \(\kappa_j\in[0, 12]\) (the first lines of the solution build the data; you may copy them). 2. Fit a one-hidden-layer network (\(N=8\), \(\tanh\), with output bias) to these 12 points, in PyTorch with L-BFGS. Rescale the input to \([-1,1]\) first. 3. Compare the network with the exact \(E_0(\kappa)\) on a fine grid of 100 points. 4. Use autograd on the network to get \(dE_0/d\kappa\) and compare with the exact derivative (Hellmann–Feynman). Is the derivative of a good fit also a good approximation of the derivative?

Solution


Code
xg = np.linspace(-6, 6, 300); dxg = xg[1] - xg[0]
H_kin = -0.5 / dxg**2 * (np.diag(np.ones(299), 1) - 2 * np.eye(300) + np.diag(np.ones(299), -1))
def E0_and_dE0(kappa):
    """Exact ground-state energy and its derivative (Hellmann-Feynman) for barrier height kappa."""
    E, psi = np.linalg.eigh(H_kin + np.diag(0.5 * xg**2 + kappa * np.exp(-xg**2 / 2)))
    # Hellmann-Feynman: dE0/dkappa = <psi0| dH/dkappa |psi0> with dH/dkappa = exp(-x^2/2).
    # eigh normalises sum(psi**2) = 1, so the expectation value is a plain sum (no factor dx).
    return E[0], np.sum(psi[:, 0]**2 * np.exp(-xg**2 / 2))

# 1) the 12 "expensive" data points and a fine reference grid
k_train = np.sort(np.random.default_rng(3).uniform(0, 12, 12))     # 12 random, non-equidistant points
E_train = np.array([E0_and_dE0(k)[0] for k in k_train])
k_fine = np.linspace(0, 12, 100)
# the list of 100 pairs (E0, dE0) becomes an array of shape (100, 2); .T gives shape (2, 100), whose two rows are unpacked
E_fine, dE_fine = np.array([E0_and_dE0(k) for k in k_fine]).T

# 2) network with output bias; input rescaled from [0, 12] to [-1, 1]
to_unit = lambda k: (k - 6.0) / 6.0
torch.manual_seed(0)
N = 8
# standard deviation 1 (an arbitrary choice): on the rescaled input [-1, 1] it already places the steps inside the interval
W1, b, W2 = torch.randn(N, requires_grad=True), torch.randn(N, requires_grad=True), torch.randn(N, requires_grad=True)
c = torch.tensor([E_train.mean()], requires_grad=True)
net = lambda k: torch.tanh(to_unit(k)[:, None] * W1 + b) @ W2 + c

kt, Et = torch.tensor(k_train), torch.tensor(E_train)
opt = torch.optim.LBFGS([W1, b, W2, c], lr=1, max_iter=50, line_search_fn="strong_wolfe")
def closure():
    opt.zero_grad()
    L = torch.mean((net(kt) - Et)**2)
    L.backward()
    return L
for _ in range(10):          # with 25 parameters and 12 points the loss stops changing after 5 outer steps
    L = opt.step(closure)
print(f"training loss: {L.item():.2e}")

# 3) and 4) prediction and its derivative on the fine grid (autograd w.r.t. the INPUT kappa)
kf = torch.tensor(k_fine, requires_grad=True)
E_pred = net(kf)
# E_pred[j] depends only on kf[j], so the gradient of the SUM w.r.t. kf is the vector of derivatives dE_pred[j]/dkappa_j.
# torch.autograd.grad returns a tuple (one entry per input); (dE_pred,) = ... unpacks its single element.
(dE_pred,) = torch.autograd.grad(E_pred.sum(), kf)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4))
axes[0].plot(k_fine, E_fine, "k", lw=2, label="exact")
axes[0].plot(k_fine, E_pred.detach(), "--", label="network")
axes[0].plot(k_train, E_train, "o", color="C3", label="12 training points")
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$E_0(\kappa)$"); axes[0].legend()
axes[1].semilogy(k_fine, np.abs(E_pred.detach().numpy() - E_fine))
axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$|E_0^{\rm net} - E_0^{\rm exact}|$")
axes[2].plot(k_fine, dE_fine, "k", lw=2, label="exact (Hellmann-Feynman)")
axes[2].plot(k_fine, dE_pred, "--", label="autograd of the network")
axes[2].set_ylabel(r"$dE_0/d\kappa$"); axes[2].legend()
for ax in axes: ax.set_xlabel(r"$\kappa$")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
inside = (k_fine >= k_train.min()) & (k_fine <= k_train.max())     # between the smallest and largest training kappa
err_E, err_dE = np.abs(E_pred.detach().numpy() - E_fine), np.abs(dE_pred.numpy() - dE_fine)
print(f"training kappa from {k_train.min():.2f} to {k_train.max():.2f}")
print(f"max error of E0 :  inside {err_E[inside].max():.1e},  outside {err_E[~inside].max():.1e}")
print(f"max error of dE0:  inside {err_dE[inside].max():.1e},  outside {err_dE[~inside].max():.1e}")
# Between the smallest and largest training kappa (interpolation) the errors are much smaller than outside the
# sampled range (extrapolation, see Section 10). Inside, the derivative is less accurate than the energy itself:
# the loss contains only values of E0, nothing constrains the slope directly. The network has 25 parameters
# for 12 data points, so it can pass through all of them; the fit is nevertheless smooth here because E0(kappa)
# itself is smooth. (Adding the Hellmann-Feynman derivatives to the loss is known as Sobolev training.)


training loss: 6.09e-07





training kappa from 1.03 to 9.62
max error of E0 :  inside 2.1e-03,  outside 7.8e-02
max error of dE0:  inside 1.5e-02,  outside 1.5e-01





Exercise 5 (advanced) — Two dimensions
The UAT holds in any dimension. Fit \(g(x,y) = \sin(2x)\cos(y) e^{-(x^2+y^2)/4}\) on \([-3,3]^2\) (a \(30\times30\) grid of training points) with nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, N), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(N, 1)) for \(N = 8, 32, 128\), using Adam (lr=1e-2, 1500 steps; kept small for speed, 3000 or more steps give smaller errors). Here nn.Linear(n_in, n_out) is the affine map \(\mathbf W\mathbf x + \mathbf b\) from \(n_{\rm in}\) to \(n_{\rm out}\) components (with trainable \(\mathbf W\) and \(\mathbf b\)), and nn.Sequential chains the layers, applying them one after another. Show the target, the fit and the error as images (imshow), one row per \(N\). The first lines of the solution build the data (you may copy them): torch.meshgrid(xs, xs, indexing="xy") returns two \(30\times30\) arrays X, Y with the \(x\) and \(y\) coordinates of all grid points (with "xy" the rows correspond to \(y\), the layout that imshow expects), and reshape(-1) flattens them into lists of 900 points.

Solution


Code
import torch.nn as nn
n_grid = 30
xs = torch.linspace(-3, 3, n_grid)
X, Y = torch.meshgrid(xs, xs, indexing="xy")
G = torch.sin(2 * X) * torch.cos(Y) * torch.exp(-(X**2 + Y**2) / 4)
inputs = torch.stack([X.reshape(-1), Y.reshape(-1)], dim=1)   # shape (900, 2): each row is a point (x, y)
targets = G.reshape(-1, 1)                                    # shape (900, 1)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(12, 11))
for row, N in enumerate([8, 32, 128]):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    # nn.Linear creates its weights and biases with PyTorch's default random initialisation (scaled by 1/sqrt(n_in))
    net2d = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, N), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(N, 1))
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(net2d.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
    for _ in range(1500):
        opt.zero_grad()
        L = torch.mean((net2d(inputs) - targets)**2)
        L.backward()
        opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        F_net = net2d(inputs).reshape(n_grid, n_grid)
    for ax, img, title in zip(axes[row], [G, F_net, F_net - G],
                              ["target", f"network N = {N}", f"error, MSE = {L.item():.1e}"]):
        im = ax.imshow(img, origin="lower", extent=[-3, 3, -3, 3], cmap="RdBu_r")
        fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8)
        ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
# The error decreases from N = 8 to N = 32; beyond that the result is limited by the 1500 Adam steps, not by N
# (N = 32 and N = 128 give the same MSE).

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
section: 1. Notation: a network as a composition of layers
text:
1. Notation: a network as a composition of layers
A fully connected (dense) network with layer sizes \(n_0, n_1, \dots, n_L\) maps an input \(\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}\) to an output in \(\mathbb R^{n_L}\) through \[\mathbf h^{(0)} = \mathbf x,\qquad \mathbf h^{(l)} = \sigma\big(\mathbf W^{(l)}\mathbf h^{(l-1)} + \mathbf b^{(l)}\big),\quad l = 1,\dots,L-1,\qquad
f(\mathbf x) = \mathbf W^{(L)}\mathbf h^{(L-1)} + \mathbf b^{(L)} .\] - \(\mathbf W^{(l)}\) is a matrix of shape \(n_l\times n_{l-1}\) and \(\mathbf b^{(l)}\) a vector of length \(n_l\): layer \(l\) has \(n_l(n_{l-1}+1)\) parameters. - \(\sigma\) is applied element-wise in the hidden layers. The last layer usually has no activation (regression), or one adapted to the task (e.g. softmax for classification, which in PyTorch is usually applied inside the loss function rather than as a layer; see Section 14.2). - In PyTorch one layer \(\mathbf h \mapsto \mathbf W\mathbf h + \mathbf b\) is nn.Linear(n_in, n_out); it stores weight with shape (n_out, n_in) and bias with shape (n_out,). - Data are processed in batches: an input tensor has shape (B, n_0), one row per sample, and the output has shape (B, n_L). For a batch, the layer computes H_out = H_in @ W.T + b. The transpose appears because every sample is a row of H_in: the row form of \(\mathbf h_{\rm out} = \mathbf W\mathbf h_{\rm in} + \mathbf b\) is \(\mathbf h_{\rm out}^T = \mathbf h_{\rm in}^T\mathbf W^T + \mathbf b^T\), applied to all rows at once.
The list \([n_0, n_1, \dots, n_L]\) together with the choice of \(\sigma\) is the architecture of the network.

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
section: 2. A function that draws network architectures
text:
2. A function that draws network architectures
Every architecture in this notebook is drawn with the following function. Each circle is a node (neuron), each grey line a weight. The function uses only basic plotting commands (plot, scatter, text); its code does not need to be studied to follow the rest of the notebook. Layers with more than max_nodes nodes are drawn shortened, with “…” marking the omitted nodes. The parameter count in the title is computed from the formula \(\sum_l n_l(n_{l-1}+1)\) above.


Code
def draw_network(layer_sizes, activations=None, title="", max_nodes=10, ax=None,
                 input_labels=None, output_labels=None):
    """
    Draw a fully connected network.
    layer_sizes : e.g. [1, 8, 1] = 1 input, one hidden layer with 8 nodes, 1 output
    activations : names of the activation functions of the hidden layers, e.g. ["tanh"]
    max_nodes   : larger layers are drawn with max_nodes nodes and a vertical "..." in the middle
    input_labels, output_labels : optional texts written next to the input and output nodes, e.g. ["$x$"]
    """
    if ax is None:
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(1.9 * len(layer_sizes) + 1, 4.2))
    n_layers = len(layer_sizes)
    positions = []                                   # list of (x, y) arrays, one per layer
    for i, n in enumerate(layer_sizes):
        shown = min(n, max_nodes)
        y = np.linspace(-1, 1, shown) if shown > 1 else np.array([0.0])
        positions.append((np.full(shown, float(i)), y * min(1.0, shown / max_nodes + 0.15)))
    # connections between neighbouring layers
    for i in range(n_layers - 1):
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = positions[i], positions[i + 1]
        for a in y0:
            for b in y1:
                ax.plot([x0[0], x1[0]], [a, b], color="0.7", lw=0.6, zorder=1)
    # nodes and labels
    for i, (n, (xs, ys)) in enumerate(zip(layer_sizes, positions)):
        if i == 0:
            color, name = "C2", "input"
        elif i == n_layers - 1:
            color, name = "C3", "output"
        else:
            act = activations[i - 1] if activations is not None else ""
            color, name = "C0", f"hidden {i}" + (f"\n{act}" if act else "")
        ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=260, color=color, edgecolor="k", zorder=3)
        if n > max_nodes:                            # mark omitted nodes
            ax.text(xs[0] + 0.2, 0.0, "...", rotation=90, fontsize=14, va="center", ha="center",
                    bbox=dict(facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", pad=1), zorder=4)
        ax.text(xs[0], -1.35, f"{name}\n{n} node" + ("s" if n > 1 else ""), ha="center", va="top", fontsize=10)
    if input_labels is not None:
        for y, lab in zip(positions[0][1], input_labels):
            ax.text(-0.18, y, lab, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=12)
    if output_labels is not None:
        for y, lab in zip(positions[-1][1], output_labels):
            ax.text(n_layers - 1 + 0.18, y, lab, ha="left", va="center", fontsize=12)
    n_params = sum(n_in * n_out + n_out for n_in, n_out in zip(layer_sizes[:-1], layer_sizes[1:]))
    ax.set_title((title + "\n" if title else "") + f"layer sizes {layer_sizes},  {n_params} parameters", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.8, n_layers - 0.2); ax.set_ylim(-2.1, 1.3)
    ax.axis("off")
    return ax

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
section: 3. Example A: one input, one hidden layer with \(N\) nodes, one output
text:
3. Example A: one input, one hidden layer with \(N\) nodes, one output
This is the network of the Universal Approximation Theorem from the lecture, \[f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} W^{(2)}_{i}\,\tanh\big(W^{(1)}_{i} x + b^{(1)}_i\big) + b^{(2)},\] with layer sizes \([1, N, 1]\). We take \(N = 8\).


Code
N = 8
draw_network([1, N, 1], activations=["tanh"], title="Example A", input_labels=["$x$"], output_labels=["$f(x)$"])
plt.show()






3.1 Way 1: nn.Sequential
nn.Sequential(layer_1, layer_2, ...) stores the layers in order. Calling the model applies them one after another to the input. This is the shortest way to write a network whose computation is a plain chain of layers.


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
model_seq = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(1, N),      # W^(1): shape (N, 1),  b^(1): shape (N,)
    nn.Tanh(),            # element-wise activation, no parameters
    nn.Linear(N, 1),      # W^(2): shape (1, N),  b^(2): shape (1,)
)
print(model_seq)


Sequential(
  (0): Linear(in_features=1, out_features=8, bias=True)
  (1): Tanh()
  (2): Linear(in_features=8, out_features=1, bias=True)
)


The layers are numbered 0, 1, 2 in the order given. The parameters carry the number of their layer in their name:


Code
for name, p in model_seq.named_parameters():
    print(f"{name:10s} shape {tuple(p.shape)}")
n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model_seq.parameters())
print("total number of parameters:", n_params, "  (formula: 3N + 1 =", 3 * N + 1, ")")
print("first layer:", model_seq[0])          # layers can be accessed by index


0.weight   shape (8, 1)
0.bias     shape (8,)
2.weight   shape (1, 8)
2.bias     shape (1,)
total number of parameters: 25   (formula: 3N + 1 = 25 )
first layer: Linear(in_features=1, out_features=8, bias=True)




3.2 Way 2: a class derived from nn.Module
The same network as a class. In __init__ the layers are created and stored as attributes (this registers their parameters); forward describes the computation.


Code
class OneHiddenLayer(nn.Module):
    """f(x) = W2 tanh(W1 x + b1) + b2  with N hidden nodes."""

    def __init__(self, n_hidden):
        super().__init__()                        # set up the internal bookkeeping of nn.Module
        self.hidden = nn.Linear(1, n_hidden)      # first layer: 1 -> n_hidden
        self.activation = nn.Tanh()
        self.output = nn.Linear(n_hidden, 1)      # second layer: n_hidden -> 1

    def forward(self, x):
        h = self.activation(self.hidden(x))       # hidden layer: shape (B, n_hidden)
        return self.output(h)                     # output: shape (B, 1)

torch.manual_seed(0)
model_cls = OneHiddenLayer(N)
print(model_cls)
for name, p in model_cls.named_parameters():
    print(f"{name:15s} shape {tuple(p.shape)}")


OneHiddenLayer(
  (hidden): Linear(in_features=1, out_features=8, bias=True)
  (activation): Tanh()
  (output): Linear(in_features=8, out_features=1, bias=True)
)
hidden.weight   shape (8, 1)
hidden.bias     shape (8,)
output.weight   shape (1, 8)
output.bias     shape (1,)


The parameter names now come from the attribute names (hidden.weight, …) instead of layer numbers; the shapes are the same.


3.3 Both ways give the same function
The two models were initialised with the same random seed, and the layers were created in the same order, so they even start with the same random numbers. To make the comparison independent of this, we copy the parameters of model_seq into model_cls explicitly and compare the outputs.
a.copy_(b) writes the values of b into the existing tensor a (the trailing underscore marks a method that changes the tensor in place). An assignment model_cls.hidden.weight = model_seq[0].weight would not copy anything: both models would then share one and the same tensor, and training one of them would change the other.


Code
with torch.no_grad():                                   # copying values is not part of any gradient computation
    model_cls.hidden.weight.copy_(model_seq[0].weight)
    model_cls.hidden.bias.copy_(model_seq[0].bias)
    model_cls.output.weight.copy_(model_seq[2].weight)
    model_cls.output.bias.copy_(model_seq[2].bias)

x = torch.linspace(-3, 3, 200).reshape(-1, 1)           # a batch of 200 inputs, shape (200, 1)
with torch.no_grad():
    y_seq, y_cls = model_seq(x), model_cls(x)
print("input shape :", tuple(x.shape), "  output shape:", tuple(y_seq.shape))
print("max |difference| between the two models:", (y_seq - y_cls).abs().max().item())


input shape : (200, 1)   output shape: (200, 1)
max |difference| between the two models: 0.0




3.4 The forward pass by hand
To see that there is nothing hidden in the model, we repeat the computation with the stored matrices, following the formula of Section 1. The argument of the activation, \(W^{(1)}_i x + b^{(1)}_i\), is called the pre-activation of node \(i\). In the left panel, ax.plot(x, h) receives an array h with \(N\) columns; matplotlib then draws one curve per column, i.e. one curve per hidden node.


Code
W1, b1 = model_seq[0].weight, model_seq[0].bias        # shapes (N, 1) and (N,)
W2, b2 = model_seq[2].weight, model_seq[2].bias        # shapes (1, N) and (1,)
with torch.no_grad():
    pre_activation = x @ W1.T + b1                      # (200, 1) @ (1, N) + (N,)  ->  (200, N)
    h = torch.tanh(pre_activation)                      # (200, N): the N hidden nodes for every input
    y_hand = h @ W2.T + b2                              # (200, N) @ (N, 1) + (1,)  ->  (200, 1)
print("shapes:", tuple(pre_activation.shape), tuple(h.shape), tuple(y_hand.shape))
print("max |model - by hand|:", (y_seq - y_hand).abs().max().item(), " (rounding of float32 numbers, about 1e-7)")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4))
axes[0].plot(x, h, lw=1)
axes[0].set_title(r"the $N$ hidden nodes $\tanh(W^{(1)}_i x + b^{(1)}_i)$"); axes[0].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[0].set_ylabel("$h_i(x)$")
axes[1].plot(x, y_seq, "k", lw=2)
axes[1].set_title("output $f(x)$ = weighted sum of the hidden nodes + $b^{(2)}$"); axes[1].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[1].set_ylabel("$f(x)$")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


shapes: (200, 8) (200, 8) (200, 1)
max |model - by hand|: 1.1920928955078125e-07  (rounding of float32 numbers, about 1e-7)





Each curve on the left is a smoothed step \(\tanh(W_i x + b_i)\) centred at \(x = -b_i/W_i\); \(|W_i|\) sets its steepness and the sign of \(W_i\) its direction. The initial weights are small (\(|W_i| \le 1\)), so the steps are gentle, and a node with \(W_i\) close to zero is almost constant (two such nodes appear here). The output on the right is the sum of these curves with the weights \(W^{(2)}_i\), plus \(b^{(2)}\). Training will move the centres, steepnesses and weights.


3.5 Way 3: explicit parameters and einsum
A third style writes the parameters as nn.Parameter tensors and the forward pass as index formulas with torch.einsum. For a batch \(x_{b}\) the layer formulas read \(h_{bj} = \tanh\big(\sum_i x_{bi} W^{(1)}_{ji} + b^{(1)}_j\big)\) and \(f_{bk} = \sum_j h_{bj}W^{(2)}_{kj} + b^{(2)}_k\), which einsum takes literally: "bi,ji->bj" (sum over \(i\), keep the batch index \(b\)).
This is still a class derived from nn.Module; what changes is that nothing is hidden in nn.Linear. The price is that the initialisation must be written by hand: below, PyTorch’s default for nn.Linear is reproduced (uniform in \([-1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}, 1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}]\) for weights and biases). The factor \(1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}\) keeps the sum \(\sum_i W_{ji} h_i\) over the \(n_{\rm in}\) inputs of a layer of order one whatever the width of the layer, so that the \(\tanh\) nodes start neither saturated nor all near zero.
Two functions appear here for the first time. torch.empty(n, m) reserves memory for a tensor of shape (n, m) without setting its values (the entries are whatever was in memory). .uniform_(a, b) then overwrites the entries, in place, with random numbers distributed uniformly in \([a, b]\).


Code
class OneHiddenLayerEinsum(nn.Module):
    # f(x) = W2 tanh(W1 x + b1) + b2, written with explicit parameters and einsum

    def __init__(self, n_hidden, n_in=1, n_out=1):
        super().__init__()
        bound1, bound2 = 1 / n_in**0.5, 1 / n_hidden**0.5
        # nn.Parameter registers a tensor as trainable; uniform_(a, b) fills it with uniform random numbers
        self.W1 = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(n_hidden, n_in).uniform_(-bound1, bound1))     # (N, n_in), as in nn.Linear
        self.b1 = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(n_hidden).uniform_(-bound1, bound1))           # (N,)
        self.W2 = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(n_out, n_hidden).uniform_(-bound2, bound2))    # (n_out, N)
        self.b2 = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(n_out).uniform_(-bound2, bound2))              # (n_out,)

    def forward(self, x):                                   # x: (B, n_in)
        h = torch.tanh(torch.einsum("bi,ji->bj", x, self.W1) + self.b1)    # h_bj = tanh(sum_i x_bi W1_ji + b1_j)
        return torch.einsum("bj,kj->bk", h, self.W2) + self.b2             # f_bk = sum_j h_bj W2_kj + b2_k

model_ein = OneHiddenLayerEinsum(N)
print("parameters:", [(name, tuple(p.shape)) for name, p in model_ein.named_parameters()])

with torch.no_grad():                                       # copy the parameters of the Sequential model
    model_ein.W1.copy_(model_seq[0].weight); model_ein.b1.copy_(model_seq[0].bias)
    model_ein.W2.copy_(model_seq[2].weight); model_ein.b2.copy_(model_seq[2].bias)
    print("max |Sequential - einsum model|:", (model_seq(x) - model_ein(x)).abs().max().item())


parameters: [('W1', (8, 1)), ('b1', (8,)), ('W2', (1, 8)), ('b2', (1,))]
max |Sequential - einsum model|: 1.1920928955078125e-07


All three ways give the same function. Way 3 is useful for teaching (the code is the formula), for operations that are not a plain matrix product (contractions over several axes, e.g. in attention layers of transformers or in tensor-network models used in physics), and for layers with unusual parameter shapes. For ordinary dense layers nn.Linear is preferable: it is equally fast (for such products einsum calls the same matrix-multiplication routine), shorter, and its initialisation is handled by PyTorch.
The network is untrained: its parameters are random, so \(f(x)\) is a random smooth function. Training (Section 10) changes the parameters so that \(f\) approximates data.
Which way to choose? All kinds of models are used in exactly the same way afterwards: model(x), model.parameters(), training. The choice depends only on how the data flow through the model; Section 8.3 discusses it in detail.

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
text:
4. Example B: two hidden layers
Layer sizes \([1, 16, 16, 1]\) with \(\tanh\) in both hidden layers: \[\mathbf h^{(1)} = \tanh(\mathbf W^{(1)}x + \mathbf b^{(1)}),\quad \mathbf h^{(2)} = \tanh(\mathbf W^{(2)}\mathbf h^{(1)} + \mathbf b^{(2)}),\quad f(x) = \mathbf W^{(3)}\mathbf h^{(2)} + b^{(3)} .\]


Code
draw_network([1, 16, 16, 1], activations=["tanh", "tanh"], title="Example B", input_labels=["$x$"], output_labels=["$f(x)$"])
plt.show()





Both constructions of Example B, followed by a comparison of their parameter counts with the formula \(\sum_l n_l(n_{l-1}+1)\):


Code
# Way 1: nn.Sequential
model_B_seq = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(1, 16), nn.Tanh(),       # hidden layer 1
    nn.Linear(16, 16), nn.Tanh(),      # hidden layer 2
    nn.Linear(16, 1),                  # output layer (no activation)
)

# Way 2: a class
class TwoHiddenLayers(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n1, n2):
        super().__init__()
        self.layer1 = nn.Linear(1, n1)
        self.layer2 = nn.Linear(n1, n2)
        self.layer3 = nn.Linear(n2, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        h1 = torch.tanh(self.layer1(x))      # the activation can also be applied as a function
        h2 = torch.tanh(self.layer2(h1))
        return self.layer3(h2)

model_B_cls = TwoHiddenLayers(16, 16)

for model in [model_B_seq, model_B_cls]:
    # type(model) is the class of the object, and .__name__ its name as a string
    print(type(model).__name__, ": parameters =", sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()),
          "  formula:", 16 * (1 + 1) + 16 * (16 + 1) + 1 * (16 + 1))


Sequential : parameters = 321   formula: 321
TwoHiddenLayers : parameters = 321   formula: 321


Way 3 for Example B: the parameters of all layers are kept in a nn.ParameterList, and forward applies the same einsum formula to every layer.
The loop over the layers uses zip(layer_sizes[:-1], layer_sizes[1:]). For layer_sizes = [1, 16, 16, 1], layer_sizes[:-1] is [1, 16, 16] (the last entry dropped) and layer_sizes[1:] is [16, 16, 1] (the first entry dropped); zip pairs them into (1, 16), (16, 16), (16, 1), the input and output sizes of every layer. This idiom is used for all automatically built networks below.


Code
class MLPEinsum(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, layer_sizes):
        super().__init__()
        self.weights, self.biases = nn.ParameterList(), nn.ParameterList()   # lists that register their parameters
        for n_in, n_out in zip(layer_sizes[:-1], layer_sizes[1:]):
            bound = 1 / n_in**0.5
            self.weights.append(nn.Parameter(torch.empty(n_out, n_in).uniform_(-bound, bound)))
            self.biases.append(nn.Parameter(torch.empty(n_out).uniform_(-bound, bound)))

    def forward(self, h):
        n_layers = len(self.weights)
        for l, (W, b) in enumerate(zip(self.weights, self.biases)):
            h = torch.einsum("bi,ji->bj", h, W) + b          # the same formula for every layer
            if l < n_layers - 1:                              # no activation after the last layer
                h = torch.tanh(h)
        return h

model_B_ein = MLPEinsum([1, 16, 16, 1])
print("parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in model_B_ein.parameters()), "(as for the other two ways: 321)")


parameters: 321 (as for the other two ways: 321)


In the class, the activation is applied with the function torch.tanh instead of a layer object nn.Tanh(): activations have no parameters, so both forms are equivalent. The parameter count follows \(n_1(n_0+1) + n_2(n_1+1) + n_3(n_2+1) = 32 + 272 + 17 = 321\).

5. Example C: several inputs and several outputs
Nothing changes in the construction except the sizes of the first and the last layer. A physics example: the input is a point \((x, y)\) in a plane, the output three numbers, e.g. a potential \(V\) and the two components of the force \((F_x, F_y)\). Layer sizes \([2, 32, 32, 3]\). The input batch has shape (B, 2) (one row = one point), the output (B, 3).


Code
draw_network([2, 32, 32, 3], activations=["tanh", "tanh"], title="Example C",
             input_labels=["$x$", "$y$"], output_labels=["$V$", "$F_x$", "$F_y$"])
plt.show()

model_C = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 32), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(32, 32), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(32, 3))
points = torch.rand(5, 2)                        # a batch of 5 points (x, y)
print("input shape :", tuple(points.shape))
print("output shape:", tuple(model_C(points).shape), " -> column 0: V, column 1: F_x, column 2: F_y")





input shape : (5, 2)
output shape: (5, 3)  -> column 0: V, column 1: F_x, column 2: F_y

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
section: 6. Example D: a classifier for images
text:
6. Example D: a classifier for images

6.1 The task and the data
In Examples A–C the network returned a number (regression). Here it has to decide which of several categories an input belongs to (classification). The categories are called classes. This word has nothing to do with Python classes: it is the standard name for the possible answers of a classifier.
The data set is MNIST, the standard first example of image classification (lecture; Section 14 trains the network of this example on it): 70 000 grey-scale images of handwritten digits, 60 000 for training and 10 000 for testing, each of \(28\times28\) pixels and each labelled with the digit it shows. The classes are therefore the ten digits \(0, 1, \dots, 9\), and the label of an image is its class, an integer from 0 to 9.
The package torchvision (installed in Colab together with PyTorch) contains a loader for MNIST. datasets.MNIST(root="data", train=False, download=True) downloads the data (about 12 MB, a few seconds) into a folder data the first time it is called and reads it from there afterwards; train=False selects the 10 000 test images, which are enough for looking at the data. The download prints a long progress bar; contextlib.redirect_stdout and redirect_stderr send this text into an unused string buffer (io.StringIO()) instead of the screen. If the download fails (for example without internet access), the except branch replaces the images by random numbers, so that the rest of the notebook still runs.
.data holds the images as one tensor of shape \((10000, 28, 28)\) with integer pixel values from 0 (background) to 255 (full ink intensity), and .targets the labels. torch.bincount(labels) counts how often each value \(0, 1, \dots, 9\) occurs.


Code
import contextlib, io

try:
    from torchvision import datasets
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()), contextlib.redirect_stderr(io.StringIO()):
        mnist = datasets.MNIST(root="data", train=False, download=True)
    images_raw, labels = mnist.data, mnist.targets
    print("MNIST test set loaded")
except Exception as err:
    print("MNIST could not be loaded:", err)
    print("random images are used instead")
    images_raw = torch.randint(0, 256, (10000, 28, 28), dtype=torch.uint8)
    labels = torch.randint(0, 10, (10000,))

print("images:", tuple(images_raw.shape), images_raw.dtype,
      "  pixel values from", images_raw.min().item(), "to", images_raw.max().item())
print("labels:", tuple(labels.shape), "  first ten labels:", labels[:10].tolist())
print("number of images per class 0..9:", torch.bincount(labels).tolist())


MNIST test set loaded
images: (10000, 28, 28) torch.uint8   pixel values from 0 to 255
labels: (10000,)   first ten labels: [7, 2, 1, 0, 4, 1, 4, 9, 5, 9]
number of images per class 0..9: [980, 1135, 1032, 1010, 982, 892, 958, 1028, 974, 1009]


The ten classes are about equally frequent (between about 890 and 1140 images each), so a classifier that guesses at random is right in about 10% of the cases.
Three examples of every class. torch.nonzero(labels == k) returns the positions of all images with label \(k\) (as a column, hence [:3, 0] for the first three); imshow draws a \(28\times28\) array as an image, and the colour map "gray_r" (reversed grey) shows 0 as white and 255 as black, as on paper.


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 10, figsize=(12, 4))
for k in range(10):
    positions = torch.nonzero(labels == k)[:3, 0]       # first three images of class k
    for row in range(3):
        ax = axes[row, k]
        ax.imshow(images_raw[positions[row]], cmap="gray_r")
        ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
        if row == 0:
            ax.set_title(f"class {k}")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The network does not see a picture but \(28\times28 = 784\) numbers. The first test image with its pixel values written into the cells (only the non-zero ones; all other pixels are 0):


Code
img = images_raw[0]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
ax.imshow(img, cmap="gray_r")
for i in range(28):                          # row
    for j in range(28):                      # column
        if img[i, j] > 0:
            ax.text(j, i, str(img[i, j].item()), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6, color="tab:red")
ax.set_title(f"test image 0, label {labels[0].item()}: a 28 x 28 array of integers 0..255")
plt.show()







6.2 The network
The network for these images, as in the lecture: a \(28\times28\) image is flattened to a vector of \(784\) pixel values, two hidden layers with ReLU, and \(10\) outputs, one per class. The outputs are arbitrary real numbers (logits); softmax turns them into probabilities \(q_k\), \(k = 0, \dots, 9\), which are compared with the true label by the cross-entropy (lecture). The predicted class is the one with the largest probability (argmax). nn.Flatten() is a layer without parameters that reshapes (B, 28, 28) into (B, 784).
The pixel values are divided by 255 and converted to floating-point numbers (.float()), so that the inputs lie in \([0, 1]\): inputs of order one (the default initialisation of nn.Linear assumes inputs of order one; Section 10.1 explains what happens otherwise).
Two choices differ from Examples A–C: - ReLU instead of tanh. \(\mathrm{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z)\) is cheap to compute and does not saturate for \(z > 0\), which makes it the standard choice for classifiers and deep networks. A ReLU network is piecewise linear in its input. For regression of smooth physical functions (Examples A–C, Section 10) \(\tanh\) is preferred, because the fitted function is then smooth and can be differentiated any number of times. - The widths 128 and 64. They are illustrative; widths of order 10–1000 are all in use for this task. Decreasing widths (\(784\to128\to64\to10\)), which compress the input step by step, are a common convention but not a requirement. The same holds for the widths 8, 16 and 32 in Examples A–C.


Code
draw_network([784, 128, 64, 10], activations=["ReLU", "ReLU"], title="Example D",
             output_labels=[f"{k}" for k in range(10)])
plt.show()

model_D = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Flatten(),                         # (B, 28, 28) -> (B, 784)
    nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(64, 10),                    # logits, one per class
)
images = images_raw.float() / 255         # integers 0..255 -> floats in [0, 1]
logits = model_D(images[:5])              # the first five test images
probs = torch.softmax(logits, dim=1)      # softmax over the class dimension
print("logits shape:", tuple(logits.shape), "  largest |logit|:", round(logits.abs().max().item(), 3))
# .detach() is needed before .numpy() because probs was computed with gradient tracking
for i in range(5):
    print(f"image {i}: true class {labels[i].item()},  predicted {probs[i].argmax().item()},  probabilities",
          probs[i].detach().numpy().round(2))
# float32 rounding: the sum differs from 1 by about 1e-7
print("sum of the probabilities of image 0:", probs[0].sum().item())

predicted = model_D(images).argmax(dim=1)                       # predicted class of all 10 000 test images
print(f"fraction of correctly classified test images: {(predicted == labels).float().mean().item():.3f}")
print("how often each class 0..9 is predicted:", torch.bincount(predicted, minlength=10).tolist())
print("parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in model_D.parameters()))





logits shape: (5, 10)   largest |logit|: 0.211
image 0: true class 7,  predicted 7,  probabilities [0.11 0.09 0.11 0.09 0.09 0.11 0.08 0.12 0.09 0.11]
image 1: true class 2,  predicted 7,  probabilities [0.11 0.09 0.1  0.09 0.09 0.11 0.09 0.12 0.09 0.12]
image 2: true class 1,  predicted 7,  probabilities [0.11 0.09 0.11 0.09 0.09 0.11 0.09 0.11 0.09 0.11]
image 3: true class 0,  predicted 7,  probabilities [0.11 0.09 0.1  0.09 0.1  0.11 0.09 0.12 0.09 0.11]
image 4: true class 4,  predicted 7,  probabilities [0.11 0.09 0.11 0.09 0.09 0.11 0.09 0.12 0.09 0.11]
sum of the probabilities of image 0: 0.9999999403953552
fraction of correctly classified test images: 0.105
how often each class 0..9 is predicted: [44, 0, 0, 0, 0, 4, 0, 9918, 0, 34]
parameters: 109386


The untrained classifier assigns roughly equal probabilities (\(\approx 0.1\)) to all ten classes. The largest of these nearly equal numbers, however, belongs to the same class for almost every image (the line “how often each class 0..9 is predicted” printed above): the small differences between the ten logits come mostly from the random initial weights and biases, which are the same for every input, and only a little from the image. The fraction of correct answers, about 10%, is therefore roughly the share of that one class among the test images: no better than guessing. The probabilities are all close to 1/10 because of the initialisation: the ten logits of the untrained network are small (the largest absolute value is printed above), and the softmax \(q_k = e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}\) of ten nearly equal numbers is nearly \(1/10\) each. Training with the cross-entropy loss (Section 14) changes the \(109\,386\) parameters so that the probability of the correct class approaches 1. Almost all of these parameters belong to the first layer (\(784\times128\) weights), as the summary in Section 9 shows.

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
section: 7. Building networks automatically from a list of layer sizes
text:
7. Building networks automatically from a list of layer sizes
Writing every layer by hand is error-prone for deep networks. Since a dense network is determined by the list \([n_0, \dots, n_L]\) and the activation, the layers can be created in a loop.

7.1 With nn.Sequential
nn.Sequential(*layers) accepts a Python list of layers; the star unpacks the list into separate arguments.


Code
def make_mlp(layer_sizes, activation=nn.Tanh):
    """Dense network with the given layer sizes; `activation` (a class such as nn.Tanh) after every hidden layer."""
    layers = []
    for i in range(len(layer_sizes) - 1):
        n_in, n_out = layer_sizes[i], layer_sizes[i + 1]
        layers.append(nn.Linear(n_in, n_out))
        is_last_layer = (i == len(layer_sizes) - 2)
        if not is_last_layer:                     # no activation after the output layer
            layers.append(activation())           # a new activation object for every layer
    return nn.Sequential(*layers)

model_auto = make_mlp([1, 32, 32, 32, 1], activation=nn.Tanh)
print(model_auto)
print("parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in model_auto.parameters()))
draw_network([1, 32, 32, 32, 1], activations=["tanh"] * 3, title="make_mlp([1, 32, 32, 32, 1])")
plt.show()


Sequential(
  (0): Linear(in_features=1, out_features=32, bias=True)
  (1): Tanh()
  (2): Linear(in_features=32, out_features=32, bias=True)
  (3): Tanh()
  (4): Linear(in_features=32, out_features=32, bias=True)
  (5): Tanh()
  (6): Linear(in_features=32, out_features=1, bias=True)
)
parameters: 2209





The same function produces the networks of Sections 3–5; Example D (Section 6) additionally needs nn.Flatten() in front and ReLU activations (activation=nn.ReLU). For instance make_mlp([1, 8, 1]) is Example A and make_mlp([2, 32, 32, 3]) is Example C. Width and depth can now be varied with one argument:


Code
for depth in [1, 2, 4, 8]:
    sizes = [1] + [32] * depth + [1]
    m = make_mlp(sizes)
    print(f"{depth} hidden layers of width 32: layer sizes {sizes}, parameters = {sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters())}")


1 hidden layers of width 32: layer sizes [1, 32, 1], parameters = 97
2 hidden layers of width 32: layer sizes [1, 32, 32, 1], parameters = 1153
4 hidden layers of width 32: layer sizes [1, 32, 32, 32, 32, 1], parameters = 3265
8 hidden layers of width 32: layer sizes [1, 32, 32, 32, 32, 32, 32, 32, 32, 1], parameters = 7489


Every additional hidden layer of width 32 adds \(32\times(32+1) = 1056\) parameters.


7.2 With a class and nn.ModuleList
In a class, a variable number of layers is stored in an nn.ModuleList, a list that registers the parameters of its elements. The loop over the layers is then written in forward. This form is useful when forward has to do something between the layers (Section 8).
The argument activation has a different form in the two constructions. make_mlp receives a class (nn.Tanh) and creates a new layer object activation() for every position in the chain, because nn.Sequential accepts only layer objects. In forward of the class below any function can be called directly, so the function torch.tanh is passed.


Code
class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, layer_sizes, activation=torch.tanh):
        super().__init__()
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList(
            [nn.Linear(n_in, n_out) for n_in, n_out in zip(layer_sizes[:-1], layer_sizes[1:])]
        )
        self.activation = activation

    def forward(self, x):
        for layer in self.layers[:-1]:            # all layers except the last one
            x = self.activation(layer(x))
        return self.layers[-1](x)                 # last layer without activation

model_list = MLP([1, 32, 32, 32, 1])
print("parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in model_list.parameters()))
print("number of Linear layers:", len(model_list.layers))


parameters: 2209
number of Linear layers: 4




7.3 A common mistake: a plain Python list
If the layers are kept in an ordinary Python list, nn.Module does not see them: their parameters are not registered, model.parameters() does not contain them, and an optimiser would never change them. No error is raised.


Code
class BrokenMLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, layer_sizes):
        super().__init__()
        self.layers = [nn.Linear(a, b) for a, b in zip(layer_sizes[:-1], layer_sizes[1:])]   # plain list: WRONG

    def forward(self, x):
        for layer in self.layers[:-1]:
            x = torch.tanh(layer(x))
        return self.layers[-1](x)

broken = BrokenMLP([1, 32, 32, 1])
print("output shape:", tuple(broken(torch.zeros(3, 1)).shape), "  <- forward works")
print("registered parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in broken.parameters()), "  <- but there are none")


output shape: (3, 1)   <- forward works
registered parameters: 0   <- but there are none

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
text:
8. Architectures beyond nn.Sequential

8.1 A skip (residual) connection
In a residual layer the input is added to the output: \(\mathbf h \mapsto \mathbf h + \tanh(\mathbf W\mathbf h + \mathbf b)\). Such connections make very deep networks trainable (ResNets). The addition of the input cannot be expressed as a chain of layers, so a class is needed.


Code
class ResidualMLP(nn.Module):
    """input layer -> n_blocks residual blocks of width `width` -> output layer."""

    def __init__(self, n_in, width, n_blocks, n_out):
        super().__init__()
        self.input_layer = nn.Linear(n_in, width)
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(width, width) for _ in range(n_blocks)])
        self.output_layer = nn.Linear(width, n_out)

    def forward(self, x):
        h = torch.tanh(self.input_layer(x))
        for block in self.blocks:
            h = h + torch.tanh(block(h))          # skip connection: the input of the block is added to its output
        return self.output_layer(h)

res = ResidualMLP(n_in=1, width=16, n_blocks=4, n_out=1)
print("output shape:", tuple(res(torch.zeros(5, 1)).shape), "  parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in res.parameters()))


output shape: (5, 1)   parameters: 1137




8.2 A physics constraint built into the network
A wavefunction of a particle in a box \([0, 1]\) must vanish at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 1\). An unconstrained network \(\mathrm{NN}(x)\) does not satisfy this, but the ansatz \[\psi(x) = x\,(1-x)\,\mathrm{NN}(x)\] does, for every value of the parameters. The boundary conditions are then never violated during training. The network inside can be any model, e.g. one made with make_mlp.


Code
class BoxWavefunction(nn.Module):
    """psi(x) = x (1 - x) NN(x): vanishes at x = 0 and x = 1 for any parameters of NN."""

    def __init__(self, layer_sizes):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = make_mlp(layer_sizes)          # a network inside a network: its parameters are registered as well

    def forward(self, x):
        return x * (1 - x) * self.net(x)

psi = BoxWavefunction([1, 16, 16, 1])
x_box = torch.linspace(0, 1, 101).reshape(-1, 1)
with torch.no_grad():
    values = psi(x_box)
print("psi(0) =", values[0].item(), "  psi(1) =", values[-1].item())
print("parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in psi.parameters()), "(all inside psi.net)")


psi(0) = -0.0   psi(1) = -0.0
parameters: 321 (all inside psi.net)


Both boundary values are zero. The printed sign of \(-0.0\) is an artefact of floating-point numbers, which have a signed zero: \(0\) multiplied by a negative number gives \(-0.0\), which equals \(0.0\) in every comparison.


8.3 When to use nn.Sequential and when a class
The rule. nn.Sequential describes exactly one kind of computation: one input tensor passes through a fixed chain of layers, and the output of each layer is the input of the next one. Whenever the computation can be drawn as such a chain, nn.Sequential is the shortest and clearest choice. For everything else a class with a forward method is needed, because forward can contain arbitrary Python code.

In practice the two are combined: the chain-like parts of a model are written as nn.Sequential blocks (or built with make_mlp), and a class connects them. The following class shows several items of the table at once: an even wavefunction \(\psi(x) = A\,[\,g(x) + g(-x)\,]\), where the same network \(g\) is applied twice (shared weights enforce \(\psi(-x) = \psi(x)\)), \(A\) is a trainable number outside any layer, and forward can also return the intermediate values \(g(\pm x)\).


Code
class EvenFunction(nn.Module):
    # psi(x) = A * (g(x) + g(-x)): even in x for any parameters of g and any A

    def __init__(self, layer_sizes):
        super().__init__()
        self.g = make_mlp(layer_sizes)                 # a Sequential block inside the class
        self.amplitude = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(1))   # a trainable number that is not part of any layer;
                                                       # it starts at 1 (any non-zero value works, it is trained)

    def forward(self, x, return_parts=False):
        g_plus = self.g(x)                             # the same network (same weights) ...
        g_minus = self.g(-x)                           # ... applied a second time
        psi = self.amplitude * (g_plus + g_minus)
        if return_parts:                               # ordinary Python control flow
            return psi, g_plus, g_minus
        return psi

even = EvenFunction([1, 16, 16, 1])
x_sym = torch.linspace(-2, 2, 9).reshape(-1, 1)
with torch.no_grad():
    psi_vals, gp, gm = even(x_sym, return_parts=True)
print("psi(x)  :", psi_vals.squeeze().numpy().round(4))
print("psi(-x) :", psi_vals.flip(0).squeeze().numpy().round(4), "  <- identical: the symmetry holds exactly")
print("parameters:", [name for name, _ in even.named_parameters()][:3], "...")
print("number of parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in even.parameters()), "= parameters of g + 1 (the amplitude)")


psi(x)  : [-0.2476 -0.2854 -0.3438 -0.4036 -0.4297 -0.4036 -0.3438 -0.2854 -0.2476]
psi(-x) : [-0.2476 -0.2854 -0.3438 -0.4036 -0.4297 -0.4036 -0.3438 -0.2854 -0.2476]   <- identical: the symmetry holds exactly
parameters: ['amplitude', 'g.0.weight', 'g.0.bias'] ...
number of parameters: 322 = parameters of g + 1 (the amplitude)


flip(0) reverses the order of the rows; since the grid is symmetric around 0, it turns the values at \(x\) into the values at \(-x\). The network \(g\) appears once in the list of parameters although it is used twice: its weights are shared.

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
text:
9. Inspecting a model
Three tools are used constantly: - named_parameters() — names and tensors of all trainable parameters; - state_dict() — a dictionary name \(\to\) tensor with all parameters (used for saving, Section 12); - passing a batch through the layers one by one and printing the shapes — the quickest way to find shape errors.


Code
def summary(model, x):
    """Print the output shape and the number of parameters of every layer of an nn.Sequential model for the input batch x."""
    print(f"{'layer':35s} {'output shape':15s} parameters")
    print(f"{'input':35s} {str(tuple(x.shape)):15s}")
    total = 0
    for layer in model:                             # an nn.Sequential can be iterated over
        x = layer(x)
        n = sum(p.numel() for p in layer.parameters())
        total += n
        print(f"{str(layer):35s} {str(tuple(x.shape)):15s} {n}")
    print(f"total parameters: {total}")

summary(model_D, images[:4])                    # four MNIST test images (Section 6)
