title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
text:
10. The training loop in detail

10.1 Data
We simulate a measurement of a damped oscillation, \(y(t) = e^{-0.2t}\cos(2t)\), at \(K = 200\) random times \(t\in[0, 10]\) with Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(0.05\). The data are split at random into three parts with different roles: - the training set (120 points) is used to change the parameters; - the validation set (40 points) is used to monitor training and to make choices (architecture, learning rate, number of epochs); the parameters never see it, but our decisions do; - the test set (40 points) is used once, at the very end, to estimate how well the final model works on new data. Because no decision was based on it, this estimate is not biased by our choices.
The fractions 60 / 20 / 20 % are a convention; splits between about 60–80 % for training and 10–20 % each for validation and test are common. The exact values are not critical, but the validation and test sets must contain enough points for their mean losses to be meaningful averages. The noise level \(0.05\) is also arbitrary: small compared with the amplitude 1 of the signal, but large enough to be visible in the plot.
Two practical details: - PyTorch layers expect inputs of shape (B, n_in), here (B, 1); targets must have the same shape as the outputs, (B, 1). - The input \(t\in[0, 10]\) is rescaled to \([-1, 1]\). With one input, the default initialisation of nn.Linear draws the first-layer weights and biases uniformly from \([-1, 1]\) (the bound is \(1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}} = 1\)), so the pre-activations \(W t + b\) are of order \(|t|\). For \(t\sim10\) most of them lie far in the flat part of \(\tanh\) (\(\tanh 3 \approx 0.995\)): these nodes start saturated, their gradients are small, and training slows down (Section 13.4 shows the effect).
Two new operations appear in the code. torch.randperm(K) returns the integers \(0, \dots, K-1\) in random order; the first 120 of them become the training indices, and so on. It receives its own random-number generator torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), so that the split is reproducible and does not depend on how many random numbers were drawn earlier in the notebook. X_all[train_idx], indexing with a tensor of integers, selects the rows with these indices in this order; since inputs and targets are indexed with the same indices, every input stays paired with its target.


Code
def damped_oscillation(t):
    return np.exp(-0.2 * t) * np.cos(2 * t)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
K = 200
t_data = rng.uniform(0, 10, K)
y_data = damped_oscillation(t_data) + 0.05 * rng.normal(size=K)

def scale(t):
    """Map t in [0, 10] to [-1, 1]."""
    return t / 5.0 - 1.0

# tensors of shape (K, 1); float32 is the PyTorch default and matches the model parameters
X_all = torch.tensor(scale(t_data), dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
Y_all = torch.tensor(y_data, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)

perm = torch.randperm(K, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0))   # random order of the indices 0..K-1
train_idx, val_idx, test_idx = perm[:120], perm[120:160], perm[160:]   # 120 / 40 / 40 points
X_train, Y_train = X_all[train_idx], Y_all[train_idx]
X_val, Y_val = X_all[val_idx], Y_all[val_idx]
X_test, Y_test = X_all[test_idx], Y_all[test_idx]
print("training set  :", tuple(X_train.shape), tuple(Y_train.shape))
print("validation set:", tuple(X_val.shape), tuple(Y_val.shape))
print("test set      :", tuple(X_test.shape), tuple(Y_test.shape), " <- not used until Section 12")

t_plot = np.linspace(0, 10, 500)
X_plot = torch.tensor(scale(t_plot), dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.5))
ax.plot(t_plot, damped_oscillation(t_plot), "k", lw=1, label="true function (unknown in practice)")
# t_data is a NumPy array, so it is indexed with the NumPy version of the index tensor
ax.plot(t_data[train_idx.numpy()], Y_train, "o", ms=4, label="training data")
ax.plot(t_data[val_idx.numpy()], Y_val, "s", ms=4, label="validation data")
ax.plot(t_data[test_idx.numpy()], Y_test, "^", ms=4, label="test data")
ax.set_xlabel("$t$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$"); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show()


training set  : (120, 1) (120, 1)
validation set: (40, 1) (40, 1)
test set      : (40, 1) (40, 1)  <- not used until Section 12







10.2 Model, loss function, optimiser

model: make_mlp([1, 32, 32, 1]);
loss function: nn.MSELoss() computes \(\frac1B\sum_i (f(x_i) - y_i)^2\) for a batch (equivalent to torch.mean((pred - y)**2));
optimiser: an object from torch.optim that holds references to the parameters and implements the update rule.

Two hidden layers of 32 nodes are a modest size for a one-dimensional function with about three periods of oscillation on the interval; Section 12 compares this choice with smaller and larger networks. The learning rate 0.1 of SGD is arbitrary here: the next cell performs a single step only, to check the update rule, and any value would serve. torch.manual_seed(1) immediately before the model is created fixes its initial parameters, so that the runs below start from the same point and can be compared; the value of the seed is arbitrary.


Code
torch.manual_seed(1)
model = make_mlp([1, 32, 32, 1])
loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)     # plain gradient descent first, to check it by hand




10.3 One training step in slow motion
One step consists of five lines. We follow three of the parameters (the first three biases of the first layer) and their gradients through the step, and check that optimizer.step() for SGD is exactly the update \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,\partial\mathcal L/\partial\theta\), where \(\theta\) is any parameter, \(\mathcal L\) the loss and \(\eta\) the learning rate (lr).


Code
p = model[0].bias                                   # a parameter tensor of shape (32,); we print its first 3 entries
print("before the step:     p[:3] =", p[:3].detach().numpy(), "  p.grad =", p.grad)

# 1) forward pass: predictions for the whole training set
pred = model(X_train)                               # shape (120, 1)
# 2) loss: a single number (a tensor with one element) that depends on all parameters
loss = loss_fn(pred, Y_train)
print("loss:", loss.item())
# 3) reset the gradients stored from a previous step (here there are none yet, but this line is always needed)
optimizer.zero_grad()
# 4) backward pass: compute d loss / d parameter for every parameter, stored in .grad
loss.backward()
print("after backward():    p.grad[:3] =", p.grad[:3].numpy())
p_old, grad_old = p.detach().clone(), p.grad.clone()  # copies, for the check below
# 5) update the parameters with the rule of the optimiser
optimizer.step()
print("after step():        p[:3] =", p[:3].detach().numpy())
print("p_old - lr * grad:         ", (p_old - 0.1 * grad_old)[:3].numpy())
print("max |difference|:", (p.detach() - (p_old - 0.1 * grad_old)).abs().max().item())


before the step:     p[:3] = [ 0.6600598 -0.9111377 -0.9508084]   p.grad = None
loss: 0.21944643557071686
after backward():    p.grad[:3] = [ 0.0114674  -0.01462021  0.01155732]
after step():        p[:3] = [ 0.6589131  -0.90967566 -0.95196414]
p_old - lr * grad:          [ 0.6589131  -0.90967566 -0.95196414]
max |difference|: 0.0


Before the first backward() no gradient has been computed, so p.grad is None rather than a tensor of zeros. The copies p_old, grad_old are made with clone() because optimizer.step() changes p in place: without clone(), p_old would be a second name for the same memory and would change together with p. detach() excludes the copy from the gradient computation.
The optimiser changed every parameter by \(-\eta\times\) its gradient, as gradient descent prescribes. More advanced optimisers (momentum, Adam) use the same .grad tensors but a different update rule.


10.4 The complete loop (full batch)
Repeating the five lines gives the training loop. In every iteration we also compute the validation loss, inside torch.no_grad() (no gradients are needed for monitoring, which saves memory and time). We use Adam (an optimiser that adapts the step size of every parameter using running averages of its gradients; see the lecture), which converges faster here.
The learning rate \(10^{-2}\) is a common starting value for Adam on small problems. In this example values between about \(3\cdot10^{-3}\) and \(3\cdot10^{-2}\) bring the training loss to the noise level within 2000 steps; with \(10^{-3}\) the loss decreases more slowly and reaches the noise level only near the end of the 2000 steps, and with \(10^{-1}\) the loss fluctuates from step to step. With \(10^{-2}\) the training loss is within a few per cent of its final value after about 1000 steps; the number of steps, 2000, leaves a margin and is otherwise arbitrary.


Code
torch.manual_seed(1)
model = make_mlp([1, 32, 32, 1])
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
n_steps = 2000
train_hist, val_hist = [], []

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for step in range(n_steps):
    pred = model(X_train)                         # 1) forward
    loss = loss_fn(pred, Y_train)                 # 2) loss
    optimizer.zero_grad()                         # 3) reset gradients
    loss.backward()                               # 4) backward
    optimizer.step()                              # 5) update

    with torch.no_grad():                         # monitoring only
        val_loss = loss_fn(model(X_val), Y_val)
    train_hist.append(loss.item())
    val_hist.append(val_loss.item())
print(f"{n_steps} steps in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s;  final training loss {train_hist[-1]:.2e}, validation loss {val_hist[-1]:.2e}")
print(f"noise variance 0.05^2 = {0.05**2:.1e}")


2000 steps in 1.2 s;  final training loss 2.67e-03, validation loss 4.64e-03
noise variance 0.05^2 = 2.5e-03


Left: training and validation loss versus the step (logarithmic scale). Right: the trained network on a dense grid of times, together with the training data and the true function.


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4))
axes[0].semilogy(train_hist, label="training loss"); axes[0].semilogy(val_hist, label="validation loss")
axes[0].axhline(0.05**2, color="gray", ls=":", label="noise variance")
axes[0].set_xlabel("step"); axes[0].set_ylabel("MSE"); axes[0].legend()
with torch.no_grad():
    y_fit = model(X_plot)
axes[1].plot(t_plot, damped_oscillation(t_plot), "k", lw=1, label="true function")
axes[1].plot(t_data[train_idx.numpy()], Y_train, "o", ms=3, alpha=0.5, label="training data")
axes[1].plot(t_plot, y_fit, "C3", lw=2, label="network")
axes[1].set_xlabel("$t$"); axes[1].set_ylabel("$y$"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The training loss decreases to about the variance of the noise, \(0.05^2 = 2.5\cdot10^{-3}\): the remaining error is the noise in the data, which no model can predict. Indeed, if the network were exactly the true function \(g\), then \(f(t_i) - y_i = g(t_i) - (g(t_i) + \varepsilon_i) = -\varepsilon_i\), and the mean of \(\varepsilon_i^2\) over many points is the variance \(\sigma^2 = 0.05^2\). A training loss far below \(\sigma^2\) would mean that the network reproduces the noise itself. The validation loss is somewhat larger (printed above): with only 120 training points the network also fits part of the noise of these particular points, which does not carry over to new points. The difference between training and validation loss measures this effect; it becomes large when a network overfits.

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
text:
11. Mini-batches, epochs and validation

11.1 Mini-batches
For large data sets the full-batch loss is too expensive to compute in every step. The training set is then split into mini-batches; every step uses one mini-batch, and one pass over all mini-batches is an epoch. The gradient of a mini-batch is a noisy estimate of the full gradient (this is stochastic gradient descent). PyTorch provides two helpers: - TensorDataset(X, Y) pairs inputs with targets; - DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=..., shuffle=True) returns the mini-batches of one epoch, in a new random order every epoch.
The batch size is a free choice; powers of two between 16 and 256 are customary. Smaller batches give noisier gradients and more updates per epoch, larger batches the opposite. Here 32 is chosen so that an epoch of 120 samples consists of a few (four) steps.


Code
from torch.utils.data import TensorDataset, DataLoader

train_set = TensorDataset(X_train, Y_train)
loader = DataLoader(train_set, batch_size=32, shuffle=True)

print("number of training samples:", len(train_set))
print("mini-batches per epoch    :", len(loader), " (= 120 / 32 rounded up; the last batch has 24 samples)")
for i, (xb, yb) in enumerate(loader):              # one epoch
    print(f"  batch {i}: inputs {tuple(xb.shape)}, targets {tuple(yb.shape)}")


number of training samples: 120
mini-batches per epoch    : 4  (= 120 / 32 rounded up; the last batch has 24 samples)
  batch 0: inputs (32, 1), targets (32, 1)
  batch 1: inputs (32, 1), targets (32, 1)
  batch 2: inputs (32, 1), targets (32, 1)
  batch 3: inputs (24, 1), targets (24, 1)




11.2 The loop with mini-batches
The five lines are the same; they are now inside a loop over the mini-batches, which is inside a loop over the epochs. The training loss of an epoch is the plain average of its mini-batch losses (np.mean(batch_losses)). It is collected while the parameters are still changing and it gives the shorter last batch (24 samples) the same weight as the others, so it differs slightly from the loss of the final model on the full training set.
model.train() and model.eval() switch layers such as dropout and batch normalisation (introduced later in the course) between their training and evaluation behaviour. Our model has no such layers, so the calls change nothing here, but they belong to the standard loop.


Code
torch.manual_seed(1)
model_mb = make_mlp([1, 32, 32, 1])
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model_mb.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
n_epochs = 500                                     # 500 epochs x 4 batches = 2000 steps, as in Section 10.4
train_hist_mb, val_hist_mb = [], []

for epoch in range(n_epochs):
    model_mb.train()
    batch_losses = []
    for xb, yb in loader:
        loss = loss_fn(model_mb(xb), yb)           # forward + loss on one mini-batch
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        batch_losses.append(loss.item())
    model_mb.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        val_hist_mb.append(loss_fn(model_mb(X_val), Y_val).item())
    train_hist_mb.append(np.mean(batch_losses))

print(f"final training loss {train_hist_mb[-1]:.2e}, validation loss {val_hist_mb[-1]:.2e}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.semilogy(np.arange(1, n_steps + 1), val_hist, label="full batch (1 step per epoch)")
# epoch e of the mini-batch run ends after e * 4 updates: both curves are plotted against the number of updates
ax.semilogy(np.arange(1, n_epochs + 1) * len(loader), val_hist_mb, label="mini-batches of 32 (4 steps per epoch)")
ax.axhline(0.05**2, color="gray", ls=":", label="noise variance")
ax.set_xlabel("number of parameter updates"); ax.set_ylabel("validation MSE"); ax.legend()
plt.show()


final training loss 2.83e-03, validation loss 4.65e-03





Both runs perform 2000 parameter updates. The mini-batch curve is noisier, because every step uses a different random subset of the data. For this small data set the full batch is cheap; for real data sets (millions of samples) only mini-batches are feasible.

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
section: 12. A reusable training function; saving and loading a model
text:
12. A reusable training function; saving and loading a model
The loop of Section 11.2 is written once as a function and then used to compare architectures.
The four architectures span almost three orders of magnitude in the number of parameters (13 to 8513), from too small to more than enough; any similar sequence shows the same trend. The default n_epochs=300 (1200 updates) is smaller than the 2000 updates of Sections 10–11 to keep the comparison fast.


Code
def train(model, X_train, Y_train, X_val, Y_val, n_epochs=300, batch_size=32, lr=1e-2, seed=0):
    """Train `model` with Adam and mini-batches; return the training and validation loss per epoch."""
    torch.manual_seed(seed)                                    # reproducible shuffling of the mini-batches
    loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(X_train, Y_train), batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True)
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()
    history = {"train": [], "val": []}
    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        model.train()
        batch_losses = []
        for xb, yb in loader:
            loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
            batch_losses.append(loss.item())
        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            history["val"].append(loss_fn(model(X_val), Y_val).item())
        history["train"].append(np.mean(batch_losses))
    return history

architectures = [[1, 4, 1], [1, 32, 1], [1, 32, 32, 1], [1, 64, 64, 64, 1]]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4))
trained = {}
for sizes in architectures:
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    m = make_mlp(sizes)
    hist = train(m, X_train, Y_train, X_val, Y_val)
    trained[str(sizes)] = m          # a list cannot be a dictionary key, so its text "[1, 4, 1]" is used
    n_par = sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters())
    axes[0].semilogy(hist["val"], label=f"{sizes}  ({n_par} parameters)")
    with torch.no_grad():
        axes[1].plot(t_plot, m(X_plot), lw=1.5, label=str(sizes))
    print(f"{str(sizes):20s} parameters {n_par:6d}   final validation MSE {hist['val'][-1]:.2e}")
axes[0].axhline(0.05**2, color="gray", ls=":"); axes[0].set_xlabel("epoch"); axes[0].set_ylabel("validation MSE"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].plot(t_plot, damped_oscillation(t_plot), "k", lw=1, label="true function")
axes[1].set_xlabel("$t$"); axes[1].set_ylabel("$y$"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


[1, 4, 1]            parameters     13   final validation MSE 9.86e-02


[1, 32, 1]           parameters     97   final validation MSE 9.25e-02


[1, 32, 32, 1]       parameters   1153   final validation MSE 4.95e-03


[1, 64, 64, 64, 1]   parameters   8513   final validation MSE 4.62e-03





The two one-hidden-layer networks are far from the noise level, although Section 3 introduced exactly this kind of network through the Universal Approximation Theorem. The theorem guarantees that suitable parameters exist for a large enough \(N\); it says nothing about whether a given optimiser finds them within a given number of steps. Here the networks with one hidden layer converge much more slowly and are far from converged after 300 epochs: trained longer (measured separately, same seeds), [1, 32, 1] reaches a validation MSE of about \(9\cdot10^{-3}\) after 1000 epochs and \(7\cdot10^{-3}\) after 3000, while [1, 32, 32, 1] is at about \(4\cdot10^{-3}\) already after 1000 epochs. With a fixed training budget the deeper networks reach a good fit much faster.
Choosing a model and testing it. The architecture is chosen by the validation loss. Only for the chosen model is the test loss computed, once; it estimates the error on new data. (Choosing by the test loss would make the test set a second validation set, and the estimate would be too optimistic.)


Code
val_final = {}
for name, m in trained.items():
    m.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        val_final[name] = loss_fn(m(X_val), Y_val).item()
# min over a dictionary runs over its keys; key=val_final.get compares the keys by their values val_final[name],
# so the result is the name of the architecture with the smallest validation loss
best_name = min(val_final, key=val_final.get)
best = trained[best_name]
with torch.no_grad():
    test_loss = loss_fn(best(X_test), Y_test).item()
print("validation MSE per architecture:", {k: f"{v:.2e}" for k, v in val_final.items()})   # dictionary comprehension, for formatting only
print(f"chosen: {best_name};  test MSE = {test_loss:.2e}  (noise variance {0.05**2:.1e})")


validation MSE per architecture: {'[1, 4, 1]': '9.86e-02', '[1, 32, 1]': '9.25e-02', '[1, 32, 32, 1]': '4.95e-03', '[1, 64, 64, 64, 1]': '4.62e-03'}
chosen: [1, 64, 64, 64, 1];  test MSE = 5.30e-03  (noise variance 2.5e-03)


The two largest networks have nearly equal validation losses. The difference is smaller than the spread caused by the random initialisation alone: repeated with the seeds 0–4, the final validation MSE varies between \(4.5\cdot10^{-3}\) and \(6.1\cdot10^{-3}\) for [1, 32, 32, 1] and between \(4.0\cdot10^{-3}\) and \(8.4\cdot10^{-3}\) for [1, 64, 64, 64, 1]. The smaller network would therefore be an equally good and cheaper choice; the rule “smallest validation loss” applied to a single run is a simplification.
Saving and loading. A trained model is saved as its state_dict (the parameter tensors). To load it, a model with the same architecture is created and the stored tensors are copied into it.
torch.save(obj, filename) writes a Python object containing tensors to a file (the extension .pt is a convention), and torch.load(filename) reads it back. The state_dict contains only names and numbers, so the file does not depend on the Python code of the model; that code (here make_mlp and the list of layer sizes) is needed to rebuild the architecture before load_state_dict fills in the values.


Code
torch.save(best.state_dict(), "damped_oscillation_model.pt")      # the chosen model, as a file in the current directory

sizes_by_name = {str(sizes): sizes for sizes in architectures}     # "[1, 32, 1]" -> [1, 32, 1]
restored = make_mlp(sizes_by_name[best_name])                      # same architecture, new random parameters
restored.load_state_dict(torch.load("damped_oscillation_model.pt"))
restored.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    print("max |original - restored|:", (best(X_plot) - restored(X_plot)).abs().max().item())


max |original - restored|: 0.0

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
text:
13. Common bugs

13.1 Output and target of different shapes
The model returns shape (B, 1). If the targets have shape (B,), broadcasting turns pred - y into a (B, B) matrix of all pairwise differences. nn.MSELoss only warns; a hand-written torch.mean((pred - y)**2) does not even warn. The loss value is wrong and training fits the wrong objective.
Python’s module warnings normally prints a warning once and does not pass it to the program. To show the message in the output below, it is captured: warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) collects the warnings raised inside the with block into the list w, and simplefilter("always") makes sure the warning is recorded even if the same warning was shown before.


Code
import warnings
pred = best(X_train).detach()                 # shape (120, 1)
y_wrong = Y_train.reshape(-1)                 # shape (120,)  <- the bug
print("shape of pred - y_wrong:", tuple((pred - y_wrong).shape))
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    wrong = loss_fn(pred, y_wrong).item()
    print("warning raised by nn.MSELoss:", str(w[0].message)[:90] if w else "none")
print(f"loss with correct shapes: {loss_fn(pred, Y_train).item():.2e}   with the shape bug: {wrong:.2e}")


shape of pred - y_wrong: (120, 120)
warning raised by nn.MSELoss: Using a target size (torch.Size([120])) that is different to the input size (torch.Size([1
loss with correct shapes: 3.02e-03   with the shape bug: 2.52e-01




13.2 Forgetting optimizer.zero_grad()
Gradients accumulate in .grad. Without resetting them, .grad holds the sum of all gradients computed so far: it grows from step to step, and the updates no longer follow the gradient of the current loss. Below, the Adam training of Section 10.4, shortened to 1000 steps, once with and once without zero_grad(); we also print the norm of the gradient stored in the first layer at the end, and the cosine of the angle between the stored gradient (all parameters joined into one vector) and the true gradient of the current loss, computed separately with torch.autograd.grad. A cosine of \(+1\) means the same direction, \(-1\) the opposite one.


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
for reset in [True, False]:
    torch.manual_seed(1)
    m = make_mlp([1, 32, 32, 1])
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(m.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
    hist = []
    for step in range(1000):
        loss = loss_fn(m(X_train), Y_train)
        if reset:
            opt.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
        hist.append(loss.item())
    label = "with zero_grad()" if reset else "without zero_grad()"
    ax.semilogy(hist, label=label)
    stored = torch.cat([p.grad.flatten() for p in m.parameters()])                     # what the optimiser uses
    true = torch.cat([g.flatten() for g in torch.autograd.grad(loss_fn(m(X_train), Y_train), list(m.parameters()))])
    cosine = torch.dot(stored, true) / (stored.norm() * true.norm())
    print(f"{label:20s}: loss after 1000 steps = {hist[-1]:.2e},  |grad| of first layer = {m[0].weight.grad.norm().item():.1e},"
          f"  cosine(stored, true gradient) = {cosine.item():+.3f}")
ax.set_xlabel("step"); ax.set_ylabel("training MSE"); ax.legend(); plt.show()


with zero_grad()    : loss after 1000 steps = 2.74e-03,  |grad| of first layer = 1.0e-04,  cosine(stored, true gradient) = +0.548


without zero_grad() : loss after 1000 steps = 2.84e+02,  |grad| of first layer = 2.0e+02,  cosine(stored, true gradient) = -0.999





Without zero_grad() the stored gradient becomes much larger than the true gradient (in a re-run, about two orders of magnitude; the true gradient is itself large because the loss is large), and the loss grows instead of decreasing. The first-layer norms printed above (\(2\cdot10^{2}\) against \(10^{-4}\)) compare the two runs, not the stored and the true gradient of the same run. The size alone would not harm Adam much, since Adam divides each update by a running average of the gradient size. The harm comes from the direction: the stored .grad is the sum of all past gradients, dominated by the old ones, and no longer follows the gradient of the current loss. At the end of this run the cosine printed above is close to \(-1\): the updates point uphill. (With zero_grad() the cosine is positive but below 1 because the stored gradient belongs to the parameters before the last step(), while the true gradient is computed after it.) No error is raised; only the loss curve reveals the bug.


13.3 Data in float64, model in float32
Arrays created by NumPy are float64; model parameters are float32. Mixing them raises an error in the first layer.


Code
x64 = torch.tensor(scale(t_data[:5])).reshape(-1, 1)           # dtype float64, taken over from NumPy
try:
    best(x64)
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("RuntimeError:", e)
print("fixed:", tuple(best(x64.float()).shape))                 # .float() converts to float32


RuntimeError: mat1 and mat2 must have the same dtype, but got Double and Float
fixed: (5, 1)




13.4 Inputs on a large scale
The same network trained on the raw times \(t\in[0, 10]\) instead of the rescaled \([-1, 1]\):


Code
X_train_raw = torch.tensor(t_data[train_idx.numpy()], dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
X_val_raw = torch.tensor(t_data[val_idx.numpy()], dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
# every value of the dictionary is a pair (training inputs, validation inputs); (Xt, Xv) unpacks the pair
for name, (Xt, Xv) in {"rescaled input [-1, 1]": (X_train, X_val), "raw input [0, 10]": (X_train_raw, X_val_raw)}.items():
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    m = make_mlp([1, 32, 32, 1])
    hist = train(m, Xt, Y_train, Xv, Y_val)
    ax.semilogy(hist["val"], label=name)
    print(f"{name:25s} final validation MSE {hist['val'][-1]:.2e}")
ax.axhline(0.05**2, color="gray", ls=":", label="noise variance")
ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("validation MSE"); ax.legend(); plt.show()


rescaled input [-1, 1]    final validation MSE 4.95e-03


raw input [0, 10]         final validation MSE 1.84e-02





With the raw input the first-layer nodes \(\tanh(W t + b)\) are saturated over most of the interval, their gradients are small, and the same number of epochs gives a worse result. Rescaling inputs (and, for targets of very different size, outputs) to order one is a standard preprocessing step.

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
section: 14. Training the image classifier on MNIST
text:
14. Training the image classifier on MNIST
Section 6 built the classifier and showed that the untrained network guesses. With the training loop of Sections 10–12 it can now be trained. The only new ingredient is the loss function for classification.

14.1 Data
The 10 000 test images of Section 6 (images, labels) remain the test set, used once at the end. The 60 000 training images (train=True, already downloaded in Section 6, since torchvision always downloads both parts) are split at random into 50 000 for training and 10 000 for validation.


Code
try:
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()), contextlib.redirect_stderr(io.StringIO()):
        mnist_train = datasets.MNIST(root="data", train=True, download=True)
    X_all, y_all = mnist_train.data.float() / 255, mnist_train.targets
except Exception as err:
    print("MNIST training set could not be loaded:", err, " -> random images (the results below are then meaningless)")
    X_all, y_all = torch.rand(60000, 28, 28), torch.randint(0, 10, (60000,))

perm = torch.randperm(60000, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0))   # a random order of the 60 000 indices
X_tr, y_tr = X_all[perm[:50000]], y_all[perm[:50000]]                      # training set
X_va, y_va = X_all[perm[50000:]], y_all[perm[50000:]]                      # validation set
X_te, y_te = images, labels                                                # test set (Section 6)
print("training:", tuple(X_tr.shape), "  validation:", tuple(X_va.shape), "  test:", tuple(X_te.shape))


training: (50000, 28, 28)   validation: (10000, 28, 28)   test: (10000, 28, 28)




14.2 Loss function and accuracy
For classification the loss is the cross-entropy (lecture). For one image with true class \(y\) and predicted probabilities \(q_k = \mathrm{softmax}(z)_k\), \[\ell = -\log q_y ,\] the negative logarithm of the probability that the network gives to the correct class: \(\ell = 0\) if \(q_y = 1\), and \(\ell\) grows without bound as \(q_y \to 0\). The loss of a batch is the mean over its images.
nn.CrossEntropyLoss() (stored as ce_loss, so that loss_fn, the MSE loss of Section 10 used again in the exercises, is not overwritten) takes the logits of shape (B, 10) and the labels as integers of shape (B,) (dtype int64, which labels already has); it applies the softmax itself, so the model must not end with a softmax layer. The label is used as an index: it picks \(q_y\) out of the ten probabilities.
The accuracy, the fraction of correctly classified images, is what we are interested in, but it cannot be used as a loss: it changes only when an image switches class, so its gradient with respect to the parameters is zero almost everywhere. The cross-entropy changes smoothly with the parameters.
A check before training: an untrained network gives \(q_k \approx 1/10\) for every class (Section 6), so the loss should be close to \(-\log(1/10) = \ln 10 \approx 2.30\).


Code
ce_loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

def accuracy(logits, y):
    """Fraction of images whose largest logit is at the true class."""
    return (logits.argmax(dim=1) == y).float().mean().item()

torch.manual_seed(0)
clf = nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10))
with torch.no_grad():
    z = clf(X_va)
    print(f"untrained: loss {ce_loss(z, y_va).item():.3f}  (ln 10 = {np.log(10):.3f}),  accuracy {accuracy(z, y_va):.3f}")


untrained: loss 2.303  (ln 10 = 2.303),  accuracy 0.108




14.3 The training loop
The loop is that of Section 11 with mini-batches, written out here because the loss and the recorded quantities differ: - mini-batches of 64 images, a new random order in every epoch (torch.randperm), Adam with learning rate \(10^{-3}\) (the default of Adam; 64 is a common batch size, values from 32 to 256 work as well); - after every epoch the loss and accuracy on the training and validation sets are computed for all images at once, inside torch.no_grad() (Section 10.4). The training loss is evaluated after the epoch, with the final parameters of that epoch, so that it can be compared with the validation loss; - 10 epochs (10 passes over the 50 000 training images). One epoch takes about a second on a CPU; the number is chosen so that the cell runs in about ten seconds and shows where the validation loss stops improving.
model.train() and model.eval() (Section 11.2) make no difference for this network (no dropout or batch normalisation) and are written for completeness.


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
clf = nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10))
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(clf.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
batch_size, n_epochs = 64, 10
log = {"train loss": [], "val loss": [], "train acc": [], "val acc": []}

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for epoch in range(1, n_epochs + 1):
    clf.train()
    order = torch.randperm(len(X_tr))                     # new random order of the training images
    for start in range(0, len(X_tr), batch_size):
        idx = order[start:start + batch_size]             # indices of one mini-batch
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = ce_loss(clf(X_tr[idx]), y_tr[idx])
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

    clf.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        z_tr, z_va = clf(X_tr), clf(X_va)
        log["train loss"].append(ce_loss(z_tr, y_tr).item()); log["train acc"].append(accuracy(z_tr, y_tr))
        log["val loss"].append(ce_loss(z_va, y_va).item());   log["val acc"].append(accuracy(z_va, y_va))
    print(f"epoch {epoch:2d}:  loss train {log['train loss'][-1]:.4f}  val {log['val loss'][-1]:.4f}   "
          f"accuracy train {log['train acc'][-1]:.4f}  val {log['val acc'][-1]:.4f}")
print(f"training took {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")


epoch  1:  loss train 0.1856  val 0.2002   accuracy train 0.9473  val 0.9434


epoch  2:  loss train 0.1144  val 0.1393   accuracy train 0.9669  val 0.9581


epoch  3:  loss train 0.0860  val 0.1140   accuracy train 0.9747  val 0.9665


epoch  4:  loss train 0.0649  val 0.1044   accuracy train 0.9808  val 0.9691


epoch  5:  loss train 0.0504  val 0.0947   accuracy train 0.9847  val 0.9736


epoch  6:  loss train 0.0338  val 0.0844   accuracy train 0.9902  val 0.9747


epoch  7:  loss train 0.0353  val 0.0984   accuracy train 0.9891  val 0.9725


epoch  8:  loss train 0.0233  val 0.0852   accuracy train 0.9928  val 0.9753


epoch  9:  loss train 0.0205  val 0.0867   accuracy train 0.9940  val 0.9747


epoch 10:  loss train 0.0152  val 0.0898   accuracy train 0.9956  val 0.9770
training took 10 s




14.4 Learning curves


Code
epochs = np.arange(1, n_epochs + 1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
axes[0].plot(epochs, log["train loss"], "o-", label="training")
axes[0].plot(epochs, log["val loss"], "s-", label="validation")
axes[0].set_ylabel("cross-entropy loss")
axes[1].plot(epochs, log["train acc"], "o-", label="training")
axes[1].plot(epochs, log["val acc"], "s-", label="validation")
axes[1].set_ylabel("accuracy")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.legend()
plt.show()





Both losses fall quickly during the first epochs. Afterwards they separate: the training loss keeps falling (from about 0.19 after the first epoch to about 0.015 after the tenth), while the validation loss reaches its smallest value after about 6 epochs (about 0.085) and then stays at that level or rises slightly. This is the onset of overfitting: the network begins to adapt to details of the 50 000 training images that do not carry over to new images. The same is seen in the accuracies: about 99.6% on the training set but about 97.7% on the validation set.
The validation accuracy still increases a little while the validation loss no longer decreases. The two measure different things: the accuracy counts only whether the largest probability is at the right class, the cross-entropy also measures how confident the network is. As training continues, the network gets a few more images right, but it also becomes more confident everywhere, and pays a large loss \(-\log q_y\) for every image on which it is confidently wrong.


14.5 Evaluation on the test set
The test set is used once, for the final numbers. Besides the accuracy two views show which mistakes the network makes: - the confusion matrix \(C_{ij}\), the number of test images of true class \(i\) that were classified as \(j\). Correct answers lie on the diagonal. It is computed with one bincount: the pair \((i, j)\) is encoded as the single number \(10i + j\), the occurrences of every number \(0, \dots, 99\) are counted, and the counts are arranged as a \(10\times10\) matrix with reshape; - a few misclassified images with their true and predicted classes.


Code
with torch.no_grad():
    pred_te = clf(X_te).argmax(dim=1)
print(f"test accuracy: {(pred_te == y_te).float().mean().item():.4f}   ({(pred_te != y_te).sum().item()} of {len(y_te)} test images misclassified)")

C = torch.bincount(10 * y_te + pred_te, minlength=100).reshape(10, 10)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 5.5))
im = ax.imshow(torch.log10(C + 1), cmap="Blues")         # logarithmic colours: the diagonal (about 1000) would hide the rest
for i in range(10):
    for j in range(10):
        if C[i, j] > 0:
            ax.text(j, i, str(C[i, j].item()), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7,
                    color="white" if i == j else "black")
ax.set_xticks(range(10)); ax.set_yticks(range(10))
ax.set_xlabel("predicted class $j$"); ax.set_ylabel("true class $i$"); ax.set_title("confusion matrix (test set)")
plt.show()

wrong = torch.nonzero(pred_te != y_te)[:, 0]             # positions of the misclassified test images
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 8, figsize=(12, 3.6))
for ax, k in zip(axes.flat, wrong[:16]):
    ax.imshow(images_raw[k], cmap="gray_r")
    ax.set_title(f"true {y_te[k].item()}, pred {pred_te[k].item()}", fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


test accuracy: 0.9756   (244 of 10000 test images misclassified)








The test accuracy (about 97.5%, i.e. about 250 misclassified images out of 10 000) agrees with the validation accuracy of the last epoch: since neither set was used for training, both estimate the accuracy on new images.
In the confusion matrix almost all images lie on the diagonal. The largest off-diagonal entries in our run are true 5 classified as 3, true 9 classified as 4, and true 9 classified as 3: pairs of digits whose shapes are similar. The misclassified images show that a part of the mistakes concerns digits that are hard to read also for a human; others are well readable and are genuine errors of the network.
The network reaches this accuracy without any notion that the input is an image: it treats the 784 pixels as an unordered list of numbers. Convolutional networks, which use the two-dimensional arrangement of the pixels, reach above 99% on MNIST; they are the subject of a later lecture.

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
text:
15. Summary

A dense network is defined by its layer sizes \([n_0,\dots,n_L]\) and activation; layer \(l\) has a weight matrix \(n_l\times n_{l-1}\) and a bias vector of length \(n_l\).
nn.Sequential(...) builds a chain of layers; a class derived from nn.Module (layers in __init__, computation in forward) builds any architecture. Both are used in the same way: model(x), model.parameters(), model.state_dict().
Networks of arbitrary depth are built in a loop: a list of layers passed to nn.Sequential(*layers), or an nn.ModuleList in a class (never a plain Python list).
Training step: forward, loss, zero_grad(), backward(), step(). Mini-batches via DataLoader; one epoch = one pass over the training data.
Three data sets: training (fit the parameters), validation (monitor, choose), test (final estimate, used once).
Monitor the validation loss inside torch.no_grad(); use model.train() / model.eval(); save with torch.save(model.state_dict(), ...).
Check shapes ((B, 1) vs (B,)), dtypes (float32) and the scale of the inputs.
Classification (Section 14): one output per class, nn.CrossEntropyLoss on the logits with integer labels, accuracy and confusion matrix for evaluation.

16. Exercises


Exercise 1 — One architecture, three constructions
Build the network with layer sizes \([2, 32, 32, 1]\) and \(\tanh\) activations in three ways: (a) nn.Sequential written out layer by layer, (b) make_mlp, (c) the class MLP of Section 7.2. Draw it with draw_network, check that all three have the same number of parameters, and compare it with the formula \(\sum_l n_l(n_{l-1}+1)\). Then copy the parameters of (a) into (c) and verify that both give the same output for a batch of 10 random points. Hint: the Linear layers of (a) are model_a[0], model_a[2], model_a[4]; those of (c) are model_c.layers[0], [1], [2].

Solution


Code
sizes = [2, 32, 32, 1]
draw_network(sizes, activations=["tanh", "tanh"], title="Exercise 1", input_labels=["$x$", "$y$"], output_labels=["$f$"])
plt.show()

# (a) written out layer by layer
model_a = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 32), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(32, 32), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(32, 1))
# (b) from the list of layer sizes
model_b = make_mlp(sizes)
# (c) the class with nn.ModuleList
model_c = MLP(sizes)

formula = sum(n_out * (n_in + 1) for n_in, n_out in zip(sizes[:-1], sizes[1:]))
for name, m in [("(a) Sequential by hand", model_a), ("(b) make_mlp", model_b), ("(c) MLP class", model_c)]:
    print(f"{name:25s} parameters = {sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters())}")
print("formula:", formula, "= 32*(2+1) + 32*(32+1) + 1*(32+1)")

# copy the parameters of (a) into (c): Linear layers of (a) are at positions 0, 2, 4 (the others are activations)
with torch.no_grad():
    for layer_c, layer_a in zip(model_c.layers, [model_a[0], model_a[2], model_a[4]]):
        layer_c.weight.copy_(layer_a.weight)
        layer_c.bias.copy_(layer_a.bias)
points = torch.rand(10, 2)
with torch.no_grad():
    print("max |output (a) - output (c)|:", (model_a(points) - model_c(points)).abs().max().item())

Exercise 2 — Fitting a function of two variables
Fit the 2D double-well potential \(V(x, y) = (x^2 - 1)^2 + \tfrac12 y^2\) on \([-1.5, 1.5]\times[-1.5, 1.5]\). 1. Generate 2000 random points \((x, y)\) in the square with values \(V(x,y)\) and split them into training (1400), validation (300) and test (300) sets. Inputs have shape (B, 2), targets (B, 1). 2. Train make_mlp([2, 64, 64, 1]) with the function train of Section 12 (mini-batches of 64, 200 epochs, lr=1e-2). Plot training and validation loss versus epoch. 3. Compute the test MSE once at the end. Show the true potential, the network and their difference as images on a \(100\times100\) grid.
The inputs \(x, y\in[-1.5, 1.5]\) and the values \(V\in[0, 2.7]\) are already of order one, so no rescaling is needed. A function of two variables needs more samples than one of a single variable to cover its domain, hence 2000 points and a somewhat wider network. The batch size, the number of epochs and the learning rate are reasonable defaults, not tuned values: changing any one of them by a factor of 2–3 (measured: batch 32 or 128, 100 or 400 epochs, lr \(3\cdot10^{-3}\) or \(3\cdot10^{-2}\)) gives final validation errors between \(1\cdot10^{-4}\) and \(2\cdot10^{-3}\), all small compared with the range of \(V\).

Solution


Code
def V2d(x, y):
    return (x**2 - 1)**2 + 0.5 * y**2

# 1) data: random points in the square, split 1400 / 300 / 300
rng2 = np.random.default_rng(1)
P = rng2.uniform(-1.5, 1.5, size=(2000, 2))                  # each row is a point (x, y)
Z = V2d(P[:, 0], P[:, 1])
X2 = torch.tensor(P, dtype=torch.float32)                    # shape (2000, 2)
Y2 = torch.tensor(Z, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)     # shape (2000, 1)
X2_train, X2_val, X2_test = X2[:1400], X2[1400:1700], X2[1700:]   # the points are already in random order
Y2_train, Y2_val, Y2_test = Y2[:1400], Y2[1400:1700], Y2[1700:]

# 2) training
torch.manual_seed(0)
model_2d = make_mlp([2, 64, 64, 1])
t0 = time.perf_counter()
hist_2d = train(model_2d, X2_train, Y2_train, X2_val, Y2_val, n_epochs=200, batch_size=64, lr=1e-2)
print(f"training took {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")

# 3) test loss (once) and images
model_2d.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    test_mse = loss_fn(model_2d(X2_test), Y2_test).item()
print(f"final training MSE {hist_2d['train'][-1]:.2e}, validation MSE {hist_2d['val'][-1]:.2e}, test MSE {test_mse:.2e}")

g1 = np.linspace(-1.5, 1.5, 100)
GX, GY = np.meshgrid(g1, g1)
# ravel() turns each 100 x 100 grid into a list of 10 000 numbers; stack(..., axis=1) puts them side by side as the
# columns x and y, giving the batch of shape (10000, 2) that the network expects. reshape(100, 100) undoes this for the image.
grid_points = torch.tensor(np.stack([GX.ravel(), GY.ravel()], axis=1), dtype=torch.float32)
with torch.no_grad():
    V_net = model_2d(grid_points).numpy().reshape(100, 100)
V_true = V2d(GX, GY)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(20, 4))
axes[0].semilogy(hist_2d["train"], label="training"); axes[0].semilogy(hist_2d["val"], label="validation")
axes[0].set_xlabel("epoch"); axes[0].set_ylabel("MSE"); axes[0].legend()
for ax, img, title in zip(axes[1:], [V_true, V_net, V_net - V_true], ["true $V$", "network", "network $-$ true"]):
    im = ax.imshow(img, origin="lower", extent=[-1.5, 1.5, -1.5, 1.5], cmap="viridis" if title != "network $-$ true" else "RdBu_r")
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8); ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
# The square root of the test MSE is the typical error of the network in the units of V: about 0.03,
# compared with values of V between 0 and 2.7. The difference image shows where these errors are located.


training took 4 s
final training MSE 8.47e-04, validation MSE 8.06e-04, test MSE 6.87e-04








Exercise 3 — A classification task
Points \((x, y)\) belong to class 0 if their distance from the origin is below 1 and to class 1 if it is between 1.3 and 2 (two rings, no point in between). 1. Generate 600 points of each class (sample the radius uniformly in the ring and the angle uniformly), shuffle them and split 800 / 200 / 200. 2. Train make_mlp([2, 16, 16, 2]) (two outputs = two class scores) with nn.CrossEntropyLoss, which takes the scores of shape (B, 2) and the integer labels of shape (B,) (dtype torch.long), and applies softmax internally. One score per class (rather than a single output) makes the same code work for any number of classes. The labels are integers because the loss uses them as indices, to pick the score of the correct class. Use Adam, lr=1e-2, full batch, 300 steps; record training and validation loss. 3. Report the accuracy (fraction of correctly classified points) on the validation and, at the end, on the test set. 4. Plot the decision boundary: the predicted class on a grid of points, with the data on top.
(The function train of Section 12 uses nn.MSELoss; write the loop by hand here.)

Solution


Code
# 1) data: two rings
rng3 = np.random.default_rng(2)
def ring(n, r_min, r_max):
    r = rng3.uniform(r_min, r_max, n)
    phi = rng3.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n)
    return np.stack([r * np.cos(phi), r * np.sin(phi)], axis=1)

points_rings = np.concatenate([ring(600, 0.0, 1.0), ring(600, 1.3, 2.0)])
labels_rings = np.concatenate([np.zeros(600), np.ones(600)])
order = rng3.permutation(1200)                                      # shuffle points and labels together
Xc = torch.tensor(points_rings[order], dtype=torch.float32)
Yc = torch.tensor(labels_rings[order], dtype=torch.long)                  # integer class labels, shape (1200,)
Xc_train, Xc_val, Xc_test = Xc[:800], Xc[800:1000], Xc[1000:]
Yc_train, Yc_val, Yc_test = Yc[:800], Yc[800:1000], Yc[1000:]

# 2) model and training loop
torch.manual_seed(0)
clf_rings = make_mlp([2, 16, 16, 2])                                      # outputs: one score (logit) per class
ce_loss_rings = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
opt = torch.optim.Adam(clf_rings.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
hist_tr, hist_va = [], []
for step in range(300):
    loss = ce_loss_rings(clf_rings(Xc_train), Yc_train)                         # scores (800, 2) vs labels (800,)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        hist_va.append(ce_loss_rings(clf_rings(Xc_val), Yc_val).item())
    hist_tr.append(loss.item())

# 3) accuracy: the predicted class is the one with the larger score.
# argmax(dim=1) gives, for every row, the index of the largest entry. Softmax does not change the order of the
# scores, so this is also the class of highest probability, and softmax need not be computed.
# (... == Y) is a tensor of True/False; .float() turns it into 1.0/0.0, and its mean is the fraction of correct answers.
def accuracy_of(model, X, Y):
    with torch.no_grad():
        return (model(X).argmax(dim=1) == Y).float().mean().item()
print(f"validation accuracy: {accuracy_of(clf_rings, Xc_val, Yc_val):.3f}")
print(f"test accuracy (computed once at the end): {accuracy_of(clf_rings, Xc_test, Yc_test):.3f}")
# The two classes are separated by an empty ring (1 < r < 1.3), so a perfect classification is possible.
# Without the gap (e.g. class 1 for 1 < r < 2) points near r = 1 would be harder, and the accuracy would drop below 1.

# 4) decision boundary
g = np.linspace(-2.2, 2.2, 200)
GX, GY = np.meshgrid(g, g)
grid = torch.tensor(np.stack([GX.ravel(), GY.ravel()], axis=1), dtype=torch.float32)
with torch.no_grad():
    pred_class = clf_rings(grid).argmax(dim=1).numpy().reshape(200, 200)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))
axes[0].plot(hist_tr, label="training"); axes[0].plot(hist_va, label="validation")
axes[0].set_yscale("log"); axes[0].set_xlabel("step"); axes[0].set_ylabel("cross-entropy"); axes[0].legend()
# the classes are the integers 0 and 1: boundaries at -0.5, 0.5, 1.5 give exactly one colour to each class
axes[1].contourf(GX, GY, pred_class, levels=[-0.5, 0.5, 1.5], colors=["C0", "C1"], alpha=0.25)
# Xc_train[Yc_train == 0]: indexing with a True/False tensor keeps the rows where the condition holds (shape (n, 2));
# .T turns it into two rows x and y, and * passes them as the two arguments of scatter
axes[1].scatter(*Xc_train[Yc_train == 0].T, s=5, color="C0", label="class 0")
axes[1].scatter(*Xc_train[Yc_train == 1].T, s=5, color="C1", label="class 1")
axes[1].set_aspect("equal"); axes[1].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[1].set_ylabel("$y$"); axes[1].legend(loc="upper right")
axes[1].set_title("predicted class (background) and training data")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


validation accuracy: 1.000
test accuracy (computed once at the end): 1.000








Exercise 4 — Boundary conditions built into the network
The ground state of a particle in a box \([0, 1]\) is \(\psi_\ast(x) = \sqrt2\sin(\pi x)\). Fit it from 15 noisy samples (\(\sigma = 0.05\)) at random points in \([0, 1]\) with (a) BoxWavefunction([1, 16, 16, 1]) of Section 8.2 and (b) an unconstrained make_mlp([1, 16, 16, 1]). Train both with Adam (lr=1e-2, full batch, 2000 steps). Compare the values at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 1\) and the maximal error on a dense grid, and plot both fits. Which model respects the physics, and where does the unconstrained one go wrong?
Few samples are used on purpose: the regions between the outermost samples and the walls are then not covered by data, which exposes the difference between the two models.

Solution


Code
rng4 = np.random.default_rng(3)
x_s = np.sort(rng4.uniform(0, 1, 15))
y_s = np.sqrt(2) * np.sin(np.pi * x_s) + 0.05 * rng4.normal(size=15)
Xs = torch.tensor(x_s, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
Ys = torch.tensor(y_s, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)

def fit(model, steps=2000):
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
    for _ in range(steps):
        loss = loss_fn(model(Xs), Ys)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return model

torch.manual_seed(0); constrained = fit(BoxWavefunction([1, 16, 16, 1]))
torch.manual_seed(0); free = fit(make_mlp([1, 16, 16, 1]))

x_dense = torch.linspace(0, 1, 401).reshape(-1, 1)
exact = np.sqrt(2) * np.sin(np.pi * x_dense.numpy())
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.plot(x_dense, exact, "k", lw=3, alpha=0.4, label=r"exact $\sqrt{2}\sin(\pi x)$")
ax.plot(x_s, y_s, "ko", ms=5, label="15 noisy samples")
for name, m in [("x(1-x) NN(x)", constrained), ("unconstrained NN(x)", free)]:
    with torch.no_grad():
        values = m(x_dense).numpy()
    ax.plot(x_dense, values, lw=2, label=name)
    print(f"{name:20s} psi(0) = {values[0, 0]:+.3f}   psi(1) = {values[-1, 0]:+.3f}   max |error| = {np.max(np.abs(values - exact)):.3f}")
ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\psi(x)$"); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show()
# The constrained model vanishes exactly at both walls for any parameters. The unconstrained model is only
# determined where there are samples; between the outermost samples and the walls it is not forced to zero.


x(1-x) NN(x)         psi(0) = +0.000   psi(1) = +0.000   max |error| = 0.082
unconstrained NN(x)  psi(0) = -0.035   psi(1) = +0.793   max |error| = 0.793








Exercise 5 (advanced) — Deep plain network vs. residual network
Train on the damped-oscillation data of Section 10 two networks of the same depth (10 hidden layers of width 16): make_mlp([1] + [16] * 10 + [1]) and ResidualMLP(1, 16, 9, 1) (one input layer plus 9 residual blocks), both with train (300 epochs). Plot their validation losses versus epoch. Before training, print the norm of the gradient of the first layer’s weights for both models (one backward pass on the training set): what does it tell us about how the signal propagates backwards through a deep plain network?

Solution


Code
torch.manual_seed(0); plain = make_mlp([1] + [16] * 10 + [1])
torch.manual_seed(0); resnet = ResidualMLP(1, 16, 9, 1)
print("parameters: plain", sum(p.numel() for p in plain.parameters()), "  residual", sum(p.numel() for p in resnet.parameters()))

# gradient of the first layer before training
for name, m, first in [("plain", plain, plain[0]), ("residual", resnet, resnet.input_layer)]:
    m.zero_grad()
    loss_fn(m(X_train), Y_train).backward()
    print(f"{name:9s} |dL/dW of first layer| = {first.weight.grad.norm().item():.2e}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
for name, m in [("plain, 10 hidden layers", plain), ("residual, 9 blocks", resnet)]:
    hist = train(m, X_train, Y_train, X_val, Y_val, n_epochs=300)
    ax.semilogy(hist["val"], label=name)
    print(f"{name:25s} final validation MSE {hist['val'][-1]:.2e}")
ax.axhline(0.05**2, color="gray", ls=":", label="noise variance")
ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("validation MSE"); ax.legend(); plt.show()
# In the plain network the gradient reaching the first layer is the product of many factors (one per layer), each
# typically smaller than one for tanh with the default initialisation: it is much smaller than in the residual network,
# where the skip connections pass the gradient directly. This is the vanishing-gradient problem.

plain     |dL/dW of first layer| = 8.37e-05
residual  |dL/dW of first layer| = 4.23e-01

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
text:
1. The architecture

1.1 Drawing
The network analysed in this notebook has layer sizes \([1, 64, 64, 64, 1]\) with \(\tanh\) activations: one input, three hidden layers of 64 nodes, one output.
Why this network: it is deliberately much larger than the 30 training points of Section 2 require (8513 parameters, counted in Section 1.3), so that it is able to overfit them (Section 4). Three hidden layers make the effects of depth on activations and gradients visible. \(\tanh\) is used because for it “saturated” has a simple meaning (Section 2.3). The width 64 itself is arbitrary: with widths 32 and 128 the same training run also shows a minimum of the validation loss followed by a rise.


Code
layer_sizes = [1, 64, 64, 64, 1]
torch.manual_seed(0)                 # fixes the random initial weights; Section 3 uses the same seed, so it trains exactly this network
model = make_mlp(layer_sizes)
draw_network(layer_sizes, activations=["tanh"] * 3, title="the network analysed in this notebook",
             input_labels=["$x$"], output_labels=["$f(x)$"])
plt.show()
print(model)





Sequential(
  (0): Linear(in_features=1, out_features=64, bias=True)
  (1): Tanh()
  (2): Linear(in_features=64, out_features=64, bias=True)
  (3): Tanh()
  (4): Linear(in_features=64, out_features=64, bias=True)
  (5): Tanh()
  (6): Linear(in_features=64, out_features=1, bias=True)
)




1.2 A table of the layers
We pass a small batch through the layers one by one and record, for each layer, its type, the shapes of its input and output, the shapes of its parameters, and the number of parameters. A pandas.DataFrame is a convenient container for such a table.
An nn.Sequential behaves like a list of layers: for layer in model runs over them in order, and model[0], model[-1] select the first and the last layer. In the table, index is the position of the module in the Sequential; it is not the layer index \(l\) of Section 1.3. type(layer).__name__ gives the name of the class of an object as a string (e.g. 'Linear'), and p.numel() the number of entries of a tensor.


Code
def layer_table(model, x):
    """One row per layer of an nn.Sequential model, for the input batch x."""
    rows = []
    for i, layer in enumerate(model):
        x_in = x
        x = layer(x)                                            # pass the batch through this layer
        params = list(layer.parameters())
        rows.append({
            "index": i,
            "layer": type(layer).__name__,
            "input shape": tuple(x_in.shape),
            "output shape": tuple(x.shape),
            "parameter shapes": [tuple(p.shape) for p in params],
            "parameters": sum(p.numel() for p in params),
            "trainable": sum(p.numel() for p in params if p.requires_grad),
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

table = layer_table(model, torch.zeros(8, 1))                   # 8 dummy inputs; batch size and values are arbitrary, only the shape (B, 1) matters

Reading the table: each Linear layer from \(n_{\rm in}\) to \(n_{\rm out}\) nodes has a weight matrix of shape \((n_{\rm out}, n_{\rm in})\) and a bias of length \(n_{\rm out}\); activation layers have no parameters and keep the shape. The batch dimension (8) is carried through unchanged.


1.3 Counting parameters
The layers are numbered \(l = 0, 1, \dots, L\), with \(n_0\) the number of inputs and \(n_L\) the number of outputs; for \([1, 64, 64, 64, 1]\), \(n_0 = 1\), \(n_1 = n_2 = n_3 = 64\), \(n_4 = 1\). The Linear layer from layer \(l-1\) to layer \(l\) has \(n_l n_{l-1}\) weights and \(n_l\) biases, i.e. \(n_l(n_{l-1}+1)\) parameters. The total from the table is compared with the formula \(\sum_{l=1}^{L} n_l\,(n_{l-1}+1)\) and with PyTorch’s own count.


Code
by_formula = sum(n_out * (n_in + 1) for n_in, n_out in zip(layer_sizes[:-1], layer_sizes[1:]))
by_table = table["parameters"].sum()
by_pytorch = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"formula: {by_formula},  table: {by_table},  PyTorch: {by_pytorch}")
for n_in, n_out in zip(layer_sizes[:-1], layer_sizes[1:]):
    print(f"  Linear({n_in}, {n_out}): {n_out} x {n_in} weights + {n_out} biases = {n_out * (n_in + 1)}")


formula: 8513,  table: 8513,  PyTorch: 8513
  Linear(1, 64): 64 x 1 weights + 64 biases = 128
  Linear(64, 64): 64 x 64 weights + 64 biases = 4160
  Linear(64, 64): 64 x 64 weights + 64 biases = 4160
  Linear(64, 1): 1 x 64 weights + 1 biases = 65




1.4 Number of parameters against width and depth
For a network \([1, W, \dots, W, 1]\) with \(D\) hidden layers of width \(W\) the count is \(W(1+1) + (D-1)\,W(W+1) + (W+1)\). The three terms are the first layer (\(W\) weights and \(W\) biases), the \(D-1\) layers from width \(W\) to width \(W\) (\(W^2\) weights and \(W\) biases each) and the output layer (\(W\) weights and one bias). The count is therefore linear in the depth \(D\) and, for \(D\ge2\), quadratic in the width \(W\). On the log-log axes below a power law \(W^k\) is a straight line of slope \(k\).


Code
widths = np.array([4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
for depth in [1, 2, 3, 5]:
    counts = [sum(p.numel() for p in make_mlp([1] + [w] * depth + [1]).parameters()) for w in widths]
    ax.loglog(widths, counts, "o-", label=f"{depth} hidden layer" + ("s" if depth > 1 else ""))
ax.loglog(widths, 3 * widths**2, "k:", label=r"$\propto W^2$")    # only the slope 2 matters; the factor 3 places the line near the data
ax.set_xlabel("width $W$ (nodes per hidden layer)"); ax.set_ylabel("number of parameters"); ax.legend()
plt.show()





With one hidden layer the count grows only linearly (\(3W+1\)); every additional hidden layer adds a \(W\times W\) matrix, so the deeper networks follow the \(W^2\) line.


1.5 Trainable and frozen parameters
Setting requires_grad = False for a parameter freezes it: no gradient is computed for it, and an optimiser leaves it unchanged. Freezing is used, for example, when a pretrained part of a network is kept fixed. Here we freeze the first layer of a copy of the model and recount.
The copy must be made with copy.deepcopy. A plain assignment frozen_model = model only gives a second name to the same network, and a shallow copy.copy(model) creates a new container that still holds the same parameter tensors: freezing it would freeze model as well. copy.deepcopy duplicates every parameter.


Code
frozen_model = copy.deepcopy(model)              # an independent copy, so that `model` itself stays unchanged
for p in frozen_model[0].parameters():           # module 0 of the `Sequential`, i.e. the first `Linear` layer
    p.requires_grad = False

trainable = sum(p.numel() for p in frozen_model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)
total = sum(p.numel() for p in frozen_model.parameters())
print(f"total parameters: {total},  trainable: {trainable},  frozen: {total - trainable}  (= 64 weights + 64 biases of the first Linear layer)")


total parameters: 8513,  trainable: 8385,  frozen: 128  (= 64 weights + 64 biases of the first Linear layer)




1.6 Memory and computational cost
Every parameter is stored as a float32 number of 4 bytes. One forward pass for one input needs, in every Linear layer, \(n_{\rm in}\,n_{\rm out}\) multiplications and as many additions (a multiply-add per weight). These numbers set the scale for large networks: a model with \(10^9\) parameters needs 4 GB only to store its weights.
The count of multiply-adds includes only the multiplications by weights; the bias additions and the activations add about \(n_{\rm out}\) operations per layer, which is small compared with \(n_{\rm in}n_{\rm out}\) for wide layers. In the printout 1 kB is taken as 1024 bytes.


Code
n_bytes = sum(p.numel() * p.element_size() for p in model.parameters())     # element_size() = bytes per number
mult_adds = sum(n_in * n_out for n_in, n_out in zip(layer_sizes[:-1], layer_sizes[1:]))
print(f"memory of the parameters: {n_bytes} bytes = {n_bytes / 1024:.1f} kB")
print(f"multiply-adds per input sample in one forward pass: {mult_adds}")


memory of the parameters: 34052 bytes = 33.3 kB
multiply-adds per input sample in one forward pass: 8320




1.7 The same with ready-made tools
Everything in Sections 1.1–1.6 was computed by hand from the definitions, because this shows what each number means. In practice the same information is obtained with ready-made tools. PyTorch itself offers basic pieces (print(model), parameters(), requires_grad, modules(), and the operation counter FlopCounterMode); a table of the layers and a drawing come from small additional packages: - torchinfo: the function torchinfo.summary prints a table of the layers with output shapes and parameter counts, the numbers of trainable and frozen parameters, and estimates of memory and cost; - torchview: draws the network as a graph of layers and tensor shapes (it uses the program Graphviz, installed in Colab); - torch.utils.flop_counter.FlopCounterMode (part of PyTorch) counts the floating-point operations of a computation.
The two packages are not part of Colab’s standard installation. %pip install installs Python packages from inside a notebook into the Python environment that runs the notebook (-q: print less); it takes a few seconds and is needed once per Colab session. The note printed by %pip about restarting the kernel concerns packages that were already imported before the installation; torchinfo and torchview are imported only after it, so no restart is needed.


Code
%pip install -q torchinfo torchview


Note: you may need to restart the kernel to use updated packages.


The table of torchinfo.summary for the model of Section 1 and the batch shape \((8, 1)\) of Section 1.2. The function returns an object that is displayed as the table and whose attributes hold the numbers, so they can be compared with our own counts. verbose=0 prevents the table from being printed a second time.


Code
import torchinfo

info = torchinfo.summary(model, input_size=(8, 1), verbose=0)
print(info)
print("total parameters: torchinfo", info.total_params, "  our count", by_pytorch)
print("trainable:        torchinfo", info.trainable_params)

The last lines need a comment: - “Params size (MB): 0.03” is the memory of the parameters, \(8513\times4\) bytes \(= 34\,052\) bytes, the number of Section 1.6 (here in units of \(10^6\) bytes). - “Total mult-adds” is counted differently from Section 1.6. torchinfo counts one multiply-add per parameter, the biases included, and for the whole batch: \(8 \times 8513 = 68\,104 \approx 0.07\) M. Section 1.6 counted only the multiplications by weights, for one sample: \(8320 = 8513 - 193\), where 193 is the number of biases. Such counts are estimates of the cost, and different tools use different conventions; it is always necessary to check what a tool counts.
For the copy with the frozen first layer (Section 1.5), col_names selects the columns, and the column “Trainable” shows which layers are frozen:

FlopCounterMode records every operation executed inside the with block. For a matrix product it counts 2 floating-point operations (one multiplication, one addition) per multiply-add; bias additions and activations are not counted. For one input sample this gives \(2\times8320\), twice the count of Section 1.6.


Code
from torch.utils.flop_counter import FlopCounterMode

with FlopCounterMode(display=False) as counter:   # display=False: no printed table (it would need the package tabulate)
    model(torch.zeros(1, 1))                      # one forward pass for one sample
print("floating-point operations:", counter.get_total_flops(), "  = 2 x", mult_adds)


floating-point operations: 16640   = 2 x 8320


The number of layers of each type is obtained from model.modules(), which runs over the model itself and all layers inside it:


Code
n_linear = sum(isinstance(m, nn.Linear) for m in model.modules())    # True counts as 1, False as 0
n_tanh = sum(isinstance(m, nn.Tanh) for m in model.modules())
print(f"Linear layers: {n_linear},  Tanh layers: {n_tanh}")


Linear layers: 4,  Tanh layers: 3


Finally the drawing by torchview. draw_graph passes a batch of the given shape through the model and records every layer it meets; .visual_graph is the resulting picture; display(...) (available in every Jupyter/Colab notebook without import) shows it, which is needed here because the picture is created inside a try block. Every box is one layer with the shapes of its input and output; the first dimension (8) is the batch. Unlike our draw_network, which draws individual nodes (up to max_nodes per layer), this drawing shows layers and shapes, and it works for any model, also for models with skip connections. If Graphviz is missing, the except branch prints a message instead.


Code
try:
    from torchview import draw_graph
    graph = draw_graph(model, input_size=(8, 1))
    display(graph.visual_graph)
except Exception as err:
    print("torchview drawing not available:", err)





The tools are faster to use, and they are the right choice for large models. The hand-made versions of Sections 1.1–1.6 remain useful: they show what the numbers mean, and they can be extended to any quantity a tool does not provide (e.g. the saturation of the activations in Section 2.3).

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
text:
2. The network before training

2.1 Data
Noisy measurements of a damped oscillation \(y(t) = e^{-0.2t}\cos(2t)\), \(t\in[0, 10]\), with noise of standard deviation \(\sigma = 0.1\) and deliberately few training points, so that overfitting (Section 4) becomes visible: 30 points for training, 40 for validation, 40 for testing. The input is rescaled to \([-1, 1]\).
The numbers are chosen for this purpose: - The noise \(0.1\) is about 10% of the amplitude of the signal (\(y(0) = 1\)): large enough for overfitting to be visible, small enough for the oscillation to remain recognisable. - With only 30 training points the network of Section 1 (8513 parameters) can memorise the training set. The validation and test sets are larger (40 points each) because their losses are used to choose and to evaluate the model, and a larger set gives a less noisy estimate. - The positions \(t\) are drawn uniformly at random, so the three sets cover the interval in the same way. All \(30+40+40 = 110\) points are drawn at once, and the first 30, the next 40 and the last 40 form the three sets. - t_plot (400 equally spaced values) and the corresponding network input X_plot are not data: they are a dense grid on which functions are evaluated for plotting, and on which the hidden layers are examined in Section 2.3. - The rescaling \(t \to t/5 - 1\) maps \([0, 10]\) onto \([-1, 1]\). \(\tanh\) changes only for arguments of order one; with the raw inputs (up to 10) and first-layer weights in \([-1, 1]\), 52% of the first-layer activations of the untrained network would be saturated (Section 2.3), with the rescaled inputs below 0.1%.


Code
def damped_oscillation(t):
    return np.exp(-0.2 * t) * np.cos(2 * t)

noise = 0.1
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
t_all = rng.uniform(0, 10, 110)
y_all = damped_oscillation(t_all) + noise * rng.normal(size=110)

def to_tensor(t, y):
    """Inputs rescaled to [-1, 1] and targets, both of shape (B, 1), float32."""
    X = torch.tensor(t / 5.0 - 1.0, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
    Y = torch.tensor(y, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
    return X, Y

X_train, Y_train = to_tensor(t_all[:30], y_all[:30])        # the points are in random order already
X_val, Y_val = to_tensor(t_all[30:70], y_all[30:70])
X_test, Y_test = to_tensor(t_all[70:], y_all[70:])
print("training:", tuple(X_train.shape), " validation:", tuple(X_val.shape), " test:", tuple(X_test.shape))

t_plot = np.linspace(0, 10, 400)
X_plot = torch.tensor(t_plot / 5.0 - 1.0, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.5))
ax.plot(t_plot, damped_oscillation(t_plot), "k", lw=1, label="true function")
ax.plot(t_all[:30], y_all[:30], "o", label="training (30)")
ax.plot(t_all[30:70], y_all[30:70], "s", ms=4, label="validation (40)")
ax.plot(t_all[70:], y_all[70:], "^", ms=4, label="test (40)")
ax.set_xlabel("$t$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$"); ax.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=2); plt.show()


training: (30, 1)  validation: (40, 1)  test: (40, 1)







2.2 Weights
PyTorch initialises the weights of nn.Linear(n_in, n_out) uniformly in \([-1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}},\ 1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}]\). The first layer (\(n_{\rm in}=1\)) therefore has weights in \([-1, 1]\), the hidden layers (\(n_{\rm in}=64\)) in \([-0.125, 0.125]\). The histograms below show the weights of every Linear layer of the untrained model, with these bounds as dashed lines. The biases are drawn from the same interval.
The scale \(1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}\) keeps the size of the weighted sum \(\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\rm in}} w_i x_i\) independent of the number of inputs: for independent \(w_i\) and \(x_i\) with zero mean its variance is \(n_{\rm in}\,{\rm Var}(w)\,{\rm Var}(x)\), which does not grow with \(n_{\rm in}\) when \({\rm Var}(w)\propto 1/n_{\rm in}\).


Code
linear_layers = [layer for layer in model if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear)]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(linear_layers), figsize=(16, 3.2))
for k, (ax, layer) in enumerate(zip(axes, linear_layers)):
    w = layer.weight.detach().numpy().ravel()
    bound = 1 / np.sqrt(layer.in_features)
    ax.hist(w, bins=30)                                         # bins: enough to show the shape, a matter of readability
    ax.axvline(-bound, color="k", ls="--"); ax.axvline(bound, color="k", ls="--")
    ax.set_title(f"Linear {k + 1}: {layer.in_features} -> {layer.out_features}\n{w.size} weights")
    ax.set_xlabel("weight value")
axes[0].set_ylabel("count")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The weight histograms above are flat between the dashed bounds, as expected for a uniform distribution; the panels with only 64 weights are irregular because 64 samples are few.


2.3 Activations and saturated nodes
To see what the hidden layers do, we pass the 400 inputs of the dense grid X_plot through the network and record the output of every activation layer. A node computes \(h = \tanh(z)\), where \(z\) is its weighted input, and \(\frac{d}{dz}\tanh z = 1 - \tanh^2 z = 1 - h^2\). A node with \(|h| > 0.95\) is saturated: its derivative \(1-h^2 < 0.0975 \approx 0.1\) is small, so gradients passing through it are damped by a factor of ten or more. The threshold 0.95 is a convention; any value between about 0.9 and 0.99 gives the same qualitative picture. The saturated fraction of a layer, shown in the panel titles below, is the fraction of activation values \(h\) (over all nodes and all 400 inputs) with \(|h|>0.95\).


Code
def hidden_activations(model, x):
    """Outputs of all activation layers of an nn.Sequential model for the input batch x."""
    outputs = []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for layer in model:
            x = layer(x)
            if not isinstance(layer, nn.Linear):     # keep the outputs of the activation layers only
                outputs.append(x.numpy().copy())   # .numpy() shares memory with the tensor; copy() makes the stored array independent
    return outputs

acts = hidden_activations(model, X_plot)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(acts), figsize=(15, 3.2))
for k, (ax, h) in enumerate(zip(axes, acts)):
    saturated = np.mean(np.abs(h) > 0.95)
    ax.hist(h.ravel(), bins=40, range=(-1, 1))     # the full range of tanh, the same in every panel so that they can be compared
    ax.set_title(f"hidden layer {k + 1}: std {h.std():.3f},\nsaturated {100 * saturated:.0f}%")
    ax.set_xlabel("activation $h$")
axes[0].set_ylabel("count")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





With the default initialisation practically no activation is saturated (below 0.1%), and the spread of the activations shrinks from layer to layer: the signal becomes weaker with depth.


2.4 Gradients in every layer
One forward and one backward pass on the training set give the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight matrix. Its norm tells how strongly each layer would be changed by the first step of gradient descent.
model.zero_grad() first sets the stored gradients to zero, because PyTorch adds new gradients to those already in .grad. nn.functional.mse_loss(a, b) is the function form of nn.MSELoss()(a, b) and gives the same value. For a matrix, .norm() is the Frobenius norm \(\sqrt{\sum_{ij} g_{ij}^2}\), the length of the matrix viewed as one long vector.


Code
def gradient_norms(model, X, Y):
    """Norm of dL/dW for the weight matrix of every Linear layer (one backward pass)."""
    model.zero_grad()
    nn.functional.mse_loss(model(X), Y).backward()
    return [layer.weight.grad.norm().item() for layer in model if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear)]

for k, g in enumerate(gradient_norms(model, X_train, Y_train)):
    print(f"Linear {k + 1}: |dL/dW| = {g:.2e}")


Linear 1: |dL/dW| = 1.41e-02
Linear 2: |dL/dW| = 4.85e-01
Linear 3: |dL/dW| = 5.12e-01
Linear 4: |dL/dW| = 7.12e-01


The gradient of the first layer is the smallest. Gradient norms of different layers are, however, not directly comparable: the first weight matrix has only \(64\) entries, the hidden ones \(64\times64 = 4096\), and the norm sums over all entries. Comparisons are meaningful for the same layer between different models or different epochs, as in Sections 2.5 and 3.2.


2.5 The influence of the initialisation scale
The analysis of Sections 2.3–2.4 is repeated for a deeper network (6 hidden layers of width 64) whose weights are drawn from \(\mathcal N(0, (c/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}})^2)\), the normal (Gaussian) distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation \(c/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}\), for three values of \(c\). The table lists, for every hidden layer, the standard deviation of the activations and the fraction of saturated nodes, and the gradient norm of every weight matrix.

The three values stand for a too small, a standard and a too large scale. Their effect is multiplied once per layer, so a deeper network than in Section 1 makes it easier to see.
A normal distribution is used instead of PyTorch’s uniform one; only the standard deviation matters for the argument. For comparison, the default uniform distribution on \([-1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}, 1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}]\) has standard deviation \(1/\sqrt{3n_{\rm in}}\), i.e. \(c = 1/\sqrt3 \approx 0.58\); this is why the activations of Section 2.3 shrink with depth.
The functions of nn.init overwrite the values of an existing tensor in place (in PyTorch a trailing underscore, as in normal_, marks an in-place operation). The biases are set to zero so that only the weight scale is varied.
The activations are measured on the dense grid X_plot, which samples the input interval evenly; the gradients are those of the training loss and need the training data.
pivot rearranges the long table (one row per pair (\(c\), layer)) into a wide one with one row per layer and one column per quantity and value of \(c\), so that the three values of \(c\) stand side by side. round(4) only affects the display.



Code
def init_scaled(layer_sizes, c, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    m = make_mlp(layer_sizes)
    for layer in m:
        if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear):
            nn.init.normal_(layer.weight, mean=0.0, std=c / np.sqrt(layer.in_features))
            nn.init.zeros_(layer.bias)
    return m

deep_sizes = [1] + [64] * 6 + [1]
rows = []
for c in [0.5, 1.0, 3.0]:
    m = init_scaled(deep_sizes, c)
    acts = hidden_activations(m, X_plot)
    grads = gradient_norms(m, X_train, Y_train)
    for k, h in enumerate(acts):
        rows.append({"c": c, "hidden layer": k + 1, "activation std": h.std(),
                     "saturated (%)": 100 * np.mean(np.abs(h) > 0.95), "|dL/dW| of this layer": grads[k]})
init_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
init_table.pivot(index="hidden layer", columns="c", values=["activation std", "saturated (%)", "|dL/dW| of this layer"]).round(4)
