\(c = 0.5\): the activations shrink by about a factor of two per layer, and all gradients are more than twenty times smaller than for \(c = 1\), decreasing slightly towards the first layers: the signal fades in both directions (vanishing gradients).
\(c = 1\): the activations decrease with depth only slowly (for \(\tanh\) the derivative is below 1, so \(c=1\) does not exactly preserve the signal), and the gradients are of similar size in hidden layers 2–6 (layer 1 has only 64 weights, so its norm is smaller; see Section 2.4).
\(c = 3\): a large fraction of the nodes (up to about half in the deeper layers) is saturated, and the gradients are tens of times larger than for \(c = 1\): the first optimisation steps would be very large (exploding gradients).

The weight scale therefore has to be chosen with the depth and the activation in mind; standard choices are derived from such arguments. Xavier (Glorot) initialisation uses \({\rm Var}(w) = 2/(n_{\rm in}+n_{\rm out})\), i.e. \(c = 1\) for square layers, and is meant for \(\tanh\)-like activations. He initialisation uses \({\rm Var}(w) = 2/n_{\rm in}\) (\(c = \sqrt2\)), which compensates for the activation ReLU, \(\mathrm{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z)\), which sets negative inputs (about half of them) to zero.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
text:
3. Monitoring training
The training function below is a standard training loop (full batch, Adam) with additional bookkeeping. After every epoch it records: - the training loss and the validation loss; - the norm of the gradient of every weight matrix; - the relative change of every weight matrix since the start, \(\|W(e) - W(0)\| / \|W(0)\|\), where \(e\) is the epoch; - a copy of the parameters at the epoch with the smallest validation loss so far (used in Section 4).
Details of the code: - log is a dictionary of lists, one entry appended per epoch. For the gradients and weight changes each entry is a list of 4 numbers (one per Linear layer); at the end np.array turns this list of lists into an array of shape (number of epochs, 4), so that log["grad"][:, k] is the history of layer \(k+1\). - Full batch. The 30 training points form one batch, so every epoch is a single exact gradient step and the loss curves contain no noise from a random choice of mini-batches. - lr=1e-2, 3000 epochs. \(10^{-2}\) is a common starting value for Adam on small problems; it was not tuned. With learning rates \(10^{-3}\), \(3\cdot10^{-3}\), \(10^{-2}\) and \(3\cdot10^{-2}\) the smallest validation loss is reached at epochs 753, 419, 293 and 281, and in every case the validation loss rises afterwards. 3000 epochs is far more than needed to reach the minimum, so that the overfitting after it can be seen. - W0 = [... .detach().clone() ...]. optimizer.step() changes the weights in place. Without clone() the list would hold the current weight tensors themselves and the relative change would always be zero. detach() keeps the copy out of the gradient computation. - best = {"val": np.inf, ...}. Starting from infinity, the validation loss of the first epoch is always smaller and becomes the first “best” model. - copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict()). state_dict() returns a dictionary of the parameter tensors themselves, not of copies. Without deepcopy the stored “best” state would follow every later optimiser step and end up equal to the final parameters. - model.train(), model.eval() switch layers such as dropout and batch normalisation between their training and evaluation behaviour. This network has no such layers, so here the calls change nothing; they are kept because a general training loop needs them. - The training loss of an epoch is computed before optimizer.step(), the validation loss after it. The two curves are shifted by one step, which is irrelevant on a scale of thousands of epochs. - torch.manual_seed(0) before make_mlp gives the same initial weights as in Sections 1–2: the model trained here is exactly the one analysed above.


Code
def train_monitored(model, n_epochs=3000, lr=1e-2):
    linear = [layer for layer in model if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear)]
    W0 = [layer.weight.detach().clone() for layer in linear]          # initial weights, for the relative change
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()
    log = {"train": [], "val": [], "grad": [], "change": []}
    best = {"val": np.inf, "epoch": None, "state": None}
    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        model.train()
        loss = loss_fn(model(X_train), Y_train)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        log["grad"].append([layer.weight.grad.norm().item() for layer in linear])    # read the gradients before the step
        optimizer.step()

        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            val_loss = loss_fn(model(X_val), Y_val).item()
            log["change"].append([((layer.weight - w0).norm() / w0.norm()).item() for layer, w0 in zip(linear, W0)])
        log["train"].append(loss.item())
        log["val"].append(val_loss)
        if val_loss < best["val"]:                                     # remember the best model so far
            best = {"val": val_loss, "epoch": epoch, "state": copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())}
    log["grad"], log["change"] = np.array(log["grad"]), np.array(log["change"])
    return log, best

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = make_mlp(layer_sizes)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
log, best = train_monitored(model)
train_time = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"training took {train_time:.1f} s;  smallest validation loss {best['val']:.3e} at epoch {best['epoch']}")


training took 2.7 s;  smallest validation loss 1.941e-02 at epoch 293



3.1 Loss on the training and validation sets versus epoch
The most important plot of every training run. The dotted line is the noise variance \(\sigma^2 = 0.01\), the smallest mean squared error that any model can reach on new data; the vertical line marks the epoch with the smallest validation loss.


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))
ax.semilogy(log["train"], label="training loss")
ax.semilogy(log["val"], label="validation loss")
ax.axhline(noise**2, color="gray", ls=":", label=r"noise variance $\sigma^2$")
ax.axvline(best["epoch"], color="C3", ls="--", label=f"smallest validation loss (epoch {best['epoch']})")
ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("MSE"); ax.legend()
plt.show()
print(f"at the end: training loss {log['train'][-1]:.2e}, validation loss {log['val'][-1]:.2e}")





at the end: training loss 3.65e-03, validation loss 8.35e-02


Two phases are visible: 1. At first both losses decrease together: the network learns the function that the training and validation points have in common. 2. Later the training loss keeps decreasing, below the noise variance, while the validation loss increases. Below \(\sigma^2\) the network can only improve on the training set by reproducing its particular noise, which is useless (in fact harmful) for new points. This is overfitting. (With 30 points even the true function has a training MSE that fluctuates by about \(\sigma^2\sqrt{2/30} \approx 25\%\) around \(\sigma^2\), so only a training loss well below \(\sigma^2\), as here at the end of training, is a clear sign of fitting the noise.)


3.2 Gradients and weight changes per layer
The gradient norms vary over several orders of magnitude and are plotted on a logarithmic axis; the relative weight changes stay between 0 and about 3 and are readable on a linear axis.


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4))
for k in range(log["grad"].shape[1]):
    axes[0].semilogy(log["grad"][:, k], lw=1, label=f"Linear {k + 1}")
    axes[1].plot(log["change"][:, k], label=f"Linear {k + 1}")
axes[0].set_xlabel("epoch"); axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$\|\partial L/\partial W\|$"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_xlabel("epoch"); axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$\|W(e) - W(0)\|\,/\,\|W(0)\|$"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].axvline(best["epoch"], color="C3", ls="--")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()






The gradient norms decay during long stretches, interrupted by sudden spikes: at a spike the Adam step overshoots, the loss jumps up for a few epochs and then decreases again. These episodes are also visible as small jumps in the right panel.
The right panel shows how far each weight matrix has moved from its initial values. Relative changes of order one mean that training has substantially rewritten the layer; changes that keep growing after the best epoch (dashed line) are the parameters adapting to the noise of the training set.

4. Overfitting and the choice of the epoch

train_monitored kept a copy of the parameters from the epoch with the smallest validation loss. Loading it gives the model that would have been obtained by stopping the training there (early stopping). Both models are compared with the data.
A state_dict contains only numbers, not the architecture. A network with the same layer sizes is therefore built first, and its random initial parameters are then overwritten by load_state_dict. final_model = model is not a copy, only a second name for the trained network.


Code
final_model = model                                   # parameters after the last epoch
best_model = make_mlp(layer_sizes)
best_model.load_state_dict(best["state"])             # parameters from the epoch with the smallest validation loss

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))
ax.plot(t_plot, damped_oscillation(t_plot), "k", lw=1, label="true function")
ax.plot(t_all[:30], y_all[:30], "o", color="C0", label="training data")
with torch.no_grad():
    ax.plot(t_plot, final_model(X_plot), "C3", lw=1.5, label=f"after the last epoch ({len(log['train'])})")
    ax.plot(t_plot, best_model(X_plot), "C2", lw=2, label=f"at the best epoch ({best['epoch']})")
ax.set_xlabel("$t$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$"); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show()





The model after the last epoch passes close to the training points and makes large excursions in the gaps between them (e.g. around \(t \approx 5\)). The model from the best epoch is smooth and follows the true function over most of the interval, but it misses the small oscillations for \(t \gtrsim 6\). The best epoch was chosen with the validation set: the test set has not been used yet.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
section: 5. The final evaluation on the test set
text:
5. The final evaluation on the test set
Now, and only now, the chosen model is evaluated on the test set. Its test loss is the estimate of the error on new data that would be reported. For illustration only, the test loss of the overfitted final model is printed as well; it was not used to make any choice.


Code
loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()
best_model.eval(); final_model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    test_best = loss_fn(best_model(X_test), Y_test).item()
    test_final = loss_fn(final_model(X_test), Y_test).item()
    pred_test = best_model(X_test).numpy().ravel()
print(f"chosen model (best epoch {best['epoch']}): test MSE = {test_best:.3e}")
print(f"final model (for comparison only)   : test MSE = {test_final:.3e}")
print(f"noise variance                       : {noise**2:.3e}")

residuals = pred_test - Y_test.numpy().ravel()
print(f"residuals: mean {residuals.mean():+.3f}, standard deviation {residuals.std():.3f} (noise level sigma = {noise})")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4))
axes[0].plot(Y_test.numpy(), pred_test, "o")
lims = [Y_test.min().item() - 0.1, Y_test.max().item() + 0.1]      # the margin 0.1 only extends the diagonal beyond the data
axes[0].plot(lims, lims, "k--", lw=1)
axes[0].set_xlabel("measured $y$ (test set)"); axes[0].set_ylabel("predicted $y$"); axes[0].set_title("prediction vs. measurement")
axes[1].hist(residuals, bins=12)                                  # few bins: only 40 residuals
axes[1].set_xlabel("residual (predicted - measured)"); axes[1].set_ylabel("count"); axes[1].set_title(f"residuals, std {residuals.std():.3f}")
axes[2].plot(t_all[70:], residuals, "o"); axes[2].axhline(0, color="k", lw=1)
axes[2].set_xlabel("$t$"); axes[2].set_ylabel("residual"); axes[2].set_title("residuals vs. input")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


chosen model (best epoch 293): test MSE = 3.197e-02
final model (for comparison only)   : test MSE = 7.065e-02
noise variance                       : 1.000e-02
residuals: mean -0.027, standard deviation 0.177 (noise level sigma = 0.1)





For an ideal model the points of the left panel lie around the diagonal, the residuals have a standard deviation equal to the noise level \(\sigma = 0.1\), and they show no trend with the input \(t\). Even for an ideal model the standard deviation of 40 residuals fluctuates by about \(\sigma/\sqrt{2\cdot 40} \approx 0.011\) around \(0.1\) (for \(n\) Gaussian values the sample standard deviation scatters by about \(\sigma/\sqrt{2n}\)). Note also that residuals.std() subtracts the mean residual, so a constant offset of the model does not enter it, while \(\sqrt{\text{test MSE}}\) includes it. Here the residual standard deviation (in the title of the middle panel) is larger than \(\sigma\) by much more than this fluctuation, and the right panel shows why: for \(t \gtrsim 9\) all residuals are negative, i.e. the model is systematically too low in this region (it misses the last oscillation, see Section 4), and between \(t \approx 7\) and \(8.3\) all residuals are positive (the minimum of \(y\) near \(t \approx 7.9\) is too shallow in the model). In the left panel the points with \(t \gtrsim 9\) form a horizontal row: the model predicts almost the same value, about \(-0.08\), for all of them, whatever the measured value. Residual plots reveal such systematic errors, which a single number such as the test MSE hides.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
section: 6. A summary table of the characteristics of a model
text:
6. A summary table of the characteristics of a model
The quantities of this notebook are collected for two models trained on the same data: the network analysed so far and a small network with one hidden layer of 16 nodes. Both are evaluated at their best epoch. The small network (\(16\cdot 2 + 17 = 49\) parameters) serves as a contrast: with one narrow hidden layer it can represent only smooth functions, so it overfits much more slowly; its smallest validation loss is reached only at epoch 2880, near the end of the 3000 epochs, and at that epoch its training loss, \(7.8\cdot10^{-3}\), is only slightly below \(\sigma^2\). (With 30 points the training MSE of even the true function fluctuates by about \(\sigma^2\sqrt{2/30} \approx 25\%\) around \(\sigma^2\).) Its width 16 is arbitrary.
DataFrame.style.format changes only how the numbers are displayed, not the stored values: "{:.2f}" means two decimal places, "{:.2e}" scientific notation with two decimals. The training time depends on the computer and on other running processes; it is useful only to compare models trained on the same machine.


Code
def characterise(sizes, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    m = make_mlp(sizes)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    lg, bst = train_monitored(m)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
    m.load_state_dict(bst["state"]); m.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        tr = loss_fn(m(X_train), Y_train).item()
        te = loss_fn(m(X_test), Y_test).item()
    return {
        "layer sizes": str(sizes),
        "parameters": sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters()),
        "memory (kB)": sum(p.numel() * p.element_size() for p in m.parameters()) / 1024,
        "best epoch": bst["epoch"],
        "train MSE": tr, "val MSE": bst["val"], "test MSE": te,
        "train time (s)": elapsed,
    }

summary_table = pd.DataFrame([characterise([1, 16, 1]), characterise(layer_sizes)])
summary_table.style.format({"memory (kB)": "{:.2f}", "train MSE": "{:.2e}", "val MSE": "{:.2e}", "test MSE": "{:.2e}", "train time (s)": "{:.1f}"})

Reading the table: with these 30 training points the small network has the smaller validation and test errors (test MSE about 0.014 against 0.032). Here, with few data, more parameters do not give a better model. The large network reaches its best validation loss early (epoch 293), when its training error is still above the noise variance; later it improves only on the training set. The small network has a lower training error at its best epoch, because that epoch comes much later.
Such a table is the minimum documentation of a trained model: architecture and size, how it was selected (best epoch by validation loss), and its errors on the three data sets. Only the test column is an unbiased estimate of the error on new data.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
text:
7. Summary

Architecture: layer table (shapes, parameters per layer), total and trainable parameters (requires_grad), memory (\(4\) bytes per float32 parameter) and multiply-adds per sample. Parameters grow linearly with depth and quadratically with width.
Before training: weight and activation histograms, fraction of saturated nodes, gradient norms per layer; the initialisation scale controls whether signals and gradients shrink, survive or saturate with depth.
During training: training and validation loss versus epoch; gradient norms and relative weight changes per layer.
Overfitting: the training loss falls below the noise level while the validation loss rises; the parameters at the epoch with the smallest validation loss are kept (early stopping).
Test set: used once, for the chosen model; residual plots show whether errors are random or systematic.

8. Exercises


Exercise 1 — Analysing an image classifier
The image classifier nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10)) assigns a \(28\times28\) grey-scale image of a handwritten digit (the MNIST data set) to one of 10 classes, the digits \(0, \dots, 9\): it has \(784\) inputs, one per pixel, and 10 outputs, one per class. 1. Load the MNIST test images (torchvision.datasets.MNIST, train=False) and show one example of every class with its label. 2. Draw the network and produce its layer table with layer_table for a batch of 16 test images (pixel values divided by 255). 3. Which layer holds most of the parameters, and what fraction? Why is it this layer? 4. Compute the memory of the parameters and the number of multiply-adds per image. 5. Freeze everything except the last layer and report the number of trainable parameters. Check the totals with torchinfo.summary (Section 1.7).

Solution


Code
import contextlib, io

# 1) data: the MNIST test set (random numbers if the download fails)

    from torchvision import datasets
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()), contextlib.redirect_stderr(io.StringIO()):
        mnist = datasets.MNIST(root="data", train=False, download=True)
    images_raw, labels = mnist.data, mnist.targets
except Exception as err:
    print("MNIST could not be loaded:", err)
    images_raw = torch.randint(0, 256, (10000, 28, 28), dtype=torch.uint8)
    labels = torch.randint(0, 10, (10000,))
images = images_raw.float() / 255                    # pixel values in [0, 1]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 10, figsize=(12, 1.8))
for k, ax in enumerate(axes):
    first = torch.nonzero(labels == k)[0, 0]          # position of the first image of class k
    ax.imshow(images_raw[first], cmap="gray_r")
    ax.set_title(f"class {k}"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.show()

clf = nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10))

# 2) drawing and table
draw_network([784, 128, 64, 10], activations=["ReLU", "ReLU"], title="image classifier",
             output_labels=[f"{k}" for k in range(10)])
plt.show()
clf_table = layer_table(clf, images[:16])            # 16 test images, shape (16, 28, 28)
print(clf_table.to_string(index=False))              # print the whole table without the row-number column

# 3) share of the largest layer
total = clf_table["parameters"].sum()
largest = clf_table.loc[clf_table["parameters"].idxmax()]   # idxmax(): row label of the largest value; .loc[label]: that row
print(f"\nlargest layer: index {largest['index']} ({largest['layer']}) with {largest['parameters']} of {total} parameters "
      f"= {100 * largest['parameters'] / total:.1f}%")
# It is the first Linear layer: every one of its 128 nodes has one weight per pixel, 784 x 128 weights in total.

# 4) memory and multiply-adds
n_bytes = sum(p.numel() * p.element_size() for p in clf.parameters())

# 5) freeze all parameters, then unfreeze the last layer
for p in clf.parameters():

for p in clf[-1].parameters():

print("trainable parameters after freezing:", sum(p.numel() for p in clf.parameters() if p.requires_grad), "(= 64 x 10 + 10)")

Exercise 2 — Early stopping with patience
In practice training is stopped automatically once the validation loss has not improved for a number of epochs (the patience). Modify the training loop so that it stops after 200 epochs without a new minimum of the validation loss, restore the best parameters, and report the stopping epoch, the best epoch, the time saved compared with 3000 epochs, and the test loss of the restored model.
The patience must be longer than the temporary rises of the validation loss (the spikes of Section 3.2), otherwise training stops at one of them. With the network and data of this notebook a patience of 100 epochs stops at epoch 213 with the best epoch 113 and validation loss 0.036, nearly twice the minimum found in Section 3; patience 200 and 500 both find the minimum at epoch 293.

Solution


Code
def train_early_stopping(model, max_epochs=3000, patience=200, lr=1e-2):
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    best_val, best_epoch, best_state = np.inf, 0, None
    train_hist, val_hist = [], []
    for epoch in range(max_epochs):
        model.train()
        loss = loss_fn(model(X_train), Y_train)
        optimizer.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); optimizer.step()
        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            val = loss_fn(model(X_val), Y_val).item()
        train_hist.append(loss.item()); val_hist.append(val)
        if val < best_val:
            best_val, best_epoch, best_state = val, epoch, copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())
        elif epoch - best_epoch >= patience:          # no improvement for `patience` epochs
            break                                     # leave the loop; `epoch` keeps its last value
    model.load_state_dict(best_state)                 # restore the best parameters
    return epoch, best_epoch, train_hist, val_hist

torch.manual_seed(0)
m = make_mlp(layer_sizes)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
stop_epoch, best_epoch, tr_h, va_h = train_early_stopping(m)
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
with torch.no_grad():
    test_mse = loss_fn(m(X_test), Y_test).item()
print(f"stopped at epoch {stop_epoch}, best epoch {best_epoch}, {elapsed:.1f} s instead of about {train_time:.1f} s for 3000 epochs")
print(f"test MSE of the restored model: {test_mse:.3e}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.semilogy(tr_h, label="training"); ax.semilogy(va_h, label="validation")
ax.axvline(best_epoch, color="C3", ls="--", label="best epoch"); ax.axvline(stop_epoch, color="k", ls=":", label="stop")
ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("MSE"); ax.legend(); plt.show()


stopped at epoch 493, best epoch 293, 0.4 s instead of about 2.7 s for 3000 epochs
test MSE of the restored model: 3.197e-02








Exercise 3 — More training data
Repeat the training of Section 3 (same network, same validation set) with 30, 100 and 300 training points (generate the additional points with the same function and noise). Plot the training and validation loss versus epoch for the three cases in one figure (same colour per case, solid = training, dashed = validation). How does the gap between training and validation loss change with the amount of data?

Solution


Code
rng_extra = np.random.default_rng(10)                         # a different seed: new, independent points
t_extra = rng_extra.uniform(0, 10, 270)
y_extra = damped_oscillation(t_extra) + noise * rng_extra.normal(size=270)
X_val_fixed, Y_val_fixed = X_val, Y_val                       # only new names: the validation set is the same in all three runs

for color, n in zip(["C0", "C1", "C2"], [30, 100, 300]):
    t_n = np.concatenate([t_all[:30], t_extra[:n - 30]])        # the original 30 points plus new ones (np.concatenate joins arrays end to end)
    y_n = np.concatenate([y_all[:30], y_extra[:n - 30]])

    torch.manual_seed(0)
    m = make_mlp(layer_sizes)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(m.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
    tr_h, va_h = [], []
    for epoch in range(3000):
        loss = loss_fn(m(Xn), Yn)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
        with torch.no_grad():
            va_h.append(loss_fn(m(X_val_fixed), Y_val_fixed).item())

    ax.semilogy(tr_h, color=color, label=f"{n} points: training")
    ax.semilogy(va_h, color=color, ls="--", label=f"{n} points: validation")
    print(f"{n:3d} training points: final training MSE {tr_h[-1]:.2e}, final validation MSE {va_h[-1]:.2e}, smallest validation MSE {min(va_h):.2e}")
ax.axhline(noise**2, color="gray", ls=":", label="noise variance")
ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("MSE"); ax.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=2); plt.show()
# With more data the network cannot reproduce the noise of every training point any more: the training loss stays
# closer to the noise variance, the validation loss rises less, and the gap between the two shrinks.

Exercise 4 — Training only the last layer
Freeze all layers of a fresh make_mlp(layer_sizes) except the last Linear layer and train it as in Section 3. The network is then a linear combination of 64 fixed random functions (the outputs of the last hidden layer) plus a constant (the bias): 65 trainable parameters. Compare the number of trainable parameters, the smallest validation loss and the fit with the fully trained network. Plot the 64 fixed functions.

features = hidden_activations(m_last, X_plot)[-1]      # (400, 64): the fixed functions of the last hidden layer

title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
section: 1. Getting the data: the original MNIST files
text:
1. Getting the data: the original MNIST files

1.1 Download
MNIST is distributed as four compressed files (.gz): images and labels, each for the training part (\(60\,000\) images) and the test part (\(10\,000\) images). Libraries such as torchvision or keras download exactly these files and decode them for you. Here we do both steps ourselves.
urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, path) downloads a file from the internet and saves it on disk. The original web page of Y. LeCun no longer serves the files reliably, so we use two public copies (mirrors) and take the first one that works. A file that is already on disk is not downloaded again.


Code
DATA_DIR = "data/MNIST_raw"
MIRRORS = ["https://ossci-datasets.s3.amazonaws.com/mnist/",          # copy used by torchvision
           "https://storage.googleapis.com/cvdf-datasets/mnist/"]     # copy used by tensorflow
FILES = {"train_images": "train-images-idx3-ubyte.gz",
         "train_labels": "train-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz",
         "test_images":  "t10k-images-idx3-ubyte.gz",
         "test_labels":  "t10k-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz"}

def download(filename):
    # Download one MNIST file into DATA_DIR (only if it is not there yet) and return its path.
    path = os.path.join(DATA_DIR, filename)
    if os.path.exists(path):
        return path
    os.makedirs(DATA_DIR, exist_ok=True)
    for mirror in MIRRORS:
        try:
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(mirror + filename, path)
            return path
        except Exception as err:
            print(f"  {mirror} failed: {err}")
            if os.path.exists(path):
                os.remove(path)                 # remove a partially downloaded file
    raise RuntimeError(f"could not download {filename}")

paths = {key: download(name) for key, name in FILES.items()}
for key, path in paths.items():
    print(f"{key:13s} {path:45s} {os.path.getsize(path) / 1e6:5.2f} MB")


train_images  data/MNIST_raw/train-images-idx3-ubyte.gz      9.91 MB
train_labels  data/MNIST_raw/train-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz      0.03 MB
test_images   data/MNIST_raw/t10k-images-idx3-ubyte.gz       1.65 MB
test_labels   data/MNIST_raw/t10k-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz       0.00 MB




1.2 The IDX file format
After decompression each file is a sequence of bytes (ubyte = unsigned byte, an integer \(0\dots255\)) in the very simple IDX format:







bytes
content




0–1
always 0, 0


2
data type; 8 (hex 0x08) means unsigned bytes


3
number of dimensions \(d\): 3 for images (number, rows, columns), 1 for labels


4 … \(4+4d-1\)
the \(d\) sizes, each a 4-byte integer, most significant byte first (big-endian)


then
the data, one byte per pixel or label, row after row



gzip.open decompresses on the fly. We read the first 16 bytes of the training images:


Code
with gzip.open(paths["train_images"], "rb") as f:
    header = f.read(16)                                       # 4 bytes "magic number" + 3 sizes of 4 bytes
print("first 16 bytes:", list(header))

sizes = np.frombuffer(header, dtype=">i4")                     # ">i4" = big-endian 4-byte integer
print("as four big-endian integers:", sizes)
print("data type byte:", header[2], " number of dimensions:", header[3])


first 16 bytes: [0, 0, 8, 3, 0, 0, 234, 96, 0, 0, 0, 28, 0, 0, 0, 28]
as four big-endian integers: [ 2051 60000    28    28]
data type byte: 8  number of dimensions: 3


The four integers are \(2051\) (the “magic number” \(=\) 0x00000803: data type 08, \(3\) dimensions), \(60\,000\) images, \(28\) rows and \(28\) columns. For example, \(60\,000 = 0\cdot256^3 + 0\cdot256^2 + 234\cdot256 + 96\), which are bytes 4–7 above.
A complete reader is a few lines. np.frombuffer interprets raw bytes as an array without copying; offset skips the header.


Code
def read_idx(path):
    # Read an IDX file (gzip-compressed) into a NumPy array of unsigned bytes.
    with gzip.open(path, "rb") as f:
        raw = f.read()
    assert raw[0] == 0 and raw[1] == 0 and raw[2] == 0x08, "not an IDX file of unsigned bytes"
    n_dims = raw[3]
    shape = np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=">i4", count=n_dims, offset=4)          # the d sizes
    data = np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=np.uint8, offset=4 + 4 * n_dims)        # all the rest
    return data.reshape(shape)

X_train_full = read_idx(paths["train_images"])
y_train_full = read_idx(paths["train_labels"])
X_test_raw   = read_idx(paths["test_images"])
y_test_raw   = read_idx(paths["test_labels"])

for name, a in [("X_train_full", X_train_full), ("y_train_full", y_train_full), ("X_test_raw", X_test_raw), ("y_test_raw", y_test_raw)]:
    print(f"{name:13s} shape {str(a.shape):16s} dtype {a.dtype}   values {a.min()} ... {a.max()}")
print("first 20 training labels:", y_train_full[:20])


X_train_full  shape (60000, 28, 28)  dtype uint8   values 0 ... 255
y_train_full  shape (60000,)         dtype uint8   values 0 ... 9
X_test_raw    shape (10000, 28, 28)  dtype uint8   values 0 ... 255
y_test_raw    shape (10000,)         dtype uint8   values 0 ... 9
first 20 training labels: [5 0 4 1 9 2 1 3 1 4 3 5 3 6 1 7 2 8 6 9]


That is the whole data set: an array of \(60\,000\) images \(28\times 28\) with integer pixel values \(0\) (background) to \(255\) (ink), the corresponding labels \(0\dots9\), and the same for the \(10\,000\) test images. Everything that follows works with these NumPy arrays.

title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
text:
2. A look at the data

2.1 Examples of every class
imshow draws a 2D array as an image; the colour map "gray_r" shows \(0\) as white and \(255\) as black, as on paper.


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 10, figsize=(12, 5))
for k in range(10):
    positions = np.flatnonzero(y_train_full == k)[:4]         # first four training images with label k
    for row, p in enumerate(positions):
        ax = axes[row, k]
        ax.imshow(X_train_full[p], cmap="gray_r")
        ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    axes[0, k].set_title(f"digit {k}")
fig.suptitle("MNIST training images")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()







2.2 Images per class
np.bincount(y, minlength=10) counts how often each of the values \(0,\dots,9\) occurs.


Code
counts_train = np.bincount(y_train_full, minlength=10)
counts_test = np.bincount(y_test_raw, minlength=10)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.2))
ax.bar(np.arange(10) - 0.2, counts_train / counts_train.sum(), width=0.4, label="training file (60 000)")
ax.bar(np.arange(10) + 0.2, counts_test / counts_test.sum(), width=0.4, label="test file (10 000)")
ax.axhline(0.1, color="k", lw=0.8, ls="--")
ax.set_xticks(range(10)); ax.set_xlabel("digit"); ax.set_ylabel("fraction of images"); ax.legend(loc="lower right")
plt.show()
print("training counts:", counts_train)
print("test counts    :", counts_test)





training counts: [5923 6742 5958 6131 5842 5421 5918 6265 5851 5949]
test counts    : [ 980 1135 1032 1010  982  892  958 1028  974 1009]


The classes are nearly balanced (between about \(9\%\) and \(11\%\) each), so a model that always answers the same digit would be right in only about \(10\%\) of the cases, and so would random guessing. Any useful model must do much better than \(10\%\).


2.3 The mean image of every class
Averaging all training images of one digit shows the “typical” shape and how much it varies (blurred regions = places where different writers put the ink differently).


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 10, figsize=(12, 1.6))
for k in range(10):
    axes[k].imshow(X_train_full[y_train_full == k].mean(axis=0), cmap="gray_r")
    axes[k].set_title(f"mean {k}"); axes[k].axis("off")
plt.show()







2.4 From an image to a vector: flattening
The networks of this notebook (dense / fully connected) take a vector as input. A \(28\times28\) image becomes a vector of \(m = 784\) numbers by writing the rows one after another: pixel \((i, j)\) (row \(i\), column \(j\)) goes to position \(28\,i + j\). This is what reshape does (NumPy and PyTorch store arrays row by row, so no data are moved).


Code
img = X_train_full[0]                         # one image, shape (28, 28)
vec = img.reshape(784)                        # the same numbers, shape (784,)
i, j = 6, 14
print(f"pixel (row {i}, column {j}) = {img[i, j]},   vector element {28 * i + j} = {vec[28 * i + j]}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 3), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 4]})
axes[0].imshow(img, cmap="gray_r"); axes[0].set_title(f"image, label {y_train_full[0]}")
axes[1].plot(vec, lw=0.8)
for r in range(1, 28):
    axes[1].axvline(28 * r, color="grey", lw=0.3)              # boundaries between image rows
axes[1].set_xlim(0, 784); axes[1].set_xlabel("position in the vector  (= 28 * row + column)"); axes[1].set_ylabel("pixel value")
axes[1].set_title("the same image as a vector of 784 numbers (grey lines: start of a new image row)")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


pixel (row 6, column 14) = 253,   vector element 182 = 253





Each bump in the right panel is one image row crossing the stroke. The network sees only this list of \(784\) numbers: it does not know which pixels are neighbours. (Convolutional networks, discussed later in Chapter 2, use the 2D arrangement.)

title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
text:
3. Splitting the data set (Box 2.10)

3.1 Training, validation, test

The training set is used to change the parameters (gradient descent).
The validation set is used during development: to watch for overfitting and to choose settings (number of epochs, learning rate, architecture).
The test set is used once, at the very end, to report the final quality. If it were used to choose settings, it would no longer measure performance on new data. For teaching purposes the analyses and exercises below also look at the test set; in a real project such comparisons would be made on the validation set.

The MNIST test file is our test set. The \(60\,000\) training images are split at random into \(50\,000\) for training and \(10\,000\) for validation. The split must be random: a data file may be ordered (by class, by writer, by date of collection), and the first images of a file need not be representative of the rest. rng.permutation(n) returns the numbers \(0,\dots,n-1\) in a random order; the first \(50\,000\) of them select the training images.


Code
n_full = len(X_train_full)
perm = rng.permutation(n_full)                     # a random order of 0, ..., 59999
idx_train, idx_val = perm[:50_000], perm[50_000:]
print("first 10 entries of the permutation:", perm[:10])
print("training indices:", len(idx_train), "  validation indices:", len(idx_val))
print("common indices:", len(np.intersect1d(idx_train, idx_val)),
      "  together they cover all images:", np.array_equal(np.sort(np.concatenate([idx_train, idx_val])), np.arange(n_full)))

X_tr_img, y_tr_np = X_train_full[idx_train], y_train_full[idx_train]
X_va_img, y_va_np = X_train_full[idx_val],   y_train_full[idx_val]
X_te_img, y_te_np = X_test_raw,              y_test_raw


first 10 entries of the permutation: [ 4013 23840 29603 43011 58703  2290 55984 52800 34316 12976]
training indices: 50000   validation indices: 10000
common indices: 0   together they cover all images: True


Indexing a NumPy array with an array of indices (X_train_full[idx_train]) picks the rows in that order. No image is in both sets, and together they use every image exactly once. The random split gives training and validation sets with the same class proportions, which also match the test file:


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.2))
for shift, (name, y) in zip([-0.27, 0, 0.27], [("training", y_tr_np), ("validation", y_va_np), ("test", y_te_np)]):
    ax.bar(np.arange(10) + shift, np.bincount(y, minlength=10) / len(y), width=0.27, label=f"{name} ({len(y)})")
ax.set_xticks(range(10)); ax.set_xlabel("digit"); ax.set_ylabel("fraction"); ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)
plt.show()







3.2 Flattening and standardisation
As in the chapter, the input vectors are standardised to mean \(0\) and standard deviation \(1\): \[\mathbf x \;\leftarrow\; \frac{\mathbf x - \mu}{s},\] with one number \(\mu\) (mean) and one number \(s\) (standard deviation) computed over all pixels of all training images. Inputs of order one keep the pre-activations \(\mathbf W\mathbf x + \mathbf b\) in the range where the sigmoid is not flat, which makes gradient descent work well.
\(\mu\) and \(s\) are computed from the training set only and then applied unchanged to validation and test data. Using statistics of the test set would let information about the test data leak into the model (data leakage); in a real application the test data are not even available when the model is built.
Finally the arrays are converted to PyTorch tensors: inputs as float32 (the default type of PyTorch parameters), labels as int64 (the type PyTorch expects for class indices).


Code
def flatten(images):
    # (N, 28, 28) uint8  ->  (N, 784) float32
    return images.reshape(len(images), -1).astype(np.float32)

X_tr_flat, X_va_flat, X_te_flat = flatten(X_tr_img), flatten(X_va_img), flatten(X_te_img)
mu, s = X_tr_flat.mean(), X_tr_flat.std()          # from the TRAINING set only
print(f"training-set pixel statistics: mean {mu:.2f}, std {s:.2f}  (on the 0..255 scale)")

X_tr = torch.from_numpy((X_tr_flat - mu) / s)
X_va = torch.from_numpy((X_va_flat - mu) / s)
X_te = torch.from_numpy((X_te_flat - mu) / s)
y_tr = torch.from_numpy(y_tr_np.astype(np.int64))
y_va = torch.from_numpy(y_va_np.astype(np.int64))
y_te = torch.from_numpy(y_te_np.astype(np.int64))

for name, X, y in [("train", X_tr, y_tr), ("val", X_va, y_va), ("test", X_te, y_te)]:
    print(f"{name:5s}  X {tuple(X.shape)} {X.dtype}  mean {X.mean():+.3f} std {X.std():.3f}   y {tuple(y.shape)} {y.dtype}")


training-set pixel statistics: mean 33.33, std 78.57  (on the 0..255 scale)
train  X (50000, 784) torch.float32  mean +0.000 std 1.000   y (50000,) torch.int64
val    X (10000, 784) torch.float32  mean -0.001 std 1.000   y (10000,) torch.int64
test   X (10000, 784) torch.float32  mean +0.006 std 1.008   y (10000,) torch.int64


The training inputs have mean \(0\) and standard deviation \(1\) by construction; validation and test inputs are close to that but not exactly, since they were transformed with the training statistics. The background pixels (\(0\)) become \(-\mu/s \approx -0.42\), full ink (\(255\)) becomes about \(2.8\).

title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
text:
4. Mini-batches

4.1 Batching by hand
The gradient of the loss is an average over images. Computing it over all \(50\,000\) images before every parameter update (full-batch gradient descent, as in the chapter’s equations) is expensive. Instead, in every epoch (one pass over the training set):

the training indices are put in a new random order,
the order is cut into consecutive pieces of batch_size indices (mini-batches),
for each mini-batch the loss and its gradient are computed on these images only, and the parameters are updated.

Every image is used exactly once per epoch; one epoch makes \(\lceil 50\,000/B\rceil\) updates (with \(B\) the batch size). The gradient of a mini-batch is a noisy estimate of the full gradient (stochastic gradient descent), but many cheap noisy steps are much faster than a few exact ones.
The function below produces the index arrays of the mini-batches. It is a Python generator: yield hands out one value and pauses the function until the next value is requested by the for loop, so the batches are produced one at a time.


Code
def batch_indices(n, batch_size, shuffle=True, generator=None):
    # Yield index tensors of consecutive mini-batches covering 0, ..., n-1 once.
    order = torch.randperm(n, generator=generator) if shuffle else torch.arange(n)
    for start in range(0, n, batch_size):
        yield order[start:start + batch_size]          # the last batch may be shorter

batch_size = 64
batches = list(batch_indices(len(X_tr), batch_size, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)))
print("number of mini-batches per epoch:", len(batches), "  ( = ceil(50000 / 64) =", int(np.ceil(50000 / 64)), ")")
print("sizes of the first three and of the last batch:", [len(b) for b in batches[:3]], len(batches[-1]))
print("first batch indices:", batches[0][:10].tolist(), "...")
all_used = torch.sort(torch.cat(batches)).values
print("every training image used exactly once:", torch.equal(all_used, torch.arange(len(X_tr))))


number of mini-batches per epoch: 782   ( = ceil(50000 / 64) = 782 )
sizes of the first three and of the last batch: [64, 64, 64] 16
first batch indices: [36044, 49165, 37807, 11341, 6091, 16904, 36293, 28026, 24681, 17849] ...
every training image used exactly once: True


\(50\,000 = 781\cdot 64 + 16\), hence \(782\) batches, the last one with \(16\) images. A batch of data is then X_tr[idx], y_tr[idx]: a matrix \(X_i\in\mathbb R^{64\times784}\) (one image per row, as in the chapter’s feed-forward pass) and a vector of \(64\) labels.


Code
idx = batches[0]
xb, yb = X_tr[idx], y_tr[idx]
print("one mini-batch: inputs", tuple(xb.shape), "  labels", tuple(yb.shape))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 16, figsize=(13, 3.8))
for ax, x, y in zip(axes.flat, xb, yb):
    ax.imshow(x.reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray_r")        # back to 28 x 28 for display only
    ax.set_title(str(y.item()), fontsize=9); ax.axis("off")
fig.suptitle("the first mini-batch of 64 images (in random order, with their labels)")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


one mini-batch: inputs (64, 784)   labels (64,)







4.2 The same with PyTorch: Dataset and DataLoader
PyTorch packages these two steps into two classes from torch.utils.data:

a Dataset knows how many samples there are (__len__) and returns sample number i (__getitem__), here a pair (image vector, label);
a DataLoader takes a Dataset, shuffles the indices in every epoch, cuts them into batches, calls __getitem__ for every index of a batch, and stacks the results into batch tensors (collate).

Writing our own Dataset shows that there is nothing more to it. (For tensors already in memory PyTorch also offers the ready-made TensorDataset, which does the same.) For large data sets that do not fit into memory, __getitem__ would read one image from disk; the DataLoader can then load batches in parallel processes (num_workers). This is the main reason the classes exist.


Code
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader

class MNISTDataset(Dataset):
    # Pairs (image vector, label) stored as two tensors in memory.
    def __init__(self, X, y):
        self.X, self.y = X, y

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.X)

    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return self.X[i], self.y[i]

ds_tr = MNISTDataset(X_tr, y_tr)
x0, y0 = ds_tr[0]                                       # calls __getitem__(0)
print("len(ds_tr) =", len(ds_tr), "   ds_tr[0]: image", tuple(x0.shape), " label", y0.item())

loader_tr = DataLoader(ds_tr, batch_size=64, shuffle=True, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0))
print("batches per epoch: len(loader_tr) =", len(loader_tr))
xb_dl, yb_dl = next(iter(loader_tr))                   # the first batch of one epoch
print("one batch from the DataLoader:", tuple(xb_dl.shape), tuple(yb_dl.shape))


len(ds_tr) = 50000    ds_tr[0]: image (784,)  label 1
batches per epoch: len(loader_tr) = 782
one batch from the DataLoader: (64, 784) (64,)


With shuffle=False both methods must give identical batches, and indeed they do. The timing shows the price of the generality: the DataLoader calls __getitem__ \(50\,000\) times per epoch and stacks single images, while X_tr[idx] copies a whole batch in one operation.


Code
loader_fixed = DataLoader(ds_tr, batch_size=64, shuffle=False)
same = all(torch.equal(xd, X_tr[idx]) and torch.equal(yd, y_tr[idx])
           for (xd, yd), idx in zip(loader_fixed, batch_indices(len(X_tr), 64, shuffle=False)))
print("DataLoader(shuffle=False) gives the same batches as batching by hand:", same)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for idx in batch_indices(len(X_tr), 64):
    xb, yb = X_tr[idx], y_tr[idx]
t_hand = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for xb, yb in loader_tr:
    pass
t_dl = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"one epoch of batches: by hand {t_hand:.3f} s,  DataLoader {t_dl:.3f} s")


DataLoader(shuffle=False) gives the same batches as batching by hand: True


one epoch of batches: by hand 0.015 s,  DataLoader 0.199 s


Both ways are used below: Part A (regression) uses the hand-written batching, Part B (cross-entropy) the DataLoader. Each mini-batch has the same size and is drawn the same way, so the choice does not affect the comparison of the two models.

title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
section: 5. Part A — Classification as regression with a single sigmoid output
text:
5. Part A — Classification as regression with a single sigmoid output

5.1 The idea
The chapter imagines an unknown function \(G:\mathbb R^{784}\to\{0,\dots,9\}\) that maps the pixels of an image to the digit it shows, and treats learning \(G\) as non-linear curve fitting (regression), just as in the one-dimensional example of the Universal Approximation Theorem:

the network has one output node with a sigmoid, so \(\bar y = f_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf x)\in(0,1)\);
the target of an image with digit \(y\) is the rescaled digit \(y/10\in\{0, 0.1, \dots, 0.9\}\);
the loss is the mean squared error over a batch of \(B\) images, \[\mathcal L = \frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B \big(\bar y_i - y_i/10\big)^2 ;\]
the predicted digit is \(10\,\bar y\) turned into an integer.

Turning \(10\bar y\) into an integer: int() in Python (and .long() in PyTorch) truncates, e.g. \(2.97\to2\), although the output is closest to the target \(3\). The correct choice is rounding to the nearest integer, then clipping to \(0\dots9\). (With the sigmoid, \(10\bar y\in(0,10)\), so \(9.6\) would round to \(10\).)


Code
outputs = torch.tensor([0.031, 0.297, 0.304, 0.649, 0.951])         # example values of the sigmoid output
print("10 * y_bar       :", (10 * outputs).tolist())
print("truncated (int)  :", (10 * outputs).long().tolist())
print("rounded + clipped:", (10 * outputs).round().clamp(0, 9).long().tolist())

def predict_digit_regression(y_bar):
    # sigmoid output in (0,1)  ->  digit 0..9
    return (10 * y_bar).round().clamp(0, 9).long()


10 * y_bar       : [0.3100000023841858, 2.9699997901916504, 3.0399999618530273, 6.489999771118164, 9.510000228881836]
truncated (int)  : [0, 2, 3, 6, 9]
rounded + clipped: [0, 3, 3, 6, 9]




5.2 The network
As in the chapter: the input is the flattened standardised image (\(m = 784\) numbers), followed by one hidden layer of \(N^{(1)} = 21\) nodes and the output node, all with the sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\): \[\bar{\mathbf h} = \sigma\big(\mathbf x W^{(1)T} + \mathbf b^{(1)}\big)\in(0,1)^{21},\qquad \bar y = \sigma\big(\bar{\mathbf h}W^{(2)T} + b^{(2)}\big)\in(0,1).\] The number of hidden nodes is kept in the variable N_HIDDEN, so that it can be changed in one place (Exercise 4 shows what wider and deeper networks do). nn.Linear(n_in, n_out) holds \(W\) of shape (n_out, n_in) and \(\mathbf b\) of length n_out, and computes \(\mathbf x W^T + \mathbf b\) for a batch of row vectors \(\mathbf x\). (The chapter has no bias in the output layer; with one extra parameter this makes no difference.)


Code
N_HIDDEN = 21                                     # nodes in the hidden layer, as in the chapter

def make_regression_model():
    return nn.Sequential(
        nn.Linear(784, N_HIDDEN), nn.Sigmoid(),      # hidden layer
        nn.Linear(N_HIDDEN, 1),   nn.Sigmoid(),      # ONE output node, value in (0, 1)
    )

torch.manual_seed(0)
model_reg = make_regression_model()
print(model_reg)
for name, p in model_reg.named_parameters():
    print(f"  {name:9s} {str(tuple(p.shape)):11s} {p.numel():7d} parameters")
print("total:", sum(p.numel() for p in model_reg.parameters()))

with torch.no_grad():
    out = model_reg(X_tr[:5])
print("output for 5 images, shape", tuple(out.shape), ":", out.squeeze(1).tolist())


Sequential(
  (0): Linear(in_features=784, out_features=21, bias=True)
  (1): Sigmoid()
  (2): Linear(in_features=21, out_features=1, bias=True)
  (3): Sigmoid()
)
  0.weight  (21, 784)     16464 parameters
  0.bias    (21,)            21 parameters
  2.weight  (1, 21)          21 parameters
  2.bias    (1,)              1 parameters
total: 16507
output for 5 images, shape (5, 1) : [0.49288123846054077, 0.5091497898101807, 0.5078026056289673, 0.48742517828941345, 0.5129513144493103]


The output has shape (B, 1), one column. The targets will have shape (B,), so the output is reshaped with .squeeze(1) before the loss is computed: nn.MSELoss given shapes (B, 1) and (B,) would broadcast them to a (B, B) matrix and compute something else; PyTorch only prints a warning, which is easy to overlook (a classic bug).
The untrained network gives nearly the same output \(\approx 0.5\) for every image (small random differences): it has not learned anything yet.


5.3 Loss and evaluation
A function that evaluates a model on a whole data set (all images at once, without gradients) returns the loss and the accuracy, the fraction of images whose predicted digit equals the label. The accuracy is what we care about, but it cannot be minimised by gradient descent: it is piecewise constant in the parameters, so its gradient is zero almost everywhere. The MSE changes smoothly.


Code
mse = nn.MSELoss()

def evaluate_regression(model, X, y):
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        y_bar = model(X).squeeze(1)                     # shape (N,)
        loss = mse(y_bar, y.float() / 10).item()
        acc = (predict_digit_regression(y_bar) == y).float().mean().item()
    return loss, acc

loss0, acc0 = evaluate_regression(model_reg, X_va, y_va)
print(f"untrained network on the validation set: MSE {loss0:.4f}, accuracy {acc0:.3f}")


untrained network on the validation set: MSE 0.0879, accuracy 0.087




5.4 The training loop
Everything is written out:

optimiser: Adam with learning rate \(10^{-3}\) (the chapter uses plain gradient descent; Adam is discussed in the section The Zoo of Optimization Algorithms and is much less sensitive to the choice of the learning rate; plain gradient descent is used in Exercise 5);
one epoch = one pass over the \(782\) mini-batches of Section 4.1; for each batch: forward pass, loss, zero_grad (clear old gradients), backward (compute \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\boldsymbol\theta\)), step (update the parameters);
the loss of every mini-batch is stored (it is cheap and shows the noise of stochastic gradient descent);
after every epoch, loss and accuracy on the full training and validation sets are computed with evaluate_regression.

model.train() / model.eval() switch layers (such as dropout, which randomly switches off nodes during training) between training and evaluation behaviour. This network has no such layers, but the calls are a habit worth keeping.


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
model_reg = make_regression_model()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model_reg.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
n_epochs, batch_size = 20, 64

hist_reg = {"batch loss": [], "train loss": [], "val loss": [], "train acc": [], "val acc": []}

t_start = time.perf_counter()
for epoch in range(1, n_epochs + 1):
    model_reg.train()
    for idx in batch_indices(len(X_tr), batch_size, shuffle=True, generator=shuffle_gen):
        xb, yb = X_tr[idx], y_tr[idx]                    # one mini-batch: (B, 784) and (B,)
        target = yb.float() / 10                         # digit / 10
        y_bar = model_reg(xb).squeeze(1)                 # forward pass, shape (B,)
        loss = mse(y_bar, target)

        optimizer.zero_grad()                            # clear gradients of the previous step
        loss.backward()                                  # backpropagation
        optimizer.step()                                 # theta <- theta - (Adam step)
        hist_reg["batch loss"].append(loss.item())

    tr_loss, tr_acc = evaluate_regression(model_reg, X_tr, y_tr)
    va_loss, va_acc = evaluate_regression(model_reg, X_va, y_va)
    for key, v in zip(["train loss", "train acc", "val loss", "val acc"], [tr_loss, tr_acc, va_loss, va_acc]):

Left: the MSE. The thin line is the loss of the individual mini-batches (x-axis converted to epochs: batch \(k\) is at epoch \(k/782\)); the markers are the losses on the full training and validation sets after every epoch. Right: the accuracies.


Code
def plot_history(hist, loss_name, title):
    n_ep = len(hist["train loss"])
    epochs = np.arange(1, n_ep + 1)
    batch_x = np.arange(1, len(hist["batch loss"]) + 1) / (len(hist["batch loss"]) / n_ep)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
    axes[0].plot(batch_x, hist["batch loss"], color="lightgrey", lw=0.5, label="mini-batches")
    axes[0].plot(epochs, hist["train loss"], "o-", label="training set")
    axes[0].plot(epochs, hist["val loss"], "s-", label="validation set")
    axes[0].set_yscale("log"); axes[0].set_ylabel(loss_name)
    axes[1].plot(epochs, hist["train acc"], "o-", label="training set")
    axes[1].plot(epochs, hist["val acc"], "s-", label="validation set")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("accuracy")
    for ax in axes:
        ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.legend()
    fig.suptitle(title); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

plot_history(hist_reg, "MSE loss", "Part A: single sigmoid output + MSE")





The network learns, but slowly and not far: the validation accuracy rises from about \(9\%\) before training and \(36\%\) after one epoch to about \(60\%\) after four epochs and then creeps up to about \(64\%\) after twenty. The loss on the validation set flattens after about seven epochs, while the training loss continues to decrease slightly: the small hidden layer cannot do much better with this formulation of the task. The accuracy curve is jagged: a small change of the parameters can push many outputs across a rounding boundary \(k\pm0.5\) at once.


5.6 Evaluation on the test set: the confusion matrix (Box 2.11)
The confusion matrix \(C\) counts, for every pair (true digit \(i\), predicted digit \(j\)), how many images of digit \(i\) (in a given set) were predicted as \(j\). We show it for all three sets: training (the data the parameters were fitted to), validation (used during training to monitor the model) and test (used only now). Each row is normalised to sum to one, so \(C_{ij}\) is the fraction of images of digit \(i\) that were classified as \(j\); the diagonal element \(C_{ii}\) is the fraction of digit \(i\) recognised correctly. The mean of the diagonal is the accuracy averaged over classes (Box 2.11); since the MNIST classes are nearly balanced it is almost equal to the plain accuracy.
The matrix is built with one bincount: the pair \((i, j)\) is encoded as the single number \(10i + j \in\{0,\dots,99\}\), the occurrences are counted and arranged as a \(10\times10\) matrix.


Code
def confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, k=10):
    C = torch.bincount(k * y_true + y_pred, minlength=k * k).reshape(k, k).float()
    return C / C.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)              # each row (true class) sums to 1

def plot_confusion(ax, C, title):
    im = ax.imshow(C, cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    for i in range(10):
        for j in range(10):
            if C[i, j] >= 0.005:
                ax.text(j, i, f"{C[i, j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.5,
                        color="white" if C[i, j] > 0.5 else "black")
    ax.set_xticks(range(10)); ax.set_yticks(range(10))
    ax.set_xlabel("predicted digit $j$"); ax.set_ylabel("true digit $i$")
    ax.set_title(f"{title}\nmean of diagonal = {C.diagonal().mean():.3f}", fontsize=10)
    return im

pred_reg_te = predict_digit_regression(y_bar_te)

C_reg_tr = confusion_matrix(y_tr, pred_reg_tr)
C_reg_va = confusion_matrix(y_va, pred_reg_va)
C_reg = confusion_matrix(y_te, pred_reg_te)
print(f"accuracy (regression):  training {(pred_reg_tr == y_tr).float().mean():.3f}"
      f"   validation {(pred_reg_va == y_va).float().mean():.3f}   test {acc_reg_te:.3f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 5.3))
plot_confusion(axes[0], C_reg_tr, "Part A: regression, training set")

The test accuracy is about \(65\%\), higher than the \(56\%\) reported in the chapter, which uses full-batch gradient descent instead of Adam with mini-batches (see Exercise 5). The three matrices look almost the same. Training and test accuracies differ by only about 2–3 points, so overfitting is mild; validation and test agree, so the validation set, which we watched during training, was a reliable estimate of the performance on new data. The model is limited by the task as posed. The confusion matrix shows the characteristic pattern of the regression: the errors form bands next to the diagonal. A \(5\) is predicted as \(4\) or \(6\) in almost half of the cases, an \(8\) as \(7\) or \(9\) and a \(2\) as \(1\) or \(3\) in more than a third. Confusions between digits of similar shape but distant value (such as \(4\) and \(9\)) do not appear as such.
The continuous output shows why. For every true digit we plot the distribution of \(10\,\bar y\) over the test images (a violin plot: the width is the histogram of the values). The dashed horizontal lines are the rounding boundaries \(k\pm 0.5\); an image is classified correctly when its value lies in the band around its own digit.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.5))
ax.violinplot([10 * y_bar_te[y_te == k].numpy() for k in range(10)], positions=range(10), widths=0.8, showmedians=True)
for b in np.arange(-0.5, 10, 1):
    ax.axhline(b, color="grey", lw=0.5, ls="--")
ax.plot(range(10), range(10), "k_", ms=25, mew=2, label="target")
ax.set_xticks(range(10)); ax.set_yticks(range(10))
ax.set_xlabel("true digit"); ax.set_ylabel(r"network output $10\,\bar y$"); ax.legend(loc="upper left")
ax.set_title("Part A: continuous output of the regression network on the test set")
plt.show()

wrong predictions: 3480 of 10000;  of these off by exactly 1: 76%


The output for each digit is centred near the target, but the distributions are wide, about one unit for most digits, and have long tails (the blue horizontal bars mark the minimum, median and maximum; the black bars the targets). Everything that leaks across a dashed line becomes a wrong digit, and leaking across one line is far more likely than across several: about three quarters of the wrong predictions are off by exactly one. \(0\), \(1\) and \(6\) are narrowest; \(5\) and \(8\), which sit in the middle of many other digits on the number line, are the widest and the worst recognised.

title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
section: 6. Part B — Ten outputs, softmax and categorical cross-entropy
text:
6. Part B — Ten outputs, softmax and categorical cross-entropy

6.1 One-hot encoding, softmax and the cross-entropy
Instead of one number, the network now returns \(K = 10\) numbers \(z_0,\dots,z_9\) (the logits), one per class. The softmax \[q_k = \mathrm{SoftMax}(\mathbf z)_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=0}^{9} e^{z_j}}\] turns them into a probability distribution \(\mathbf q\): \(q_k > 0\) and \(\sum_k q_k = 1\). \(q_k\) is read as the probability, according to the network, that the image shows digit \(k\). The predicted digit is the most probable one, \(\arg\max_k q_k\).
The label \(y\) is written as a one-hot vector \(\mathbf p\) with \(p_k = \delta_{k,y}\) (Box 2.7): the “true” distribution, all probability on the correct class. Two distributions are compared with the Kullback–Leibler divergence (Box 2.8), \[\mathrm{KL}(\mathbf p\,\|\,\mathbf q) = \sum_k p_k\log\frac{p_k}{q_k} = \underbrace{\sum_k p_k\log p_k}_{-\,\mathcal H(\mathbf p)\ \text{(no }\boldsymbol\theta\text{)}}\;\underbrace{-\sum_k p_k\log q_k}_{\mathcal L_{\rm ce}} .\] (Here and below \(\log\) denotes the natural logarithm.) Only the second term depends on the network, so the loss is the categorical cross-entropy, averaged over the batch of \(B\) images. For a one-hot \(\mathbf p\) only the term of the true class survives: \[\mathcal L_{\rm ce} = -\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^{B}\sum_{k=0}^{9} p_{ik}\log q_{ik} = -\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^{B}\log q_{i,y_i} .\] It is \(0\) if the network gives probability \(1\) to the true class and grows without bound as that probability goes to \(0\).
In PyTorch, nn.CrossEntropyLoss takes the logits of shape (B, 10) and the labels as integers of shape (B,). It applies the softmax itself (in a numerically stable form, via \(\log\sum_j e^{z_j}\)), so the model must not end with a softmax layer. The cell checks on random logits that the formula above, written out with one-hot vectors, gives the same number.


Code

y5 = y_tr[:5]                                           # their true labels

q = torch.softmax(z, dim=1)                             # probabilities, each row sums to 1
p = nn.functional.one_hot(y5, num_classes=10).float()   # one-hot labels, shape (5, 10)
print("labels:", y5.tolist())
print("one-hot p:\n", p.int())
print("row sums of q:", q.sum(dim=1).tolist())

ce_by_hand = -(p * torch.log(q)).sum(dim=1).mean()
ce_torch = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(z, y5)
print(f"cross-entropy by hand: {ce_by_hand:.6f}   nn.CrossEntropyLoss: {ce_torch:.6f}")

6.2 The network: the same, except the output layer
The hidden layer is exactly that of Part A. Only the output layer changes: \(10\) nodes instead of \(1\), and no sigmoid (the softmax is inside the loss).


Code
def make_classification_model():
    return nn.Sequential(
        nn.Linear(784, N_HIDDEN), nn.Sigmoid(),      # hidden layer   (as in Part A)
        nn.Linear(N_HIDDEN, 10),                     # TEN output nodes: logits z_0 ... z_9
    )

torch.manual_seed(0)
model_ce = make_classification_model()
print(model_ce)
print("parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in model_ce.parameters()),
      "  (Part A:", sum(p.numel() for p in model_reg.parameters()), ";  difference 9 * (N_HIDDEN + 1) =", 9 * (N_HIDDEN + 1), ")")


Sequential(
  (0): Linear(in_features=784, out_features=21, bias=True)
  (1): Sigmoid()
  (2): Linear(in_features=21, out_features=10, bias=True)
)
parameters: 16705   (Part A: 16507 ;  difference 9 * (N_HIDDEN + 1) = 198 )


An untrained network gives roughly equal probabilities \(q_k\approx 1/10\) to all classes, so the cross-entropy should start near \(-\log(1/10) = \log 10 \approx 2.30\):


Code
ce = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

def evaluate_classification(model, X, y):
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        logits = model(X)                               # shape (N, 10)
        loss = ce(logits, y).item()
        acc = (logits.argmax(dim=1) == y).float().mean().item()
    return loss, acc

loss0, acc0 = evaluate_classification(model_ce, X_va, y_va)
print(f"untrained: cross-entropy {loss0:.3f} (ln 10 = {np.log(10):.3f}),  accuracy {acc0:.3f}")


untrained: cross-entropy 2.356 (ln 10 = 2.303),  accuracy 0.072




6.3 The training loop
The same loop as in Part A with three differences: the batches come from a DataLoader as in Section 4.2, the target is the integer label itself, and the loss is the cross-entropy of the \(10\) logits. Optimiser, learning rate, batch size and number of epochs are the same as in Part A.


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
model_ce = make_classification_model()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model_ce.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
n_epochs, batch_size = 20, 64

                       generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(1))
hist_ce = {"batch loss": [], "train loss": [], "val loss": [], "train acc": [], "val acc": []}

t_start = time.perf_counter()
for epoch in range(1, n_epochs + 1):
    model_ce.train()
    for xb, yb in loader_tr:                             # the DataLoader shuffles and batches
        logits = model_ce(xb)                            # forward pass, shape (B, 10)
        loss = ce(logits, yb)                            # target: integer labels, shape (B,)

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        hist_ce["batch loss"].append(loss.item())

    tr_loss, tr_acc = evaluate_classification(model_ce, X_tr, y_tr)
    va_loss, va_acc = evaluate_classification(model_ce, X_va, y_va)
    for key, v in zip(["train loss", "train acc", "val loss", "val acc"], [tr_loss, tr_acc, va_loss, va_acc]):
        hist_ce[key].append(v)
    if epoch == 1 or epoch % 2 == 0:
        print(f"epoch {epoch:2d}:  CE train {tr_loss:.4f}  val {va_loss:.4f}   accuracy train {tr_acc:.3f}  val {va_acc:.3f}")

7. Comparison: why the output layer and the loss matter

7.1 Same hidden layer, different output layer and loss
Both networks have the same hidden layer, the same optimiser, learning rate, batch size and number of epochs. They differ only in the output layer and the loss.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 4.8), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.2, 1, 1]})

axes[0].plot(epochs, hist_reg["train acc"], "o--", color="tab:blue", alpha=0.5, label="A: training")
axes[0].plot(epochs, hist_ce["val acc"], "s-", label="B: 10 outputs + CE (validation)")

axes[0].set_xlabel("epoch"); axes[0].set_ylabel("accuracy"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)

plot_confusion(axes[2], C_ce, "B: cross-entropy")

test accuracy                          0.652              0.948
misclassified test images               3480                516


This is the central result of the notebook. With the same hidden layer, data and training, the single-output regression reaches about \(65\%\) test accuracy and the ten-output cross-entropy network about \(95\%\), with about seven times fewer errors. The difference comes from how the task is posed, that is, from the output layer and the loss together; Exercise 2 shows that the ten outputs account for most of the gain. Model B is better in every epoch: after one epoch it is already far beyond the best value model A ever reaches. The confusion matrices show two different kinds of errors: bands along the diagonal (A: neighbouring values) versus rare, scattered errors (B: similar shapes).


Code
top2 = q_te.topk(2, dim=1)                                # two largest probabilities and their digits
a, b = top2.indices[:, 0], top2.indices[:, 1]
doubtful = torch.nonzero((top2.values[:, 1] > 0.25) & ((a - b).abs() >= 3))[:, 0]
print("test images on which model B hesitates between two distant digits:", len(doubtful))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(show), figsize=(2 * len(show), 2.9))
for ax, n in zip(np.atleast_1d(axes), show):
